Experimentally, we validate enhanced approximation accuracy and demonstrate the simultaneous approximation of 4,136 distinct nonlinear functions using a compact, single-layer diffractive processor under five-wavelength illumination. These results establish wavelength diversity as an additional physical resource for scaling the expressive power of optical computing and enhancing the accuracy of parallel nonlinear function approximation.
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.comment: 34 Pages, 10 Figures

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: SpikeQ: Spike-Guided Post-Training Quantization for Spiking Neural Networks
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: On neuromorphic chips, spiking neural networks (SNNs) consume far less energy than artificial neural networks (ANNs), but the limited memory of these chips requires low-bit synaptic weights and membrane potentials. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods provide them without retraining and, like those for ANNs, minimize numerical errors such as the mean squared error (MSE). In an SNN, however, a quantization error reaches later layers only through the spikes it flips. We find that errors of equal MSE can cause very different accuracy losses, whereas errors that flip the same fraction of spikes cause the same loss. We therefore propose SpikeQ, a spike-guided PTQ framework. For weights, we select the level of each weight by simulating the downstream neurons and minimizing their spike errors. For membrane potentials, most existing methods quantize the state after the reset, whereas neuromorphic chips compare the threshold with the membrane potential stored at a fixed bit width. We target this pre-fire quantization and build a reset-aware grid that places the threshold on a rounding boundary, so rounding never flips the spike at the current time step. We evaluate SpikeQ on seven benchmarks of image classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection. With 2-bit pre-fire membrane potentials, every existing grid collapses, whereas SpikeQ retains most of the full-precision accuracy. With both at 4 bits, the models stay within 2.59 points of full precision, shrink their memory footprint 7.8--7.9 times, and use 6.4--6.9 times less energy.

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: Disentanglement with Biological Constraints: A Theory of Functional Cell Types
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Neurons in the brain are often finely tuned for specific task variables. Moreover, such disentangled representations are highly sought after in machine learning. Here we mathematically prove that simple biological constraints on neurons, namely nonnegativity and energy efficiency in both activity and weights, promote such sought after disentangled representations by enforcing neurons to become selective for single factors of task variation. We demonstrate these constraints lead to disentanglement in a variety of tasks and architectures, including variational autoencoders. We also use this theory to explain why the brain partitions its cells into distinct cell types such as grid and object-vector cells, and also explain when the brain instead entangles representations in response to entangled task factors. Overall, this work provides a mathematical understanding of why single neurons in the brain often represent single human-interpretable factors, and steps towards an understanding task structure shapes the structure of brain representation.

Atomic Physics.title: A Rydberg atom array coupled to a high-cooperativity optical cavity
Atomic Physics.summary: Integrating Rydberg-state control of atom-atom interactions with cavity control of atom-light interactions enables the combination of local entangling operations with photon-mediated long-range coupling, measurement, and communication. Such integration is challenging because electric fields generated by charges on cavity optics and by cavity-stabilizing actuators may disturb Rydberg-state coherence. Here, we couple a Rydberg tweezer array to a high-cooperativity optical cavity, suppressing the electric fields produced by cavity length actuation so that the residual field variation of about $3~\mathrm{mV/cm}$ rms does not limit Rydberg coherence. We demonstrate two capabilities that neither system provides alone. First, we use Purcell-enhanced fluorescence to read out atoms directly in the ground-Rydberg basis within $7.5~μ\mathrm{s}$, well within the Rydberg-state lifetime, with ground- and Rydberg-state detection infidelities of $3\%$ and $5\%$, respectively, and with low atom loss. Second, we use Rydberg-Rydberg interactions to control collective light-atom scattering into the cavity mode. Specifically, we drive blockaded Rabi oscillations between a state with two ground-state atoms, which scatter collectively with a superradiant or subradiant rate controlled by the atomic positions, and an entangled state with a single Rydberg excitation, which scatters like a single atom. These capabilities open routes toward networked Rydberg processors, mid-circuit measurements in analog quantum simulators, and many-body quantum optics with entangled emitters coupled collectively to light.

Atomic Physics.title: Exponential-SWAP gate between bosonic motional modes of trapped ions
Atomic Physics.summary: The exponential-SWAP (eSWAP) gate generates a coherent superposition of identity and SWAP operations, with continuously tunable amplitudes. We experimentally implement this gate between two bosonic motional modes of trapped ions using spin-independent and spin-dependent beam splitter interactions. Measurements of selected slices of the joint characteristic function for distinct input states test the gate and demonstrate continuous control of the identity-SWAP superposition. This implementation provides a tunable interaction for hybrid qubit-bosonic quantum information processing.

Atomic Physics.title: Precision measurement of the ground-state hyperfine constant for $^9Be^+$ in a linear Paul trap via magnetically insensitive hyperfine transitions
Atomic Physics.summary: Direct measurements of the ground-state magnetically insensitive hyperfine transition |F=2,mF=0>->|F=1,mF=0> of $^9Be^+$ ions have been performed using microwave-driven state transfer. The $^9Be^+$ ions are confined and laser-cooled in a linear Paul trap, forming a Coulomb crystal. The transition frequencies have been measured over a magnetic field range of $ \pm 0.5 mT $ centered at zero magnetic field, and the acquired data were fitted accounting for the high-order Zeeman effect. The hyperfine constant A is determined to be -625.008840(35) MHz, achieving a relative precision of $ 5.6 \times 10^{-8}$.

Atomic Physics.title: Fully relativistic calculation of thermal shifts in spectra of hydrogen molecular ion
Atomic Physics.summary: Within a fully relativistic framework, we discuss the one-loop self-energy correction, generalized to the presence of external blackbody radiation, for a bound electron in the hydrogen molecular ion. The calculations rely on the thermal part of the photon propagator from finite-temperature quantum electrodynamics. The Dirac equation with a two-center potential is solved using the dual kinetic balance condition, extended to axially symmetric systems, and a B-spline-based trial function. The results are obtained within the Born-Oppenheimer adiabatic approximation. Thermal shift for the ground term of the hydrogen molecular ion is computed as a function of the internuclear distance. Including this correction, we present the resulting shifts of the vibrational levels. The analysis focuses on the dynamical effect, a comparison is made with data available in the current literature.

Atomic Physics.title: A large nonmagnetic aluminum-and-Viton vacuum chamber suitable for vacuum pressures down into the extremely-high-vacuum (XHV) regime
Atomic Physics.summary: A recently constructed large nonmagnetic vacuum chamber is described and characterized. The vacuum chamber was machined from 19-inch cubes of aluminum and are sealed using dual Viton O-rings (with the interspace between the O-rings evacuated by a separate vacuum pump). 17-inch-diameter openings on all six sides allow for easy access to the experimental apparatus and for vacuum pumps with very large pumping speeds. These 17-inch holes were bored straight through the aluminum cube, resulting in an interior volume of 100 L (almost 90\% of the total volume of the 19-inch cube). The 17-inch openings are sealed with 19-inch-diameter aluminum flanges. The system is modular in that the cubes can be connected to one another to form larger vacuum systems. The chamber is designed to allow for vacuum pressures of $10^{-12}$ torr. In many respects (including nonmagnetic properties, outgassing rate after low-temperature baking, weight, cost, ease of machining, and ease of baking due to the chamber's high thermal conductivity) this system is superior to standard stainless-steel metal-sealed CF vacuum systems and is highly recommended for use by others.

Atomic Physics.title: Rossi-alpha Benchmark Validation of a Static Alpha Eigenvalue Capability in OpenMC
Atomic Physics.summary: A static alpha eigenvalue capability was implemented in a modified version of the open-source Monte Carlo radiation transport code OpenMC and validated against Rossi-alpha measurements from 21 delayed-critical benchmark experiments and 33 subcritical configurations spanning fast, intermediate, and thermal systems with U-233, HEU, IEU, LEU, and plutonium fuels. The effective delayed neutron fraction was calculated using the k-prompt method, and the prompt neutron lifetime was calculated using the iterated fission probability method, both evaluated within the standard k-eigenvalue power iteration. The delayed-critical alpha eigenvalue was calculated from these quantities using the point kinetics equation alpha_dc = -beta_eff / ell_p. Agreement was generally within 10% for fast metal systems and within 5% for thermal solution systems. Subcritical extrapolation studies derived from the SHE-8 and STACY benchmark families show that alpha_dc remains stable as the system is driven subcritical.

Atomic Physics.title: Symmetry and Quantum Interference in the Attosecond Domain
Atomic Physics.summary: In this review, we examine the interplay of symmetry and quantum interference in the attosecond domain primarily through one- and two-electron photoelectron momentum distributions. Using our own work, we discuss how tailored laser fields provide control over dynamical symmetries, and how quantum-orbit methods make it possible to connect the resulting momentum-space structures to specific ionisation, propagation, and rescattering pathways. Particular emphasis is placed on ultrafast photoelectron holography and nonsequential double ionisation through recollision excitation with subsequent ionisation, where several distinct forms of quantum interference can be identified and manipulated. We also discuss how target properties, including the binding potential, orbital symmetry and parity, modify this mapping. Finally, we consider emerging opportunities offered by non-classical states of light, for which photon statistics and quantum fluctuations provide additional degrees of freedom for controlling symmetry and strong-field electron dynamics.

Biological Physics.title: Blinking membrane patterns induced by protein binding/unbinding
Biological Physics.summary: Nonequilibrium membrane pattern formation is studied using meshless membrane simulation. Bound proteins are considered to have two states that generate different membrane spontaneous curvatures. Protein binding and unbinding occur cyclically owing to chemical potential differences, as an off-lattice active Potts model. It is found that this cyclic binding/unbinding can induce blinking domains, with oscillating size: convex domains of the proteins with a higher spontaneous curvature grow, and subsequently, the proteins change to the other state with a lower spontaneous curvature, resulting in domain shrinkage. These processes repeat. In thermal equilibrium, hexagonal convex domains are formed by the competition between bending and surface tension energies, so that they are stably formed only under positive surface tension. However, blinking domains can form even in tensionless membranes.

Biological Physics.title: When is vaccine prioritization worth optimizing?
Biological Physics.summary: Optimizing vaccine prioritization is often treated as the default policy response when vaccine supply is limited. Yet optimized prioritization carries administrative, ethical and communication costs, motivating an upstream question: whether differences among vaccine allocations can alter epidemic outcomes enough to make optimization epidemiologically necessary. We show that optimization is not always worth pursuing: in some regimes, vaccination markedly reduces epidemic burden, but many feasible allocation rules perform almost equally well, making the necessity of optimization low. We quantify this necessity as the range of epidemic outcomes generated by different allocations under fixed supply and show that it is governed by competition between vaccinating high-contact groups to slow transmission and vaccinating groups that benefit most directly: necessity is low when these protection routes are balanced and high when one dominates. Increasing transmission intensity changes this balance and drives a transition in the optimal allocation from transmission-focused prioritization toward direct protection. Different prevention objectives exhibit distinct transition thresholds, creating regimes in which optimizing one objective substantially compromises another, thereby revealing when the choice of prevention target matters most. This framework reframes vaccine prioritization as a prior decision problem, identifying when optimization is warranted, when simpler rules suffice, and when prevention goals conflict.

Biological Physics.title: Non-Monotonic Exciton Transport Efficiency in Multi-layer Ring-shaped Quantum Networks inspired by Photosystem I
Biological Physics.summary: Photosystem I (PSI) is one of the most efficient natural photosynthetic complexes and serves as a structural prototype for understanding excitation energy transfer (EET) and designing artificial light-harvesting systems. Here, we construct a multilayer elliptical-conical quantum network inspired by PSI to investigate how antenna architecture affects EET. Excitation dynamics are simulated using the quantum jump approach combined with coherent modified Redfield theory (QJA-CMRT). The transfer efficiency exhibits a pronounced nonmonotonic dependence on pigment density, reaching a maximum of 0.86 at x=6 in the five-layer network. The optimal configuration contains 91 pigments, close to the number of core antenna pigments in natural PSI. Our combined density-of-states and kinetic analyses reveal that this nonmonotonic dependence originates from a trade-off: at low pigment densities, enhanced band overlap promotes energy transfer, whereas at high densities, excessive exciton delocalization compromises funnel directionality and reduces efficiency; the optimal configuration is consequently achieved at x=6. These findings provide insights into PSI antenna organization and offer guidelines for designing efficient artificial light-harvesting systems.

Biological Physics.title: Comprehensive Analysis of Relative Pressure Estimation in Type B Aortic Dissection Utilizing 4D-Flow MRI
Biological Physics.summary: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can estimate three-dimensional (3D) time-resolved blood velocity fields using 4D-flow MRI, providing rich relative pressure field information. Clinical alternatives---catheterization and Doppler echocardiography---provide one-dimensional pressure drops. While the accuracy of one-dimensional pressure drops from 4D-flow has been explored, the accuracy of 3D relative pressure field estimates requires further evaluation. This work analyzes three state-of-the-art relative pressure estimators: virtual Work-Energy Relative Pressure (vWERP), the Pressure Poisson Estimator (PPE), and the Stokes Estimator (STE). Spatiotemporal characteristics and noise sensitivity were determined in silico via comparison with CFD-derived relative pressure fields. Estimators were then validated using a type B aortic dissection (TBAD) flow phantom with varying tear geometry and twelve catheter pressure measurements. Finally, each estimator was evaluated across eight patient cases in a clinical feasibility analysis. Estimators were cross-compared and evaluated for coherence since no reference catheter pressure measurements were available. PPE outperformed STE in the in silico relative pressure analysis, while both outperformed vWERP in plane-to-plane assessment. High velocity gradients and low spatial resolution contributed most significantly to local variations in 3D relative pressure field errors. Low temporal resolution led to systematic underestimation of highly transient peak pressure events. In the flow phantom analysis, vWERP was the most accurate method, followed by STE and then PPE. Each relative pressure estimator was strongly correlated with ground truth relative pressure values, despite the tendency to underestimate peak relative pressure. Patient case results demonstrated that each relative pressure estimator could be feasibly integrated into a clinical workflow.
Biological Physics.comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging. 15 pages, 11 figures. \c{opyright} 2026 IEEE

Chemical Physics.title: Gap edge eigenpairs from density matrix purification using moments of the Dirac distribution
Chemical Physics.summary: In this work, we propose a simple method to resolve the eigenstates located at the band gap edges of an electronic eigenspectrum using only the quasi-purified one-particle density matrix as input. The theoretical framework relies on the decomposition of the occupation number variance into a particle and a hole moment. These moments, when purified using power narrowing iterations, allow us to isolate the highest occupied and lowest unoccupied single-state projectors, \colp{giving ready access} to the corresponding eigenpairs. We demonstrate that when degeneracy is encountered, power narrowing remains able to deliver relevant mixed states. From a benchmark of selected molecules, we show that the method is robust and efficient since it requires from four to sixteen matrix-matrix multiplications in the worst case. The possibility of reducing the computational cost using the Lanczos subspace approach is discussed. The algorithm simplicity of power narrowing makes it very easy to implement in electronic structure codes or libraries already featuring Fermi operator expansion or density matrix purification.
Chemical Physics.comment: [Revision 1] manuscript submitted to J. Chem. Phys

Chemical Physics.title: Analysis of Transient Microscopy Data in Reciprocal Space
Chemical Physics.summary: Transient microscopy has evolved to include a family of well-established techniques for studying the spatiotemporal dynamics of excited states in a variety of materials systems. In these methods, a laser pulse is focused to locally excite a material, and the subsequent evolution of the excited species is visualized to extract transport parameters such as diffusivities. Typically, transport coefficients are extracted from experimental datasets using curve-fitting methods to analyze the change in the mean squared displacement (MSD) of the spatial profiles over time. However, this approach can lead to inaccurate or misleading diffusivity values under many common experimental conditions, and is only formally accurate for the case of a single diffusing species. In this work, we introduce a new approach to the analysis of transient microscopy data based on the evolution of profile shapes in reciprocal space. We use simulated datasets to quantitatively analyze the performance of our proposed methods and compare them to current state-of-the-art analysis techniques. We demonstrate that reciprocal-space-based analysis methods have the highest overall performance in terms of accuracy and precision for normal diffusive transport over a range of realistic initial conditions and signal-to-noise ratios. Furthermore, we highlight the limitations of using MSD alone to characterize anomalous transport in materials, and we show how analysis of spatial frequencies can yield a more comprehensive understanding of complex excited-state dynamics and their underlying physical mechanisms. Our results show that reciprocal-space-based analysis methods are powerful tools for characterizing and quantifying many different types of transport behaviors.

Chemical Physics.title: AceFF: A State-of-the-Art Machine Learning Potential for Small Molecules
Chemical Physics.summary: We introduce AceFF, a pre-trained machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) optimized for small molecule drug discovery. While MLIPs have emerged as efficient alternatives to Density Functional Theory (DFT), generalizability across diverse chemical spaces remains difficult. AceFF addresses this by refining the TensorNet2 architecture and training it on a comprehensive dataset of drug-like compounds. This approach yields a force field that balances high-throughput inference speed with DFT-level accuracy. We introduce two models sharing the same architecture: \mbox{AceFF-2}, trained on our own dataset of small molecules and supporting the essential medicinal chemistry elements (H, B, C, N, O, F, Si, P, S, Cl, Br, I); and \mbox{AceFF-2-OMOL}, trained on a subset of OMol25 containing the AceFF-2 elements plus the common biomolecular ion elements Na and K. The models are explicitly trained to handle charged states. Validation against rigorous benchmarks, including complex torsional energy scans, molecular dynamics trajectories, batched minimizations, and tests of force and energy accuracy, demonstrates that AceFF is state-of-the-art for organic molecules in the accuracy and speed regime important for drug discovery. The AceFF-2 and AceFF-2-OMol model weights and inference code are available at https://huggingface.co/Acellera/AceFF-2.0 and https://huggingface.co/Acellera/AceFF-2-OMOL.

Chemical Physics.title: Geometry-Dependent Electronic Coupling and Singlet Fission Pathways in Carotenoid Dimers
Chemical Physics.summary: Using the density matrix renormalization group method, we solve the Pariser--Parr--Pople model of $π$-electron systems to determine the character and energies of the low-lying eigenstates of a lycopene dimer comprising two 22-carbon-atom chains. To complement these calculations, we use the molecular-exciton, valence-bond model of polyene systems to derive selection rules governing interchain coupling, which provide a physical framework for interpreting the DMRG results. We find that dimer geometry strongly influences both the character and energetics of the low-lying eigenstates. In vertically stacked dimers, neither the bright-dimer state nor the triplet-pair states contain any interchain charge-transfer (CT) character. In contrast, in slip-stacked dimers, both the bright-dimer state and triplet-pair states do contain interchain CT character. We also find that increasing the interchain coupling preferentially stabilizes states with greater interchain character, leading to a reordering of the low-lying eigenstates. These results have direct implications for energetically possible singlet fission (SF) mechanisms in carotenoid aggregates. For vertically stacked dimers, the only energetically viable pathway identified here proceeds through intermediate intrachain triplet-pair states, whereas slip-stacked geometries allow an additional SF pathway mediated by interchain CT states. Our results establish a direct connection between carotenoid packing geometry, symmetry-controlled electronic coupling, and the energetically accessible pathways for SF.

Chemical Physics.title: Vibro-polaritonic Raman spectroscopy via cavity Born-Oppenheimer perturbation theory
Chemical Physics.summary: We derive a vibro-polaritonic Raman activity from third-order cavity Born-Oppenheimer perturbation theory (CBO-PT) accounting for weak interactions between electrons and low-frequency cavity modes in the vibrational strong coupling (VSC) regime. This work extends the recently presented CBO-PT linear response approach [J. Phys. Chem. Lett. 2024, 15, 2262-2269] from infrared (IR) to vibro-polaritonic Raman spectroscopy. In a first step, we discuss cavity-induced corrections to the static dipole polarizability tensor, which manifest as molecular and cavity mode contribution determined by the polarization-projected static hyperpolarizability tensor. We then obtain the corresponding vibro-polaritonic Raman activity in double harmonic approximation, which contains molecular, cavity and mixed contributions similar to previously discussed CBO-PT IR intensities. The cavity Raman activity can be interpreted as effective transmission component, which is exclusively determined by the polaritonic Raman response. The methodology and its relation to vibro-polaritonic IR spectroscopy is illustrated for a formaldehyde molecule under VSC. An implementation of the CBO-PT linear response approach for vibro-polaritonic Raman and IR spectroscopies is provided via the open-source Python package CBOvibSpec.

Chemical Physics.title: Single-electron fluorine bonding. II. Benchmarking Minnesota density functional approximations and popular ab initio methods for binding energies (BEs) and F-bond distances
Chemical Physics.summary: Companion paper I (Khanal and Arunan, in this issue; arXiv:2610.16629 [physics.chem-ph]) reported reference BEs and F-bond distances for two new databases SEFB-15 (DF$\cdots$CH$_3$) and CSFB-14 (DF$\cdots$NH$_3$). Here, we assess performance of popular ab initio methods (MP2, MP3, MP4(DQ), MP4(SDQ), CCSD, and QCISD) with valence- and full-electron correlation treatments, and sixteen Minnesota DFAs, including M06-2X already assessed in companion paper I. CCSD/AVDZ reproduces reference F-bond distances closely, although BEs predicted by it deviate more. Among the 16 Minnesota DFAs, M08-HX reliably reproduces both reference values for DF$\cdots$CH$_3$ and DF$\cdots$NH$_3$, comparable to M05-2X and M06-2X for DF$\cdots$NH$_3$. Selected meta-GGAs (M06-L, M11-L, and MN15-L) exhibit spurious fractional charge transfer in cationic complexes even at infinite separation, whereas hybrid Minnesota DFAs do not, except M05 and M06 for NH$_3$F$^+\cdots$CH$_3$ and NH$_2$F$_2^+\cdots$CH$_3$. Although M08-HX shows slightly larger monomer delocalization error than M05-2X and M06-2X, it is more reliable for predicting BEs of SEFB complexes, indicating that monomer delocalization error alone does not govern DFA performance. Bader's intermolecular delocalization indices (DIs) further support M08-HX as more reliable than M05-2X and M06-2X for SEFB, while the larger DIs from M05-2X and M06-2X explain the degraded performance of their dispersion-corrected variants for DF$\cdots$CH$_3$, with only a minor impact for DF$\cdots$NH$_3$, highlighting the system-dependent nature of functional delocalization error. Present work reveals that M08-HX is more reliable than M05-2X and M06-2X for open-shell DF$\cdots$CH$_3$ complexes, while all three functionals show comparable reliability for closed-shell DF$\cdots$NH$_3$ complexes.

Chemical Physics.title: Isomer-resolved ion-molecule reaction kinetics of HCO+ and HOC+
Chemical Physics.summary: The HCO$^+$/HOC$^+$ abundance ratio has been observed to vary significantly in different astrophysical environments, making it an important diagnostic tool for exploring the interstellar medium. However, uncertainties in the reaction rates and branching ratios of key chemical reactions involving these ions affect the conclusions drawn from observations of either these species or other species that are derived on their basis. Here, we present isomer-resolved ion-molecule reaction rate coefficients of reactions involving HCO$^+$ and HOC$^+$ using a cryogenic ion trap experiment. We measured the rate coefficients of the isomerization reaction of HOC$^+$ to HCO$^+$ with H$_2$ and CO, as well as three different reactions producing both isomers: CO$^+$ + H$_2$ , H$_3^+$ + CO, and ArH$^+$ + CO. Our results show that the reaction of CO$^+$ with H$_2$ predominantly produces HCO$^+$ with a negligible yield of HOC$^+$ . This result is in agreement with recent theoretical predictions, but in major contrast to the generally accepted branching ratio based on previous experimental results. We also find that the isomerization reaction of HOC$^+$ to HCO$^+$ is efficient with both H2 and CO. We were able to assess the impact of our new measured reaction rate coefficients on the predicted HCO$^+$/HOC$^+$ abundance ratio using a state-of-the-art astrochemical model.

Chemical Physics.title: Towards decoding the structure of water-magnetite interface
Chemical Physics.summary: The molecular structure of water at iron-oxide interfaces is determined by the protonation state, orientation and population of interfacial OH species. These microscopic features can be decoded by combining surface-specific vibrational spectroscopy with reactive and accurate molecular dynamics simulations. In this way, it could be possible to connect the measured nonlinear optical response to specific molecular configurations at the magnetite-water interface, resolving the interfacial water structure. We investigated magnetite films in contact with liquid water at neutral and alkaline pH using phase-resolved sum-frequency generation (SFG) spectroscopy in the OH/OD stretching region and Fresnel correction of the optical response. In parallel, neural-network-potential molecular dynamics simulations were used to model the water-magnetite interface and identify interfacial water species, quantify their orientations, hydrogen-bonding environments and lifetimes, and compute species resolved SFG spectra. The combined analysis assigns distinct spectral features to dissociated surface OH groups, hydroxyls and water molecules adsorbed on octahedral iron sites, water bound at dissociation sites and water molecules above tetrahedral rows. The simulations reveal a reactive interfacial hydroxyl network with nanosecond-scale rearrangements and strong species-dependent hydrogen bonding. Experimentally, the SFG spectra show pronounced pH dependence, consistent with changes in surface charge and hydroxylation. A systematic difference between measured and computed SFG spectra indicates that the assumed surface model of magnetite does not fully represent the aqueous interface. This discrepancy provides a molecular constraint for improved models of magnetite-water interfaces and highlights SFG spectroscopy/ML-MD comparison as a valuable route to resolving oxide-water interfacial structures.

Chemical Physics.title: Electrochemical Molecular Dynamics within the Finite-Field Framework
Chemical Physics.summary: Electrochemical processes at charged interfaces lie at the heart of modern technologies and their continued improvement depends on insights into the relevant atomistic processes. However, the necessary tools to impose constant-voltage conditions in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations typically directly target the electrode charge, making their extension to methods that go beyond an empirical description of metals more cumbersome. In this work, we propose an MD protocol to realize a thermodynamic ensemble in which voltage control is attained, but which is formulated purely within the framework of finite-field simulations in 3D periodic boundary conditions. We show a derivation and implementation of such a control device, which we coin an electrostat, in the ELECTRODE package within LAMMPS. Our simulations systematically benchmark the derived theory against other established approaches, for example, showing its equivalence to a potentiostat, and quantify the importance of properly accounting for ensemble fluctuations. We find that for systems of several thousands of atoms, one obtains the same equilibrium properties with the electrostat as with a simpler constant-field simulation. The difference between the two methods only manifests itself at smaller length scales, thereby establishing practical limits for the inclusion of voltage fluctuations in atomistic simulations of electrochemical systems. The strength of this framework also lies in its simplicity of extension to first-principles ab initio and reactive machine-learning potentials.
Chemical Physics.comment: Main text: 16 pages, 6 figures, 3 appendices. Supporting information: 20 pages, 8 figures

Chemical Physics.title: Learning the information contained in the microstructure of data distributions
Chemical Physics.summary: Understanding how much and where information is nested in sets of data obtained using different parameters and metrics is a typical problem in the analysis of high-dimensional datasets. Approaches based on relative data-driven metrics may be poorly quantitative and difficult to interpret, while accurate methods may be computationally expensive and impractical for large datasets. Here, we report an efficient, quantitative, and transferable method useful to this end, which we call "Micro-Information Analysis". Its foundation is based on the tight relationship that exists between the microscopic features of data distributions and the information they contain. The method performs preliminary unsupervised clustering, capturing microstructural features of data distributions such as the dominant Gaussian microdomains (microstates) present in them, their population, separation, and their residual non-Gaussian fraction. Leveraging the principle of clustering-and-minimization of Shannon entropy, this allows quantifying in bit (that is, in absolute metric) the information contained in the microstructure of the data, and how much information is nested in each Gaussian and non-Gaussian microdomain. The output of the analysis is a set of easily interpretable Information-Microstructure plots that allow to readily compare and rank data based on their information content and to graphically map the information breakdown among their various microenvironments in diagrams that are easy to interpret. We prove the efficiency of our method by analyzing and ranking data generated synthetically or from molecular simulations, demonstrating how "Micro-Information Analysis" is a physically-grounded quantitative tool useful for the study of physical systems from their data and for data science in general.

Chemical Physics.title: Permutationally Invariant Polynomial Descriptors as Colored Multigraphs
Chemical Physics.summary: The combinatorial explosion in monomial counts limits the extension of global permutationally invariant polynomial (PIP) potential energy surfaces to larger molecular systems. We use graph-theoretic language to reformulate PIPs as colored multigraphs and develop a series of theoretical and computational tools. First, we introduce an offline PIP generation algorithm whose cost has an upper bound independent of atom count for a fixed degree cutoff and number of element types. Second, we introduce a new online PIP evaluation algorithm, termed tensor-network descent. For the full PIP set through degree $d$ in a system of $M$ atoms, the evaluation complexity for $1\le d\le14$ is $O\!\left(f(d)M^{\left\lfloor(\sqrt{1+8d}+1)/2\right\rfloor}\right)$. At the commonly used cutoff of $d=5$, the online evaluation complexity decreases from the $M^{10}$ scaling of conventional explicit term-by-term computation to $M^3$. Numerical tests using the full PIP set through degree 5 show that our method achieves speedups of several orders of magnitude on most MD17 systems and remains computationally affordable for systems containing more than one thousand atoms. The method has a native tensor form, supports automatic differentiation, and provides a unified theoretical construction of four classes of PIP descriptors defined consistently across systems---global, atom-centered, bond-centered, and cluster-centered---establishing a representation and computational foundation for PIP potentials for large systems and for transfer across systems. Together, these results show that PIPs are neither inherently restricted to small systems nor intrinsically nontransferable.

Chemical Physics.title: Diffusion-controlled reactions with time-dependent surface reactivity
Chemical Physics.summary: We investigate diffusion-controlled reactions on a reactive surface with time-dependent reactivity. Starting from a conventional formulation via diffusion equation with Robin boundary condition for the macroscopic concentration of particles, we aim at quantifying how temporal variations of reactivity affect the survival probability and the associated first-reaction time (FRT) of a single particle on the reactive surface. Using an adiabatic description, we first identify five long-time regimes of the first-reaction time distribution, ranging from exponential and stretched-exponential to power-law decay. In particular, sufficiently rapid decay of the reactivity leads to a nonzero probability of never reacting, despite diffusion in a bounded domain. Second, we provide a probabilistic reformulation of this problem and compare it with a different scenario of encounter-dependent reactivity. Our theoretical predictions are validated via extensive Monte Carlo simulations.

Chemical Physics.title: Low-Cost Third-order Algebraic Diagrammatic Construction Method for Excited States Using Tensor Hypercontraction and State-Specific Frozen Natural Orbitals
Chemical Physics.summary: We have developed a reduced-cost framework for excited-state calculations by combining the state-specific frozen natural orbital (SS-FNO) approach with the third-order algebraic diagrammatic construction [ADC(3)] method and tensor hypercontraction (THC). This strategy enables a systematic and controllable truncation of the virtual orbital space, while significantly lowering the computational scaling through the THC representation of the electron repulsion integrals. The method allows black-box application via adjustable thresholds and includes a perturbative correction that compensates for the truncation error. We have used the CIS(D) method to generate the natural orbitals for the excited states. The performance of the SS-FNO-THC-ADC(3) method is assessed for valence, Rydberg, and charge-transfer excitations. Benchmark calculations demonstrate that the combined approach achieves excellent agreement with the canonical ADC(3) results. The efficiency of the present implementation is demonstrated by calculating the excitation energy of a molecule containing 31 atoms and more than one thousand basis functions.

Chemical Physics.title: Tersoff-NN: Hybrid Machine-Learned Bond-Order Extension of the Tersoff Potential
Chemical Physics.summary: Accurate, robust, and efficient interatomic potentials are highly desirable for large-scale molecular dynamics simulations. Although machine-learning interatomic potentials can reproduce first-principles potential-energy surfaces with high accuracy, they typically incur higher computational costs than conventional empirical potentials and may be less reliable outside their training domains. We developed Tersoff-NN, a hybrid machine-learning potential for Si, which retains the analytical radial interactions and cutoff structure of the Tersoff potential while representing its environment-dependent bond-order factor using compact neural networks (NNs). Benchmarks for 32,768-atom systems show that Tersoff-NN is 4-12 times faster than the Behler-Parrinello-type NN potentials tested in this study. Tersoff-NN improves the short-range structure of liquid Si relative to the conventional Tersoff potential, closely reproduces the ab initio radial and angular distributions, and reproduces the equilibrium structure of diamond Si and qualitative energetic trends among several crystalline phases. Furthermore, melt-quench simulations reveal a disordered solid with predominantly four-coordinated, tetrahedral-like local environments. Additionally, characteristic reconstruction motifs are retained on Si surfaces despite their exclusion from the training dataset. A direct comparison with an alternative atom-centered bond-order NN highlights the critical role of physical constraints in ensuring dynamic stability. Despite exhibiting comparable validation errors, the selected triplet-based architecture remains stable, while an alternative model exhibits unphysical bond-order growth and atomic collapse. These results confirm that learning only the bond-order term improves the description of diverse Si environments while retaining substantial computational efficiency and enhancing dynamical stability.

Chemical Physics.title: Programming the Nonlinear Optics of a Nanoporous Photonic Metamaterial by Confined Crystallization
Chemical Physics.summary: A membrane traversed by a dense array of nanochannels acts as a photonic metamaterial: with channels far smaller than the wavelength of light, the optical response is set by the architecture rather than by the constituent materials. Here each nanochannel is turned into a nonlinear optical meta-atom by filling anodic aluminum oxide (AAO) with benzil (BZL), a noncentrosymmetric molecular crystal, and the crystallization pathway programs their orientation. In free-standing membranes every channel solidifies independently, the orientations remain uncorrelated, and the effective second-harmonic generation (SHG) response is nearly polarization isotropic; its magnitude follows a core - shell model in which an optically inactive interfacial layer of 2.6 nm reduces the active volume of each meta-atom, reproducing on bare alumina the value previously found on alkyl-grafted silica and indicating a host-insensitive limit. Seeding crystallization from a bulk benzil layer instead aligns the meta-atoms over submillimeter domains and produces a macroscopically anisotropic effective susceptibility. Channel diameters from 32 to 270 nm span the transition out of the subwavelength regime, and the anomalous directional SHG emission reported here is confined to the metamaterial limit. Confined crystallization thus offers a route to nonlinear optical metamaterials whose effective susceptibility tensor is written during processing.

Chemical Physics.title: Shape-Constrained Bayesian Active Learning of Self-Limiting Saturation Curves
Chemical Physics.summary: Saturation curves, monotone responses that rise from zero to a plateau, recur across gas adsorption, enzyme kinetics, and self-limiting growth. Learning one from a few costly, noisy measurements is a common bottleneck. We present a Bayesian active-learning platform built on a penalized monotone I-spline. Non-negative weights make every posterior draw rise from zero and never fall, a survey measurement anchors the plateau in place of a flatness prior, and the input reaching any saturation level is read from the posterior by level crossing, assuming no kinetic form. Each measurement is placed where the surrogate is least certain, which beats random designs and edges a log-spaced grid of the same budget. One fixed configuration recovers five kinetically distinct regimes from twenty measurements to a saturation error of 0.037 to 0.041, below the output noise, and averages 0.045 on 250 curves from an unseen distribution. Running unconstrained Gaussian processes (GPs) and two unpenalized monotone bases through the same loop separates each ingredient's contribution. Logarithmic resolution and the roughness penalty carry the accuracy, while monotonicity guarantees a level crossing unique on every draw. The penalty keeps the surrogate the most accurate model at every noise level, and its second-order form centers the recommended input for saturation where a first-order penalty reads late (a bias of +0.32 s with 94% coverage, against +0.44 s and 64% for the matched unconstrained GP). Because the recommended input lies where the curve is nearly flat, no method can pin it down precisely, and we report it as a cost-indexed quantile with the probability of falling short.

Computational Physics.title: Gap edge eigenpairs from density matrix purification using moments of the Dirac distribution
Computational Physics.summary: In this work, we propose a simple method to resolve the eigenstates located at the band gap edges of an electronic eigenspectrum using only the quasi-purified one-particle density matrix as input. The theoretical framework relies on the decomposition of the occupation number variance into a particle and a hole moment. These moments, when purified using power narrowing iterations, allow us to isolate the highest occupied and lowest unoccupied single-state projectors, \colp{giving ready access} to the corresponding eigenpairs. We demonstrate that when degeneracy is encountered, power narrowing remains able to deliver relevant mixed states. From a benchmark of selected molecules, we show that the method is robust and efficient since it requires from four to sixteen matrix-matrix multiplications in the worst case. The possibility of reducing the computational cost using the Lanczos subspace approach is discussed. The algorithm simplicity of power narrowing makes it very easy to implement in electronic structure codes or libraries already featuring Fermi operator expansion or density matrix purification.

Computational Physics.title: Active Learning for Interatomic Potentials: A Review of Uncertainty-Driven Data Efficiency
Computational Physics.summary: Developing a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) that is accurate for the specific conditions under which it will be applied, rather than simply for the predefined configurations chosen by the model developer, is a significant challenge in atomistic simulation. Active learning (AL) addresses this challenge by closing the loop between candidate generation, data selection, reference calculation, and model updating. Here, we survey more than seventy studies, with an emphasis on work from 2020 to 2026, to understand how active learning has evolved from a niche, on-the-fly training technique for query-by-committee and Gaussian process force fields into a diverse family of data-efficient strategies. he reviewed examples include on-the-fly molecular dynamics, active data selection for fine-tuning pretrained models, kernel- and representation-based acquisition using frozen pretrained models, and reaction-aware sampling for chemical systems far from equilibrium. We explore the use of active learning in elemental and alloy mechanics, hydrogen and ion diffusion, ferroelectrics and effective Hamiltonians of functional materials, reactive and photochemical dynamics, high-entropy and compositionally disordered materials, as well as generative and autonomous material discovery pipelines. Drawing on a growing body of critical, methodologically self-aware literature, we also show that this achievement carries systematic caveats. Uncertainty estimates are not interchangeable across model architectures and are frequently the least reliable exactly where they matter most. We close by discussing the outlook for standardized, uncertainty-calibrated, and observable-targeted active-learning workflows in the foundation-model era.

Computational Physics.title: Plastic Flow Rule Based on Dislocation Link Velocity
Computational Physics.summary: We develop a theory for the plastic shear rate $\dotγ_i$ on each slip system $i$ of face-centered cubic (FCC) single crystals, by integrating the shear rate contributions $\dotγ_i(l)$ from dislocation links of length $l$. A generalized Orowan equation expresses $\dotγ_i(l)$ in terms of the link density $n_i(l)$ and the average link velocity $v_i(l)$. This model accurately reproduces the discrete dislocation dynamics (DDD) shear-rate data for all 12 slip systems across 99 loading orientations. In particular, it explains why the plastic shear rate depends exponentially on the resolved shear stress $τ_i$, as reported previously, in the absence of any thermally activated mechanism. This dependence arises from the exponential tail of $n_i(l)$ filtered through the threshold-like velocity function $v_i(l)$. Furthermore, $v_i(l)$ is well approximated by a single two-dimensional function $v(τ_i,l)$ for all these slip systems. The link velocity is therefore governed mainly by $τ_i$ and $l$, with only a minor effect from the complex interactions between slip systems. These interactions instead manifest themselves mainly through $n_i(l)$. As a demonstration of the effect of the link-length distribution on the slip rate, we show that even when $τ_i$ is limited to a narrow window, the shear rates still span two orders of magnitude. The supply of long links is therefore the dominant factor controlling slip-system activity, outweighing the direct effect of $τ_i$ on the link velocity.

Computational Physics.title: Foundation-Model Supervision of Distilled Potentials for Million-Atom Molecular Dynamics
Computational Physics.summary: Machine-learned interatomic potentials distilled from foundation models enable fast large-scale molecular dynamics (MD), but they can fail locally in chemical environments that their training data did not sample. System-averaged error metrics and small random audits often miss such sparse or isolated failures. Here we use an exact equivariant foundation model, MACE-MPA-0, to check every atom of million-atom production simulations. Reorganizing two-layer MACE inference into a receiver-chunked three-pass schedule that keeps no per-edge intermediates resident reduces the marginal memory per atom 340-fold, evaluates up to $2.86\times10^{7}$ atoms on a single H200 GPU, and supervises $10^{6}$-atom trajectories in LAMMPS at 1.3% of the run time. Distilled MACE students run four to nine times slower than NEP89 with 0.95-1.28 times the teacher's force error against density functional theory (DFT). In molten SiO$_2$, whole-system checks uncover a persistent tail of under-coordinated atoms hidden by the system-averaged error and an isolated, unphysical O-O contact that a 1% random audit misses 94% of the time. On-the-fly retraining on teacher-labelled 13-Å clusters, with the force loss restricted to their inner 6 Å, removes three quarters of the failure tail and the kilobar-level pressure biases in SiO$_2$ and compressed water; the repair converges to the teacher, not to DFT.
Computational Physics.comment: 31 pages, 6 figures, 1 table; Supporting Information (21 pages, 12 figures, 18 tables) appended after the references

Computational Physics.title: Simulation of centrifugal separation of particles with equal sedimentation velocities
Computational Physics.summary: Conventional centrifugal sedimentation cannot readily separate particles with the same sedimentation velocities. Density gradient centrifugation, although highly selective, exposes delicate particles such as drug delivery system (DDS) nanoparticles and exosomes to high osmotic pressure that can cause shrinkage, rupture, or expansion. To separate particles with equal or similar sedimentation velocities while preserving their properties, we propose two methods that exploit thermal fluctuations (Brownian motion): the centrifugal Brownian ratchet method, which uses asymmetric structures, and the centrifugal wavy-channel method, which uses geometric barriers. Two-dimensional Brownian dynamics simulations combining Stokes-Einstein diffusion with centrifugal sedimentation were performed, and particle transport was analyzed using the Péclet number. In the ratchet method, particles with identical sedimentation velocities but different Péclet numbers showed statistically distinct mean arrival positions and times. In the wavy-channel method, periodic entropic barriers interacting with differences in transport properties produced arrival-time differences, achieving temporal separation even for particles with identical sedimentation velocities or Péclet numbers. Both methods separate particles without relying on sedimentation-velocity differences and are expected to preserve particle properties. Because they neither depend on electrical properties nor require a change of medium, they may also be applicable to particles in liquid metals, oils, organic solvents, and ionic liquids.

Computational Physics.title: Geometric inflation of deviations challenges neural quantum states in dynamics of quantum Ising models
Computational Physics.summary: Neural quantum states (NQS) have emerged as a powerful framework for simulating non-equilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated quantum systems, offering scalable variational representations of highly entangled states. Yet, accurate NQS simulations have been found to be surprisingly challenging in some physical regimes of limited complexity. Here, we address paradigmatic quench dynamics of a one-dimensional quantum Ising model as a controlled benchmark. Through supervised state reconstruction we establish substantially tighter empirical upper bounds on the required parameter count than previous estimates, ruling out representational limitations as the key obstruction. Instead, we uncover a geometric inflation of small deviations as a hitherto overlooked challenge for accurate solutions of the infinitesimal time-dependent variational principle (TDVP): the dynamical rotation of the kernel of the quantum geometric tensor (QGT) can suddenly lend physical significance to previously irrelevant parameter deviations. The stability of matrix product state solutions of the same TDVP suggests that the non-linearity of the neural network ansatz is the origin of the sensitivity. These results identify QGT-null-space rotation as a geometric diagnostic of sensitive NQS dynamics and as a concrete target for improving TDVP algorithms.

Computational Physics.title: When is vaccine prioritization worth optimizing?
Computational Physics.summary: Optimizing vaccine prioritization is often treated as the default policy response when vaccine supply is limited. Yet optimized prioritization carries administrative, ethical and communication costs, motivating an upstream question: whether differences among vaccine allocations can alter epidemic outcomes enough to make optimization epidemiologically necessary. We show that optimization is not always worth pursuing: in some regimes, vaccination markedly reduces epidemic burden, but many feasible allocation rules perform almost equally well, making the necessity of optimization low. We quantify this necessity as the range of epidemic outcomes generated by different allocations under fixed supply and show that it is governed by competition between vaccinating high-contact groups to slow transmission and vaccinating groups that benefit most directly: necessity is low when these protection routes are balanced and high when one dominates. Increasing transmission intensity changes this balance and drives a transition in the optimal allocation from transmission-focused prioritization toward direct protection. Different prevention objectives exhibit distinct transition thresholds, creating regimes in which optimizing one objective substantially compromises another, thereby revealing when the choice of prevention target matters most. This framework reframes vaccine prioritization as a prior decision problem, identifying when optimization is warranted, when simpler rules suffice, and when prevention goals conflict.

Computational Physics.title: PINN-LPCDD: Physics-Informed Neural Network with Learnable and Physically Consistent Domain Decomposition for Compressible Multi-Medium Flows
Computational Physics.summary: The physics-informed neural network (PINN) faces significant challenges when solving compressible multi-medium flows, including the inability to locate interface positions, poor approximation of discontinuities, and difficulty in handling high-pressure-ratio problems between media with large stiffness differences. To address these issues, we propose PINN with Learnable and Physically Consistent Domain Decomposition (PINN-LPCDD), a framework that incorporates the sharp interface method (SIM) into PINNs for solving compressible multi-medium flows. Firstly, we design separate sub-networks for each medium with learnable parameters to automatically learn interface positions, so that the domain decomposition is physically consistent, and the contact discontinuity at the interface is naturally sharp. Secondly, the Euler equations with artificial viscosity are solved to enhance robustness when handling problems involving shock waves. Lastly, the scaling invariance of the Euler equations is exploited to facilitate the solution of high pressure ratio problems. Numerical experiments on air-air, air-helium, air-water, and air-R22 problems demonstrate the acceptable accuracy of the proposed method in simulating multi-medium flows.

Computational Physics.title: ZStar: A unified toolkit for polarization, Born effective charges, dielectric and piezoelectric responses, and infrared and Raman spectra
Computational Physics.summary: Born effective charge (BEC) tensors link atomic displacements to polarization, thereby connecting lattice vibrations with dielectric response and infrared activity. We present ZStar, an open-source Python toolkit that automates calculations of polarization, BEC, phonons, static and frequency-dependent dielectric response, and infrared and Raman spectra. ZStar supports bulk crystals, two-dimensional materials, one-dimensional structures, and molecules through an integrated workflow for input preparation, execution, and response analysis. Berry-phase polarization and real-space dipoles describe responses along periodic and open directions, respectively. Its unified, symmetry-adapted finite-displacement framework jointly determines BEC and zone-center force constants from the same calculations, improving computational efficiency while preserving numerical accuracy. Strain-response calculations further provide proper piezoelectric coefficients and their internal-relaxation contributions for bulk crystals. In the ABACUS+PYATB route, electronic Hamiltonian data are reused to obtain Raman response without additional self-consistent calculations. Native response implementations from VASP and CP2K are also integrated. Matched infrared/Raman benchmarks against the implemented separate workflows achieve speedups of up to 8.4. An accompanying agent skill provides an agent-friendly interface for workflow integration. ZStar therefore offers an efficient and automated route for exploring polarization, BEC, dielectric and piezoelectric responses, and vibrational spectra across different material dimensionalities.

Computational Physics.title: Azimuthal Instability in Oscillating Liquid Jets by the Weber Number Variations
Computational Physics.summary: This paper investigates the dependence of azimuthal mode growth rate of oscillating liquid laminar jets on the Weber number. The oscillating liquid laminar jets were simulated over a range of Weber numbers. The simulation setup was validated by comparing the instantaneous interface shapes and the visible azimuthal mode from experimental measurements. As the Weber number increases, the spreading angle rises due to the small surface tension, and higher azimuthal modes are observed. Fourier Transform analysis is used to find the exact azimuthal mode of the simulation results. The dominant azimuthal mode increases as the Weber number increases. A power-law dependence of the growth rate on the Weber number is identified, with the obtained exponents showing good agreement with linear instability analysis. Furthermore, the rescaled Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) results collapse onto a single growth curve for each azimuthal mode, validating the proposed power-law for predicting the growth rates of oscillating liquid jets.
Computational Physics.comment: The following article has been submitted to Physics of Fluids

Computational Physics.title: Rossi-alpha Benchmark Validation of a Static Alpha Eigenvalue Capability in OpenMC
Computational Physics.summary: A static alpha eigenvalue capability was implemented in a modified version of the open-source Monte Carlo radiation transport code OpenMC and validated against Rossi-alpha measurements from 21 delayed-critical benchmark experiments and 33 subcritical configurations spanning fast, intermediate, and thermal systems with U-233, HEU, IEU, LEU, and plutonium fuels. The effective delayed neutron fraction was calculated using the k-prompt method, and the prompt neutron lifetime was calculated using the iterated fission probability method, both evaluated within the standard k-eigenvalue power iteration. The delayed-critical alpha eigenvalue was calculated from these quantities using the point kinetics equation alpha_dc = -beta_eff / ell_p. Agreement was generally within 10% for fast metal systems and within 5% for thermal solution systems. Subcritical extrapolation studies derived from the SHE-8 and STACY benchmark families show that alpha_dc remains stable as the system is driven subcritical.

Computational Physics.title: Boundary Element Modeling for THz-SNOM Near-Field Probes
Computational Physics.summary: Terahertz scanning near-field optical microscopy (THz-SNOM) enables spatially and spectrally resolved investigation of low-energy collective and topological states in quantum materials and nano-structured devices by exploiting the strongly localized near field generated by a polarized atomic force microscopy (AFM) tip. Because the THz near-field response is highly sensitive to tip geometry, understanding how geometric parameters control field confinement and decay is essential for selecting tip designs that provide the spatial resolution required for specific experiments. In this work, we develop a boundary element method (BEM) for modeling the electrostatic near-field of a conducting AFM tip in response to an external background field. The tip is represented by a simplified closed, blunt-cone geometry with its surface discretized into panels using increased mesh density near the apex. A modified Green's function is used to calculate interactions between surface panels, while an augmented linear system simultaneously enforces the equipotential boundary condition on the conducting surface and overall charge neutrality to determine the induced surface-charge distribution. We validate the BEM by comparing the resulting near-field decay with that obtained from a three-dimensional quasi-static COMSOL Multiphysics simulation. The BEM accurately reproduces the COMSOL field-decay behavior while requiring orders of magnitude fewer mesh elements and substantially reducing computational cost. These results demonstrate that the BEM provides an accurate and computationally efficient framework for systematically investigating the dependence of THz near-field confinement on AFM tip geometry. This framework can be extended to more complex and experimentally realistic tip geometries, providing a route toward rational tip selection and design for application-specific spatial-resolution requirements.

Computational Physics.title: QRecoupling.jl: numerical and exact computation of classical and quantum recoupling coefficients
Computational Physics.summary: QRecoupling.jl is a Julia package for numerical, exact and symbolic evaluation of classical and quantum recoupling coefficients and generic finite sums of quantum factorials, with one interface across the classical limit, principal unitary levels and real or complex deformation. A compact factorial rule and its cyclotomic exponents expose factor cancellation, polynomial structure and level support. The package covers quantum Clebsch-Gordan coefficients, 3j and 6j symbols and user-defined sums. Its adaptive numerical evaluation is combined with exact decisions for sums that cancel to zero. Classical 3j and 6j symbols are evaluated at a speed comparable to that of WIGXJPF, which is based on prime factorization tables, at the smallest spins, and about 6 and 10 times faster at spin cutoff 500. Under real, root-of-unity and complex deformation, the largest relative error measured against independent high-precision references is $3.5 \times 10^{-14}$ for spins up to 400. Fusion matrices with 401 channels are computed about 100 times faster than by loops over their entries.

Computational Physics.title: Commutative Coarse-graining on the Sphere
Computational Physics.summary: Filtering by spatial convolution underlies coarse-graining and Large Eddy Simulation, the analysis of multiscale dynamics, and data processing across the sciences. Yet, as commonly practiced on the sphere, it violates a basic consistency requirement: commutation with differential operators, which is necessary for deriving coarse-grained dynamics and preserving the physics across lengthscales. We discuss the root of the problem, which is intrinsic to the curved geometry rather than being a result of metric terms, coordinate system, or numerical grid. A recently proposed generalized spherical convolution is, for a given scalar kernel, the unique linear operator commuting with the radial projection, divergence, and curl. Any consistent linear operator, be it spectral truncation, wavelet transform, diffusion, Green's-function inversion, or a machine-learned convolution, necessarily takes this form. From a simulation of an unstable jet, we demonstrate commutation to within numerical round-off, whereas common filtering that ignores curvature produces significant spurious divergence where none exists and gradient errors comparable to the gradients themselves.
Computational Physics.comment: 7 pages + 1 page Supplementary Material, submitted to Europhysics Letters: Focus Issue on Complex Flows and Complex Fluids

Computational Physics.title: Residual Carleman lift for nonlinear lattice Boltzmann simulations
Computational Physics.summary: Low-order Carleman embeddings replace nonlinear dynamics by a larger linear system, but truncation errors can accumulate even when the underlying nonlinear model is accurately approximated by a quadratic equation. We construct a residual Carleman lift (RC2) of lattice Boltzmann dynamics in which an independently evolved spectral background supplies the coefficients and forcing of a second-order residual lift. In a double-shear-layer test, conventional fixed-rest Carleman reaches $87.3\%$ final error, whereas prepared RC2 achieves $0.136\%$ through vortex roll-up, without restarting the lift or using fine-reference feedback. The results demonstrate control of the finite-time accuracy of a fixed-order linear embedding through nonlinear preparation.

Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.title: Equiprobability Anomaly Detector Using Angular Distributions
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.summary: We use the angular distribution of top quark pairs ($t\bar{t}$) in the semileptonic final state $b\bar{b}\,\ellνq\bar{q}'$ to construct an anomaly detector for non-$t\bar{t}$ events. Wigner $D$ functions expand the distribution with coefficients determined by orthogonal series density estimation. Its equiprobable surfaces bin the events, the non-$t\bar{t}$ concentrate at low $t\bar{t}$ density. The separation is quantified by the Kullback-Leibler divergence, which makes connection to variational autoencoders. The performance is comparable to normalizing flows at parton level, but is limited by jet assignments at reconstruction level.
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.comment: 8 pages, 6 figures

Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.title: Autonomous self-harmonic drift in Langevin dynamics causes a compaction of underlying domain for the density of Stochastic Localization
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.summary: Our recent research on Langevin dynamics with self-harmonic drift and classical spins has revealed a strong connection to ``Stochastic Localization," a concept attracting attention in the fields of mathematical geometry and data science. Roughly speaking, the former can be viewed as a version of the latter in which the $n$-dimensional Euclidean space - the domain of the probability distribution function appearing in the latter - is ``compactified'' to the surface of an $n$-dimensional sphere. By comparing the two frameworks, we argue that this compactification is a consequence of requiring the drift to be autonomous. The relationship between the two approaches may expand the scope of Stochastic Localization.
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.comment: 5 pages. 1 table. 0 figure: Submission to SciPost

Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.title: Distributional signatures of computation: inferring mechanisms from computation time distributions
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.summary: Computational complexity theory provides a framework for analysing abstract models of computation, whereas computational systems operate as finite physical implementations whose behaviour is shaped by their architecture and physical substrate. In such systems, computational organisation cannot be directly characterised from algorithms or internal representations. Building on the use of reaction time distributions to constrain mechanisms in cognitive science, we introduce an empirical framework for investigating computation in physical systems by inferring computational mechanisms from observable computation time distributions. The framework combines empirical benchmarking, which characterises computational efficiency through the scaling of computation time with problem size, with distributional analysis, which treats computation time distributions as signatures of the stochastic dynamics generated by different computational mechanisms. We demonstrate the framework using a scalable visual search paradigm, comparing human performance with three computational models that employ distinct mechanisms of evidence accumulation. Benchmarking reveals broadly similar scaling behaviour for the models and human observers, whereas distributional analysis distinguishes between these models. We show that computation time distributions provide an empirical level of description linking observable computational behaviour to underlying computational mechanisms. This framework complements computational complexity theory by extending the empirical study of computation from measuring computational performance to characterising computational organisation. It provides an empirical approach for comparing finite computational systems across diverse physical implementations, including biological, classical, neuromorphic, and quantum systems, without requiring access to their internal algorithms or architectures.
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, separate supplementary information

Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.title: When Should Team KPIs Be Absolute or Relative for Match-Outcome Prediction?
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.summary:
In rugby union and association football, team key performance indicators (KPIs) can be represented in absolute terms or relative to the opponent. Relativisation sometimes improves match-outcome prediction and sometimes harms it. There has been no general account of when each occurs.
  The answer depends on how much the two teams differ in variability and how strongly their KPI values rise and fall together. We combine these properties into the Paired Efficiency Factor (PEF), which generalises Fisher's paired-efficiency result to the unequal-variance conditions typical of competitive sport. The PEF also connects a KPI's statistical efficiency to how much information its relative form carries about the outcome. Combined KPIs can interact in complex ways, so we analyse each indicator on its own.
  Across 86 team KPIs from professional rugby union and association football, the PEF places every metric in one of four regimes. Anti-correlation is common among these KPIs, especially for high-volume competitive counts, and absolute measures are then usually preferable. Relativisation can still improve prediction when a noisier difference carries more outcome information. An idealised simulation and one representative KPI from each regime confirm both signs under team-blocked cross-validation. The same pairing geometry appears in healthcare, genomics, finance, and manufacturing.
  The PEF is a diagnostic for when to relativise a performance metric and when not to.
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.comment: 32 pages

Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.title: Learning the information contained in the microstructure of data distributions
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.summary: Understanding how much and where information is nested in sets of data obtained using different parameters and metrics is a typical problem in the analysis of high-dimensional datasets. Approaches based on relative data-driven metrics may be poorly quantitative and difficult to interpret, while accurate methods may be computationally expensive and impractical for large datasets. Here, we report an efficient, quantitative, and transferable method useful to this end, which we call "Micro-Information Analysis". Its foundation is based on the tight relationship that exists between the microscopic features of data distributions and the information they contain. The method performs preliminary unsupervised clustering, capturing microstructural features of data distributions such as the dominant Gaussian microdomains (microstates) present in them, their population, separation, and their residual non-Gaussian fraction. Leveraging the principle of clustering-and-minimization of Shannon entropy, this allows quantifying in bit (that is, in absolute metric) the information contained in the microstructure of the data, and how much information is nested in each Gaussian and non-Gaussian microdomain. The output of the analysis is a set of easily interpretable Information-Microstructure plots that allow to readily compare and rank data based on their information content and to graphically map the information breakdown among their various microenvironments in diagrams that are easy to interpret. We prove the efficiency of our method by analyzing and ranking data generated synthetically or from molecular simulations, demonstrating how "Micro-Information Analysis" is a physically-grounded quantitative tool useful for the study of physical systems from their data and for data science in general.

Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.title: Reliable data clustering with Bayesian community detection
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.summary: From neuroscience and genomics to systems biology and ecology, researchers rely on clustering similarity data to uncover modular structure. Most methods work in two steps: first reduce noise, then cluster. The first step runs without regard to the second: it forces arbitrary choices, discards useful information, and can impose structure where none exists. Here we bring the two steps together. Using established Bayesian community detection methods, we let one minimum description length criterion choose both how much to sparsify the data and how to cluster it. This one-step approach keeps all the samples for inference, removes the arbitrary threshold choice, and returns a single cluster when there is no real structure. On synthetic data, our approach recovers clusters under more noise and with fewer samples than standard methods. On gene co-expression data from the human brain, it finds more coherent and more stable clusters than WGCNA, the standard tool in the field. Uniting sparsification and clustering in a single model-selection step provides a principled, noise-resistant way to uncover modular structure in similarity data across fields.

Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.title: Emergence of Correlations Between Records and Maximum in Random Time Series
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.summary: We compute exactly the covariance between the maximum $M$ and the number of records $K$ in a discrete time series of $n$ entries as a quantitative probe of the history leading to an extreme event. For continuous IID series, with a common probability distribution function (PDF) $p(x)$, we find the striking result that $M$ and $K$ are uncorrelated for any $n \geq 1$. We show that this independence is rather fragile and the covariance $C_q(n)$ between $M$ and $K$ becomes nonzero when $p(x)$ becomes discontinuous due to a delta-component at $x=0$ with an amplitude $0< q < 1$. This time series models the occurrence of dry days with probability $q$ in a precipitation time series when there is no rainfall. We show that there is an interesting shape transition at a critical value $q_c$ where the covariance $C_q(n)$, as a function of $n$, changes from monotonic ($q<q_c$) to non monotonic behavior (for $q>q_c$). We compute the critical strength $q_c$ exactly. Furthermore, for large $n$, we show that $C_q(n)$ decays as a power law, with an exponent that depends on the tail of $p(x)$. We then compare our theoretical predictions with real precipitation data from several weather stations across Germany, finding a very good agreement.
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.comment: Letter: 5+2 pages and 6 figures; Supp. Mat.: 15 pages and 5 figures

Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.title: Residual diagnostics for detecting the breakdown of the single power-law approximation in photoelectron yield spectroscopy: application to doped silicon
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.summary: Our automated analysis of photoelectron yield spectroscopy (PYS) estimates the threshold Ith and the exponent n of a single power law for every spectrum. When this model fits poorly, however, the analysis cannot tell whether the data or the model is at fault. Here we present residual diagnostics that separate the two causes. The exponent is scanned continuously on a 1/n-power fit with an Akaike information criterion (AIC) based on the mean absolute error (MAE), and the spread of the resulting Akaike weights ($P \times Δn$) quantifies the uncertainty of the estimate. The normalized MAE (NMAE) and the RMSE-to-MAE ratio (RMR) assess the data quality, the Durbin-Watson (DW) statistic assesses the model adequacy, and the three checks are reported in parallel. With criteria set from an Au reference, the diagnostics were applied to 60 continuous measurements in air of four HF-treated Si samples. For heavily doped p-type Si, DW fell below its criterion, whereas the means of NMAE and RMR remained within their criteria. Prompted by this flag, we fitted the spectrum with a two-component model with fixed exponents (n = 1 and 2.5); the AIC decreased by 56, DW increased from 0.86 to 1.99, and the two components set in at 4.70 and 5.28 eV. For heavily doped n-type Si, the change during air exposure was consistent with a single component. The diagnostics thus identify the spectra that require a multi-component analysis without assuming an emission mechanism.
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.comment: 35 pages, 4 figures and 2 tables; Supplementary Material (10 figures, 6 tables) included. Submitted to Science and Technology of Advanced Materials: Methods (TSTM-2026-0073). v2: restructured and retitled; the estimation part is condensed with citations to our previous papers, and the paper now centers on the residual diagnosis and its verification by a two-component fit
