Repository continuous integration (CI) validates publishing manifests, the engine loader performs syntactic, structural, and static semantic checks before every simulation, and published model artefacts are versioned and immutable, so that an earlier validated version can be selected by pinning its identifier. The platform runs as containerised microservices on Kubernetes with engine adaptations that externalise inputs and results and expose lifecycle control. An initial case study on bus route 22 in Riga exercises the lifecycle on an offline model with roughly 115,000 DEVS atomic components and reports single-container throughput and concurrent job execution on one Kubernetes node. Behavioural validation and multi-node evaluation remain future work.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: v2: revised version. Corrects the case study of v1 (bus route 22 only; the v1 scenario had also included the trolleybus route of the same number) and all reported measurements; adds a Kubernetes concurrency experiment, a SysML v2 comparison and a validation walk-through. Submitted to Software and Systems Modeling (Springer). Under review

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: HyCo: Hybrid Drafting for Cost-Efficient Mobile-Cloud Speculative Decoding
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Device-cloud speculative decoding reduces server computation, but growing a deep draft tree with a small language model (SLM) requires repeated passes on a mobile neural processing unit (NPU). We present HyCo, which assigns depth to the server model's native multi-token prediction (MTP) head, executed on the device, and alternative branches to one SLM pass. The server returns the hidden state, input embedding, and key-value entries needed by the head instead of executing its sequential steps. Quantization, a restricted vocabulary, and a 1K-token window fit both drafters to the NPU. An ε-threshold rule additionally relaxes exact preservation of the verifier's sampling distribution. In single-client runs with a Galaxy S26 Ultra over LTE/5G, HyCo reduces server GPU time per output token relative to server-side MTP self-speculation by 38.6% on Spec-Bench and 29.2% on 32K-token summarization. With the same acceptance rule, three Spec-Bench runs per system show 9.0 percentage points more saving and 1.9x delivery speed than an SLM-only drafter. HyCo differs from Cloud+MTP by +0.2 judge-score points (paired 95% CI: -0.9 to +1.3); exploratory translation favors SpecEdge-ε. Without relaxation, HyCo exact saves 27.7% and 11.9% on the two datasets.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Under review at ACL Rolling Review (October 2026)

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: AdaBool: Sparse Boolean Matrix Processing with Adaptive Data Representation
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
Many data processing tasks revolve around determining whether logical relationships exist between two sets of entities, a pattern that can be naturally modeled as Sparse Boolean Matrix Multiplication (SpBMM). Under Boolean semantics, matrix representations no longer need to store numerical values and instead focus on encoding the positions of non-zero elements, making it highly amenable to data compression for substantially lower memory access overhead. The key challenge, however, is that the most effective compression depends heavily on sparsity distribution: different methods perform best at different sparsity levels, while real-world matrices often contain sharply varying sparsity across regions. Consequently, forcing the entire matrix into any fixed, monolithic representation leaves considerable optimization opportunities untapped.
  We present AdaBool, a SpBMM framework designed to reconcile this tension through an adaptive data representation. AdaBool partitions matrices into fine-grained element blocks and represents each block with the encoding best matched to its local sparsity. On top of this adaptive encoding, AdaBool introduces a heterogeneous GPU execution model that groups blocks by encoding type and maps them to matching processing paths, enabling efficient execution and scheduling across GPU resources. We implement AdaBool end to end with low-level system optimizations, evaluate it on both production and public workloads, and show that it outperforms representative baselines by over an order of magnitude.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Accepted to ACM SIGMOD 2027 (Proceedings of the ACM on Management of Data). 16 pages, 21 figures, 7 tables

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Coordination-Free Workload Regularization for Variable-Cost Distributed Training
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Synchronous data-parallel training usually assigns every rank the same number of records, even when record costs vary by orders of magnitude. For variable-length models, this converts input variation into idle time because each step waits for its most expensive rank-local batch. We present Batch Cost Lookahead (BCL), a coordination-free data-loading policy that buffers a bounded rank-local window and repartitions it into fixed-cardinality packs with balanced estimated cost. BCL preserves the trainer's record-count contract and requires neither cross-rank metadata exchange nor runtime modification. In simulation over public workload distributions, enabling BCL reduces per-rank estimated batch-cost variability by up to 82.8%. Across 13 NeMo-RL SFT corpora on eight H200 GPUs, rank-local BCL runs 1.050 to 1.167 times faster than pooled MFFD. Compiled H200 measurements on an internal sequence workload show speedups of 1.197 to 1.343 times over packed execution from one to four nodes. We also identify a memory-feasibility boundary: a p99 cap for high-variance or OOM-prone data bounds outliers before BCL balances the rest. These results show that substantial variable-cost imbalance can be removed at the data-loader boundary, while clarifying when data preparation or broader coordination is still necessary.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: TensorDex: A Compact, Tensor-Centric Storage System for Modern AI Models
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
Modern model hubs store hundreds of petabytes of large language models (LLMs), with fine-tuned variants dominating the storage footprint. These variants contain substantial cross-model redundancy that delta compression can exploit by storing only the difference between a target and a reference model. However, compression effectiveness depends critically on choosing a similar reference. At model-hub scale, this is challenging because model lineage metadata is often missing or unreliable, and different tensors within the same model may be most similar to tensors from different models. Consequently, model-level pairing leaves substantial redundancy unexploited.
  We present TensorDex, a lossless, tensor-centric storage system that performs delta compression at tensor granularity. TensorDex decomposes models into tensors, uses compact bit-level fingerprints to predict tensor-pair compressibility, and incrementally organizes tensors into multi-center clusters to select effective bases as new models arrive. Evaluated on 2,890 randomly sampled Hugging Face models, TensorDex reduces storage footprint by 70.5%, 37% lower than the state-of-the-art design. It achieves 22.9 GB/s compression and 28.4 GB/s decompression throughput, 3.86x and 1.49x faster than the next-best system, respectively.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 12 pages, 6 figures. Systems paper on AI model storage

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: ZenFlow: Enabling Stall-Free Offloading for LLM Training
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) often exceeds GPU memory limits, prompting systems to offload model states to CPU memory. However, existing offloaded training frameworks like ZeRO-Offload treat all parameters equally and update the full model on the CPU, causing severe GPU stalls, where fast, expensive GPUs sit idle, waiting for slow CPU updates and limited-bandwidth PCIe transfers. We present ZenFlow, a new offloaded training framework that decouples updates between GPU and CPU by prioritizing important gradients. ZenFlow performs in-place updates of important gradients on GPU while offloading and accumulating less important ones on CPU without blocking training iterations, fully overlapping CPU work with GPU computation. To make this importance-aware design scalable, ZenFlow leverages a novel spatio-temporal locality of important gradients, concentrated in specific positions that remain stable across iterations, to make important gradient identification efficient and lightweight while preserving fidelity. Evaluation shows that ZenFlow achieves up to 5x end-to-end speedup, 2x lower PCIe traffic, 85% less GPU stalls, and up to 72% lower cloud GPU cost, all while preserving accuracy.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 13 pages, 16 figures

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Helix: A Unified Programmable Accelerator for Diverse Krylov Subspace Solvers
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Domain-specific accelerators deliver high performance and energy efficiency through specialization but often lack support for extensible algorithm families. Existing FPGA accelerators for Krylov subspace methods, which iteratively solve sparse linear systems, typically support a single solver or require separate hardware configurations. Helix follows a systematic algorithm-family design methodology that first abstracts common computational primitives from diverse Krylov solvers and builds the architecture around efficient, programmable primitive kernels. Helix then introduces programmable datapaths to coordinate these primitives. Its architecture decouples hardware implementation from solver-specific execution, enabling HBM reuse and zero solver-switching latency. Finally, Helix provides a DSL compiler that efficiently maps different solvers onto the architecture while optimizing vector-operation performance for each solver. We prototype Helix on a Xilinx Alveo U55C FPGA and evaluate Helix's practicality and performance by using it to compile and execute eight solvers. Helix achieves up to 7.91x and 1.16x speedups over Xilinx XcgSolver and the state-of-the-art FPGA accelerator Callipepla, respectively, both of which support only JPCG. Across the eight solvers, Helix sustains 47.5% - 96.9% of the throughput of an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU while delivering 2.29x - 4.66x higher energy efficiency and 1.89x - 3.85x higher throughput per unit peak memory bandwidth. The programmable components incur 0.25% - 0.57% execution-time overhead and 4.7% LUT and 4.0% FF overhead, demonstrating negligible overhead for programmability.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Probabilistic Optical-Layer Surrogate for Risk-Aware Control-Plane Decision Making
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: In this paper, we propose a generative surrogate for the optical layer. Current control-plane decisions in optical transport networks are made using analytical impairment models, deterministic learned predictors, or quantile-regression-based uncertainty estimates. These approaches expose only a limited, static summary of the optical layer at any given time. This forces the control plane to rely on conservative fixed margins that leave capacity underutilized. Our proposed surrogate is a conditional generative model trained on traces from optical simulators with validated physical models. The surrogate produces a full conditional distribution over physical-layer metrics such as OSNR, Q-margin, nonlinear penalty, and feasibility. This output allows the controller to estimate violation probability and tail risk at arbitrary thresholds at runtime. This is different from existing approaches because no retraining is required for each decision. We present the first case study in fast path feasibility estimation using a generative surrogate for the optical layer. We compare the surrogate against simulators, deterministic learned predictors, and quantile-regression estimators. We evaluate the surrogate along nine research questions (RQ1--RQ9) covering prediction accuracy, inference latency, uncertainty quality, controller integration, cross-emulator generalization, dynamic reconfiguration under span degradation, topology scalability, GNPy-validated generalization, and finally, inference latency on real-world live hardware traces. The core contribution is an optical-layer control abstraction where physical-layer behavior is exposed as a fast probabilistic query mechanism instead of an offline simulation output or a deterministic feasibility rule.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 20 pages, 6 figures, 11 tables. Accepted at ACM CoNEXT 2026. Published in Proc. ACM Netw. 4, CoNEXT4, Article 44 (December 2026)

Discrete Mathematics.title: Rational decomposition of polyhedra and a conjecture of Brlek and Reutenauer
Discrete Mathematics.summary: We prove in the affirmative a conjecture of Brlek and Reutenauer (2003), which relates unambiguous rational sets to a well known result due to Khovanskii and Pukhlikov (1992) and independently to Lawrence (1990) on the valuations of the algebra spanned by the indicator functions of polyhedra.

Discrete Mathematics.title: An improved randomized algorithm for finding sinks of Acyclic Unique Sink Orientations of the binary hypercube
Discrete Mathematics.summary: Acyclic Unique Sink Orientations (AUSOs) of the binary hypercube form an elegant abstraction of various optimization problems, ranging from linear programs whose feasibility region is a combinatorial hypercube, to 2-player turn-based stochastic games (2TBSGs) in which one of the players has two actions from each one of its states. The currently fastest known randomized algorithm for finding the sink of such AUSOs is the Random-Facet algorithm of Kalai (STOC 1992), and of Matoušek, Sharir and Welzl (SoCG 1992), adapted to the binary hypercube by Gärtner (RSA 2002). The expected number of vertex queries made by the algorithm is at most $e^{2\sqrt{n}}$, where $n$ is the dimension of the cube. We design an improved randomized sink-finding algorithm that performs an expected number of only $e^{\sqrt{(2+o(1))n}}$ queries. This is the first improved bound for the problem in over two decades. The improved algorithm is obtained by adapting improved versions of the Random-Facet algorithm for solving general linear programs, and LP-type problems, developed by Kalai (STOC 1992), Gärtner (FOCS 1992), and by Hansen and Zwick (STOC 2015). The improved bound is not implied by these much more general algorithms. A key feature of the improved algorithm and its analysis is its simplicity. The structure of binary AUSOs enables a simpler description and a much simpler analysis of the adapted algorithm. In particular, the recurrence relations bounding the complexity of the algorithm depend on only one variable, and not two, and they can be solved using fairly straightforward techniques.

Discrete Mathematics.title: Asymptotic dimension of graphs excluding an induced or fat minor
Discrete Mathematics.summary:
Asymptotic dimension is a large-scale invariant of metric spaces that was introduced by Gromov (1993). A major open problem in coarse graph theory asks whether, for every fixed graph $H$, the class of graphs excluding $H$ as a fat minor has bounded asymptotic dimension. A weaker conjecture asserts the same conclusion for graphs excluding $H$ as an induced minor.
  We substantially expand the range of graphs $H$ for which these conjectures are known to hold. Specifically, we prove bounded asymptotic dimension for the following classes of graphs: graphs excluding a fixed planar graph as a fat minor; and graphs excluding a fixed string graph as an induced minor. All of our results also hold for the stronger notion of Assouad--Nagata dimension, a refinement of asymptotic dimension.
  These results have a number of applications, two of which we mention here. First they imply that an induced minor-closed class is $χ$-bounded if and only if it does not contain some Burling graph. Second they imply that, in graph classes excluding a fixed planar graph as an induced minor, treewidth is polynomial in maximum degree.

Discrete Mathematics.title: There is no $8$-regular $K_3$-irregular graph
Discrete Mathematics.summary: A graph is $K_3$-irregular if its vertices belong to pairwise distinct numbers of triangles. We prove that no $8$-regular $K_3$-irregular graph exists, settling the last unresolved case. Following the initial discovery of such graphs for regularities $r \in \{10,11,12\}$ (Stevanovi'c et al., 2024), our previous work (Hak et al., 2025) showed that no such graphs exist for $r \le 7$, provided the first example for $r=9$, and proved that any $8$-regular candidate must have between $17$ and $22$ vertices. We exclude these possible orders for $r=8$ by combining careful analysis of triangle degrees with integer linear programming techniques. Meanwhile, a recent construction (Zhang, 2026) established that regular $K_3$-irregular graphs do exist for all $r \ge 9$. Together with our results, this establishes that an $r$-regular $K_3$-irregular graph exists if and only if $r\geq 9$.
Discrete Mathematics.comment: Updated version, any comments are welcome

Discrete Mathematics.title: Efficient sampling of the unlabeled structure of uniform random mappings and surjections
Discrete Mathematics.summary:
This article deals with the sampling and statistics of uniform random mappings and surjections from $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ to $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$. More precisely, we focus on statistics that are invariant under relabeling of the domain and codomain. The structure of a mapping or surjection up to relabeling is captured by a compact representation called its profile. The profile records, for each occurring preimage size, the number of preimages of that size.
  We provide a complete set of algorithms that directly sample the profiles of uniform random mappings and surjections, covering the full parameter space. Their expected running times match the expected length of their outputs up to logarithmic factors. It is important to note that we make no assumption about the relationship between $n$ and $k$; in particular, we do not assume that $n/k$ is constant. All our guarantees are uniform in $n$ and $k$. Achieving this uniformity substantially complicates the analysis. Our algorithms are based on exact-size Boltzmann samplers, which we accelerate by optimizing the cost of each sampling round and increasing the acceptance probability.
  As spin-off results, we answer, up to a logarithmic factor, an open question of Devroye and Los~25 on sampling profiles of random mappings when $n>k\log k$, and obtain a sampler for uniform random surjections with expected running time $O(n\log k)$, valid across the full parameter space.

Discrete Mathematics.title: Geometric Graph Representations via Compact SAT Encodings
Discrete Mathematics.summary:
We present compact SAT encodings and certifying exact solvers for boxicity and cubicity. The boxicity of a graph is the minimum dimension in which it is the intersection graph of axis-aligned boxes; cubicity is defined analogously using unit cubes. Grid-based formulations face a geometric discretization bottleneck, growing rapidly with the target dimension. We avoid this bottleneck by encoding the total order of interval endpoints in each coordinate. For an $n$-vertex graph and target dimension $d$, our boxicity encoding uses $O(n^2d)$ variables and $O(n^3d)$ clauses, both linear in $d$. Requiring the left- and right-endpoint orders to agree yields a cubicity encoding of the same asymptotic size.
  Satisfying models are decoded into independently checked geometric representations, while unsatisfiable instances used as lower-bound evidence carry mechanically verified DRAT certificates. In a controlled evaluation with 186 trials per encoding on standard and structured graph families, the order encoding solves 96.8% of trials, compared with 71.0% for the known grid formulation, and reduces mean PAR-2 time from 178.21 to 21.70 seconds.
  The pipeline also certifies exact values for several named graphs. We turn one such value into a reusable obstruction by proving that every Kneser graph $K(n,k)$ with $k\ge3$ and $n\ge2k+1$ contains an induced Desargues graph. The resulting lower bound, together with an explicit three-dimensional representation of $K(7,3)$, establishes $\operatorname{boxicity}(K(7,3))=3$. This disproves the conjecture of Caoduro and Sebo that $\operatorname{boxicity}(K(n,k))=n-k$ for all $k\ge3$ and $n\ge2k+1$.

Discrete Mathematics.title: Connectivity Bounds for GHZ Graphs
Discrete Mathematics.summary: Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states are multipartite entangled quantum states that play a central role in quantum information theory, with applications in quantum communication, cryptography, and distributed quantum computing. A major experimental goal is to create high-dimensional GHZ states using multiple entangled parties. Krenn, Gu and Zeilinger discovered a surprising bridge between these quantum-optical experiments and graph theory: certain photonic experiments can be represented by edge-coloured, edge-weighted graphs, and the dimension of the produced GHZ state equals the number of feasible monochromatic inherited vertex colourings. This led Krenn and Gu to conjecture that every GHZ graph with more than four vertices has dimension at most $2$. A counterexample would give a new high-dimensional multipartite GHZ construction, while a proof would clarify fundamental resource limitations in quantum optics. It is known that the conjecture holds for graphs of vertex connectivity at most $2$ [MFCS 2024], and that simple GHZ graphs with $n>4$ vertices have dimension less than $n/\sqrt{2}$ [Quantum 2024]. However, no general upper bound depending only on vertex connectivity was known. We prove that every simple connected GHZ graph $G$ with at least four vertices has dimension at most $2^{κ(G)-1}+\binom{κ(G)}{2}$, where $κ(G)$ is the vertex connectivity of $G$. We also prove new bounds in terms of edge connectivity and maximum degree.

Discrete Mathematics.title: On balanced subfamilies of maximum complement-free families in the middle layer of the Boolean lattice
Discrete Mathematics.summary: We study balanced subfamilies of the middle layer $\binom{[2n]}{n}$ of the Boolean lattice $2^{[2n]}$. A family $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\binom{[2n]}{n}$ is said to be balanced if every element in $[2n]$ appears in the same number of members of $\mathcal{F}$. A balanced subfamily of size 2 is exactly a complementary pair $\{A,[2n]\setminus A\}$, and therefore a family with no balanced subfamily of size $2$ has at most $\frac{1}{2}\binom{2n}{n}$ members. We show that for every $k\geq 1$ and all sufficiently large $n$, this maximum size is compatible with delaying the smallest size of a balanced subfamily until $2k+2$. More precisely, there exists a family $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\binom{[2n]}{n}$ of size $\frac{1}{2}\binom{2n}{n}$ with no balanced subfamilies of sizes $2,4,\ldots,2k$, but with a balanced subfamily of size $2k+2$. The proof is constructive and uses a general lifting from simple games to self-dual selectors in the middle layer. This provides an efficient constructive proof of a recent conjecture of Moss and Pedersen.
Discrete Mathematics.comment: Added complexity discussion, Improved construction complexity, added two references, and an open question. 12 pages and 1 table

Discrete Mathematics.title: Barrier Log-Concavity of Large Forests
Discrete Mathematics.summary: We prove that the independence sequence of every sufficiently large forest is strictly barrier log-concave: whenever $i_{k+1}>i_k$, one has $i_k^2>i_{k-1}i_{k+1}$. Consequently, every common downward coefficient tilt is unimodal, with one order threshold valid simultaneously for all $0<t\le1$. As an application, we prove that every sufficiently large well-covered tree has a strictly log-concave independence polynomial. More generally, the latter conclusion holds for well-covered forests with sufficiently large matching number. Every sufficiently large forest with a palindromic independence polynomial is also strictly log-concave, with its modes at the central ranks. The proof establishes local coefficient-curvature estimates uniformly over forests of unbounded maximum degree and over activities tending to zero. Combined with the fixed-density theorem of Fang, Lu, Nevo, Yao, and Zheng, these estimates complete the strict log-concavity interval down to rank one through $\lfloor17α/25\rfloor$; the terminal fraction is inherited. The classical decreasing tail then yields the barrier property. A cumulative-coefficient corona theorem transfers barrier log-concavity of the base forest to full strict log-concavity of its leaf corona.
Discrete Mathematics.comment: 26 pages, 2 figures; optional 16-page quantitative supplement and verification code/data in ancillary files

Discrete Mathematics.title: Burling graphs in graphs with large chromatic number
Discrete Mathematics.summary:
A graph class is $χ$-bounded if the only way to force large chromatic number in graphs from the class is by forming a large clique. In the 1970s, Erdős conjectured that intersection graphs of straight-line segments in the plane are $χ$-bounded, but this was disproved by Pawlik et al. (2014), who showed another way to force large chromatic number in this class -- by triangle-free graphs $B_k$ with $χ(B_k)=k$ constructed by Burling (1965). This also disproved the celebrated conjecture of Scott (1997) that classes of graphs excluding induced subdivisions of a fixed graph are $χ$-bounded.
  We prove that in broad classes of graphs excluding induced subdivisions of a fixed graph, including the increasingly more general classes of segment intersection graphs, string graphs, region intersection graphs, and hereditary classes of graphs with finite asymptotic dimension, large chromatic number can be forced only by large cliques or large graphs $B_k$.
  One corollary is that the hereditary closure of $\{B_k\colon k\geq 1\}$ forms a minimal hereditary graph class with unbounded chromatic number -- the second known graph class with this property after the class of complete graphs. Another corollary is that the decision variant of approximate coloring in the aforementioned graph classes can be solved in polynomial time by exhaustively searching for a sufficiently large clique or copy of $B_k$. We also discuss how our results along with some results of Chudnovsky, Scott, and Seymour on the existence of colorings can be turned into polynomial-time algorithms for the search variant of approximate coloring in string graphs (with intersection model in the input) and other aforementioned graph classes. Such an algorithm has not yet been known for any graph class that is not $χ$-bounded.

Discrete Mathematics.title: Minimizing the makespan in job shop scheduling under conflict graph constraints
Discrete Mathematics.summary: We study the job shop scheduling problem with a conflict graph, in which adjacent jobs cannot be processed simultaneously on different machines, with the objective of minimizing the makespan. We establish a polynomial equivalence with a resource-constrained job shop problem having unit-capacity resources and binary resource requirements The problem is strongly NP-hard even on two machines with unit-time operations. For this setting, we derive an optimal-makespan formula and a linear-time algorithm when the conflict graph is a cluster graph, given the clique partition. We also develop a polynomial-time $4/3$-approximation algorithm for arbitrary conflict graphs on two machines when each job has exactly two unit-time operations. For the general problem, we propose four mixed-integer linear formulations, lower bounds, and a genetic algorithm with active, non-delay, and hybrid decoding procedures. Computational experiments on instances derived from the Lawrence and Taillard benchmarks and on randomly generated generalized job shop instances evaluate the proposed methods and show that the genetic algorithm generally improves on constructive heuristics.

Discrete Mathematics.title: Reweighted Spectral Partitioning Works: A Simple Algorithm for Vertex Separators in Special Graph Classes
Discrete Mathematics.summary:
We establish that a practical polynomial-time algorithm obtains near-optimal $\frac23$-balanced vertex separators for a number of graph classes, including genus-$g$ graphs, $K_h$-minor-free graphs, and geometric graphs. For many of these classes, our polynomial-time separator bounds improve on previous work. Moreover, unlike previous work, all these separators are produced by a single unified algorithm that has no specialization for the graph class, and this algorithm admits a scalable implementation with good empirical results. Furthermore, our approach is robust to graphs falling just outside these classes, making it appropriate for practical applications like road networks.
  A key distinction of our approach, compared to previous work, is the disentanglement of our algorithm and its analysis for specific graph classes. Our algorithm is based on a newly improved form of a recent Cheeger-style inequality relating the value of a special semidefinite program to vertex expansion. Our analysis then only has to directly bound the value of this semidefinite program for each graph class, and constructions for these bounds need not be algorithmic. Finally, we obtain several results of independent interest. These include an improved (existential) separator theorem for intersection graphs of $k$-ply $d$-dimensional balls, an improved bound on the Fiedler value of genus-$g$ graphs, and a complete spectral proof of the planar separator theorem.

Discrete Mathematics.title: Computing bounded solutions to linear Diophantine equations with the sum of divisors
Discrete Mathematics.summary: We propose an efficient computational method for finding all solutions $n\leq U$ to the Diophantine equation $aσ(n)=bn+c$, where $a,b,c$ are fixed integer coefficients, $U$ is a given upper bound, and $σ(n)$ denotes the sum of divisors of $n$. The method combines advanced pruning of possible prime factors of $n$ and their combinations with several optimization techniques, organized around a \emph{prime-wheel} data structure developed for this purpose. It is implemented in the {\sc SageMath} computer algebra system within the framework of recursively enumerated sets and supports native {\sc MapReduce} parallelization. We apply the method to numerous previously studied equations, discovering new solutions, certifying complete solution lists below substantially larger bounds than previously reported, and substantially improving lower bounds in several open problems involving the sum-of-divisors function.

Discrete Mathematics.title: Empirical Quantum Advantage in Constrained Optimization from Encoded Unitary Designs
Discrete Mathematics.summary:
We introduce the Constraint-Enhanced Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (CE-QAOA), a shallow, constraint-aware ansatz that operates inside the one-hot product space [n]^m, where m is the number of blocks and each block is initialized in an n-qubit W_n state. We give an ancilla-free, depth-optimal encoder that prepares W_n using n-1 two-qubit rotations per block, and a two-local block-XY mixer that preserves the one-hot manifold and has a constant spectral gap on the one-excitation sector. At the level of expressivity, we establish per-block controllability, implying approximate universality per block. At the level of distributional behavior, we show that, after natural block and symbol permutation twirls, shallow CE-QAOA realizes an encoded unitary 1-design and supports approximate second-moment (2-design) behavior; combined with a Paley-Zygmund argument, this yields finite-shot anticoncentration guarantees.
  Algorithmically, we wrap constant-depth sampling with a deterministic feasibility checker to obtain a polynomial-time hybrid quantum-classical solver (PHQC) that returns the best observed feasible solution in O(S n^2) time, where S is a polynomial shot budget. We obtain two advantages. First, when CE-QAOA fixes r >= 1 locations different from the start city, we achieve a Theta(n^r) reduction in shot complexity even against a classical sampler that draws uniformly from the feasible set. Second, against a classical baseline restricted to raw bitstring sampling, we show an exp(Theta(n^2)) minimax separation. In noiseless circuit simulations of traveling salesman problem instances with n in {4,...,10} locations from the QOPTLib benchmark library, we recover the global optimum at depth p = 1 using polynomial shot budgets and coarse parameter grids defined by the problem size.

Discrete Mathematics.title: A Linear-Time Algorithm for the Unbiased Claw Game on Graphs with Maximum Degree 4
Discrete Mathematics.summary:
We study the unbiased Maker-Breaker $K_{1,3}$-game, the unbiased claw game, played on the edge set of a general graph $G$. In this game, Maker and Breaker alternatingly claim edges of $G$, and Maker wins if his claimed edges contain a claw once no more edges are available. Graphs with maximum degree at least 5 are Maker's win. A graph $G$ is claw-connected if the hypergraph modeling the unbiased claw game played on $G$ is connected. We characterize Maker's win in the unbiased claw game on every claw-connected graph whose maximum degree is different from 3. Our main structural result is a complete characterization of Maker's win for claw-connected graphs with exactly one vertex of degree 4. The analysis is based on the fact that vertices of degree 4 act as forcing structures.
  Our characterization results in a linear-time algorithm for the unbiased claw game on claw-connected graphs with maximum degree different from 3. We also obtain a linear-time decomposition algorithm reducing the game on general graphs to a collection of pairwise edge-disjoint claw-connected subgraphs of maximum degree exactly 3, thereby isolating the only remaining case. This decomposition yields an $\mathcal{O}(|V(G)|^3)$-time algorithm for the unbiased claw game on general graphs, improving on the $\mathcal{O}(|V(G)|^7)$-time algorithm implied by the work of Galliot, Gravier and Sivignon (arXiv 2026). For a lower bound on the decision complexity, we prove that any agent deciding the game in the adjacency-array model makes at least $Ω(|V(G)|)$ queries in the worst case, indicating the optimality of our linear-time algorithm.

Discrete Mathematics.title: Arithmetic Circuits and Neural Networks for Regular Matroids
Discrete Mathematics.summary: We prove that there exist uniform $(+,\times,/)$-circuits of size $O(n^3)$ to compute the basis generating polynomial of regular matroids on $n$ elements. By tropicalization, this implies that there exist uniform $(\max,+,-)$-circuits and ReLU neural networks of the same size for weighted basis maximization of regular matroids. As a consequence in linear programming theory, we obtain a first example where taking the difference of two extended formulations can be more efficient than the best known individual extended formulation for the base polytope of regular matroids of size $O(n^6)$ by Aprile and Fiorini. Such differences have recently been introduced as virtual extended formulations. The proof of our main result relies on a fine-tuned version of Seymour's decomposition of regular matroids which allows us to identify and maintain graphic substructures to which we can apply a local version of the star-mesh transformation.

Discrete Mathematics.title: Investigating mixed-integer programming approaches for the $p$-$α$-closest-center problem
Discrete Mathematics.summary:
In this work, we introduce and study the $p$-$α$-closest-center problem ($pα$CCP), which generalizes the $p$-second-center problem, a recently emerged variant of the classical $p$-center problem. In the $pα$CCP, we are given sets of customers and potential facility locations, distances between each customer and potential facility location as well as two integers $p$ and $α$. The goal is to open facilities at $p$ of the potential facility locations, such that the maximum $α$-distance between each customer and the open facilities is minimized. The $α$-distance of a customer is defined as the sum of distances from the customer to its $α$ closest open facilities. If $α$ is one, the $pα$CCP is the $p$-center problem, and for $α$ being two, the $p$-second-center problem is obtained, for which the only existing algorithm in literature is a variable neighborhood search (VNS).
  We present four mixed-integer programming (MIP) formulations for the $pα$CCP, strengthen them by adding valid and optimality-preserving inequalities and conduct a polyhedral study to prove relationships between their linear programming relaxations. Moreover, we present iterative procedures for lifting some valid inequalities to improve initial lower bounds on the optimal objective function value of the $pα$CCP and characterize the best lower bounds obtainable by this iterative lifting approach.
  Based on our theoretical findings, we develop a branch-and-cut algorithm (B&C) to solve the $pα$CCP exactly. We improve its performance by a starting and a primal heuristic, variable fixings and separating inequalities. In our computational study, we investigate the effect of the various ingredients of our B&C on benchmark instances from related literature. Our B&C is able to prove optimality for 17 of the 40 instances from the work on the VNS heuristic.

Discrete Mathematics.title: Ternary Binomial and Trinomial Bent Functions in the Completed Maiorana-McFarland Class
Discrete Mathematics.summary: Two classes of ternary (vectorial) bent functions of degree four with two and three terms in the univariate representation that belong to the completed Maiorana-McFarland original class are found. Binomials are mappings $\F_{3^{4k}}\mapsto\fthreek$ given by $\Tr^{4k}_k\big(a_1 x^{2(3^k+1)}+a_2 x^{(3^k+1)^2}\big)$, where $a_1$ is a nonsquare in $\F_{3^{4k}}$ and $a_2$ is defined explicitly by $a_1$. Particular subclass of such binomial vectorial bent function is represented by the exceptional polynomials over $\fthreek$. Bent trinomials are mappings $\F_{3^{2k}}\mapsto\fthree$ given by $\Tr_{2k}\big(a_1 x^{2(3^k+2)} + a_2 x^{3^k+5} + a_3 x^2\big)$ with $k>1$ not divisible by four and coefficients explicitly defined depending on the parity of $k$. The proof is based on new criterion that allows checking bentness by analyzing the first-order derivatives of $f$ in the direction of a chosen $n/2$-dimensional subspace ($n$ is the degree of the domain of $f$ over $\fp$).

Discrete Mathematics.title: Optimal Unambiguous DNFs and Alon-Saks-Seymour
Discrete Mathematics.summary: We construct unambiguous DNFs having width $O(n)$ but $0$-certificate complexity $Ω(n^2)$. By utilizing the special structure of these DNFs, we prove a lifting theorem with a constant-sized gadget that lifts the DNF to a communication problem, while losslessly translating the separation in certificate complexity to a separation in communication complexity. This leads to an optimal refutation of the Alon-Saks-Seymour conjecture, as well as an optimal communication lower bound for the Clique versus Independent Set problem, improving the previous results of Balodis, Ben-David, Göös, Jain and Kothari (FOCS 2021, SICOMP 2023) by several doubly logarithmic factors. As further applications of our construction to query complexity and learning theory, we exhibit: (a) a family of Boolean functions that has an optimal quartic separation between certificate complexity and approximate degree, and (b) a sample compression lower bound of $Ω(\sqrt{\log c})$ for multiclass concept classes over $c$ labels.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Improved Pass Complexity for Semi-Streaming Matching in General Graphs via Budgeted Price Approach
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We present a simple deterministic semi-streaming algorithm that computes a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximate maximum matching in general graphs in $O(1/\varepsilon^{2})$ passes. This matches the pass complexity of the auction algorithm of Assadi, Liu, and Tarjan~[SOSA'21] for bipartite graphs, and answers Open Question~2 of Assadi~[SOSA'24 \& TheoretiCS'25].
  Our approach, which we call the \emph{budgeted price approach}, is very different from the previous $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$-pass semi-streaming algorithms for $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation of matching in general graphs and improves their pass complexity. All previous approaches are augmenting-path-based and use $O(1/\varepsilon^{19})$ passes by Fischer, Mitrović, and Uitto~[STOC'22], $O(1/\varepsilon^{6})$ passes by Mitrović, Mukherjee, Sankowski, and Sheu~[ICALP'25], and $O(1/\varepsilon^{4})$ passes by Izumi, Kitamura, and Yamaguchi~['25].

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Fast Distributed $(Δ+ 1)$-Edge Coloring in Bipartite Graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We show that, on bipartite $n$-vertex graphs in the LOCAL model of distributed computation, $(Δ+ 1)$-edge coloring can be solved deterministically in $O(f(Δ) \log n)$ rounds for some function $f$.
  In particular this implies a deterministic $O(\log n)$-round upper bound for $(Δ+ 1)$-edge coloring on bipartite constant-degree graphs.
  Our results improve on the previous state-of-the-art bounds (which hold already on general graphs) whose $n$-dependencies are $\widetilde{O}(\log^5 n)$ rounds deterministically and $\widetilde{O}(\log^2 n)$ rounds randomized [Bernshteyn and Dhawan, J.\ Comb.\ Theory 2025].
  In fact, we obtain the aforementioned results already for a more restrictive version of $(Δ+ 1)$-edge coloring that corresponds to a \emph{local-palette} strengthening of Vizing's theorem shown recently to hold [Christiansen, STOC 2023].
  In this version, every edge $\{u, v\}$ has to be colored with a color from $\{1, \dots, \max(\operatorname{deg}(u), \operatorname{deg}(v))+ 1\}$.
  For all of our results, the vertices do not need to know on which side of the bipartition they lie---the structural promise of bipartiteness suffices.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Hard Instances on Demand
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The conclusions of an experimental study of algorithms are only as good as the instances they are run on. Benchmark libraries for well-studied problems took decades to curate, while evaluations of new problems often fall back on random instances, which are known to be misleading: they may say more about the random generator than about the algorithmic question at hand.
  We treat instance generation as an optimization problem: parameterize the instance space, take the solver's running time as the objective, and let a black-box optimizer search for hard instances. We develop a widely applicable workflow built on the Nevergrad optimization platform and demonstrate it on four NP-hard problems: satisfiability, traveling salesperson, Hamiltonian cycle, and non-permutation flow-shop scheduling. The search needs only the solver, an instance encoder, and a compute budget. Our evolved instances beat the hardest instance of a budget-matched random draw in all four case studies, by an order of magnitude or more in three. They are often competitive with long-curated benchmark sets: our SAT champion is harder (for a three-solver portfolio) than 78% of the 498 SAT Competition formulas in its size class; our 20-city TSP champions take several times longer than the hardest measured classical TSPLIB instance (229 cities); and our flow-shop champion takes 238.6 seconds of CP Optimizer time to solve to proven optimality (versus 4.5 seconds for the hardest of 100,000 random draws) while denying CP-SAT an optimality proof. The optimizer even recovers known structure from running time alone: it locates a SAT clause/variable ratio near the phase transition and finds structurally different champions for the two scheduling engines.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Full version of a paper accepted to ALENEX 2027

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Dynamic Graph Coloring: Sequential, Parallel, and Distributed
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We present a simple randomized algorithm that can efficiently maintain a $(Δ+1)$ coloring as the graph undergoes edge insertion and deletion updates, where $Δ$ denotes an upper bound on the maximum degree. A key advantage is the algorithm's ability to process many updates simultaneously, which makes it naturally adaptable to parallel and distributed computations. Concretely, it gives a unified framework across the models, leading to the following results:
  - In the sequential setting, the algorithm processes each update in $O(1)$ expected time, worst-case. This matches and strengthens the results of Henzinger and Peng [TALG 2022] and Bhattacharya et al. [TALG 2022], who achieved an $O(1)$ bound but amortized over the sequence of updates (in expectation and with high probability, respectively), whose work improved the $O(\log Δ)$ expected amortized bound of Bhattacharya et al. [SODA'18].
  - In the parallel setting, the algorithm processes each batch of updates using $O(1)$ work per update in the batch in expectation, and in $\text{poly}(\log n)$ depth with high probability. This is, in a sense, an ideal parallelization of the above results.
  - In the distributed setting, the algorithm can maintain a coloring of the network graph as (potentially many) edges are added or deleted. The maintained coloring is always proper; it may become partial upon updates, i.e., some nodes may temporarily lose their colors, but quickly converges to a full, proper coloring. Concretely, each insertion and deletion causes at most $O(1)$ nodes to become uncolored, but this is resolved within $\tilde{O}(\log n)$ rounds with high probability (e.g., in the absence of further updates nearby--the precise guarantee is stronger, but technical). Importantly, the algorithm incurs only $O(1)$ expected message complexity and computation per update.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: An improved randomized algorithm for finding sinks of Acyclic Unique Sink Orientations of the binary hypercube
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Acyclic Unique Sink Orientations (AUSOs) of the binary hypercube form an elegant abstraction of various optimization problems, ranging from linear programs whose feasibility region is a combinatorial hypercube, to 2-player turn-based stochastic games (2TBSGs) in which one of the players has two actions from each one of its states. The currently fastest known randomized algorithm for finding the sink of such AUSOs is the Random-Facet algorithm of Kalai (STOC 1992), and of Matoušek, Sharir and Welzl (SoCG 1992), adapted to the binary hypercube by Gärtner (RSA 2002). The expected number of vertex queries made by the algorithm is at most $e^{2\sqrt{n}}$, where $n$ is the dimension of the cube. We design an improved randomized sink-finding algorithm that performs an expected number of only $e^{\sqrt{(2+o(1))n}}$ queries. This is the first improved bound for the problem in over two decades. The improved algorithm is obtained by adapting improved versions of the Random-Facet algorithm for solving general linear programs, and LP-type problems, developed by Kalai (STOC 1992), Gärtner (FOCS 1992), and by Hansen and Zwick (STOC 2015). The improved bound is not implied by these much more general algorithms. A key feature of the improved algorithm and its analysis is its simplicity. The structure of binary AUSOs enables a simpler description and a much simpler analysis of the adapted algorithm. In particular, the recurrence relations bounding the complexity of the algorithm depend on only one variable, and not two, and they can be solved using fairly straightforward techniques.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Hypothesis Selection via Weighted Medians
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Given $n$ distributions (hypotheses) $\mathcal H=\{H_1,\ldots,H_n\}$ and samples from an unknown target distribution $P$, proper hypothesis selection seeks a distribution whose total variation distance to $P$ is close to the best achievable within the known distributions. We give an algorithm that, using $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(n/δ))$ target samples, running in $O(n\varepsilon^{-2}\log(n/δ))$ time, with probability at least $1-δ$, returns $H_{\hat i}$ satisfying $d_\mathrm{TV}(P,H_{\hat i})\leq 3\min_{i\in[n]}d_\mathrm{TV}(P,H_i)+\varepsilon.$ The algorithm achieves the optimal approximation factor and sample complexity. The running time improves the dependence on the failure probability from polynomial to logarithmic in the state-of-the-art bound $\tilde{O}(n\varepsilon^{-2}δ^{-1})$ of Aamand, Aliakbarpour, Chen, and Silwal (COLT 2026), thereby answering their Question~2.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Near-Optimal Parallel $M$-Matrix Scaling
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In this paper we consider the problem of computing a positive diagonal scaling of a $d \times d$ symmetric $M$-matrix so that all row and column sums are $1$. We provide a poly-logarithmic iteration algorithm that solves this problem to high accuracy, where the cost of each iteration is dominated by the cost of solving a Laplacian system. This improves upon the recent $\tilde{O}(d^{1/3})$ iteration bound of [Vladu STOC 2025] and yields a randomized algorithm for the problem that runs in near-linear time and poly-logarithmic parallel depth.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Subgraph Counting with Local Node Differential Privacy
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the problem of approximately counting subgraphs under local node differential privacy (LNDP), a recently introduced model that enforces strong privacy guarantees in analyses of distributed social networks. We design a noninteractive $(\varepsilon,0)$-LNDP algorithm that, given any public $k$-node template graph $H$, counts occurrences of $H$ in a sensitive undirected $n$-node graph with additive error $O(n^{k-\frac{1}{2}}/\varepsilon^{k-1})$, for any constant $k$. We complement this algorithm with a lower bound showing that every noninteractive $(\varepsilon,δ)$-LNDP algorithm for counting copies of any $k$-node template graph with maximum degree greater than $1$ must have error $Ω(n^{k - \frac{1}{2}})$. Thus, our algorithm achieves optimal error for counting constant-size subgraphs, up to $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ factors.
  Our results substantially expand the types of network statistics known to be approximable under LNDP: prior work considered only functions of the degree distribution. In addition, our lower bound yields the first known $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ gap between central and local node differential privacy when accuracy is required for all input graphs. Previous separations either only involved $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ factors or only applied to promise problems.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: To appear at the ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms (SODA) 2027

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Tree Edit Distance: Near-Linear-Time Approximate, Sublinear, and Dynamic
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Tree edit distance (TED), the analog of string edit distance (ED) for hierarchical data, is the minimum number of node insertions, deletions, and substitutions transforming one labeled rooted ordered tree into another. We narrow polynomial gaps between TED and ED in near-linear-time approximation, sublinear algorithms, and dynamic algorithms.
  We give an $n^{o(1)}$-approximation in $O(n)$ time and, for every $0<δ<1$, a $(\log n)^{O(1/δ)}$-approximation in $O(n^{1+δ})$ time. This improves the previous near-linear-time $O(\sqrt n)$-approximation [Boroujeni et al., STOC'19] and brings TED to parity with ED in this regime up to polylogarithmic factors.
  With query access to the balanced-parentheses (Euler-tour) representation of the input trees, we give the first sublinear-time TED algorithm: for every $τ\in[1,n]$, it computes a $τn^{o(1)}$-approximation of $1+\mathrm{ted}$ in $O(n/τ)$ time.
  For dynamic TED, we give an exact algorithm with amortized update time $\tilde{O}(k^7)$ and a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation with amortized update time $\tilde{O}_{\varepsilon}(k)$, where $k$ caps the distance that must be reported. The exact algorithm is the first to beat recomputation in a nontrivial parameter regime. The approximation improves prior dynamic guarantees [Das et al., FOCS'25] and cannot be significantly improved in any parameter regime without a breakthrough for static $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation of ED.
  All results use dynamic programming on a new hierarchical tree decomposition, analogous to partitioning strings into blocks of geometrically decreasing sizes. It combines structural properties previously achieved only in isolation, providing a framework for transferring algorithmic ideas from ED to TED, with additional ingredients addressing the obstacles in each computational setting.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Efficient sampling of the unlabeled structure of uniform random mappings and surjections
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
This article deals with the sampling and statistics of uniform random mappings and surjections from $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ to $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$. More precisely, we focus on statistics that are invariant under relabeling of the domain and codomain. The structure of a mapping or surjection up to relabeling is captured by a compact representation called its profile. The profile records, for each occurring preimage size, the number of preimages of that size.
  We provide a complete set of algorithms that directly sample the profiles of uniform random mappings and surjections, covering the full parameter space. Their expected running times match the expected length of their outputs up to logarithmic factors. It is important to note that we make no assumption about the relationship between $n$ and $k$; in particular, we do not assume that $n/k$ is constant. All our guarantees are uniform in $n$ and $k$. Achieving this uniformity substantially complicates the analysis. Our algorithms are based on exact-size Boltzmann samplers, which we accelerate by optimizing the cost of each sampling round and increasing the acceptance probability.
  As spin-off results, we answer, up to a logarithmic factor, an open question of Devroye and Los~25 on sampling profiles of random mappings when $n>k\log k$, and obtain a sampler for uniform random surjections with expected running time $O(n\log k)$, valid across the full parameter space.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Geometric Graph Representations via Compact SAT Encodings
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We present compact SAT encodings and certifying exact solvers for boxicity and cubicity. The boxicity of a graph is the minimum dimension in which it is the intersection graph of axis-aligned boxes; cubicity is defined analogously using unit cubes. Grid-based formulations face a geometric discretization bottleneck, growing rapidly with the target dimension. We avoid this bottleneck by encoding the total order of interval endpoints in each coordinate. For an $n$-vertex graph and target dimension $d$, our boxicity encoding uses $O(n^2d)$ variables and $O(n^3d)$ clauses, both linear in $d$. Requiring the left- and right-endpoint orders to agree yields a cubicity encoding of the same asymptotic size.
  Satisfying models are decoded into independently checked geometric representations, while unsatisfiable instances used as lower-bound evidence carry mechanically verified DRAT certificates. In a controlled evaluation with 186 trials per encoding on standard and structured graph families, the order encoding solves 96.8% of trials, compared with 71.0% for the known grid formulation, and reduces mean PAR-2 time from 178.21 to 21.70 seconds.
  The pipeline also certifies exact values for several named graphs. We turn one such value into a reusable obstruction by proving that every Kneser graph $K(n,k)$ with $k\ge3$ and $n\ge2k+1$ contains an induced Desargues graph. The resulting lower bound, together with an explicit three-dimensional representation of $K(7,3)$, establishes $\operatorname{boxicity}(K(7,3))=3$. This disproves the conjecture of Caoduro and Sebo that $\operatorname{boxicity}(K(n,k))=n-k$ for all $k\ge3$ and $n\ge2k+1$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Per-State Signatures and Mean Time-to-Failure: An Algorithm for Systems With Simultaneous Failures
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We present an algorithm that computes the structural signature and the mean time-to-failure (MTTF) of a monotone binary system at every one of its states, rather than only at the state in which all components work. It makes no assumption on the structure function and evaluates it exactly once per state, as many times as needed for the signature of the complete system alone, so computing the MTTF everywhere costs only a factor polynomial in the number of components over computing it once. As a by-product, it identifies all minimal path sets. We assume exchangeable component failure times whose survivor count is a continuous-time Markov chain. This setting admits simultaneous failures, as in the Lévy-frailty Marshall-Olkin, binomial failure rate and lethal-shock models, where the simplifications available for single failures do not apply. We use the per-state MTTF to define threshold repair policies. We show that the per-state signature is a strictly finer decision criterion than the MTTF: signature dominance at a common failure count implies MTTF dominance, but not conversely. Under the Lévy-frailty Marshall-Olkin model the MTTF is monotone in the state, which yields the long-run cost rate of every threshold policy in a single pass. Experiments on 22 benchmark networks with up to 30 components and 31 failure models show that the best MTTF-threshold policy has a median excess cost of 0.36% over the optimal state-based policy, and that it is never worse than the best policy that repairs after a fixed number of failures.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: The manuscript has been submitted to IEEE Transactions on Reliability

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Asteroidal Triples and Friends in (Likely Necessary) Matrix Multiplication Time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In a seminal paper, Kratsch and Spinrad [SODA 2003 and SIAM Journal on Computing 2006] studied several important problems in structural graph theory that anticipated two trends in fine-grained complexity, both from the upper- and lower-bound side:
  * From the upper-bound side, for each of these problems the authors give an intermediate running time strictly between $n^ω$ and $n^3$, where $ω<2.371177$ is the matrix multiplication exponent. When optimized, this running time can be made $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{(3+ω)/2})$. By now, many more problems can be solved in this running time: directed unweighted or node-weighted APSP, a variety of matrix products such as max-min and dominance, RNA Folding and many more. For some of these, the community has also developed tools suggesting that this intermediate running time is necessary.
  * From the lower-bound side, the authors give lower bounds of $n^{ω-o(1)}$, conditioned on three natural hardness hypotheses on the complexity of quantified variants of triangle detection that account for different types of hardness of such problems.
  Despite this, it has remained open for over 20 years which of these two pieces of evidence reflects the truth for the problems that Kratsch and Spinrad study: whether the intermediate running time is indeed necessary and stronger lower bounds hold, or whether the hardness evidence of Kratsch and Spinrad is essentially tight. In this paper, we resolve this question and show that the latter is the case: all problems admit an $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^ω)$ time algorithm.
  As an additional contribution, we make partial algorithmic progress on further problems in structural graph theory of intermediate complexity, improving over previous work [Chiu and Lu, STACS 2022 and Information and Computation 2024][Spinrad, Discrete Applied Math 2004].
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 32 pages, 6 figures; to appear at SODA 2027

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Quality control in sublinear time: a case study via random graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Many algorithms are designed to work well on average over inputs. But when such an algorithm is run on an arbitrary input, the question arises: Can we trust the algorithm on this input? This question is especially relevant in network science, where algorithms for theoretical random graph models are often applied to individual real-world networks.
  We identify a new class of algorithmic problems addressing this, which we call "Quality Control Problems." These problems are specified by a "quality function" $ρ$ and a distribution $D$ such that, with high probability, a sample drawn from $D$ is "high quality," meaning its $ρ$-value is near $1$. The goal is to accept most inputs $x \sim D$ and reject potentially adversarially generated inputs $x$ with $ρ(x)$ far from $1$.
  In this work, we consider the sublinear version of the quality control problem, where $D \in Δ(\{0,1\}^N)$ and the goal is to solve the $(D,ρ)$-quality problem with $o(N)$ queries and time. As a case study, we consider random graphs, i.e., $D = G_{n,p}$ (and $N = \binom{n}2$), and the $k$-clique count function $ρ_k := C_k(G)/\mathbb{E}_{G' \sim G_{n,p}}[C_k(G')]$, where $C_k(G)$ is the number of $k$-cliques in $G$. In suitable parameter ranges, worst-case approximate $k$-clique counting requires $p^{-Ω(k^2)}$ queries. In contrast, we show that the quality control problem for $G_{n,p}$ (with $n\geq p^{-ck}$ for some constant $c$) with respect to $ρ_k$ can be tested with $p^{-O(k)}$ queries and time, showing quality control is provably superpolynomially more efficient in this setting. More generally, for a motif $H$ of maximum degree $Δ(H)$, we show that the corresponding quality control problem can be solved with $p^{-O(Δ(H))}$ queries and running time.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Reweighted Spectral Partitioning Works: A Simple Algorithm for Vertex Separators in Special Graph Classes
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We establish that a practical polynomial-time algorithm obtains near-optimal $\frac23$-balanced vertex separators for a number of graph classes, including genus-$g$ graphs, $K_h$-minor-free graphs, and geometric graphs. For many of these classes, our polynomial-time separator bounds improve on previous work. Moreover, unlike previous work, all these separators are produced by a single unified algorithm that has no specialization for the graph class, and this algorithm admits a scalable implementation with good empirical results. Furthermore, our approach is robust to graphs falling just outside these classes, making it appropriate for practical applications like road networks.
  A key distinction of our approach, compared to previous work, is the disentanglement of our algorithm and its analysis for specific graph classes. Our algorithm is based on a newly improved form of a recent Cheeger-style inequality relating the value of a special semidefinite program to vertex expansion. Our analysis then only has to directly bound the value of this semidefinite program for each graph class, and constructions for these bounds need not be algorithmic. Finally, we obtain several results of independent interest. These include an improved (existential) separator theorem for intersection graphs of $k$-ply $d$-dimensional balls, an improved bound on the Fiedler value of genus-$g$ graphs, and a complete spectral proof of the planar separator theorem.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Parameterized Complexity of Isometric Path Cover: Treewidth and Diameter
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the fixed-parameter tractability of the \textsc{Isometric Path Cover} problem where, given an integer $k$ and a simple, undirected, and unweighted graph $G$, the objective is to decide whether $G$ admits a set of $k$ isometric paths (i.e., shortest paths between their endpoints) whose union is the entire vertex set of $G$.
  We show that \textsc{Isometric Path Cover} is NP-hard on graphs of pathwidth (and thus treewidth) at most 287. This is an interesting contrast with the closely related problems \textsc{Isometric Path Partition} and \textsc{Path Cover}, which are both known to be XP for treewidth, see [Chakraborty et al., WG 2026] and [Foucaud et al., TCS 2026].
  On the positive side, we show, by a suitable dynamic programming scheme, that \textsc{Isometric Path Cover} admits an XP algorithm w.r.t.~the parameter combination of treewidth and diameter, running in time $n^{\diam^{O(\tw)}}$ where $\diam$, $\tw$, and $n$ denote the diameter, the treewidth, and the number of vertices of the input graph, respectively.
  However, we also prove that \textsc{Isometric Path Cover} becomes W[1]-hard for pathwidth on graphs of diameter~7, showing that an XP algorithm is the best one can hope for w.r.t.~this parameterization, under standard complexity theory assumptions.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Computing bounded solutions to linear Diophantine equations with the sum of divisors
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We propose an efficient computational method for finding all solutions $n\leq U$ to the Diophantine equation $aσ(n)=bn+c$, where $a,b,c$ are fixed integer coefficients, $U$ is a given upper bound, and $σ(n)$ denotes the sum of divisors of $n$. The method combines advanced pruning of possible prime factors of $n$ and their combinations with several optimization techniques, organized around a \emph{prime-wheel} data structure developed for this purpose. It is implemented in the {\sc SageMath} computer algebra system within the framework of recursively enumerated sets and supports native {\sc MapReduce} parallelization. We apply the method to numerous previously studied equations, discovering new solutions, certifying complete solution lists below substantially larger bounds than previously reported, and substantially improving lower bounds in several open problems involving the sum-of-divisors function.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Preprocessed 3SUM: From Reals to Integers
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The Preprocessed 3SUM problem asks to preprocess a set $A$ of $n$ numbers so that we can quickly decide whether a query subset $A' \subseteq A$ contains a solution $a+b=c$. The best known query bounds differ substantially between integer and real inputs. For integers, a series of advances with near-quadratic preprocessing reduced the query time from $\tilde O(n^{13/7})$ [Chan, Lewenstein; STOC '15] to $\tilde O(n^{11/6})$ [Chan, Vassilevska W., Xu; STOC '23], and finally to $\tilde O(n^{3/2})$ [Kasliwal, Polak, Sharma; SOSA '25]. For reals, only the first of these bounds has been achieved, by adapting the corresponding integer algorithm [Fischer; SODA '25]. Is this gap inherent to the more limited tools available for real inputs?
  We give a randomized real-to-integer reduction with $\tilde O(n^2)$ preprocessing overhead and no asymptotic increase in query time. This yields $\tilde O(n^2)$ preprocessing and $\tilde O(n^{3/2})$ query time for real inputs, closing the gap. We show how to extend our result to the setting where one set is unknown at preprocessing time. Our reduction is conceptually simple, and relies on an interesting technical toolkit around old and new tools from sparse linear algebra. More broadly, it suggests a route to real-to-integer reductions for other additive problems.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Restless Guards: Robust Guarding of Polyominoes
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The art gallery problem is a fundamental problem whose practical applications have inspired numerous variants. In this work, we investigate a setting in which full coverage of the gallery shall be ensured despite locational uncertainty of the guards.
  We study this problem for polyominoes under rectangular visibility, where a $k$-restless guard assigned to a cell may move to any cell within distance at most $k$. While all polyominoes are guardable for $k\in\{0, 1\}$, the same is not true for all $k\geq 2$. However, for a given polyomino $P$ and integer $k$, we present an algorithm that identifies a $k$-restless guard set of $P$ in polynomial time, or decides that no such set exists. For the cases $k\in\{0,1\}$, where $k$-restless guard sets always exist, we provide tight worst-case bounds on the number of $k$-restless guards that are always sufficient and sometimes necessary to guard a hole-free polyomino with $n$ vertices or $m$ cells.
  Moreover, we show that computing a minimum guard set is NP-hard. Complementing the hardness, we provide polynomial-time algorithms for solving the problem optimally for histograms, and leverage this to obtain a $20k$-approximation for polyominoes without holes.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The Sync Heap: Delete First, Ask Questions Later
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Heaps (priority queues) are among the best-studied data structures in computer science. In this paper, we critically revisit the textbook assumption that in the comparison model at least one of the two standard heap operations of inserting an element and deleting the minimum must take logarithmic time.
  By decoupling the deletion itself from the act of revealing the identity of the deleted element to the user, we avoid the sorting barrier and obtain a novel trade-off between the complexities of heap operations. This shows that the logarithmic barrier is not inherently the cost of deleting the minimum but rather the information cost of immediately learning which element was deleted. In the special case when the user inspects the heap state only constantly many times, we show that both insertions and deletions can be supported in constant amortized time. As an application, this yields a runtime improvement from $\mathcal{O}(n \log n)$ to the optimal $\mathcal{O}(n)$ for a textbook unit-time scheduling problem.
  We obtain our results by designing a new data structure, the sync heap, which gains speed by rearranging and compacting its operations until queries force it to synchronize and reveal its state. As a key component, we use the soft heap introduced by Chazelle as part of his minimum spanning tree algorithm. Our data structure is simple, comparison-based, and deterministic, and our results are asymptotically optimal.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Towards Dynamic Top-$k$ Simple Shortest Paths
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Computing the top-$k$ \textit{simple} shortest paths between two vertices of a graph, i.e., solving the P-KSSP problem, is a fundamental primitive in graph analytics. In modern scenarios, however, queries are rarely one-shot: parameters change as applications adapt their information needs, and recomputing a solution from scratch at every request quickly becomes a bottleneck. We study P-KSSP in a dynamic setting, focusing on changes of the parameter $k$: given a top-$k$ solution for a pair of vertices and a new value $k'$, the goal is to compute a top-$k'$ solution reusing the previously computed paths. Our approach rests on the \textit{pseudo-tree}, a compact representation of a collection of simple $s$--$t$ paths: we show that building it from an arbitrary, unstructured solution amounts to trie construction, and give two constructions running in time linear in the size of the collection. On top of it, we design UPD, a dynamic algorithm that updates a solution upon a change of $k$; we prove its correctness, analyze its complexity, and show that it is a general, solver-agnostic scheme, which starts from the paths alone, is parametric in the routine that generates candidate paths and combinable with known preprocessing techniques, as well as with an online pruning rule that we formalize. While a worst-case update is asymptotically comparable to recomputing from scratch, an extensive experimental evaluation shows that a variant of UPD is the fastest method in the large majority of tested configurations, often by a wide margin (with speedups over recomputation that grow with $k$ and $k'$ and exceed $60\times$), yielding a practical recipe for the configuration to deploy.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Stronger Hardness for Submodular Maximization Subject to a Matroid Constraint
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Maximizing a submodular function subject to a matroid constraint is a cornerstone problem in combinatorial optimization. The state-of-the-art algorithm for this problem obtains $0.401$-approximation~\cite{buchbinder2024constrained}, and the state-of-the-art hardness result shows that no polynomial time algorithm can obtain better than $0.478$-approximation for this problem~\cite{oveisgharan2011submodular}. In this work, we present the first improvement in $15$ years for the hardness result, showing that no polynomial time algorithm in the value-oracle model can obtain better than $8/17 \approx 0.471$-approximation, even for the special case of a cardinality or (simplified) partition matroid constraint.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 13 pages. This version adds a remark about the relationship between this work and the results of arXiv:2610.00545

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: How Hard Is It to Rig a Tournament When Few Players Can Beat or Be Beaten by the Favorite?
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In knockout tournaments, players compete in successive rounds, with losers eliminated and winners advancing until a single champion remains. Given a tournament digraph $D$, which encodes the outcomes of all possible matches, and a designated player $v^* \in V(D)$, the \textsc{Tournament Fixing} problem (TFP) asks whether the tournament can be scheduled in a way that guarantees $v^*$ emerges as the winner. TFP is known to be NP-hard, but is fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) when parameterized by structural measures such as the feedback arc set (fas) or feedback vertex set (fvs) number of the tournament digraph. In this paper, we introduce and study two new structural parameters: the number of players who can defeat $v^*$ (i.e., the in-degree of $v^*$, denoted by $k$) and the number of players that $v^*$ can defeat (i.e., the out-degree of $v^*$, denoted by $\ell$).
  A natural question is that: can TFP be efficiently solved when $k$ or $\ell$ is small? We answer this question affirmatively by showing that TFP is FPT when parameterized by either the in-degree or out-degree of $v^*$. Our algorithm for the in-degree parameterization is particularly involved and technically intricate. Notably, the in-degree $k$ can remain small even when other structural parameters, such as fas or fvs, are large. Hence, our results offer a new perspective and significantly broaden the parameterized algorithmic understanding of the \textsc{Tournament Fixing} problem.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: This work has been merged with arXiv:2602.13422. All updates will appear there

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Incremental Exact Vertex Connectivity
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the problem of maintaining the vertex connectivity $κ$ of a graph under edge insertions. For undirected graphs, our algorithm uses $O(κ^4 \log^2 n)$ amortized time per edge insertion. After each edge insertion, the algorithm outputs the current value of $κ$, plus a set of $κ$ vertices whose removal disconnects the graph. Our algorithm is Monte-Carlo randomized and works with a randomness-adaptive adversary. The algorithm also works on directed graphs against an oblivious adversary, which is equivalent to an output-adaptive adversary if we only have to output the current value of $κ$.
  Previously, algorithms for maintaining the vertex connectivity with $o(n)$ time per edge insertion were only known for $κ\le 2$, and need $\tilde{O}(\log^2 n)$ and $O(\sqrt{n})$ time per edge insertion for $κ= 1,2$, respectively. Moreover, for $κ> 4$, no algorithm faster than recomputation from scratch was known.
  We complement our algorithm with a conditional lower bound: Under the OMv conjecture, any insertions-only algorithm that outputs the current value of $κ$ after every insertion needs $Ω(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ amortized time per edge insertion for $κ= Θ(n)$. Previous conditional lower bounds for this problem only apply to worst case running time, or algorithms that support both edge insertions and edge deletions.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Decoding Failure Biases IBLT Count Measurements: A Gaussian-Selection Law at the Peeling Threshold
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In a self-sizing set-reconciliation protocol, a small first-round Invertible Bloom Lookup Table (IBLT) sketch attempts peeling decoding; after failure, the protocol estimates the difference count $d$ from the count energy and sizes the second round from a lower quantile of the measurement. This quantile must be computed conditionally on failure: the measurement and peeling success are determined by the same random mapping, so conditioning can shift the measurement law.
  In the ideal peeling model, inside the critical window where failure has nondegenerate probability, the standardized energy and a statistic of the unsigned mapping that governs the peeling outcome (the precritical score) have a joint Gaussian limit with correlation $η_kρ^2$, $ρ$ being the sign imbalance and $η_k$ a closed-form constant. The measurement conditional on failure is thus a bivariate normal truncated to a half-plane, which we call the Gaussian-selection law. Since $η_k$ changes sign between $k=4$ and $k=5$, under one-sided imbalance the unconditional threshold undercovers exactly when $k\ge5$ and is conservative for $k=3,4$.
  The key tool is a quenched CLT for a signed quadratic form on a random overlap graph; under asymptotically balanced signs, conditioning on any unsigned mapping event that is permutation-invariant and has probability bounded away from zero leaves the standard normal limit unchanged. After failure the protocol observes the total sign; inverting the selection law yields an upper confidence bound for $d$, asymptotically conservative in the critical window and, when $d/\sqrt M\to\infty$, along the whole load axis. The experiments use analytic constants, none fitted; the unconditional threshold carries a selection error that does not vanish with scale, while the corrected selection-law threshold matches per-configuration empirical quantiles.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Geometric Hashing in MPC with Applications to Clustering and Stochastic Embeddings
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In this paper we study consistent hashing (a.k.a. sparse partitions) for doubling metrics in the Massively Parallel Computation (MPC) model. A $(Γ,Λ)$-hash with diameter bound $Δ$ partitions a metric space into clusters of diameter at most $Δ$ such that every ball of radius $Δ/Γ$ intersects at most $Λ$ clusters in expectation. Consistent hashing has emerged as a central tool in geometric MPC algorithms. However, so far it has been solely used in Euclidean spaces, where it can be pre-computed.
