On the other hand, in cases where the metric space is received as input and unknown in advance, no previous parallel construction was known. We present the first fully scalable MPC algorithm over machines with local space $n^σ$, that given an $n$-point metric space with doubling dimension $d\leq O(σ\log n)$, samples a randomized $(Γ,2^{O(d/Γ)})$-hash in $O(d/σ^3)$ rounds. There is a dichotomy: if the doubling dimension is $d=Ω(σ\cdot\log n)$, a polynomial number of rounds is required to compute such a hash. We conclude by showing that this MPC primitive yields $O(d/σ^3)$-round fully scalable MPC algorithms for a broad class of fundamental geometric problems in doubling metrics, including stochastic tree embeddings with $O(\log n)$ expected distortion, constant factor approximation for facility location, bicriteria $(O(ε^{-2}),1+ε)$-approximation for $k$-median and $k$-means.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Testing Connectedness and Edge Connectedness
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We revisit the classical problem of testing connectedness of graphs represented in the adjacency lists model and obtain optimal bounds. Specifically, we show that $\varepsilon$-testing connectedness of graphs with maximum degree at most $d$ requires $Ω(\frac{1}{\varepsilon} \log \frac{1}{\varepsilon d})$ queries (when $\varepsilon \le \frac{1}{4d^5}$). Our result implies that the connectedness tester of Levi, Pallavoor, Raskhodnikova, and Varma ({\em ACM Trans.\ Comput.\ Theory, 2022}) is optimal. We also study the problem of testing $k$-edge-connectedness of both directed and undirected graphs of average degree $\overline{d}$ in the adjacency lists model and design a tester with query complexity $O(\frac{k}{\varepsilon} \log \frac{1}{\varepsilon \overline{d}})$, improving upon the bounds by Forster, Nanongkai, Saranurak, Yang, and Yingchareonthawornchai (SODA 2020). Furthermore, we complement our upper bound by showing that every one-sided error $k$-edge-connectedness tester must make $Ω(k/\varepsilon)$ queries.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A General Framework for Matching with Delays
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We present a simple deterministic $O(\log n)$-competitive algorithm for the online minimum-cost perfect matching with delays (MPMD) problem on arbitrary, unknown metric spaces, where $n$ is the (unknown) number of requests. This improves upon the recent $O(\log^5 n)$-competitive algorithm of Dufay and Wattenhofer (SODA 2026) and nearly matches the $Ω(\log n / \log \log n)$ randomized lower bound of Ashlagi et al. (APPROX 2017). Our algorithmic framework rests on two ingredients: an online moat-growing process that grows active dual variables at a deliberately slowed constant rate $α< 1$ to control temporal asymmetry, and a delayed eligibility rule that matches requests in the same dual component only after their waiting time is proportional to their time-expanded distance. The framework extends naturally to arbitrary concave delay functions, maintaining an $O(\log n)$ competitive ratio, and to $k$-way matching with delays, yielding an $O(k \log n)$-competitive deterministic algorithm.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Shortest Augmenting Path Algorithm for Linear Matroid Parity
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The matroid parity problem generalizes both graph matching and matroid intersection. Although the general version is intractable, Lovász (1981) developed a polynomial-time algorithm for the linear matroid parity problem, assuming the availability of matrix representations. Subsequently, Gabow and Stallmann (1986) presented an augmenting path algorithm, which has long been recognized as one of the fastest deterministic algorithms. Since shortest augmenting paths improved algorithms for graph matching (Micali & Vazirani, 1980) and linear matroid intersection (Cunningham, 1986), extending these techniques to linear matroid parity appears to be a natural progression. However, such an algorithm has remained elusive for four decades.
  We present the first shortest augmenting path algorithm for linear matroid parity. Our approach synthesizes the augmenting path algorithm of Gabow and Stallmann with the synchronized blossom formation of Micali and Vazirani, whose correctness was recently proven by Vazirani (2024). Our key technical contributions are threefold: (i) a linear-algebraic argument that bounds the lengths of shortest augmenting paths for linear matroid parity, which generalizes Cunningham's bound for linear matroid intersection; (ii) an a priori characterization of shortest search paths through lower bounds on their lengths; and (iii) an extension of the structural properties for graph matching established by Izumi, Kitamura, and Yamaguchi (2025) to the linear matroid parity setting.
  Our algorithm deterministically solves the linear matroid parity problem in ${\rm O}(nr^2\log r)$ time, where $n$ is the ground set size and $r$ is the matroid rank. By incorporating fast matrix multiplication, this complexity can be further reduced to ${\rm O}(nr^2)$. These results improve upon the long-standing deterministic bounds of ${\rm O}(nr^3)$ and ${\rm O}(nr^ω)$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A proximal gradient algorithm for composite log-concave sampling
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We propose an algorithm to sample from composite log-concave distributions over $\mathbb{R}^d$, i.e., densities of the form $π\propto e^{-f-g}$, assuming access to gradient evaluations of $α_f$-convex $f$ and a restricted Gaussian oracle (RGO) for $α_g$-convex $g$, where $α_g \ge 0$. The latter requirement means that we can easily sample from the density $\text{RGO}_{g,h,y}(x) \propto \exp(-g(x) -\frac{1}{2h}||y-x||^2)$, which is the sampling analogue of the proximal operator for $g$. If $f + g$ is $α$-convex and $f$ is $β$-smooth, our sampler achieves $\varepsilon$ error in total variation distance using $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(κ\sqrt d \log^4(1/\varepsilon))$ oracle calls where $κ:= 1 \vee β/α$, with $0\le α_g \le β$ and $α:= α_f + α_g > 0$, which matches prior state-of-the-art results for the case $g=0$. We further extend our results to cases where (1) $π$ is non-log-concave but satisfies a Poincaré or log-Sobolev inequality, and (2) $f$ is non-smooth but Lipschitz.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A 0.4584-approximation for DR-submodular maximization over down-closed convex sets
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We obtain a $0.4584$-approximation for nonnegative, non-monotone, $L$-smooth DR-submodular maximization over compact convex down-closed subsets of the unit cube, improving the $4/9\approx0.4444$ ratio of Aggarwal's projection-based algorithm~\cite{aggarwal2026geometry}. A recovery map combining exponential and linear-fractional branches admits a cube-wide affine upper bound. The resulting continuous-time Frank--Wolfe-type algorithm with randomized output and its randomized discrete-time implementation both satisfy $\E F(\widehat x)\ge(0.4584-\varepsilon)\OPT-δLD^2$; the implementation uses polynomially many cube-wide value/full-gradient queries and ordinary linear maximization calls, where $D$ is the feasible diameter and $\varepsilon,δ>0$ are accuracy parameters. Our guarantee and Aggarwal's hardness bound~\cite{aggarwal2026geometry} place the optimal approximation ratio for cube-wide value/full-gradient queries and linear maximization, with additive error $δLD^2$, in $[0.4584,0.4705)$. Standard multilinear sampling and pipage rounding imply an expected $(0.4584-\varepsilon)$-approximation for nonnegative submodular set-function maximization under a matroid constraint \cite[Lemma B.3]{vondrak2013symmetry}.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Deterministic Volume Estimation of Truncated Hypercubes
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We present a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for estimating the volume of a hypercube intersected by a fixed number of constraints, where each constraint is the sum of univariate functions that are each nonnegative, monotone, and convex. Such constraints include knapsack and norm-ball constraints. The case of the unit hypercube truncated by a single linear constraint (halfspace) is already #P-hard. Given a fixed number of such constraints in a given dimension, together with an error parameter, our algorithm computes a multiplicative approximation of the volume of their intersection with the unit hypercube in time polynomial in the dimension, reciprocal error, input encoding length, and output encoding length.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Efficient Agnostic Learning of Univariate Densities Under Local Differential Privacy
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We propose a general framework for non-interactive locally differentially private (LDP) learning of structured univariate distributions that can be approximated by piece-wise polynomials. This gives the first sample-efficient LDP learners for several distribution classes, including mixtures of log-concave distributions, such as Gaussian mixture models (GMMs). These learners also provide agnostic guarantees and are computationally efficient. We also prove a lower bound for learning GMMs under LDP, improving on the standard pure-DP packing lower bounds of Bun et al. [BKSW19]. To obtain our general learning framework, we develop an efficient non-interactive LDP algorithm for synthetic data generation over large domains, which may be of independent interest. We then use it together with a deterministic adaptation of the non-private piecewise polynomial learner of Acharya et al. [ADLS17].

Emerging Technologies.title: Design-Space Exploration of Distributed Neural Networks in Low-Power Wearable Nodes
Emerging Technologies.summary: Wearable devices increasingly support intelligent applications such as augmented reality, continuous health monitoring, and vision-based interaction. However, the neural networks (NNs) required by these applications often exceed the memory and energy budgets of wearable nodes. Cloud offloading reduces local computation but increases communication demand and can introduce latency and privacy concerns. TinyML reduces model complexity, potentially sacrificing accuracy without resolving the memory demands of vision workloads. This paper presents DistNN, a hardware-software framework for distributed NN inference that partitions execution between an ultra-low-power (ULP) wearable node and a nearby resource-rich hub, such as a smartphone. The node processes early NN layers and sends intermediate feature maps to the hub, which executes the remaining layers. To choose the split point, we propose a platform-independent figure of merit (FoM) based on data volume (DV) and cumulative computation cost (CC). The FoM captures the central trade-off: earlier splits reduce node computation but increase communication, whereas later splits reduce transmitted data but increase node computation. We also derive conditions for a net node-side energy benefit from distribution and demonstrate that the target autoencoder (AE) workloads cannot run monolithically on representative wearable microcontrollers. To enable ULP execution, we synthesize a custom node using low-precision fixed-point arithmetic. Post-synthesis estimates place DistNN below the 10 mW node-power target, with average node-compute power approximately 11x lower than that of the recent ML ASIC baselines evaluated. Across convolutional NNs and AEs, DistNN preserves task quality, achieving a structural similarity index (SSIM) of approximately 0.90 for image reconstruction with low-precision node features and a resource-rich hub decoder.
Emerging Technologies.comment: 10 figures, 8 tables, 16 pages

Emerging Technologies.title: Agentic AI in Automated Markets
Emerging Technologies.summary:
Automated markets increasingly host autonomous, learning trading agents and are powered by formulaic automated market makers (AMMs). We study how heterogeneous agent behavior shapes stress, risk-adjusted performance, liquidity, and volatility in these types of markets. Three behavioral archetypes are modeled as agentic reinforcement learning (RL) systems: a rational arbitrageur, a manipulator, and a retail herd-follower. Each archetype is defined by its reward function within a common, asset-agnostic exposure-control environment, and each is trained with a value-based Deep Q-Network (DQN) and with REINFORCE using a learned baseline.
  A pilot on hourly cryptocurrency data (AAVE, ETC, SUI) motivates the hypotheses. Herd-followers produce the most frequent but shortest stress episodes, manipulators the fewest but most persistent, and rational agents the most stable rolling Sharpe ratios despite higher return volatility. SHAP attributions tie these patterns to drawdown and cross-asset signals, short-term volatility and position state, and momentum, respectively. The results motivate behavior-specific regulation rather than uniform limits on volatility or turnover.
Emerging Technologies.comment: 10 pages

Emerging Technologies.title: SynDebug: A Framework to Debug Logic Bugs in Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Programs
Emerging Technologies.summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) introduces substantial systems-level complexity through quantum error correction (QEC), making debugging FTQC programs challenging. Existing quantum debugging approaches primarily target logical-level circuits and do not naturally support debugging within realistic FTQC execution flows. We present SynDebug, the first systems-level debugging framework for FTQC programs. SynDebug introduces lightweight assertion-based debugging primitives that operate directly within encoded FTQC infrastructures while avoiding additional logical surface area and minimizing temporal overhead. We evaluate SynDebug across multiple QEC code families, code distances, and encoded workloads, including state preparation, entanglement validation, and Shor-style programs. Our results demonstrate that SynDebug enables practical FTQC debugging with an average 1.8% additional circuit depth overhead (0% in most cases) and no measurable increase in the logical error rate, showing that systems-level debugging for large-scale FTQC applications is both feasible and practical.
Emerging Technologies.comment: SynDebug will appear at SIGOPS ATC 2026

Emerging Technologies.title: Empirical Quantum Advantage in Constrained Optimization from Encoded Unitary Designs
Emerging Technologies.summary:
We introduce the Constraint-Enhanced Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (CE-QAOA), a shallow, constraint-aware ansatz that operates inside the one-hot product space [n]^m, where m is the number of blocks and each block is initialized in an n-qubit W_n state. We give an ancilla-free, depth-optimal encoder that prepares W_n using n-1 two-qubit rotations per block, and a two-local block-XY mixer that preserves the one-hot manifold and has a constant spectral gap on the one-excitation sector. At the level of expressivity, we establish per-block controllability, implying approximate universality per block. At the level of distributional behavior, we show that, after natural block and symbol permutation twirls, shallow CE-QAOA realizes an encoded unitary 1-design and supports approximate second-moment (2-design) behavior; combined with a Paley-Zygmund argument, this yields finite-shot anticoncentration guarantees.
  Algorithmically, we wrap constant-depth sampling with a deterministic feasibility checker to obtain a polynomial-time hybrid quantum-classical solver (PHQC) that returns the best observed feasible solution in O(S n^2) time, where S is a polynomial shot budget. We obtain two advantages. First, when CE-QAOA fixes r >= 1 locations different from the start city, we achieve a Theta(n^r) reduction in shot complexity even against a classical sampler that draws uniformly from the feasible set. Second, against a classical baseline restricted to raw bitstring sampling, we show an exp(Theta(n^2)) minimax separation. In noiseless circuit simulations of traveling salesman problem instances with n in {4,...,10} locations from the QOPTLib benchmark library, we recover the global optimum at depth p = 1 using polynomial shot budgets and coarse parameter grids defined by the problem size.
Emerging Technologies.comment: 37 Pages, 5 figures, 2 tables

Emerging Technologies.title: Wattlytics: A Web Platform for Co-Optimizing Performance, Energy, and TCO in HPC Clusters
Emerging Technologies.summary: The escalating computational demands and energy footprint of GPU-accelerated computing systems complicate informed design and operational decisions. We present the first release of Wattlytics (https://wattlytics.netlify.app), an interactive, browser-based decision-support system. Unlike existing procurement-oriented calculators, Wattlytics uniquely integrates benchmark-driven GPU performance scaling, dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS)-aware piecewise power modeling, and multi-year total cost of ownership (TCO) analysis within a single interactive environment. Users can configure heterogeneous systems across contemporary GPU architectures (GH200, H100, L40S, L40, A40, A100, and L4), select representative scientific workloads (e.g., GROMACS, AMBER), and explore deployment scenarios under constraints such as energy prices, system lifetime, and frequency scaling. Wattlytics computes multidimensional decision metrics (TCO breakdown, work-per-TCO, power-per-TCO, and work-per-watt-per-TCO) and supports design-space exploration, what-if scenarios, sensitivity metrics (elasticity, Sobol indices, Monte Carlo) and collaborative features to guide realistic cluster design and procurement under uncertainty. We validate the fitted power and performance models and compare four deployment modes: fixed budget, fixed GPU count, fixed performance, and fixed power. Our case studies show that, under budget or energy constraints, optimally deployed energy-efficient GPUs can outperform higher-performance alternatives in overall cost-effectiveness. Wattlytics helps users explore the design parameter space and distinguish between cost- and risk-driving factors, turning HPC design into a well-informed and explainable decision-making process.

Emerging Technologies.title: Audio-Based Condition Monitoring for Agricultural Machinery: Stakeholder Needs, Adoption Barriers, and MVP Requirements
Emerging Technologies.summary: Failures of agricultural machinery are costly when breakdowns occur during narrow work windows and are discovered too late for planned service. Audio-based condition monitoring offers a low-cost retrofit sensing path because operators already treat abnormal sound as an informal diagnostic cue. Whether such systems are adopted, however, depends on how well they fit farm workflows, repair constraints, and stakeholder decision-making. This paper reports a stakeholder discovery study of audio-based condition monitoring for agricultural machinery. We synthesize semi-structured interviews with farm operators, dairy operators, dealership and service personnel, manufacturers, integrators, and domain experts, together with a short survey. Across sources, downtime avoidance emerged as the dominant value driver, and failures were most commonly recognized through unusual noise and loss of functionality. Survey responses further indicate a gap in maintenance visibility and low penetration of predictive tools. These findings narrow the opportunity from generic ``AI diagnosis'' to low-friction early warning and evidence generation for maintenance planning. Modern tractors appear to be a weaker initial wedge because many are already instrumented and supported by mature service programs. Implements, attachments, hidden rotating components, small-to-medium operations, and continuous-use settings such as dairy present clearer need because failures in these contexts are harder to perceive, sensing coverage is lower, and downtime consequences are higher. We translate these findings into requirements for a minimum viable product (MVP) that prioritizes maintenance actionability over full automation: commodity audio capture, contextual annotation, asset-specific baselines, persistent-deviation detection, temporally stable alerts, and evidence artifacts that support operator inspection and dealer triage.

General Literature.title: OnBodyAI - Why the Next AI Needs a Body
General Literature.summary: The next AI will not win by knowing more about the world. It will win because it knows you: because it lives on your body, works for you and answers to you. That is what the term OnBodyAI stands for. It describes what happens when large language models are given a body, and what research and industry need to make that happen. This article is based on my talk in the Industrial Panel at UbiComp/ISWC 2026 in Shanghai (October 13, 2026) and follows its ten key statements.
General Literature.comment: This article is based on my talk in the Industrial Panel at UbiComp/ISWC 2026 in Shanghai (October 13, 2026) and follows its ten key statements

Graphics.title: SAMS: A Structured Graph Framework for Securing Additive Manufacturing Systems
Graphics.summary: Additive manufacturing, also known as 3D printing, is significant for its use in industries such as aerospace, robotics, medicine, and construction. However, digital mesh files remain vulnerable to geometry defects which can be introduced through malicious tampering or designer error. This can lead to hampered structural integrity and impede its use due to unexpected degradation of the part. To address these challenges, we propose SAMS, a multi-layered hierarchical graph framework designed to analyze meshes to enhance the Security of Additive Manufacturing Systems. SAMS captures geometric and topological information across mesh, facet, and surface levels, providing an adaptable architecture for targeted mesh processing tasks. We evaluate SAMS's accuracy against existing mesh processing tools. The graph construction results in rich structural representation and has the potential to significantly reduce downstream analytical complexity when detecting vulnerabilities. This paper presents SAMS, its formal graph-theoretic properties, and releases an open-source Python 3.12 implementation on GitHub (https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SAMS-graph-classes/) to facilitate future research in secure additive manufacturing systems software.

Graphics.title: Three LiDARs, Twenty-Five Datasets: Cross-Source Generalization in Tree-Species Recognition
Graphics.summary: FOR-species20K is the largest public LiDAR benchmark for tree-species classification, pooling 25 independently collected terrestrial, mobile, and airborne laser-scanning datasets across 33 species. We introduce a multi-resolution, multi-view ConvNeXtV2 model that improves official hidden-test accuracy from 79.5% to 85.0%, ranking first at the time of submission. We then examine what this score measures. Because the hidden test is species-balanced, its overall accuracy is more comparable to a macro metric than to accuracy under the public set's long-tailed distribution. Moreover, the official random split places every source dataset in both training and evaluation. A logistic probe recovers source identity from out-of-fold model probabilities with 69% accuracy, while geometric features identify the source above 90% within two widely shared species; 18 of the 33 species occur in only one source. Under a source-species-cell holdout, evaluated on 5,566 trees from eight eligible species that retain the same LiDAR-type training support in other sources, the unweighted species mean falls from 82% to 36%, and tree-weighted accuracy falls from 95% to 60%. Count-matched retraining and experiments with two alternative backbones indicate that this gap is not explained by reduced training support alone, while an external PureForest experiment shows a smaller but consistent grouped-split effect. These results establish the 85% leaderboard score as strong in-distribution performance, but not as an estimate of source-disjoint generalization, motivating balanced metrics and source-aware evaluation. The code is available at: https://github.com/JaeLee18/FOR20K-lidar-tree-species

Graphics.title: CoatFusion: Controllable Material Coating in Images
Graphics.summary: We introduce Material Coating, a novel image editing task that simulates applying a thin material layer onto an object while preserving its underlying coarse and fine geometry. Material coating is fundamentally different from existing "material transfer" methods, which are designed to replace an object's intrinsic material, often overwriting fine details. To address this new task, we construct a large-scale synthetic dataset (110K images) of 3D objects with varied, physically-based coatings, named DataCoat110K. We then propose CoatFusion, a novel architecture that enables this task by conditioning a diffusion model on both a 2D albedo texture and granular, PBR-style parametric controls, including roughness, metalness, transmission, and a key thickness parameter. Experiments and user studies show CoatFusion produces realistic, controllable coatings and significantly outperforms existing material editing and transfer methods on this new task.
Graphics.comment: Accepted to ACM Transactions on Graphics (SIGGRAPH Asia 2026)

Graphics.title: SUPRA-TEX: 3D Generation with Super-Aligned Texture
Graphics.summary: Single image 3D generation aims to dress a given 3D mesh with relightable materials while faithfully preserving the visual details of a reference image. Existing methods either introduce artifacts when fusing inconsistent multi-view predictions or struggle to preserve fine details through implicit image-feature conditioning. To resolve these challenges, we introduce SUPRA-Tex, built on the principle of decoupling visible-material estimation, surface alignment, and observation-guided 3D completion. This division of labor allows the 3D generator, trained on limited 3D data, to focus its capacity on preserving visible evidence and completing unobserved surfaces. Specifically, we first train an MLLM-based image editing model to predict lighting-separated PBR maps in the reference view. We then project these maps onto the visible surface and encode them with the pretrained material VAE encoder into native observation latents that share the generation target's latent space. An interleaved flow transformer holds these latents as fixed, read-only anchors while alternating unobserved-region and full-surface updates to generate complete material latents. This design achieves super-alignment with the reference, delivering What You See Is What You Get fidelity on visible regions and coherent completion on unobserved surfaces. Trained solely on public datasets, SUPRA-Tex achieves SOTA performance in both geometry-conditioned texturing and end-to-end asset generation, matching or even exceeding leading commercial systems on in-the-wild images. Project page: https://supra-3d.github.io/supratex/

Graphics.title: ACEdit: Stable Multi-Turn Image Editing via Asymmetric Conditioning
Graphics.summary: Image editing models produce impressive results for individual edits, but their quality often deteriorates over multiple editing turns. Each editing turn introduces small distribution shifts that accumulate over successive edits, creating a gap between the input distributions encountered during the editor's original training and multi-turn inference. We introduce a training scheme that makes multi-turn image editing stable under this accumulating distribution shift. A key is to force the editor to operate on its own outputs from previous editing turns during training, bringing the principle of Self-Forcing to image editing. The main challenge is that self-generated editing trajectories deviate from ground-truth trajectories, making direct supervision unreliable. We address this challenge through a distillation objective that leverages a teacher image editor to provide a reliable training signal when the model operates on its own previous outputs. We introduce an asymmetric conditioning scheme: while the student performs edits sequentially on its own outputs, the teacher remains anchored to the original clean image and receives a compound editing instruction. Experiments show substantially reduced degradation over long multi-turn sequences while maintaining editing quality and instruction adherence.

Graphics.title: Compression of Uniformly Distributed Unit Quaternions
Graphics.summary: Unit quaternions are widely used in computer graphics making their efficient compression critical for reducing memory consumption and bandwidth requirements. In this paper, we present a novel method for encoding uniformly distributed unit quaternions. Our thorough analysis of several quaternion parameterizations compares their theoretical error properties, quantization behavior, computational cost, and memory efficiency and provides both an analytical and empirical characterization. We show that an infinity-norm parameterization with our optimized warp function consistently offers the smallest maximum error and the best storage efficiency, at a decompression cost equal to or lower than that of parameterization methods found in practice. We demonstrate the practical benefits of the proposed approach in several graphics applications, including tangent-space normal mapping, skeletal animation with blend weights, and Gaussian splatting.

Graphics.title: From Sketch to Scene: Relightable Garment Reconstruction from Marked Sketches
Graphics.summary: Sketching is one of the most natural ways for people to express visual ideas. Unlike the text prompts that most generative systems rely on today, a sketch captures spatial structure and intent directly, including where a designer wants highlights and shadows to appear. Yet current sketch-to-3D pipelines have no input for that intent: they bake the drawn shading into the texture as dark paint, and the light cannot be moved. We propose a system that transforms a rough garment sketch, marked with sparse annotations (a star for a highlight and a moon for a shadow), and a short text prompt describing the texture, into a textured 3D mesh with an explicit directional light, as a scene that can be relit and edited after generation. The two symbols are the most frequent proposals in an elicitation study with art students. From the marked sketch the system predicts the scene's directional light and, separately, a displacement field that bends the surface so that the moon-marked regions fall into shadow under that light, rather than being painted dark in the texture.
Graphics.comment: 11 pages, 5 figures. Ahmet Neçirvan Doğan and Eren Acar Başaran contributed equally

Graphics.title: Seeing Both the Forest and the Trees: Reusing Holistic 3D Priors for Part-Decomposed Generation
Graphics.summary: Generating 3D assets with explicit parts requires two properties at once: geometric detail inside each part and structural coherence across the whole object. Recent image-conditioned 3D generation models adopt a structured 3D representation that anchors tokens to explicit spatial positions, capturing both properties, but their output remains a single fused mesh. We ask how a part-decomposed generation model can inherit both properties of these holistic priors, and answer with STRUCTPARTS, a framework whose core technical contribution is a dual-frame coordinate interleaving mechanism: each shape latent is interpreted under both a part-local and an object-global reference frame, and processed through a global-local inter-leaved transformer that simultaneously reuses the prior's geometric detail at the part scale and its structural coherence at the whole-object scale. As its structural input, STRUCTPARTS uses a segmented mesh scaffold, a coarse mesh paired with a face-level segmentation mask kept entirely within the prior's native 3D representation. With only lightweight finetuning, both intra-part detail and inter-part coherence emerge from the same pretrained weights. On PartObjaverse-Tiny, STRUCTPARTS matches or surpasses prior part-decomposed models at a fraction of their training cost, while naturally supporting part-mesh refinement and part-level editing.

Graphics.title: Geometric Queries on Tessellation-Free Displaced Surfaces
Graphics.summary: Displacement maps encode fine geometric detail in compact textures and simplify surface authoring, but using them typically requires pre-tessellating surfaces into dense triangle meshes, incurring a heavy memory cost. Recent tessellation-free methods enable direct ray tracing. However, broader geometric queries such as surface sampling, specular manifold search, and closest-point queries remain less explored. Supporting these operations requires surface enclosures, area estimates, and normal bounds, which scalar height intervals alone do not fully provide. We present a first-order texture-space hierarchy that unlocks these queries directly without pre-tessellation. Each node stores a local affine height plane and a conservative residual bound, retaining spatial height variation that scalar minimum--maximum bounds discard. The plane and residual provide surface enclosures for intersection and distance searches, while the plane's height and slopes supply area estimates for sampling. Additional slope bounds support specular light-path search. Building on this representation, we develop query-specific traversal, pruning, and sampling algorithms, and demonstrate them in caustics rendering, sampling displaced emitters, and surface partial differential equation (PDE) solvers. We demonstrate memory savings over pre-tessellation and performance improvements over query-specific baselines, while retaining efficient ray tracing.

Graphics.title: Learning to Search for Executable Patternmaking from Certified Programs
Graphics.summary: Recent models generate sewing patterns from images or text, and program-based representations make these patterns executable. These systems produce a finished pattern and do not model how a patternmaker turns one pattern into another. In practice a new style is made by editing an existing pattern: lengthening the bodice, moving a dart, swapping a sleeve. Pattern archives record the results of such edits and none of the steps. We observe that the steps can be recovered by searching over editing actions until one pattern becomes the other. A deterministic compiler makes the recovered steps checkable. To this end, we present SemDraft, the first framework that learns to search for executable patternmaking programs from paired before-and-after sewing patterns without recorded editing steps. Specifically, a bounded search recovers a program of editing actions and certifies it only after three checks: it recompiles from scratch, every pair of its actions is classified as ordered or interchangeable, and an independent replay reaches the same pattern. The certified programs then train a model that ranks candidate actions inside the same search. On two frozen draws of 80 order-sensitive cases, with every other search component fixed, the learned ranker certifies 63 and 64 cases within 1,000 search executions, against at most 53 and 52 for non-learned rankers.

Graphics.title: IKMo: Image-Keyframed Motion Generation with Trajectory-Pose Conditioned Motion Diffusion Model
Graphics.summary: While text-to-motion generation is mainstream, integrating explicit spatial constraints has become a standard solution for precise animation. Existing state-of-the-art models are tailored for professional workflows, effectively processing high-quality, pre-aligned 3D inputs via unified conditioning mechanisms. However, this strictly aligned setting restricts accessibility for general users who rely on unaligned, in-the-wild 2D reference images. This accessible scenario introduces a fundamental conflict: heterogeneous geometric constraints, where user-defined global trajectories clash with local image-derived poses. To resolve this coordinate mismatch, we propose TPMDM, a diffusion model featuring a decoupled parallel control strategy that explicitly isolates and aligns these divergent signals. Furthermore, we introduce IKMo, a holistic framework that synergizes TPMDM with a VLM-powered multi-agent system. By bridging the semantic-geometric gap, IKMo translates user-friendly inputs into explicit motion constraints to drive the diffusion backbone. Experiments on HumanML3D and KIT-ML demonstrate that our method establishes a new state-of-the-art in the task of generating motions under heterogeneous trajectory and keyframe pose constraints.
Graphics.comment: 6 pages; accepted to ICME 2026 (Spotlight). Camera-ready version with updated author list and abstract

Graphics.title: Homology-Preserving Dimensionality Reduction via Adaptive Mapper and Landmark Isomap
Graphics.summary: As data becomes increasingly central across engineering and scientific disciplines, effective visualization is essential for interpreting complex, high-dimensional structures. Dimensionality reduction techniques project high-dimensional data into lower dimensions while aiming to preserve structural properties such as pairwise distances and local neighborhoods. In this paper, we focus on improving homological preservation, that is, the retention of topological features such as connected components and loops, which is critical for maintaining global shape and continuity. We first introduce AdaMapper, a Mapper-based algorithm that leverages persistence diagrams to guide both skeleton construction and landmark selection. AdaMapper incorporates an adaptive refinement strategy that automatically increases cover resolution in regions exhibiting topological loops. We then propose AdaHIsomap, which extends landmark Isomap by incorporating homology-informed landmark selection and augmenting it with random anchor points to better balance distance and homology preservation. We evaluate both methods on a diverse set of datasets, including high-dimensional point clouds, scientific simulations, networks, and image data, and benchmark their performance against state-of-the-art approaches.
Graphics.comment: Published in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (TVCG), 2026

Graphics.title: ResStreamGS: Residual-Sensitive Dual-Stream Gaussian Splatting for Mobile Volumetric Video Streaming
Graphics.summary: Real-time mobile volumetric video enables immersive free-viewpoint experiences, but delivering high-quality 3D content under constrained bandwidth and computation remains challenging. Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) systems, such as V$^3$, enable efficient mobile streaming by encoding time-varying Gaussian attributes with commodity video codecs and hardware decoding. However, existing pipelines treat all Gaussians as frame-varying signals, which is poorly suited to full-scene content where large portions remain temporally stable. Our empirical study shows that frame-wise adaptation and video coding of all Gaussians cause quality degradation in complex full-scene content, particularly in temporally stable regions. To address this issue, we propose ResStreamGS, a residual-sensitive dual-stream framework that processes Gaussians according to their temporal behavior. ResStreamGS identifies residual-sensitive primitives through lightweight probe adaptation and reuses stable Gaussians within each Group of Pictures (GOP). Stable Gaussians are transmitted once per GOP, while only residual-sensitive Gaussians remain in the frame-wise hardware-decodable video stream. Experiments on complex full-scene volumetric videos show that ResStreamGS improves post-codec PSNR by 7.51--8.35~dB over a controlled V$^3$-style all-Gaussians baseline, reduces amortized payload by up to 56.5%, and achieves 30.883~FPS on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 778G platform.

Graphics.title: RoboCloth: A Large-Scale Real Cloth Material Dataset for Neural Reflectance Reconstruction
Graphics.summary: We present RoboCloth, a dataset of 500 real cloth materials captured under flexible, calibrated camera and lighting configurations, where both are robotically controlled during acquisition. Each material is imaged in approximately 580 high-dynamic range frames spanning a wide view-light hemisphere; camera poses are refined via structure-from-motion and aligned to the robot frame, yielding per-material sparse surface geometry and structured per-point reflectance observations ready for neural material training. We demonstrate the value of this data through a two-stage neural reconstruction pipeline: Stage 1 trains a shared MLP decoder on our corpus to learn cloth material priors; Stage 2 then freezes the decoder and fits a dense 2048x2048 latent texture to each target material. Evaluating on held-out materials from our own dataset and on the independent UBO2014 benchmark, we show that a decoder trained on our captures outperforms decoders trained on existing measured reflectance datasets and analytic PBR fitting, transferring to unseen acquisition systems without modification. The dataset, calibration files, observation tensors, and train/test splits are released under CC BY 4.0 on the Hugging Face Hub.
Graphics.comment: Project page: https://theialab.github.io/robocloth/ ; Code: https://github.com/theialab/robocloth ; Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/theialab/RoboCloth . 16 pages including supplementary material

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Dynamic Auction Mechanisms in a Closed-Credit Economy: Sequential Slot Reallocation in Air Traffic Management
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Indivisible resources allocated in advance may need to be reallocated when capacity reductions make existing assignments infeasible, yet monetary compensation is often impractical or undesirable. We develop a sequential resource reallocation scheme using reusable artificial credits, where agents hold pre-existing resource rights and have heterogeneous marginal valuations over time blocks. Capacity reductions produce fractional endowments, which our closed-credit scheme resolves into indivisible final allocations. We model agents' intertemporal preferences through a predicted-value-to-go function and characterize conditions ensuring that their optimal demand is non-increasing in price. We propose an ascending-auction mechanism that partitions agents into subgroups and uses the minimum subgroup market-clearing price as a common transaction price. We show that the mechanism preserves non-myopic individual rationality and weak nontrader neutrality. Moreover, we establish Pareto efficiency under optimal-demand clearing in the unified market and bound the expected gain from misreporting by the probability that an agent changes the common price. Simulations of airport slot reallocation demonstrate reductions in total modeled delay and cancellation costs relative to a ground-delay baseline.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: StratFL: Countering Covert Model Poisoning Attacks with Strategic Federated Learning
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Advanced persistent threats (APTs) are a major concern in federated learning (FL) deployments in critical sectors such as healthcare, and finance. Traditional defense mechanisms fail to contain APTs due to their intermittent attacking behavior. This paper addresses a specific type of APT called covert model poisoning (CMP) where the attacker intermittently injects poisoned model updates in a covert manner. The interaction between the FL server and a CMP attacker is modeled as an imperfect repeated game where both players cannot observe each other's actions. A novel adversarial search algorithm called StratFL is designed alongside novel belief update algorithms at both the server and adversary. Experiments are designed using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets to evaluate and compare StratFL's performance against state-of-the-art methods. Empirical convergence of belief update algorithms is demonstrated across various security vignettes. At the same time, StratFL is found to exhibit an improved accuracy of 10% compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Auditable and Deployable Multi-Agent Motion Planning via Posetal Games from Legal Guidelines
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: When robots are deployed in the real-world, they must interact with other agents and accomplish their own goals while adhering to legal constraints. These potentially conflicting objectives are often only partially prioritized, making scalarized objectives or fully specified hierarchies unsuitable. We present a framework for multi-agent motion planning under legal requirements based on games with partially ordered preferences (posetal games). Scenario-independent legal guidelines order abstract legal concerns, from which we automatically derive agent preferences and a legal game for any concrete scenario. Agents may refine their legal preferences with private objectives, and regulators may refine the guideline as laws evolve. We prove that such customizations can only remove equilibria and thus preserve legality. To coordinate agents without explicitly communicating private preferences, we introduce belief play, which provably recovers the true equilibria from conservative local games, and a distributed iterative best-response protocol requiring less information. We apply the framework to maritime navigation, systematically lifting pairwise traffic rules to multi-vessel encounters. On seven encounters with up to four vessels, every rule violation of the committed equilibria is certified as forced by the legal hierarchy or unsatisfiable, and defectors are identified from public information in all tested cases. These results indicate that guideline-based posetal games offer an auditable route from partially specified laws to multi-agent motion planning.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Decentralized LLM Workflows via Sequential Auctions
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We present a scalable framework for solving multi-step tasks through a decentralized market of self-interested agents. Prior theoretical work demonstrated that agents organized through sequential auctions can converge to a globally optimal policy in a Markov decision process (MDP), but relied on the restrictive assumption of the existence of perfect clones as a model of perfect competition. In reality, exact clones drive agent profit to zero, violating the natural risk-reward incentives of participants. Conversely, we empirically demonstrate that the opposite extreme, absence of competition, also leads to market failure and value extraction collapse. Between these two extremes, we investigate how heterogeneous agents can survive in markets that span the critical middle ground of imperfect competition. To be profitable, agents learn to strategically shade bids to secure positive individual profit margins, while still ensuring that the marketplace functions effectively enough so that collaborative tasks posed by market consumers can still be solved. We formulate and evaluate four bidding algorithms (Mirror Descent, Thompson Sampling, Bayes-Optimal, and PPO) across three auction protocols (1st-Price, 2nd-Price, and Credit-Conserving Vickrey). Across a diverse set of domains, we demonstrate that imperfect competition successfully sustains necessary agent profit margins while maintaining high task success rates at low costs.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Smoothed analysis of policy iteration and value iteration for deterministic discounted and mean-payoff games played on any graph
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Our understanding of turn-based stochastic games is reminiscent of our understanding of linear programming in the 1970s. Instead of the simplex method, we have two families of algorithms - policy iteration and value iteration - which work well in practice but are known to run in exponential time on some input instances, and we still lack an algorithm that runs in polynomial time on all instances.
  A recent result by Loff and Skomra showed that, for deterministic discounted and mean-payoff games played on an ergodic graph, a variant of policy iteration runs in smoothed polynomial time. This offered an explanation of why policy iteration performs well in practice, analogous to Spielman and Teng's explanation for the simplex method.
  In this paper, we drop the ergodicity assumption: we show that their policy iteration algorithms run in smoothed polynomial time for any game graph. We do this by defining a condition number that naturally generalizes theirs, showing that sufficiently-perturbed games are well-conditioned with high probability, and showing that their algorithms are efficient on well-conditioned instances. Although the outline is similar, our proof requires a substantially new approach, based on log-Lipschitz distributions which recently appeared in work on the smoothed analysis of the simplex method.
  For our second contribution, we propose three new value iteration algorithms for solving deterministic mean-payoff games (also on any graph). All three are based on iterative methods for finding fixed points of non-expansive operators, which we show can be applied to the Shapley operator. The first two are simple applications of Krasnoselskii-Mann iteration and Halpern iteration. The third is quadratically faster but more complicated: it runs Zwick-Paterson and Halpern iterations in parallel. We prove that all three algorithms are correct and run in smoothed polynomial time.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Switchback Price Experiments with Forward-Looking Demand
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Switchback experiments are widely used in pricing applications. We consider a retailer running such an experiment for the price of a single product, with infinite supply. In each period, the seller chooses a price from a set of predefined prices consisting of an original price and a few discounted price levels. The goal is to estimate the demand gradient at the original price to adjust the original price and improve revenue after the experiment. In our model, in each period, a unit mass of buyers arrives on the market, with values distributed based on a time-varying process. Crucially, buyers are forward-looking with a discounted utility and will choose not to purchase now if they expect to face a discounted price in the near future. We show that such forward-looking behavior introduces bias in naive estimators of the demand gradient, due to intertemporal interference. Furthermore, although experiments with only two price points are common in practice, we prove that no estimator using data from such experiments can recover the correct demand gradient, even in the limit of an infinitely long experiment with an infinitesimal price discount. Moreover, we characterize the form of the bias of naive estimators. Finally, we show that with a simple three-price-level experiment, the seller can remove the bias due to strategic forward-looking behavior and construct an estimator for the demand gradient that asymptotically recovers the truth. Our results provide practical guidance for platforms to obtain unbiased demand gradients from price experiments in the presence of forward-looking demand.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Why Alternation Speeds Up Counterfactual Regret Minimization?
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Solving imperfect-information games at scale rests on counterfactual regret minimization with the regret matching$^{+}$ (RM$^{+}$) update, and a seemingly minor implementation choice accounts for much of its practical speed: alternating the two players' updates, so that the second player responds to the strategy the first player just produced. A widely repeated intuition explains why: seeing the opponent's fresh strategy should act like optimism. We treat this intuition as a testable hypothesis about deterministic two-player zero-sum self-play dynamics and find that its canonical additive form fails an information-matched test. On an analytic witness family we compare alternating RM$^{+}$ against a one-sided predictive RM$^{+}$ that receives the same information channel each round and differs only in where the fresh signal enters, a persistent regret state versus a transient prediction term. Our main result is a dichotomy theorem that reduces trajectory separation to the recurrence of exact-vertex play by the predictive dynamics: under an interior-band assumption on the alternating iterate, either vertex times recur and the profile distance is at least, infinitely often, an explicit constant that our measurements nearly attain, or they terminate. Across the tested self-play regimes, any correct explanation of the alternation speedup must reproduce a staleness cost present at the smallest tested stale fraction, an advantage that persists across seven orders of payoff conditioning, regime crossings of the optimism family, and a measured per-perturbation cost of weakening the injection path that is far steeper for staleness than for partial persistence.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Learning Rewards in Strategic Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Understanding the objectives that drive agents' behavior is crucial in strategic environments, where multiple agents interact and adapt to one another. This challenge arises in domains such as cybersecurity, autonomous driving, and online markets, where agents' underlying incentives are typically unknown and must be inferred from their observed behavior. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a natural framework for this problem, but extending IRL to strategic multi-agent settings introduces a fundamental challenge: a reward that explains observed behavior does not necessarily induce optimal strategies when used for decision-making. In this work, we study this problem through the lens of \emph{strategic identifiability}, and show that learning from a fixed policy pair can be insufficient to strategically identify rewards, independent of the number of expert samples $K$. Motivated by this, we introduce an active IRL algorithm for two-player repeated Stackelberg games, in which the leader adaptively selects policies to elicit informative responses about the follower's reward. Combining maximum-likelihood estimation with experimental design, we derive finite-sample guarantees on the Stackelberg sub-optimality induced by the learned reward, matching up to polylogarithmic factors a new minimax learning rate of $K^{-1/2}$. Finally, we evaluate our approach in a realistic anti-poaching setting, demonstrating the benefits of active exploration for reward recovery and downstream strategic performance.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Infinite lexicographic products of positional objectives
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: This paper contributes to the study of positional determinacy of infinite duration games played on potentially infinite graphs with neutral transitions. Recently, [Ohlmann, TheoretiCS 2023] established that positionality of prefix-independent objectives is preserved by finite lexicographic products. We propose two different notions of infinite lexicographic products indexed by arbitrary ordinals, and extend Ohlmann's result by proving that they also preserve positionality. In the context of one-player positionality, this extends positional determinacy results of [Grädel and Walukiewicz, Logical Methods in Computer Science 2006] to edge-labelled games and arbitrarily many priorities for both Max-Parity and Min-Parity. Moreover, we show that the Max-Parity objectives over countable ordinals are complete for the infinite levels of the difference hierarchy over $Σ^0_2$ and that Min-Parity is complete for the class $Σ^0_3$. We obtain therefore positional languages that are complete for all those levels, as well as new insights about closure under unions and neutral letters.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: How language model agents reshape price competition
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Repeated Bertrand competition is a stringent benchmark for algorithmic pricing: in homogeneous-goods markets, standard learning procedures typically select the stage-game Nash outcome with prices near marginal cost. We show that LLM pricing agents can escape this benchmark, depending on deployment decisions. LLMs outperform standard online learners through faster adaptation, but this advantage largely disappears against full-information learners. An extracted surrogate algorithm illustrates how LLMs in specific deployments profit from regularly undercutting slower learners. Agents that post one price every period from raw market histories that include rival prices can sustain supracompetitive regimes in self-play. Agents that periodically emit probability distributions from summarized histories of their own profits instead move toward the competitive region in self-play. Markets mixing these interfaces can generate dynamic regimes in which LLMs establish a high-price anchor and regularly undercut it to capture demand. These regimes can keep both competitors' prices above marginal cost. Deployment choices shape these outcomes, shifting the focus from stationary equilibria to dynamic pricing regimes.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Market Incentives for AI Safety Investment
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Despite their practical significance, modern AI systems pose significant societal risks, including toxicity, malicious use, and misinformation. Their mitigation depends not only on technical feasibility but also on the incentives of firms that develop and deploy these systems. We show how profit maximization shapes safety investment in an AI supply chain with an upstream LLM provider and several competing downstream firms. In our game-theoretic model, we derive the market-driven level of safety investment and compare it with the levels that maximize market welfare and industry profit. We find that downstream competition generally induces downstream firms to invest more in safety than the industry-profit-optimal level. By contrast, the upstream provider may underinvest relative to these benchmarks because it is not fully compensated for the surplus from safety investments. Finally, we analyze how different regulatory interventions affect the participants' incentives and profits, and the resulting levels of model safety.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: How Hard Is It to Rig a Tournament When Few Players Can Beat or Be Beaten by the Favorite?
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
In knockout tournaments, players compete in successive rounds, with losers eliminated and winners advancing until a single champion remains. Given a tournament digraph $D$, which encodes the outcomes of all possible matches, and a designated player $v^* \in V(D)$, the \textsc{Tournament Fixing} problem (TFP) asks whether the tournament can be scheduled in a way that guarantees $v^*$ emerges as the winner. TFP is known to be NP-hard, but is fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) when parameterized by structural measures such as the feedback arc set (fas) or feedback vertex set (fvs) number of the tournament digraph. In this paper, we introduce and study two new structural parameters: the number of players who can defeat $v^*$ (i.e., the in-degree of $v^*$, denoted by $k$) and the number of players that $v^*$ can defeat (i.e., the out-degree of $v^*$, denoted by $\ell$).
  A natural question is that: can TFP be efficiently solved when $k$ or $\ell$ is small? We answer this question affirmatively by showing that TFP is FPT when parameterized by either the in-degree or out-degree of $v^*$. Our algorithm for the in-degree parameterization is particularly involved and technically intricate. Notably, the in-degree $k$ can remain small even when other structural parameters, such as fas or fvs, are large. Hence, our results offer a new perspective and significantly broaden the parameterized algorithmic understanding of the \textsc{Tournament Fixing} problem.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: This work has been merged with arXiv:2602.13422. All updates will appear there

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Role of Degrees and Acyclic Neighborhoods in the Complexity of Tournament Fixing
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: The \textsc{Tournament Fixing} problem asks whether a knockout tournament can be scheduled to make a favorite player win when all pairwise match outcomes are given. Such tournaments are used in sports and provide models for elections and organizational decision-making. Although the problem is NP-hard in general, it is polynomial-time solvable when some structural parameters become zero. Motivated by these cases, we study its parameterized complexity using those structural parameters centered on the favorite player. We prove fixed-parameter tractability when parameterized by either the number of players who beat the favorite player or the number that the favorite player beats. We next consider four subset parameters that measure the arc or vertex deletions needed to eliminate cycles through the player or either neighborhood. For each parameter, the problem remains NP-hard even when its value is one. When both neighborhoods are acyclic, we show that the problem remains NP-hard. We also give some sufficient conditions for the existence of a winning seeding. Our results complete the tractability classification of several individual parameters centered on the favorite player, extending the parameterized complexity landscape of this problem.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: We have merged arXiv:2602.13422 and arXiv:2601.08530v1. All updates will appear here

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Equitable Auctions
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study how auction design shapes surplus division among bidders. We introduce a parsimonious ex post equity notion and examine standard multi-unit auctions. The equity-optimal pricing depends sharply on the private-common value composition. Among mixed-price auctions, at one extreme, uniform pricing is always optimal for pure common values and, at the other, pay-as-bid pricing is preferred for pure private values under standard regularity assumptions. For any fixed monotone allocation rule, we characterize a BNIC interim-IR implementation that equalizes surplus ex post across all bidders and is revenue-maximizing among those that equalize surplus ex ante; efficient allocation permits parity among winners.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Approximating the Value of Time-Bounded Weighted Timed Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: The Value Problem for weighted timed games, an extension of timed automata with weights and adversity, consists in determining, given a weighted timed game with a reachability objective and a rational threshold, whether or not the value of the game exceeds the threshold. This problem is known to be undecidable for weighted timed games, i.e., there is no algorithm that can compute the value exactly. A natural alternative is to approximate the value; however, the Approximation problem is also undecidable in general. In this paper, we prove that the Approximation problem is decidable in 4-ExpTime for weighted timed games whose executions are time-bounded.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Characterization and Computation of Normal-Form Proper Equilibria in Extensive-Form Games via the Sequence-Form Representation
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Normal-form proper equilibrium, introduced by Myerson as a refinement of normal-form perfect equilibrium, plays an important role in the equilibrium analysis of extensive-form games because of its stronger stability properties. However, the exponential growth of the normal-form representation makes existing approaches for directly computing normal-form proper equilibria computationally impractical. To address this challenge, we introduce sequence-form proper equilibrium by defining a maximal payoff function over sequences, and prove its strategic equivalence to normal-form proper equilibrium. For computation, we further derive an equivalent formulation of sequence-form proper equilibrium via a class of perturbed games in sequence form, in which the perturbed realization-plan space is induced by imposing probability lower bounds on restricted sequence sets to encode the desired perturbation hierarchy. Based on this formulation, we develop two differentiable path-following methods for computing normal-form proper equilibria. These methods rely on artificial sequence-form games in which the expected payoff functions are regularized by logarithmic or entropy terms through an auxiliary variable. For each method, as the auxiliary variable tends to zero, the limit point of the induced smooth equilibrium path can derive one or more normal-form proper equilibria of the original game. Finally, Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed methods.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Learning in Structured Stackelberg Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We initiate the study of structured Stackelberg games, a novel form of strategic interaction between a leader and a follower where contextual information can be predictive of the follower's (unknown) type. Motivated by applications such as security games and AI safety, we show how this additional structure can help the leader learn a utility-maximizing policy in both the online and distributional settings. In the online setting, we first prove that standard learning-theoretic measures of complexity do not characterize the difficulty of the leader's learning task. Notably, we find that there exists a learning-theoretic measure of complexity, analogous to the Littlestone dimension in online classification, that tightly characterizes the leader's instance-optimal regret. We term this the Stackelberg-Littlestone dimension, and leverage it to provide a provably optimal online learning algorithm. In the distributional setting, we provide analogous results by showing that two new dimensions control the sample complexity upper- and lower-bound.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Accepted as a spotlight paper to ICML 2026

Human-Computer Interaction.title: ElectroCalm: Investigating User Experience and Physiological Responses to Multi-Node Transcutaneous Electrical Stimulation for Stress Modulation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Transcutaneous Electrical Stimulation (TES) for stress modulation has largely focused on vagus nerve stimulation at the neck, yet two questions remain underexplored: how users experience electrotactile sensations at this sensitive site, and whether electrotactile feedback itself can function as a haptic stress intervention. To investigate this gap, we applied an 8-node TES array to two body sites during a cognitively demanding 2-back task: the neck, a site used in prior vagal TES research for its anatomical proximity to the cervical vagus nerve, and the arm, the most common haptic wearable site, which primarily provides cutaneous electrotactile sensation without vagal access. In a usability study, both sites were rated as comparably comfortable without disrupting task performance, though the same stimulation was interpreted differently across sites. A second study assessing the physiological effects of active versus inactive stimulation under identical electrode attachment revealed that only neck TES produced cortical and autonomic changes consistent with stress modulation, while arm TES did not differ from inactive conditions. These findings suggest that neck TES can be acceptable despite the site's sensitivity, and that both the physiological effects and the sensory experience of TES depend on placement.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 25 pages, 6 figures, to appear in Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies, Vol. 10, No. 4, December 2026

Human-Computer Interaction.title: A misinformation playbook sharpens judgement without breeding cynicism
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Misinformation harms public health and democracy, and generative artificial intelligence now writes falsehoods as persuasive as people's. Defences range from fact-checking individual claims to training people to resist falsehoods. Yet many claims are too new to check, and interventions that teach doubt can reduce belief in truth too. We propose a defence that targets not the facts of each claim but the persuasion strategies that recur across them. Here we show that learning misinformation's persuasion playbook, mapped from 214,646 fact-checked claims in 51 languages, can sharpen human and machine judgement of claims they know little about, without making either more cynical about true claims. The playbook spans social influence, information manipulation and emotional appeals, combined around a core of fear, conspiracy and fabrication. Briefed with it, plus a reminder that persuasion is not proof of falsehood, a language model better distinguished true from machine-generated false claims about events after its training data. In a pre-registered experiment, the same briefing improved people's discernment of claims they reported as unfamiliar and left their belief in true claims unchanged. Averaged over all claims, the gain was not statistically significant. Because it targets what recurs, this defence need not wait for claim-specific fact-checks.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Benchmarking Robots for Everyday Environments: From Lab Experiments to Real-World Operations
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: This study presents an interdisciplinary process for benchmarking service robots in public everyday environments, addressing the gap between laboratory metrics and real-world operation at technology readiness levels 6-7. Three robots were evaluated in three use cases: outdoor park cleaning, pedestrian underpass cleaning, and interactive assistance in a public library. Over three years (2023-2025), seven benchmarking events (a consensus workshop and six on-site evaluations, two per use case) assessed the robots in increasingly realistic settings, from controlled conditions to public operation. An interdisciplinary panel of experts in robotics, human-robot interaction, safety, and economic viability consolidated use-case-specific metrics into a shared evaluation concept refined across three phases. Rather than ranking the robots, the evaluation examined how task fulfillment, interaction quality, safety, and economic viability interact in the transition from laboratory prototype to operational system. Direct quantitative comparability across the heterogeneous use cases remained limited, characteristic of benchmarking at this maturity level. The process yielded cross-case insights: increasing environmental realism introduces challenges that uniform metrics capture only in part; the interaction-quality guideline works best as a modular instrument adapted to each use case; safety was assessed by occupational-safety and product-certification experts who adapted industrial test procedures for public settings; and economic viability proved a cross-cutting dimension. We conclude that benchmarking at higher technology readiness levels is well served by a shared procedure for selecting and documenting metrics across these four categories, with safety as mandatory, rather than by a fixed set of metrics: generalizability lies in the procedure rather than in identical metrics.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 46 pages, 14 figures, 5 tables. Accepted for publication in Frontiers in Robotics and AI (Field Robotics)

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Risk and Refusal: Mechanisms of LLM Responses to Suicidal Ideation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Refusal is a common safety mechanism in large language models (LLMs), yet in contexts of suicidal ideation (SI), refusing to engage can itself constitute a safety failure. We evaluate how eight instruction-tuned LLMs respond to SI and self-harm disclosures across three datasets, varying whether models are informed that a disclosure expresses SI and whether they receive a clinician-developed response protocol, and complement this with mechanistic analyses in six open-weight models. Our results reveal a nuanced relationship between refusal and response-level risk. At baseline, elevated risk in model responses is driven primarily by inattention to the disclosure, alongside refusal to engage. Mechanistic analyses suggest that models may refuse SI disclosures through the same direction that mediates their refusals of harmful requests. However, informing models of the SI context, or suppressing refusal directly, increases engagement without reliably lowering response risk, and may raise it. In contrast, the clinician-guided protocol consistently reduces response-level risk while also reducing refusal. Together, these analyses and ablations motivate the need for models that refuse only when warranted and engage in interactionally safe ways when users disclose SI.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Recursive Organization Improvement: A Modeling Specification for Human--Agent Organizations
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Stronger AI agents do not automatically produce better organizations: teams must also learn which work arrangements to retain and when to reconsider them, while those arrangements determine what evidence the team can learn from. We propose a modeling specification for recursive organization improvement and evaluate it through an executable checker, a public-record mapping, and two simulation studies. The specification connects actor-visible histories, organizational memory, decision rights, and the evidence used to retain changes. Study 1 crosses six decision rules, three memory conditions, and three task environments under fixed resource ceilings. In a stationary environment, cumulative evidence raises balanced evaluation's net value per task from 0.452 to 0.480, while selection regret falls from 0.029 to 0.002. After a workflow-ranking reversal, retained evidence delays adaptation. In post hoc acquisition-matched controls, the remaining contribution of program replacement depended on the memory rule: small and uncertain under an eight-round window, positive under cumulative memory after a reversal, and negative under reset evidence. Study 2 models human-agent review with shared errors, copying, and decision rights. It identifies a two-actor case in which public records conceal whether agreement comes from shared errors or copying, and shows how dependence changes the preferred placement of human judgment under a fixed budget. Paid observation can lower decision error while costing more than the deployment gain. Assessments of organizational improvement should track the evidence acquired and retained, using acquisition-matched comparisons to isolate the contribution of evaluator revision.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 23 pages (including references and appendices), 4 figures, 12 tables. Supplementary material: 16 pages, 5 tables (S1-S5)

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Harness-Driven Agentic Operation of Optical Pooled Screen Analysis
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Optical pooled screens connect genetic perturbations to changes in cell morphology and behavior, but turning the microscopy data into interpretable results takes complex, multi-day analyses. Established pipelines process this data, yet researchers still select parameters, inspect outputs, and resolve failures for each experiment. Here, we present Brieflow-auto, a pipeline-specific harness implemented as a Claude Code plugin that lets a coding large language model (LLM) operate Brieflow, an open-source end-to-end pipeline for optical pooled screening data. A researcher supplies experimental facts and approves the launch. An agent tunes parameters in an interactive notebook, and the harness validates the configuration, monitors execution, recovers from common failures, and checks output quality. For pipeline defects, the agent opens upstream issues proposing backward-compatible fixes for the broader community. In five previously analyzed screens, harness runs yielded more cells with a confident single-gene assignment than the original hand analyses. On a screen the pipeline was not designed for, the harness turned each failure into a reviewed upstream fix. More broadly, we propose that wrapping an established pipeline in a harness can substantially accelerate its use and the long-term reliability of its codebase.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Agentic Life Sciences

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Lonely Individuals Show Distinct Patterns of Social Media Engagement
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Loneliness has reached epidemic proportions globally, posing serious risks to mental and physical health. As social media platforms increasingly mediate social interaction, understanding their relationship with loneliness has become urgent. While survey-based research has examined social media use and loneliness, findings remain mixed, and little is known about when and how often people engage with social media, or about whether different types of platforms are differently associated with loneliness. Web trace data now enable objective examination of these behavioral dimensions. We asked whether objectively measured patterns of social media engagement differ between lonely and non-lonely individuals across devices and platform types. Analyzing six months of web trace data combined with repeated surveys ($N=589$ mobile users; $N=851$ desktop users), we found that greater social media use was associated with higher loneliness across both devices, with this relationship specific to social media rather than other online activities. On desktop, lonely individuals exhibited shorter sessions but more frequent daily engagement. Lonely individuals spent more time on visual-sharing ($g = -0.47$), messaging ($g = -0.36$), and networking-oriented platforms on mobile. These findings demonstrate how longitudinal web trace data can reveal behavioral patterns associated with loneliness, and more broadly illustrate the potential of digital traces for studying other psychological states. Beyond research, the results inform the responsible design of digital interventions and platform features that better support psychological well-being across different technological contexts.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Cleaned up references and fixed typos

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Hybrid Cinematography: Previsualizing and Managing Hallucination Risk in Generative Video Reshooting
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: On a film set, the camera move is committed during a take. Generative video reshooting lets filmmakers change it afterward, but may require hallucinating unrecorded content, a gap sometimes discovered only after leaving the set. We present Hybrid Cinematography, a workflow that bridges physical capture and generative reshooting to manage hallucination risk while filmmakers can still act on it. Using an editable 3D shot plan and a proxy of the take, our previsualization evaluates hallucination risk in real time. Seeing where the take lacks support, filmmakers can iteratively adjust the plan, explore moves that balance capture and generation, shoot guided pickups, or knowingly accept hallucination.
