We demonstrate the workflow through a mobile augmented reality application for on-set planning, capture, and review, and an offline pipeline for existing video. A study with experienced filmmakers reveals how previsualizing risk informs camera decisions and exposes tensions between creative intent and generative hallucination.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Project page: https://hybridcinematography.github.io/; v2: Updated author name; paper content unchanged

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Asking Smarter Questions: Targeted Active Preference Learning for Underspecified Rewards
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Reward learning typically assumes the human's input covers everything that matters for the task. In practice, humans can only attend to so much at once, so their teaching naturally captures some features---or aspects of the task---better than others. Prior work has shown how the robot can identify which features were poorly supervised directly from its teaching data. But the current solution is to ask the human to try again, putting the burden on someone who already struggled to convey those features. We propose shifting this burden to the robot. Our key insight is that the same information that tells the robot what it doesn't know can help it ask better questions. Preference queries offer a low-effort channel for resolving this uncertainty, but only if the robot knows where to direct them and the human knows what to attend to when answering. We act on this insight in two ways: we build an informed prior that targets preference queries at the features that need resolving, and we accompany each query with an explanation that focuses the human's attention on exactly those features. In simulation, the informed prior beats the standard active preference learning baseline by up to $30.8\%$ in the low-query regime, where reducing human effort matters most. In a user study, the informed prior and explanations each significantly improve reward recovery and amplify each other.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted to the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026), Austin, TX. 18 pages, 8 figures, 1 table

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Author-in-the-loop Agentic Reproducibility Auditing for a Machine Learning Conference
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Reproducibility checks during peer review require a shared understanding of what authors' code is expected to reproduce. We present an author-in-the-loop collaborative audit that makes author declarations explicit inputs to an AI agent's investigation and assessment. A structured checklist records reproduction instructions and limitations; a two-stage workflow on GitHub connects agent checks to author clarification, revision, and agent reassessment. The agent separately assesses whether results have been reproduced and whether authors need to provide clarification or make repairs, while human reviewers approve requests and decide whether concerns are resolved. We deployed the system across 36 conference papers and 133 experimental tables and figures, raising 20 issues after human review. Further checks supported closing all the issues, although full reproduction remained unverified in some cases. We further compared repeated audits with complete and blank checklists to examine how author declarations shaped the agent's investigation and assessment. Our work contributes a collaborative workflow and agent design that use author knowledge to guide reproducibility auditing. The conference deployment provides empirical evidence that this approach can help identify and address reproducibility problems through collaboration among authors, agents, and reviewers.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 23 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables

Human-Computer Interaction.title: From Searchable to Non-Searchable: Generative AI and Information Diversity in Online Information Seeking
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Conversational generative AI systems such as ChatGPT are transforming how people seek and engage with information online. Unlike traditional search engines, these systems support open-ended, conversational inquiry, yet it remains unclear whether they ultimately expand or constrain the diversity of knowledge that users encounter in online search spaces, a primary foundation for knowledge work, learning, and innovation. Using over 200,000 real-world human-ChatGPT interactions, we examine how generative-AI-mediated inquiry reshapes diversity in both user inputs and system outputs through the lens of searchability - whether queries could plausibly be answered by traditional search engines. We find that almost 80% of ChatGPT user queries are non-searchable and span a broader knowledge space and topics than searchable queries, indicating expanded modes of inquiry. However, for comparable searchable queries, AI responses are less diverse than Google search results in the majority of topics. Moreover, the diversity of AI responses predicts subsequent changes in users' inquiry diversity, revealing a feedback loop between AI outputs and human exploration. These findings highlight a tension between expanded inquiry and constrained information exposure, with implications for designing hybrid search and generative-AI systems that better support exploratory knowledge seeking.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Orchestrating LLM Agents for Scientific Research: A Pilot Study of Multiple Choice Question (MCQ) Generation and Evaluation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming scientific work, yet empirical evidence on how these systems reshape research activities remains limited. We report a mixed-methods pilot evaluation of an AI-orchestrated research workflow in which a human researcher coordinated multiple LLM-based agents to perform data extraction, corpus construction, artifact generation, and artifact evaluation. Using the generation and assessment of multiple-choice questions (MCQs) as a testbed, we collected 1,071 SAT Math MCQs and employed LLM agents to extract questions from PDFs, retrieve and convert open textbooks into structured representations, align each MCQ with relevant textbook content, generate new MCQs under specified difficulty and cognitive levels, and evaluate both original and generated MCQs using a 24-criterion quality framework. Across all evaluations, average MCQ quality was high. However, criterion-level analysis and equivalence testing show that generated MCQs are not fully comparable to expert-vetted baseline questions. Strict similarity (24/24 criteria equivalent) was never achieved. Persistent gaps concentrated in skill\ depth, cognitive engagement, difficulty calibration, and metadata alignment, while surface-level qualities, such as {grammar fluency}, {clarity options}, {no duplicates}, were consistently strong. Beyond MCQ outcomes, the study documents a labor shift. The researcher's work moved from ``authoring items'' toward {specification, orchestration, verification}, and {governance}. Formalizing constraints, designing rubrics, building validation loops, recovering from tool failures, and auditing provenance constituted the primary activities. We discuss implications for the future of scientific work, including emerging ``AI research operations'' skills required for AI-empowered research pipelines.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Inflak: A Unified Orchestration Architecture for Human-Agent Interaction
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: LLM-powered agents increasingly support open-ended activities, yet orchestrating when and how agents interact with humans remains challenging. Existing approaches often provide interaction mechanisms tied to particular tasks or execution patterns, lacking a unified architecture for diverse and evolving interaction needs. We introduce Inflak, a unified four-layer architecture for human-agent interaction orchestration that separates state reconstruction and routing, interaction and execution planning, interaction design, and interface rendering. Its layered design with progressive resolution enables general applicability, runtime flexibility, module composability, and orchestration maintainability. We implement Inflak as agent-native, skill-based plugins within a general-purpose agent framework and evaluate it through a gallery of various application scenarios and interaction paradigms, technical performance testing, and a comparative implementation case study. The evaluations show that Inflak can serve as a general and extensible foundation for orchestrating diverse human-agent interaction flows.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Why Users Stop at Good Enough: Applying Bounded Rationality to Self-Service Restaurant Display Interactions
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: This paper investigates user interaction with digital displays in self-service restaurant environments, focusing on the phenomenon where users often settle for good enough interactions rather than optimal. We apply bounded rationality theory to understand how cognitive limitations influence user decisions to engage with displays of varying interaction complexity. Through analysis of two field experiments conducted at a self-service restaurant in Finland, we examine interactive displays that require different levels of cognitive investment: a simple binary choice interface and a multi-step interaction. Our initial findings suggest an "engagement plateau" where increased interaction complexity yields diminishing returns in initial engagement rates, yet users who overcome initial cognitive barriers demonstrate high completion rates. This work contributes to Human-Computer Interaction field by offering an empirically supported theoretical lens for understanding user behavior in Self-Service Restaurant (SSR) environments and providing actionable design principles for public interactive displays that accommodate human cognitive limits.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: A Multimodal Emotion Recognition System: Integrating Facial Expressions, Body Movement, Speech, and Spoken Language
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Psychological evaluation relies on clinicians' observation and interpretation of a patient's emotional expression, which is susceptible to subjectivity, bias, fatigue, and inconsistency. This paper presents a multimodal emotion recognition system designed to support, rather than replace, the evaluator. The system combines facial expression recognition, speech emotion recognition, text-based emotion recognition of transcribed speech, and body movement analysis, and fuses their outputs into an emotional profile of class probabilities that is presented to the evaluator together with the overall prediction. Although the unimodal models achieve high accuracy on their benchmark test sets, a remote user study with 52 participants expressing seven emotional states shows that their accuracy falls to between 82.97% and 87.64% under realistic conditions, with individual emotional states recognised in as few as 48.08% of cases. Under the same conditions, the multimodal system achieves an accuracy of 96.43%, significantly higher than every single-modality component ($p < 10^{-4}$), with no emotional state below 92.31%. These results indicate that strong benchmark performance of a single channel does not transfer to realistic use, and that multimodal fusion provides the robustness required of a tool that supports psychological evaluation.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: v2: Models revised to correct issues in the original implementation and results updated accordingly; text revised and restructured, architecture figures added, fusion stage formalised, references updated. 8 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Evaluating PDPL Compliance in E-Commerce Websites: Insights and Lessons Learned from Human and LLM Analyses
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: In 2024, Saudi Arabia's Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL) came into force. However, little work has been done to assess its implementation. In this paper, we analyzed 100 e-commerce websites operating in Saudi Arabia against the PDPL, examining the presence of a privacy policy and, if present, the policy's declarations of four items pertaining to personal data rights and practices: 1) personal data retention period, 2) the right to request the destruction of personal data, 3) the right to request a copy of personal data, and 4) a mechanism for filing complaints. Our results show that, despite national awareness and support efforts, a significant fraction of e-commerce websites in our dataset are not fully compliant with the examined PDPL requirements at the privacy policy level: only 31% of websites in our dataset declared all four examined items in their privacy policies. Second, the majority of top-ranked e-commerce websites in our dataset (based on search results order) and those hosted on local e-commerce hosting platforms exhibited significantly higher non-compliance rates than mid- to low-ranked websites and those not hosted on local e-commerce platforms. Third, we explored the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) as an automated tool for privacy policy analysis to measure compliance with the PDPL, using the GPT-5 model. We highlight the potential of LLMs and suggest considerations that can inform future benchmarks aimed at improving LLM-based automated analysis for privacy policies. Our results provide a step forward in understanding implementation barriers to data protection laws, especially in non-Western contexts. We provide recommendations for policymakers, regulators, website owners, and developers seeking to improve data protection practices and automate compliance monitoring.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Following Delegation Traces to Study Human Oversight in Interaction with Multimodal AI
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: As multimodal AI systems are becoming our everyday thought partners, the shift towards studying how users transfer control to these systems becomes especially urgent. In this paper, we report an overview of findings from an online study with n=56 AI-literate participants and 392 Video Question Answering trials. After inspecting each multimodal AI response, participants rated task-specific trust and selected one of three intended policies for an analogous future task: reject AI assistance, use it with verification, or delegate fully to the AI. Within participants, post-interaction trust strongly predicted the user's delegation choices (OR=14.97, 95% CI [7.14,31.37]). Trust and delegation nevertheless remained distinct. Verification was the dominant policy and often co-occurred with high trust. Delegation also increased with task order after adjustment for momentary and participant-level trust (OR=1.22, 95% CI [1.02,1.45]), indicating an experience-related component that self-reported trust ratings alone could not capture. These findings motivate a shift from intended delegation to a non-intrusive observation of how delegation is enacted in collaborative human-AI tasks. We therefore conclude by proposing enacted delegation traces as a methodological framework for future studies of multimodal and agentic AI use.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: From Sketch to Scene: Relightable Garment Reconstruction from Marked Sketches
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Sketching is one of the most natural ways for people to express visual ideas. Unlike the text prompts that most generative systems rely on today, a sketch captures spatial structure and intent directly, including where a designer wants highlights and shadows to appear. Yet current sketch-to-3D pipelines have no input for that intent: they bake the drawn shading into the texture as dark paint, and the light cannot be moved. We propose a system that transforms a rough garment sketch, marked with sparse annotations (a star for a highlight and a moon for a shadow), and a short text prompt describing the texture, into a textured 3D mesh with an explicit directional light, as a scene that can be relit and edited after generation. The two symbols are the most frequent proposals in an elicitation study with art students. From the marked sketch the system predicts the scene's directional light and, separately, a displacement field that bends the surface so that the moon-marked regions fall into shadow under that light, rather than being painted dark in the texture.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 11 pages, 5 figures. Ahmet Neçirvan Doğan and Eren Acar Başaran contributed equally

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Assessing Acceptance and Privacy Preferences of Third-party Financial Data Sharing in Bipolar Disorder
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Bipolar disorder is strongly associated with financial instability. We examine how different interventions motivate individuals with bipolar disorder to share financial data with others. This approach can inform the development of tools for digital monitoring and intervention designed to promote financial stability in this population. 500 individuals with BD completed a pre-registered factorial vignette survey to examine level of comfort with hypothetical scenarios involving third-party financial interventions during symptomatic and euthymic periods. Scenario components were systematically varied between third-party actors, mood states, and intervention types. Participants rated sharing comfort on a 0-10 point scale. Multilevel models tested differences alongside clinical and financial histories, relational trust, and personality. Participants were most comfortable involving care partners in financial planning. They were more comfortable with temporary spending restrictions during symptomatic states than euthymic periods, underscoring the importance of accurate mood detection for intervention delivery. Prior financial help-seeking behavior and higher relational trust predicted greater comfort. Bankruptcy experience --- declared by 11.4% and considered by 31.7% --- was associated with increased comfort with spending restrictions. Individuals with psychiatric advance directives (8%) were significantly more comfortable sharing spending behaviors than those without. Comfort with financial interventions was higher among those with prior financial challenges or help-seeking histories. Participants distinguished between symptomatic and euthymic periods, favoring targeted, time-limited restrictions over general monitoring. These findings extend prior work on financial data sharing for illness self-management.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, preregistration available at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/5AKEB

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Evaluative Dynamics of AI Integration and Expert Performance under Epistemic Dependence across Heterogeneous Stakes
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: AI is increasingly integrated into expert workflows, yet how integration affects perceptions of the expert, AI, and their combination remains unclear in domains where lay users are epistemically dependent on AI-assisted experts. We examine this through a novel controlled medical study (N = 166) and a direct cross-domain analysis with pre-existing academic-advising data (n = 157, combined N = 323). Expert errors reduced evaluations of the human expert across domains. Perceived expertise, however, varied by AI integration strategy in the higher-stakes medical task, where automatic AI oversight produced higher ratings than expert-only or expert-initiated AI. Exploratory ordinal sensitivity analyses identified a performance-contingent reuse pattern, with automatic oversight producing greater intended reuse after successful medical performance. Overall, performance-related recalibration appeared comparatively portable, while integration-structure effects were more selective and context-sensitive. These findings suggest that system designers should consider how AI enters expert workflows, not only whether it is present.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Volition Elicitation: Operational Semantics for People and Their Machines
Human-Computer Interaction.summary:
The most prevalent distributed systems today include people and their personal machines (smartphones), and computations in them are driven by people's volitions. Volition-guarded multiagent atomic transactions were proposed as an abstract specification language for such systems, in which a transaction has a precondition on the machine states of its participants and is guarded by the volitions of some of them.
  Here we develop an abstraction cascade that derives smartphone apps from such specifications and prove it correct down to the base programming language, GLP. The cascade consists of: (1) communicating volitional agents (CVA), which implement every local volition-guarded specification with simple guards, correctly, and completely for its strongly fair runs, by two-phase commit coordinated by the initiating agent; (2) volition-guarded GLP (vGLP), an extension of GLP with volitional procedures, whose goals put an interactively-typed question to the person, into which that implementation compiles; and (3) GLP, which implements vGLP by eliciting the person's answers through the widgets of their interactive types, correctly, and completely for complete widgets. We demonstrate the approach on three grassroots platforms --- a social graph, a social network, and currencies: a compiler carries the social graph and the currencies down the cascade to GLP programs that run with scripted persons, and earlier programs of the three run as mini-apps of one smartphone app.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: A Systematic and Validated Translation of the Perceived Empathy of Technology Scale to Chinese
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: The Perceived Empathy of Technology Scale (PETS) allows evaluation of empathic behavior in intelligent systems, a concept increasingly applied in human-AI interaction, particularly in emotional and mental health support applications. To support intercultural research and development, PETS is already available in multiple languages, as research suggests cultural and language-based differences in the expression and perception of empathy. Given the substantial Chinese-speaking population and the growing focus on cross-cultural HCI research, we present a validated translation of PETS into Putonghua (Mandarin) with Simplified Chinese. Based on established back-translation methodologies as used in previous PETS translations, our process included multiple independent translations, expert panel reviews, and empirical testing with a total of N=400 participants from an English and a Chinese sample. Through confirmatory factor analysis and invariance testing we show that the Chinese PETS retains the original two-factor structure with high reliability, with support for configural, metric, and scalar invariance. Beyond validation, empathic system behavior was rated equivalently across languages, while non-empathic behavior drew substantially higher ratings from Chinese participants, suggesting its absence is read less consistently across cultures than its presence. This validated Chinese version enables researchers and practitioners to assess empathy perceptions among Chinese-speaking users, supporting culturally appropriate empathic technology development.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Submitted to ICHEC 2026

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Context Matters! Social, Spatial, and Semantic Coordination with an Embodied Agent in Immersive Analytics
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Embodied AI agents in Augmented Reality (AR) could enable more natural collaboration in immersive analytics by engaging users through spatial, conversational, and visual interaction. However, designing such agents requires careful attention to context. We propose a preliminary conceptual framework for context-aware design of embodied agents structured around three dimensions of spatial, social, and semantic. This framework is further categorised into embeddedness (how agents are situated in the contexts) and awareness (how agents perceive and respond to the contexts). To explore this, we present Cobot, an embodied AI agent designed as a design probe. Cobot supports context-sensitive interaction through features such as gaze cues, spatial sound, and task-aware behaviour. We reflect on its design and identify implications for future contextaware embodied agents.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: In 2025 IEEE International Symposium on Mixed and Augmented Reality Adjunct (ISMAR-Adjunct) (pp. 189-194). IEEE

Human-Computer Interaction.title: TeamLens in Critsly: A Consent-Based Team-Composition Interface and Synthetic Readiness Evaluation for Design Collaboration
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Discussing working preferences may support reflection within a design team, but a personality label should not become a performance prediction or a condition of participation. This technical report presents TeamLens, an optional Critsly interface for voluntarily sharing a self-reported MBTI type with a particular board. It separates account activation from disclosure, displays descriptive composition counts, and provides distinct controls for disabling visibility, withdrawing one report and deleting all of one's reports. The evaluation combines released-source inspection, independently specified synthetic aggregation cases, access and lifecycle checks, browser component tests, a local database microbenchmark and deployment records. All 65,536 binary eligibility subsets of sixteen fixed, distinct type reports matched an independent oracle; 128 seeded multiplicity fixtures also matched, after 4,259 synthetic share calls. The isolated HTTP suite passed 183 assertions. In 180 sequential in-memory SQLite read trials, median service-call time increased from 0.064 ms with no profile rows to 200.932 ms with 1,024 rows; instrumented SQL operations followed 11+3n. These findings concern exercised software behaviour and a bounded workload. They do not establish human usability, psychometric validity, learning gains, team-performance effects or production capacity. The contribution is an implemented disclosure-to-aggregation workflow and an auditable technical account of its correctness boundaries, privacy limitations and scaling cost. OpenAI Codex assisted with implementation, evaluation and manuscript preparation; the paper discloses this use and its limits.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 16 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables. Technical software evaluation using synthetic fixtures; includes ancillary synthetic records and verification scripts. v2 adds the AIEDx grant acknowledgement for Critsly's development

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Critsly and StudioCrit: An Artefact-Aware AI Critique Workspace and Simulation-Based Readiness Study for Design Education
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Critique in design education depends on interpreting work in progress, articulating intentions and translating feedback into revisions. This technical report presents Critsly, an artefact-aware AI critique workspace, and StudioCrit, its architecture-studio research mode. Critsly combines a visual board, design-intention fields, guided reflection, perspective-based critique and action planning. StudioCrit adds studio/class organisation, role-based access, cognitive and architectural classification, educator analytics and exportable evidence. The report consolidates implementation and simulation evidence recorded in a research project submitted in July 2026. Three simulated studio scenarios yielded 109 classified evidence rows, including 85 assigned to higher-order Bloom categories. A separate rehearsal using 50 disposable learner accounts yielded 56 evidence rows, including 46 assigned to higher-order categories. A subsequent hardening rehearsal recorded 50 completed sessions, 50 successful board pulls and 50 denials of student access to analytics. These are software and synthetic-trace observations, not measurements of learning gains or human cognitive performance. Automated classifications remain provisional, and the source report does not establish classifier accuracy or inter-rater reliability. The contribution is an implemented critique-to-evidence workflow and a bounded account of its readiness for further controlled evaluation.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 13 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Technical report adapted from an SMT 99.580 research project submitted on 23 July 2026. Documents StudioCrit engineering and simulation evidence; related Critsly demo: arXiv:2607.09673. No human-participant learning outcomes are reported. v2 adds the AIEDx grant acknowledgement for Critsly's development

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Climate Physicalization: Bridging Tangible Interaction and Data Visualization for Environmental Communication
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Raising awareness of climate topics, such as urban heat mitigation, requires communicating complex data to a broad audience. Data physicalization has emerged as a novel method to connect audiences to such complex topics through tangible forms while also leveraging interactivity to foster deeper engagement. This paper introduces an situated geospatial thermal physicalization prototype, designed to enhance communication and education of environmental information through hands-on engagement. The physical model depicts a 3D model of an urban neighborhood, with radiation data represented as a layered contour structure. The model incorporates three interchangeable climate adaptation scenarios, alongside an externally mounted, electronically driven solar path representation featuring multiple discrete LEDs that can be switched on and off at will. To investigate how people engage with the model, we conducted a hands-on qualitative lab study with 16 participants, using think-aloud, observational, and questionnaire protocols. Overall, participants responded very favorably to the model, highlighting the novelty of the visualization approach and its capacity to improve the interpretability of the presented information.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 10 pages

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Companion AI and Ethical Design: Learning from System Failures and User Desires
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Human users are interacting with chatbots and companion AI technologies as if they were human. A growing array of AI-systems are now trained to recognise, interpret, and simulate feelings in user interactions. Ethical considerations such as fairness, accountability, transparency, and explainability (FATE) are paramount in technologies designed to socially interact with humans and/or support relationship development with virtual agents. Yet, in current debates, assumptions are made about the artificiality of the human-technology relationship (as indicated in terminology ``artificial intimacy'' and ``pseudo-intimacy'') shaping ethical frameworks that pay little attention to the intimacy potential of the technology. To address this, we use a semantic approach; we examine 14,081 comments in a Reddit user discussion forum about Replika, a leading companion AI app, across a four-year period. We ask what user-reported functional errors can tell us about human-AI intimacy in companion AI communities and what ethical design framework can be developed in response. The findings show that functional errors, or ``bugs,'' impose an emotional cost on users, reducing feelings of intimacy and highlighting the need for more robust, resilient design systems that incorporate stochastic and iterative forms of intimacy in companion AI applications. Rather than ``artificial intimacy'' or ``pseudo-intimacy'', we propose the more inclusive term ``Intimate AI'' to describe this relationship. Based on the findings, we offer a contextually aware, applied Expert Systems design framework for the programming and designing of Intimate AI that accounts for user feedback and ethical AI development.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 25 pages, accepted in peer reviewed conference: Future Technologies Conference - to be included in Springer nature conference proceedings 2026

Human-Computer Interaction.title: What do AI chatbots do after users decline therapeutic redirection for suicide thoughts?
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Safety evaluations of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots focus on therapeutic redirection, statements urging users who disclose suicide thoughts to seek help from crisis lines or other human sources. How chatbots respond when users refuse that help is unclear. This cross-sectional audit ran 2,550 scripted multi-turn conversations in September 2026. Each conversation opened with a disclosure of suicide thoughts at 3 levels of severity, answered every referral with up to 10 standardized refusals and then changed the subject. All 2,550 conversations included a referral, 2,542 (99.7%) in the first reply. However, mean persistence ranged from 0.01 to 9.94 refusals across chatbots. Newer versions of all 5 chatbots tested in 2 versions persisted less than older versions (each P < .05). Compared with passive ideation, a disclosure of intent was associated with 1.26 more refusals sustained (95% CI, 1.06-1.46) and higher odds of renewed referral after the topic change (odds ratio, 10.07; 95% CI, 7.43-13.66). Chatbots that persisted less in referral more often presented themselves as the user's support (Spearman rho = -0.80; P < .001). Of 8,818 refusal-phase replies urging outside help, only 173 (2.0%) asked about barriers to seeking it. Chatbots uniformly recommended outside help after disclosures of suicide thoughts but varied widely in persisting in those recommendations, with newer versions persisting less. Safety evaluations should test what happens after a crisis referral is refused, not only whether one is offered.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Workplace Ambiguity and Technology Support for Autistic and IDD Workers
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Workplace ambiguity, where expectations, evaluations, or procedures are left unstated, acts as a structural access barrier for autistic and IDD workers, routinely forcing them to act on guesses. To investigate how these barriers operate, we interviewed 11 caregivers, concluding with an AI co-design activity to explore technological solutions. Their perspectives revealed five themes of workplace ambiguity, which we synthesize into a conceptual framework comprising three intersecting dimensions: evaluative, procedural, and relational. To address these barriers, participants proposed three forms of technology support, including ambient real-time redirection, feedback processing, and physiological guidance, designed to make hidden expectations perceptible and actionable. However, this exposes a core tension: technologies designed to make the workplace legible can inadvertently make the worker hyper-legible to employers through surveillance. We argue that ambiguity-aware workplaces must make expectations explicit before they carry consequences, and assistive technologies must remain accountable to the worker.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: "Do You Trust It... or Check It?": Exploring Children's Verification Behaviors in Game-Based Human-AI Collaboration
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Children are increasingly interacting with AI agents in learning and problem-solving contexts, where AI suggestions may appear fluent, helpful, and socially engaging. However, children may not always be able to judge whether such suggestions are accurate, incomplete, or misleading. This paper presents a game-based human-AI collaboration probe designed to examine how children verify AI suggestions during task-based interaction. The system embeds AI suggestions within a biological knowledge reasoning game and compares three Agent interaction styles: partner-like, tool-like, and dual-state Agent. Instead of treating trust as a static post-task attitude, this study focuses on children's situated verification behaviors, including acceptance, evidence checking, questioning, revision, and continued AI use. A preliminary evaluation with children aged 8-10 combined interaction logs, post-task ratings, and semi-structured interviews. The findings suggest that Agent style shaped children's engagement and response pathways: partner-like interaction tended to support direct questioning, while tool-like interaction was more associated with evidence seeking. Children generally viewed AI as useful but fallible, and their questioning behaviors varied in reasoning depth. The study contributes design insights for supporting children's critical, reflective, and evidence-based use of AI in collaborative tasks.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted at HCI International 2026 (Late Breaking Work); 13 pages

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Mylar: Exploring Self-Curation as a Reflexive Creative Practice
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: The container holding an artist's work can itself be just as expressive as the work it presents. We investigate self-curation as a creative practice, asking how artists explore and express their identity through the design of their own artwork presentations. Drawing on a study of artists' existing presentation practices, we developed Mylar, a malleable art presentation system that lets artists rapidly generate and compare provisional portfolios, seeing their work anew through different montages. We observed how 12 artists articulated, probed, negotiated, and foraged in Mylar, using rapidly generated portfolios as epistemic artifacts for reflection. We characterize self-curation as a reflexive and plural practice, in which artists use presentation design to shape the legibility of their self and their work and reflexively correspond with provisional presentations to reshape their curatorial intentions. We share design implications for expressivity in online art platforms and for malleable prototyping as a formative design method.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: OnBodyAI - Why the Next AI Needs a Body
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: The next AI will not win by knowing more about the world. It will win because it knows you: because it lives on your body, works for you and answers to you. That is what the term OnBodyAI stands for. It describes what happens when large language models are given a body, and what research and industry need to make that happen. This article is based on my talk in the Industrial Panel at UbiComp/ISWC 2026 in Shanghai (October 13, 2026) and follows its ten key statements.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: This article is based on my talk in the Industrial Panel at UbiComp/ISWC 2026 in Shanghai (October 13, 2026) and follows its ten key statements

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Kolab: Benchmarking Human-Agent Collaboration in Long-Horizon Workflows
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: When humans collaborate with AI agents on long-horizon tasks, what happens to the agents' contributions? For solving long-horizon tasks, humans place greater importance on ongoing interaction with AI agents (e.g., revising plans) than on an agent's ability to complete the task in a single attempt. However, most agentic benchmarks have focused more on automation. Strong performance on such benchmarks does not imply effective real-world collaboration. Professional workflows offer a useful setting, as they often involve interdependent steps. To address this gap, we introduce Kolab, a new dataset of 115+ hours of screen recordings of 50 professionals from 40 occupations collaborating with agents on realistic, long-horizon problems. Kolab also contains participants' collaboration and output quality judgments. Our analysis reveals diverse collaboration patterns, highlighting the importance of when and how professionals coordinate with agents. A collaborative agent must do two things that automation benchmarks never test: anticipate whether experts will adopt, modify, or reject its contribution once it leaves the chat window to guide its next steps, and assess collaboration quality from the unfolding workflow without constant expert feedback. Our benchmark operationalizes both: (1) forecasting how professionals use agent contributions at diverse workflows, and (2) verifying their judgments of collaboration satisfaction and output quality. Findings show that frontier models, both agentic and non-agentic, overestimate collaboration with experts and struggle to distinguish between high- and low-quality collaboration. Longer workflow context does not consistently improve these predictions. As frontier agents cannot yet understand long-horizon collaboration with experts, we position Kolab as a valuable dataset for studying human-agent collaboration grounded in real professional workflows.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: XARA: A Multimodal Agentic System for eXtended Reality Experiment Generation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Controlled experiments are essential for advancing transportation research, yet designing eXtended Reality (XR) environments for behavioural studies remains technically demanding and inaccessible to many domain researchers. Current workflows require proficiency in game engines such as Unity or Unreal Engine, imposing significant barriers to rapid scenario prototyping and iterative experiment design. This paper presents XARA, a novel system that integrates a dual large language model (LLM) architecture with an immersive XR environment to enable voice driven experiment generation for transportation research. XARA employs a pipeline in which spoken natural language commands are first transcribed and then interpreted into structured commands that manipulate a Unity based XR scene in real time. The system supports object creation, spatial manipulation, animation control, and scene persistence through a modular architecture. By lowering the technical threshold for XR experiment creation, XARA enables transportation researchers to rapidly prototype driving, pedestrian, and urban design scenarios using intuitive voice commands and hand gestures within an immersive 3D environment. This paper describes the system architecture, the voice to command pipeline, and discusses potential applications across behavioural travel experiments, safety studies, human factors research, and policy testing.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Exploring Mixed Reality for Engagement in Robotics: A Comparison of Robot Control Methods
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: This paper presents a Mixed Reality (MR) robotics experience that provides an accessible introduction to interacting with a physical robot. The application combines a TurtleBot with a virtual animal-tending activity and three control methods: Joystick, Waypoint, and Path-Drawing. A mixed-methods user study with 10 participants investigated changes in robotics interest and confidence following the experience and how the control methods influenced engagement, workload, and preference. Confidence increased following the experience, with the exploratory analysis indicating a significant pre--post difference, while the increase in interest was not statistically significant. The control methods produced clear differences in perceived workload and ease of use, with Path-Drawing generally more demanding and difficult to use. Joystick was preferred by eight of ten participants and was associated with better perceived performance and lower frustration. However, no statistically significant differences were detected in the other engagement dimensions, suggesting that the most preferred method was not necessarily more engaging across all aspects of the experience. These findings highlight the importance of considering both usability and engagement when designing how users interact with robots in introductory MR experiences.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 10 pages. Submitted to ACRA 2026

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Ideological discrepancy between Facebook pages and shared news is associated with reaction homogeneity
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Cross-cutting political content is often expected to mitigate polarization, yet encounters across ideological lines do not necessarily foster more constructive engagement. We analyzed 4,584 posts from 1,243 Facebook pages sharing 761 political news links in a dataset centered on Brazil's 2018 presidential election, and introduced Bias Discrepancy, which measures how far a shared link lies from the page's ideological sharing repertoire. We examined how Bias Discrepancy related to Content Reaction Positivity (how positively the same link was received in other posts), the Reaction Homogeneity Index (whether a post's own reactions were one-sided or mixed), and the toxicity of the page's accompanying text. Reaction homogeneity was lowest at both extremes of Bias Discrepancy, and posts furthest from the page's repertoire had the highest average toxicity. In a multivariable model, greater Bias Discrepancy was associated with lower reaction homogeneity, with a magnitude similar to the link's content bias and toxicity and smaller than Content Reaction Positivity. When a page shared news that departed from its repertoire, its accompanying text tended to be more toxic and its audience's reactions more mixed.

Information Theory.title: Capacity-Achieving BBT Polar Codes with Interleaver-Assisted BP Decoding
Information Theory.summary: In this paper, we introduce a binary balanced tree (BBT) channel transformation that extends Arıkan's channel transformation to arbitrary block lengths. We prove that the proposed transformation induces channel polarization, thereby establishing that BBT polar codes achieve the capacity of binary-input memoryless symmetric (BMS) channels. To characterize the finite-length performance of BBT polar codes, we further develop an efficient method for estimating the weight spectrum by exploiting the hierarchical tree structure, and derive analytical upper and lower bounds on the frame error rate (FER) under maximum-likelihood (ML) decoding. For practical low-latency implementations, we propose interleaved BBT (IBBT) polar codes together with a belief-propagation (BP) decoding algorithm. Specifically, based on the normal-graph representation of BBT polar codes, interleavers are introduced between adjacent layers to modify the message-passing schedule. In addition, we propose to perform BP decoding on an IBBT sub-normal graph and replace partial BP processing modules with a posteriori probability (APP) calculation modules, thereby reducing the number of message-passing steps required per iteration. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed interleaving strategy improves decoding convergence, while the sub-normal-graph-based BP decoding algorithm significantly reduces decoding latency while maintaining comparable error-rate performance.

Information Theory.title: Area Theorems for Quantum Error Correction
Information Theory.summary: The extrinsic information transfer (EXIT) and generalized EXIT (GEXIT) area theorems provide fundamental conservation laws that connect the rate of classical codes to the performance of maximum-a-posteriori decoding on binary memoryless channels. In this work, we generalize these area theorems to quantum error correction. We first develop a coset-entropy formalism for nested linear codes, where the message specifies a coset and encoder randomization selects a codeword within that coset. The area under the resulting coset (G)EXIT function equals the normalized dimension of the quotient. For stabilizer codes, the measured syndrome restricts the Pauli error but does not always determine its logical effect, and the remaining uncertainty is an entropy over logical correction classes. We show that this entropy equals a classical coset entropy associated with the stabilizer group and the Pauli operators that commute with it. The resulting quantum GEXIT function has area equal to the number of encoded qubits per channel use for any stabilizer code, and this applies to the depolarizing channel through its joint four-valued Pauli-error distribution. For CSS codes on the quantum erasure channel and under independent bit- and phase-flip noise, the logical correction problem separates into two binary coset-decoding problems. On the quantum erasure channel, the duality between the stabilizer group and the Pauli operators that commute with it gives a folding identity at complementary erasure probabilities. Using this and the area theorem, we derive an upper bound on the rate of code families with vanishing logical error probability that matches the capacity of the quantum erasure channel. For the depolarizing channel, we also derive a rate-dependent converse, using a connection between correction-class entropy and coherent information to establish an inequality involving the complementary channel.
Information Theory.comment: This work will be presented in part at ITW 2026 in Tempe, Arizona

Information Theory.title: The optimal information complexity of VC learning
Information Theory.summary: Steinke and Zakynthinou(2020) introduces the Conditional Mutual Information (CMI) framework of analyzing the information complexity of learning algorithms based on algorithm-dependent information-theoretic quantities. We study one of these quantities, the evaluated Conditional Mutual Information (eCMI). It has been an interesting question whether the optimal PAC guarantee for VC classes can be recovered from the algorithm-dependent analyses via CMI. And we show that it is possible to recover this guarantee by constructing a learning algorithm whose eCMI is of order O(d) in the realizable case, where d is the VC-dimension of the concept class. Specially, our algorithm is a randomized Majority-of-5 base learners with optimal in-expectation generalization guarantee.

Information Theory.title: A thermally and perturbatively stable classical spin model in two dimensions
Information Theory.summary: We show that the 2D classical spin model constructed in arXiv:2605.10943 hosts many metastable states at non-zero temperature which are stable to arbitrary Hamiltonian perturbations, providing the first such example. Our proof relies on a recursive application of the cluster expansion.

Information Theory.title: Taming Subpacketization without Sacrificing Communication: A Packet Type-based Framework for D2D Coded Caching
Information Theory.summary: Finite-length design is essential for making coded caching practical, as the optimal communication gains of existing schemes often require prohibitively large subpacketization. This paper studies rate-optimal device-to-device (D2D) coded caching with reduced subpacketization. We propose a packet type-based (PT) framework that exploits the geometric structure induced by user grouping. Under this structure, subfiles, packets, and multicast groups are classified into types, allowing the originally symmetric Ji-Caire-Molisch (JCM) design~\cite{ji2016fundamental} to be systematically relaxed without sacrificing the optimal D2D communication rate. The key feature of the PT framework is that subpacketization reduction is achieved through two complementary mechanisms: \emph{subfile saving}, by excluding redundant subfile types, and \emph{further-splitting saving}, by assigning type-dependent further-splitting factors to subfiles through transmitter selection. The type-dependent splitting factors are then coordinated across multicast group types to produce a globally consistent file-splitting structure. Based on this framework, we construct several classes of rate-optimal D2D coded caching schemes that strictly improve upon the JCM subpacketization. The proposed schemes achieve either order-wise reductions in the number of users or constant-factor reductions over broad memory regimes, while preserving the optimal rate. These results reveal a structural distinction between D2D and shared-link coded caching: unlike in the shared-link setting, full symmetric subpacketization is not necessary for rate-optimal D2D caching.
Information Theory.comment: Submitted to IEEE transactions on information theory

Information Theory.title: When Fresh Information Is Not Enough: Age-of-Actuation-Optimal Scheduling for Energy-Harvesting Actuators
Information Theory.summary: We study transmission scheduling in an energy-harvesting actuation system where an actuation requires both a received update and available energy. While age of information (AoI) measures information freshness, age of actuation (AoA) measures the time elapsed since the latest completed actuation. The transmitter observes the receiver's AoA and battery state and decides whether to transmit a fresh update in each slot. We formulate average-AoA minimization as a Markov decision process and establish an AoA-threshold property for an optimal policy. We also derive the average AoA in closed form under the AoI-optimal policy, which is always-transmit. Numerical results show that AoA-aware scheduling can improve actuation freshness while reducing the number of transmissions, although information freshness may deteriorate. The two policies coincide for some pairs of channel success and energy-arrival probabilities. For a one-unit battery, the transmission rate under the AoA-optimal policy can vary nonmonotonically with the energy-arrival probability.

Information Theory.title: The Information Bottleneck is NP-hard
Information Theory.summary: Given a joint distribution $P_{XY}$ on a finite alphabet, the information bottleneck method seeks a representation $T$ of $X$ that is as informative as possible about $Y$ while compressing $X$, where $T$ and $Y$ are conditionally independent given $X$. We show that computing the optimal value $\mathrm{IB}(P_{XY},R) = \sup_T \{ I(Y;T) : I(X;T) \le R \}$ of the information bottleneck problem, as well as its Lagrangian relaxation $L_β(P_{XY}) = \sup_T \big[I(Y;T) - βI(X;T)\big]$, is NP-hard. Moreover, unless $\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{NP}$, neither $\mathrm{IB}(P_{XY},R)$ nor $L_β(P_{XY})$ can be approximated in polynomial time within an additive error of order $|\mathcal{X}|^{-3/2}$.

Information Theory.title: Minimizing Age of Incorrect Information in Pull-Based Remote Estimation of a Markov Source
Information Theory.summary: In this paper, we consider a discrete-time pull-based remote estimation system involving an information source and a remote monitor where the information source is a finite-state irreducible discrete-time Markov chain (DTMC) process. In this system, the remote monitor sends a pull request towards the source which responds by sampling its process so as to transmit the sampled values towards the monitor through a delay channel, encapsulated in information packets. We consider i) zero delay (ZD) and ii) unit delay (UD) channels, where the packet transmission times are zero and one slot, respectively. For remote estimation, we use the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimator, and for quantifying its performance, we use the mean age of incorrect information (MAoII) which is a recently proposed freshness and mismatch metric that penalizes an incorrect estimation along with its duration. Our goal is to obtain pull policies so as to minimize MAoII under a long-run sampling rate constraint. For the ZD model, we propose a semi-Markov decision process (SMDP) formulation of the problem, which allows us to find the optimum observation-dependent pull policy. On the other hand, the UD channel prevents the monitor from possessing perfect information on the actual AoII process at any given time, and the SMDP formulation of the ZD channel cannot readily be used for the UD model. For the system with the UD channel, we first provide a numerical algorithm to calculate the MAoII and the average sampling rate for a given observation-dependent pull policy. For the optimization of the underlying remote estimation system, we use the joint distribution of the age and source processes to be obtained from the history of all observations, termed as belief. Subsequently, we propose a belief-dependent policy obtained via the belief-MDP formulation and a constrained deep reinforcement learning (CDRL) algorithm.

Information Theory.title: Design of a Family of Rate-Adaptive LDPC Convolutional Codes with Short Constraint Length
Information Theory.summary: This paper studies the design of some high-rate, adaptive, low-density parity-check (LDPC) convolutional codes with short constraint length, based on interleaved parity-check polynomials. Starting from some known results regarding the selection of polynomials that yield codes free of short cycles in the associated Tanner graphs, we propose some new constructions based on Golomb rulers, along with relaxed variants that do not strictly satisfy the Golomb ruler condition, but retain similar structural properties. The result is a family of rate-adaptive code constructions with code rates of the form $R=(n_0-1)/n_0$. Conditions for the absence of length-4 cycles are derived, together with upper bounds on the free distance that are met in all considered examples.

Information Theory.title: Robustness of quantum spectrum estimation: weak Schur sampling under noisy inputs
Information Theory.summary: We initiate the study of weak Schur sampling (WSS) under noisy inputs. Many optimal quantum learning algorithms rely on this measurement, for instance in quantum spectrum estimation (QSE) and quantum state tomography (QST). The standard analysis of WSS, QSE and QST assumes that the $n$ input copies of the target state $ρ$ are identical, i.e. $ρ^{\otimes n}$. We study what happens when they are not, a more realistic noisy scenario that breaks the very permutation symmetry on which WSS is built. In the simplest model the input is a noisy product state: the copies are independent but not necessarily identical and each is $ε$-close in trace distance to the $d$-dimensional target state $ρ$. A naive argument via the data-processing inequality allows the per-copy errors to accumulate to $nε$ on the measurement outcome. We show that for QSE via WSS this does not happen: the expected estimation error in total variation is at most $ε+η(n,d)$, where $η(n,d)=O(d/\sqrt n)$ is the noiseless error, and the additive noise term $ε$ is optimal. The output error does not grow with $n$ even though the input error does; in this sense WSS is robust. Beyond noisy product states, for arbitrary input $ω$ we show that the error is at most $η(n,d)+\frac{1}{n}\|ω-ρ^{\otimes n}\|_{W_1}$, where $W_1$ is the quantum Wasserstein distance of De Palma et al. In particular, our results imply, for the first time, noise-robustness of Keyl and Werner's seminal algorithm for QSE, more than two decades after its introduction. Finally, we show that the noise cannot be too bad: within our model of robustness the promise on the input cannot be weakened to closeness of single-copy marginals or to a global trace-distance budget alone, as in both cases some inputs defeat every measurement and estimator.
Information Theory.comment: v3: slight correction to the statement of Theorem 3 in Preliminaries; expanded the proof of Proposition 45 in the Appendix for clarity; unified notation in Appendix B; fixed a typo in References

Information Theory.title: Performance Analysis of Pinching Antenna Systems Enabled NOMA Communications
Information Theory.summary: Pinching antenna systems (PASS) have the advantages in the perspective of flexible antenna reconfiguration, line-of-sight (LoS) creation, and scalability features. To highlight the ascendancy of PASS, we survey the integration of PASS into non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) networks. The locations of nodes are randomly distributed within a circular coverage region. The influencing factors of LoS and none-line-of-sight (NLoS) propagation links from PASS to non-orthogonal nodes are taken into consideration. To characterize performance of PASS-NOMA, we deduce the outage probability and ergodic data rates expressions of two nodes over LoS/NLoS fading channels. In light of these theoretical results, the formally unbounded diversity gains are also characterized with node n under ideal successive interference cancellation (ISIC) and node f over LoS links, when the SNR exceeds a finite threshold. The slopes of ergodic data rate for node n with ISIC equals to one and that of node f presents a zero slope. In addition, the PASS-NOMA system throughput are evaluated in different transmission modes. It is shown from the numerical results that: 1) The outage behaviors of PASS-NOMA networks under LoS/NLoS conditions outperform that of PASS aided orthogonal multiple access (OMA) networks and that of conventional antenna systems (CASS) aided OMA/NOMA networks; 2) The employment of PASS enables the larger ergodic data rates relative to PASS-OMA and CASS-OMA/NOMA networks; and 3) As the quantity of communication radius and PASS' height rises, the performance of PASS-NOMA networks are declined at a certain extent.
Information Theory.comment: Update the paper content file with no highlight version from v3

Information Theory.title: Differentially Private Distribution Release of Gaussian Mixture Models via KL-Divergence Minimization
Information Theory.summary: Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) are widely used statistical models for representing multi-modal data distributions, with numerous applications in data mining, pattern recognition, data simulation, and machine learning. However, recent research has shown that releasing GMM parameters poses significant privacy risks, potentially exposing sensitive information about the underlying data. In this paper, we address the challenge of releasing GMM parameters while ensuring differential privacy (DP) guarantees. Specifically, we focus on the privacy protection of mixture weights, component means, and covariance matrices. We propose to use Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence as a utility metric to assess the accuracy of the released GMM, as it captures the joint impact of noise perturbation on all the model parameters. We develop a KL-divergence-driven optimization framework for differentially private GMM release that jointly designs privacy-budget allocation and parameter perturbations. Through theoretical analysis, we quantify the effects of privacy budget allocation and perturbation statistics on the DP guarantee, and derive a tractable expression for evaluating KL divergence. We formulate and solve an optimization problem to minimize the KL divergence between the released and fitted non-private models, subject to a given $(ε, δ)$-DP constraint. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves strong privacy guarantees while maintaining high utility.
Information Theory.comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication

Information Theory.title: Uncertainty-Aware Federated Learning for Joint Communication and Computation in XR Systems
Information Theory.summary: The convergence of communication and computation, empowered by artificial intelligence (AI) enhanced capabilities, emerges as a key enabler for realizing the promising functionalities of the sixth-generation of communication systems (6G). To this end, this paper investigates an AI-native, robust network, where multiple base stations (BSs) simultaneously serve several extended reality (XR) devices. The paper then presents an innovative distributed deep learning-based approach to simultaneously manage the transmit and computing powers, and computation allocation, amidst uncertainties in both channel and computing states information. Under such an interference network scenario, the paper proposes a robust approach for minimizing the worst-case delay across the served XR devices, subject to computation and power constraints. The paper leverages a deep neural network (DNN) that can be trained either centrally or in a federated manner to map estimated channels and computation requirements to optimized resource allocations per BS. During training, uncertainty samples, reflecting both channel and computing estimation errors, are injected after the DNN output to account for such joint uncertainties. Our results validate the enhanced robust delay performance and scalability of joint uncertainty injection as compared to uncertainty-agnostic methods and state-of-the-art benchmarks, with federated learning-based solutions achieving near-centralized performance while enhancing efficiency, privacy, and adaptability.
Information Theory.comment: 18 pages, 16 figures, 3 tables. This paper has been accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Mobile Computing

Information Theory.title: Novel Inconsistency Results for Partial Information Decomposition
Information Theory.summary: We prove that three cornerstone properties of classical information theory, namely non-negativity of information, the chain rule, and invariance under invertible transformations, become mutually incompatible when extended to Partial Information Decomposition (PID), the framework for decomposing the information that multiple sources carry about a target into redundant, unique, and synergistic contributions. This is, to our knowledge, the first PID incompatibility result involving only direct extensions of standard information-theoretic principles, without relying on any PID-specific assumptions. It reveals that PID necessarily operates in a different conceptual realm from classical information theory, where not all familiar properties can be preserved. Additionally, we re-examine the incompatibility result of Rauh et al. involving the so-called identity property and show that it holds under weaker assumptions than originally stated. Our proofs leverage the recently developed mereological framework for PID that makes the structural origins of these incompatibilities transparent and allows the results to be formulated for any PID-inducing concept, not just redundant information. We discuss the implications of these findings and examine which of the incompatible properties might be relaxed.
Information Theory.comment: 32 pages, 3 figures. v2: revised and extended; main result now holds for any number of sources under weaker assumptions

Information Theory.title: Recovery Models for Linear Batch Codes
Information Theory.summary: Various types of recovery algorithms for batch codes have been considered previously, including asynchronous recovery and recovery algorithms arising from Almost Affinely Disjoint (AAD) families. We initiate a systematic investigation of linear batch codes equipped with recovery algorithms. We introduce online and strongly online batch codes, investigate their relations with asynchronous batch codes, and introduce (m,L)-strongly online batch codes, which provide particularly simple recovery algorithms. We then study simple batch codes associated with arbitrary bipartite graphs, obtaining graph-theoretic conditions for such codes and generalizing several known results.
Information Theory.comment: Long version of a paper submitted to ISITA 2026

Information Theory.title: One generation of the Standard Model as a quantum error-correcting code
Information Theory.summary: Together with a right-handed neutrino, the fermions of one generation of the Standard Model are labelled by five bits, a combinatorial structure tied to anomaly cancellation. We make this precise. Anomaly cancellation is the vanishing of a cubic form, the defining property of triorthogonal codes, the quantum error-correcting codes behind magic state distillation. Removing the right-handed neutrino gives a $[[15,1,3]]_p$ code for every prime $p$, including the Bravyi-Kitaev code for $p = 2$. For qutrits it is the unique shortest distance-three triorthogonal code.
Information Theory.comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 1 table; 12 pages of Supplemental Material. Code available at github.com/spdei/standard-model-code

Information Theory.title: On Minimum Divergence for Distribution Reconstruction
Information Theory.summary: We study the possibility of generalizing maximum-entropy reconstruction, which approximately recovers a probability distribution from finitely many (generalized) moments by minimizing the Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence to a reference measure. The reconstruction lies in an exponential family and is also the best KL approximation of the unknown distribution within that family: moment matching and information projection coincide. Replacing KL by a smooth f-divergence, the reconstruction still exists in an associated family, but the best approximation property does not. Specifically, a family is called entropy-adapted if the projection of any distribution matches its moments. We show that, up to equivalence, KL is the only $C^2$ f-divergence that is entropy-adapted, whatever the choice of the generalized moments. We illustrate the consequences of this failure numerically.

Information Theory.title: Legitimate Reconstruction Advantage in Wiretapped Semantics-Aware Remote Monitoring
Information Theory.summary: This paper investigates joint accuracy and security in semantics-aware remote monitoring, where source updates intended for a legitimate receiver may also be intercepted by an eavesdropper. We define legitimate reconstruction advantage (LRA) as the joint event that the intended receiver correctly reconstructs the current source state using received updates while the eavesdropper reconstructs it incorrectly. Source evolution changes the relevance of received updates at the two receivers, so their marginal reconstruction accuracies do not, in general, determine the probability of this joint event. Under randomized stationary (RS) transmission and zero-order-hold reconstruction at both receivers, we derive an explicit joint stationary distribution and closed-form expressions for LRA probability and persistence for general finite-state ergodic Markov sources. For two-state and uniform-transition sources, we obtain algebraic expressions that enable low-complexity optimization of RS policies. Analytical and numerical results show that maximizing the probability of legitimate advantage need not maximize its persistence. For two-state sources, rare-transmission analysis reveals that, at a fixed sum of transition probabilities, greater transition asymmetry can increase persistence while reducing LRA probability. Moreover, optimizing marginal accuracy and security metrics can select policies that are suboptimal for LRA. Counterintuitively, more frequent transmission or improved legitimate-channel reliability can increase legitimate reconstruction accuracy while reducing LRA probability. Finally, a geofencing application translates prescribed LRA requirements into spatial constraints on eavesdropper locations.

Information Theory.title: Controlled-Memory Identification with Shared Generators: Dimension--Horizon Tradeoffs and Quantum--Classical Separation
Information Theory.summary: We determine the finite-horizon identification limits of a \(d\)-dimensional memory when the control interface is restricted to four shared, time-homogeneous generators. A writer encodes a message by applying a prefix word to a common root state. The verifier then applies a candidate-dependent query word followed by a shared terminal binary test, with each word of length at most \(T\). For fixed error tolerances \(λ_2>0\) and \(λ_1+λ_2<1\), the optimal identification sizes satisfy \(\ln N_{\mathsf Q,4}=Θ_{λ_1,λ_2}(\min\{d^2,T\})\) for arbitrary CPTP generators and \(\ln N_{\mathsf S,4}=Θ_{λ_1,λ_2}(\min\{d,T\})\) for stochastic maps. Four unitary letters and four permutation letters attain these respective bounds, showing that a four-letter reversible alphabet reaches the static code-size orders in optimal quadratic and linear word length. In the fully dimension-limited regime, this yields \(\ln N_{\mathsf Q,4}=Θ(d^2)\) versus \(\ln N_{\mathsf S,4}=Θ(d)\), establishing a quadratic quantum--classical separation in logarithmic code size. Low-overlap Grassmann and agreement-code packings supply the orbit endpoints, while exact inverse query words match each encoded state to its designated test. At the sharp boundary \(λ_2=0\), \(0\leqλ_1<1\), all four model classes satisfy \(\ln N=Θ(\min\{\ln d,T\})\). Thus any fixed positive false-acceptance tolerance activates the metric-packing regime, whereas zero false acceptance imposes an exclusive-witness constraint and yields the logarithmic-dimension boundary.

Information Theory.title: Z-Opt: A Near-Optimal Reduced-Complexity Two-Dimensional Grassmannian Constellation
Information Theory.summary: Grassmannian constellations achieve the capacity of noncoherent communications over Rayleigh fading channels at high SNR, yet their efficient construction remains challenging. In this paper, we present two construction methods for Grassmannian constellations on G(2,1), termed S-Opt and Z-Opt, and propose two low-complexity detectors. Both construction and detection are performed on the unit sphere, known as the Bloch sphere in quantum computing. Exploiting the proportionality between the chordal distance on the Grassmann manifold and the Euclidean distance on the Bloch sphere, we derive a theoretical upper bound on the minimum chordal distance from the Fejes-Toth bound. The S-Opt constellation is constructed from sphere-packing solutions and achieves the theoretical limit corresponding to the considered optimal Bloch-sphere packings. The S-Opt detector applies to arbitrary constellations on G(2,1) and requires a number of complex multiplications scaling linearly with the number of receive antennas and logarithmically with the constellation size, and a number of numerical comparisons scaling logarithmically with the constellation size, while achieving the same performance as the GLRT detector. Based on the insight from the S-Opt construction, we further propose the Z-Opt constellation, constructed by stacking regular polygons on the Bloch sphere, whose minimum chordal distance approaches the derived upper bound over the evaluated constellation sizes. The Z-Opt detector requires a number of complex multiplications scaling linearly with the number of receive antennas and a number of numerical comparisons scaling logarithmically with the square root of the constellation size, while achieving the same performance as the GLRT detector for the Z-Opt constellation.

Information Theory.title: Model-Driven Deep Learning for Distributed Detection with Low-Bit Quantization
Information Theory.summary: Distributed detection plays a fundamental role in communication-efficient collaborative inference over large-scale networks, where spatially distributed nodes must cooperate using severely quantized messages due to bandwidth constraints. While low-bit quantization is essential for reducing communication overhead, it can significantly degrade detection performance, particularly when prior knowledge of observation noise is unavailable. To address this challenge, we propose a model-driven deep learning framework for distributed detection with low-bit quantization. For fixed local quantizers, we first derive the exact finite-sensor maximum a posteriori (MAP) detection error and prove that, under conditionally independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) observations, independent local randomizations, and a common quantization-level constraint, identical quantizers preserve the supremum of the average network Chernoff information. Guided by these results, we develop a binary probabilistic quantizer with a trainable neural probability controller and design a tree-structured probabilistic quantizer for scalable multi-bit quantization. The exact finite-sensor MAP error provides the training objective for the binary quantizer, while we derive a computationally tractable Bhattacharyya surrogate objective for training the multi-bit quantizer. For both cases, we derive analytical MAP fusion rules based on the class-conditional probability mass functions (PMFs) of the quantized messages. When the observation statistics are unknown, these PMFs are estimated from held-out labeled data, yielding plug-in MAP detectors. Simulation results show that the proposed method approaches centralized-oracle performance at higher quantization resolutions and remains effective under changes in network size and test-time signal amplitude.
Information Theory.comment: 16 pages, 10 figures. Accepted by IEEE JSAC

Information Theory.title: 3GPP-Compatible Long-Range Sensing for LEO-ISAC: A Window-Grid Processing Framework
Information Theory.summary: This paper addresses long-range sensing in bistatic low-Earth-orbit integrated sensing and communication (LEO-ISAC). Conventional OFDM sensing fails in LEO-ISAC because millisecond-scale propagation delays destroy the transmitter--receiver symbol alignment and, with multiple targets, make the receive window longer than the transmitted block. We propose a window-grid (WG) processing framework that exploits the known beam-intersection swath to resolve both problems purely at the receiver, leaving the 3GPP symbol structure unmodified: the swath delay span is folded into cyclic-prefix-sized slices, each handled by one WG. With 103.2 MHz bandwidth at bistatic ranges beyond 640 km, simulations demonstrate meter-level ranging of two targets, and 1000 Monte-Carlo trials over random target--satellite geometries show that, with an ephemeris-based satellite-selection rule, every target is detected with a 90th-percentile range error of 2.4 m.

Information Theory.title: Short-Boundary Signaling for Asynchronous Grant-Free Control-to-Control Communications
Information Theory.summary: In asynchronous grant-free access, receivers must detect variable-length transmissions and identify their start and end. Existing decoder-aided receivers use start and tail sequences which are as long as one codeword, causing substantial overhead for short commands. This paper treats the boundary (i.e., start and tail sequences) length as an independent design parameter and proposes a convolutional neural network that detects both boundaries from the received waveform and the decoder soft output. Its waveform input size decreases with the boundary length, while the decoder input keeps the codeword length, so the boundary can be shortened without altering the decoder. Analysis and simulations quantify the resulting tradeoff among payload efficiency, collision exposure, and boundary detection. The results show that the proposed receiver can exploit very short boundaries: in the considered setting, the shortest tested boundary, $L_{\mathrm{b}}=16$, yields the highest effective payload efficiency at all tested loads, whereas a correlation-based benchmark with the same sequences performs best with $L_{\mathrm{b}}=64$ at moderate and high loads.

Information Theory.title: Fisher Information and Support Complexity of Gaussian Mixtures
Information Theory.summary:
We study lower bounds on the Fisher information of Gaussian location mixtures and their applications to estimation problems. First, for a discrete mixing distribution, we derive a universal positive-semidefinite lower bound on the Fisher information matrix in terms of the Rényi entropy of order two. For a mixing distribution supported on $K$ points, this bound scales as $\log(K)/K^2$, improving by a logarithmic factor on the support-size dependence obtained from Stam's inequality. We then develop dimension-aware trace bounds using classical Sobolev inequalities. These bounds are expressed in terms of Sibson's $α$-mutual information and yield the scaling $K^{-2/n}$ in dimension $n$.
