A complementary bound involving the $α$-mutual information of order $1/2$ is obtained using the sharp Young convolution inequality.
  The derived inequalities are further specialized to rotationally invariant mixing distributions supported on discrete spherical shells. In this setting, an intrinsic-dimensional bound on Sibson mutual information leads to lower bounds on the Fisher information in terms of the number of occupied shells. As applications, we study least favorable priors for bounded Gaussian mean estimation. In the scalar case, we show that the least favorable prior on $[-R,R]$ has at least $Ω(R\sqrt{\log R})$ support points and that each of its probability masses is of order at most $1/R$. In the vector case, we show that the number of occupied shells grows at least linearly with $R$. Finally, Brown's identity and the I-MMSE relationship are used to translate the Fisher-information inequalities into upper bounds on the MMSE and mutual information.

Information Theory.title: Extreme Points of the $(0,δ)$-LDP Polytope with Small Input Size and Arbitrary Output Sizes
Information Theory.summary: The structure of locally differentially private (LDP) mechanisms can be understood through the geometry of the corresponding privacy polytope. While the extreme points of the \( (ε,0)\)-LDP polytope are well characterized (Kairouz {et al.}, 2014; Holohan {et al.}, 2017), comparatively little is known for the \((ε,δ)\)-LDP polytope with \(δ>0\). Recent work (Elangovan and Jog, 2024) has shown that even in the special case \(ε=0\), the \( (0,δ) \)-LDP privacy polytope exhibits fundamentally different behaviour. In this work, we provide complete characterizations of the extreme points for the low-input-alphabet regime \(k=2\) and \(k=3\) and with arbitrary output alphabet size \(m \). We also identify new extreme mechanisms for larger input alphabet sizes \(k\), of the star configuration type, as introduced by Elangovan and Jog (2024).

Information Theory.title: How Does Probabilistic Constellation Shaping Control Ranging Sidelobe Levels in ISAC?
Information Theory.summary: Probabilistic constellation shaping (PCS), originally designed to fill the gap between finite uniform constellations and continuous capacity-achieving input distributions, has recently emerged as a central tool in adjusting the expected integrated sidelobe level (EISL) in integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). In this paper, we show that PCS goes beyond EISL: A large class of PCS methods, termed as type-based PCS, are capable of providing precise control over codeword-wise integrated sidelobe level ratio (ISLR) for systems employing orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM), thus yielding a stronger sensing performance guarantee than EISL control. We further show that OFDM is almost the only unitary modulation basis whose codeword-wise ISLR can be precisely controlled by type-based PCS. Based upon the analytical results, practical type-based PCS methods compatible with the probabilistic amplitude shaping (PAS) framework are conceived, which achieve higher communication rates than existing ISAC-oriented PCS methods under identical ISLR constraints.

Information Theory.title: Coverage Region Analysis and Optimization of FIRES-Assisted NOMA and OMA Systems
Information Theory.summary: Fluid integrated reflecting and emitting surfaces (FIRES) are investigated. In these metasurfaces, each subarea hosts an active element capable of simultaneous transmission and reflection, phase, and geometric positioning control within the subarea. We develop a coverage-centric system model for the two-user downlink scenario (one user per half-space) under spatially correlated Rician fading and imperfect phase control. First, we derive closed-form far-field line-of-sight (LoS) coverage bounds that reveal the effects of aperture size, base station (BS) distance, transmit power, energy-splitting (ES), and phase errors. Protocol-aware corollaries are then presented for both orthogonal multiple access (OMA) and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA), including conditions for successful successive interference cancellation (SIC). Second, we formulate coverage maximization as a bi-level optimization problem consisting of (i) an outer search over FIRES element positions, selecting one active preset per subarea under minimum-spacing constraints, and (ii) an inner resource allocation problem tailored to the multiple-access scheme, which is one-dimensional for OMA and a small convex program for NOMA. The proposed framework explicitly accounts for target rate constraints, ES conservation, power budgets, geometric placement limits, and decoding-order feasibility. Extensive simulations demonstrate that FIRES, by jointly exploiting geometric repositioning and passive energy control, substantially enlarges the coverage region compared with a conventional simultaneously transmitting and reflecting reconfigurable intelligent surface (STAR-RIS) under the same element budget. Furthermore, NOMA yields additional coverage gains when feasible. The analytical coverage bounds closely match the simulation results and quantify the robustness of FIRES to phase-control imperfections.

Information Theory.title: Post-Quantum Secure Aggregation via Code-Based Homomorphic Encryption
Information Theory.summary: Secure aggregation lets a server learn the sum of inputs from multiple users without learning individual contributions. Recent single-server protocols achieve this with key- and message-additive homomorphic encryption (KAHE), but existing instantiations rely on lattice assumptions. We instantiate a KAHE from the Learning Parity with Noise (LPN) assumption and analyze the challenges that arise with the Hamming metric. Decryption of the aggregate amounts to decoding over a q-ary symmetric channel whose crossover probability grows with the number of users. Security under leakage of the key sum reduces to LPN with a noise rate that is quadratic in the KAHE noise rate, and a matching attack shows that this loss is inherent when all but two users collude. Asymptotically, we characterize the optimal communication cost in closed form, showing that the overhead over the raw payload vanishes as the input length grows, and decouple the field size from the input range via the Chinese remainder theorem. In cross-silo settings, our protocol requires less communication than information-theoretically secure aggregation for moderate to high collusion.

Information Theory.title: It Takes Two Moments: Rigidity and Limits of Continuous Encoders for Over-the-Air Computation
Information Theory.summary: We study over-the-air computation of functions, such as empirical variance, formed by combining two separately postprocessed sums of locally transformed observations. We consider continuous encoders subject to pointwise peak-power constraints over a single use of a complex multiple-access channel. With four or more transmitters, we identify conditions under which exact noiseless recovery forces every continuous encoder collection into a common affine structure that preserves both sums, reducing infinite-dimensional encoder design to selecting a finite set of coefficients. To quantify resilience against channel noise, we introduce a robustness score that measures the separation of noiseless received aggregates relative to variations in the desired function value. Within this characterized encoder family, we formulate robustness maximization as an exact convex semi-infinite program, eliminating rank constraints without a relaxation gap, and construct a decoder that attains the minimum uniform noise-amplification constant. For several function classes, including empirical variance, we derive closed-form robustness-optimal encoders and scores. Under mild regularity conditions, we also establish sharp limits on the Gaussian mean squared error at high signal-to-noise ratios and show how using the input distribution reduces average error at the expense of uniform robustness.

Information Theory.title: On the structure of polynomial ideal codes and additive Reed--Solomon codes
Information Theory.summary: We study structural properties of polynomial ideal (PI) codes and additive Reed--Solomon (aRS) codes in the folded Hamming metric (equivalently, the Hamming metric over a larger alphabet). We first determine the maximum possible length of PI codes, prove that the dual of every PI code is a generalized PI code, and deduce that PI codes are dually QMDS together with an explicit formula for their weight distribution. We then show that PI codes defined by irreducible polynomials correspond to aRS codes with pairwise nonconjugate evaluation points. For these aRS codes, the previous results on PI codes apply (duality, QMDS property and weight distribution). We show that, asymptotically, aRS codes with nonconjugate evaluation points achieve the same length as PI codes. We also compute the permutation group of such aRS codes. We also extend the family of PI codes to consider arbitrary polynomial modules (not necessarily pairwise coprime), and study when these and general aRS codes satisfy the QMDS and dually QMDS properties.

Information Theory.title: A Unified Two-Stage Generative Diffusion Framework for Channel Estimation and Port Selection in Multiuser MIMO-FAS
Information Theory.summary: Fluid antenna systems (FAS) have emerged as a promising technology for next-generation wireless systems. However, practical multiuser multiple-input multiple-output FAS (MIMO-FAS) faces two inherently coupled challenges: acquiring accurate high-dimensional channel state information (CSI) from limited RF chains and solving the combinatorial port selection problem, where the effectiveness of the latter highly depends on the result of the former. In this paper, we propose a unified two-stage diffusion framework that formulates the joint task as a maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) inference problem equivalent to maximizing the posterior expected utility of the port selection, and approximates it through two sequential stages. For Stage I, we employ a continuous flow-based diffusion model as a powerful implicit prior for 2D FAS channels and perform approximate posterior sampling via a parallel guided generation scheme, enabling accurate multiuser channel recovery even under severely low sub-sampling ratios. For Stage II, we train a discrete diffusion model on optimal labels computed by exhaustive search to propose a pool of promising port selection candidates. The final selection is then determined by maximizing the empirical posterior expected utility over this pool, followed by a lightweight local refinement. Extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed framework simultaneously achieves accurate channel estimation and delivers over 90% of the deployed rate of the computationally expensive exhaustive search over the estimated channel, while substantially improving the minimum achievable rate relative to practical cascaded schemes.
Information Theory.comment: 16 pages, 9 figures. Revised version submitted to an IEEE journal for possible publication

Information Theory.title: GPU-Accelerated Robust MA--RIS Pre-Optimization for Communication and Target Illumination
Information Theory.summary: Movable antennas (MAs) and reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) offer strong spatial control for integrated sensing and communication (ISAC), but repeatedly adapting MA positions and RIS phases to each channel realization can be impractical. This letter develops a GPU-accelerated robust pre-optimization framework that jointly selects slow-timescale MA geometry and RIS phases and returns a reusable Pareto set balancing expected worst-user rate and transmit-side worst-target illumination. The illumination objective measures directional transmitted power rather than complete echo-detection or parameter-estimation performance. The proposed Regime-Aware Multiobjective Pre-optimization (RAMP) preserves regime-specific Pareto populations, regulates cross-regime mating using Pareto-survival feedback, and constructs a worst-regime robust archive. Numerical results demonstrate competitive robust Pareto quality against the considered evolutionary baselines while avoiding online physical re-optimization.

Information Theory.title: Decoding Failure Biases IBLT Count Measurements: A Gaussian-Selection Law at the Peeling Threshold
Information Theory.summary:
In a self-sizing set-reconciliation protocol, a small first-round Invertible Bloom Lookup Table (IBLT) sketch attempts peeling decoding; after failure, the protocol estimates the difference count $d$ from the count energy and sizes the second round from a lower quantile of the measurement. This quantile must be computed conditionally on failure: the measurement and peeling success are determined by the same random mapping, so conditioning can shift the measurement law.
  In the ideal peeling model, inside the critical window where failure has nondegenerate probability, the standardized energy and a statistic of the unsigned mapping that governs the peeling outcome (the precritical score) have a joint Gaussian limit with correlation $η_kρ^2$, $ρ$ being the sign imbalance and $η_k$ a closed-form constant. The measurement conditional on failure is thus a bivariate normal truncated to a half-plane, which we call the Gaussian-selection law. Since $η_k$ changes sign between $k=4$ and $k=5$, under one-sided imbalance the unconditional threshold undercovers exactly when $k\ge5$ and is conservative for $k=3,4$.
  The key tool is a quenched CLT for a signed quadratic form on a random overlap graph; under asymptotically balanced signs, conditioning on any unsigned mapping event that is permutation-invariant and has probability bounded away from zero leaves the standard normal limit unchanged. After failure the protocol observes the total sign; inverting the selection law yields an upper confidence bound for $d$, asymptotically conservative in the critical window and, when $d/\sqrt M\to\infty$, along the whole load axis. The experiments use analytic constants, none fitted; the unconditional threshold carries a selection error that does not vanish with scale, while the corrected selection-law threshold matches per-configuration empirical quantiles.

Information Theory.title: Parallel Repetition for Entangled Games via Conditional Relative Entropy
Information Theory.summary:
We give a proof of the cubic parallel-repetition bound for finite two-player entangled games using quantum conditional relative entropy. For a game with entangled value $1-\varepsilon<1$ and answer alphabets $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$, its $n$-fold repeated value is at most \[
  \exp[-Ω(\varepsilon^3n/L)],\qquad
  L:=\max\{1,\log(|\mathcal A||\mathcal B|)\}, \] for every $n\ge1$. This recovers Song's cubic rate. We also prove a threshold bound: the probability of winning a fraction at least $1-\varepsilon+δ$ is at most $\exp[-Ω(δ^5n/(\varepsilon^2L))]$ for $0<δ\le\varepsilon$.
  Our information charge is the decrease in relative entropy when a question reference is discarded. Our comparison states preserve the original conditional question law. A chain rule bounds the coordinate charges using the cost of conditioning on checked wins and retaining checked answers. Our main lemma converts small charges into nearby pure-state descriptions and local corrections, each depending only on one player's question. Together with Song's sampler, these enable approximate local preparation of the conditioned workspace.

Information Theory.title: On the Power Distance Representation of Bregman Divergences
Information Theory.summary: We express Bregman divergences between parameters as power distances between corresponding weighted points, and investigate several applications of this representation. First, we show that the Bregman closest pair and diameter problems can be reformulated as bichromatic weighted point problems under the power distance. This reformulation enables Bregman nearest and farthest neighbor queries under power distances to be handled in practice through corresponding Euclidean neighbor queries in one additional dimension, after offsetting the weights. Next, we revisit the problem of computing minimum enclosing Bregman balls (Bregman MEBs) and establish their equivalence to double-sided weight power MEBs. We further show that Bregman MEBs can be approximated by relaxing the double-sided weight power MEB problem to its single-sided weight counterpart. We then present two approaches to solving general power MEB problems: An exact algorithm based on the LP-type framework and an arbitrarily accurate approximation scheme based on iterative Frank-Wolfe optimization. Finally, we show that the potential-function lifting transformations used to construct Bregman Voronoi diagrams can be reinterpreted as classical paraboloid lifting transformations applied to the corresponding weighted point sets. This establishes a direct connection between Bregman Voronoi diagrams and power diagrams, further illustrating how Bregman divergences can be represented as power distances.

Information Theory.title: Conditioning Strengthens Classical Entropy and Matrix Inequalities: A Submodular Approach
Information Theory.summary:
Dembo, Cover, and Thomas (1991) developed an elegant information-theoretic framework for proving determinantal inequalities for positive definite matrices, which relies on the structural inequalities of differential entropy. Submodular functions, which subsume entropy, inherently satisfy these structural inequalities because they obey generalized forms of the fundamental properties of entropy -- a chain rule and the property that conditioning reduces the function's value (under an appropriate definition of conditioning). Applying subadditivity, Han's inequality (1978), and partition subadditivity (i.e., subadditivity over a partition) yields Hadamard's, Szász's, and Fischer's inequalities, respectively. Furthermore, this framework recovers Ky Fan's inequality (1955), a strengthening of Hadamard's inequality. We highlight a previously unnoticed information-theoretic insight behind this improvement: conditioning yields a tighter upper bound on the joint entropy than the unconditional one.
  In this paper, we establish conditional strengthenings of Han's inequality and partition subadditivity in the general setting of submodular functions. We derive equality conditions for these strengthened bounds and characterize when they strictly improve their unconditional counterparts. We specialize these results to differential entropy and apply them to establish strengthened versions of Szász's and Fischer's inequalities. The strengthening of Szász's inequality recovers Ky Fan's inequality as a special case, and is strictly stronger than the classical Szász's inequality for any non-diagonal positive definite matrix. We also derive an inequality concerning eigenvalues, which generalizes and strictly strengthens a corresponding eigenvalue inequality of Ky Fan. We provide numerical examples to explicitly illustrate the tightness of our proposed matrix determinantal bounds.

Information Theory.title: Iterative Bounded Distance Decoding With 2-Bit Reliability Marker For Product-Like Codes
Information Theory.summary: We propose a novel soft-aided hard-decision decoding scheme for product codes based on two-bit quantized reliability markers. In particular, one bit is used for a two-level tolerance miscorrection check to validate the bounded distance decoding (BDD) result, while the other identifies bits to be randomly flipped upon BDD failure and miscorrection. List decoding is incorporated to further facilitate the error performance. Density evolution is performed for the design of the quantization thresholds. Compared to iterative BDD, the proposed scheme requires only moderate increases in memory and computational overhead. Simulation results verify that our scheme outperforms several unquantized soft-aided decoders, while maintaining small memory costs and low BDD attempts.
Information Theory.comment: Accepted by IEEE Information Theory Workshop 2026

Information Theory.title: The Rate of the Delsarte Bound for Binary Codes and Spheres
Information Theory.summary:
We give the asymptotic rate of Delsarte's linear programming bound for binary codes and spherical codes. This extends previous work of the author which formulated and proved an analogue of the conjecture of Afkhami-Jeddi, Cohn, Hartman, de Laat, and Tajdini for binary codes, obtaining the rate of the Delsarte linear program at distance $1/2-1/π$.
  The lower bounds introduce ideas from potential theory into the study of Delsarte's bounds, whereby the measures underlying a system of orthogonal polynomials give an obstacle problem. We solve the resulting obstacle problem in the case of binary codes and spherical codes, obtaining a closed form for the lower bound in terms of elliptic integrals. For the upper bounds, we relate the $N$-qubit construction for binary codes used in previous work of the author to the constructions in OpenAI's Chapter 2 for spherical codes and observe that they both involve interlacing spectra. This leads to a variational problem involving measures constructed from these spectra under the Markov-Krein correspondence. This variational problem admits an exact solution and matches the lower bound.

Information Theory.title: Finite-History Outage Certification for Partially Observed Fluid Antenna Receivers
Information Theory.summary: Fluid antenna receivers can select a service position from partial port observations, but finite historical data leave uncertainty in the covariance used for that decision. We develop deployment-before-use reliability certification for a frozen partial-observation rule. A proper predictive density defines a history-based parameter region. Gaussian covariance envelopes, shared conditional-probability bounds and selector enclosures provide simultaneous risk bounds over continuous parameters and discontinuous port decisions. Separate history-coverage and integration budgets limit erroneous positive certification to 0.05 for a single qualification procedure under the stated stationary model and numerical assumptions. Confidence-set inclusion allows a new independent history to reuse the risk computation with the rule unchanged. In a structured Gaussian example with 32 candidate positions, five noisy probes and target outage 0.001, all 282 risk groups are qualified; the largest upper bound is 0.000999748. A separate coupled comparison gives a current-rule outage interval of $[7.6820,9.1266]\times10^{-4}$ and resolves lower outage than two observed-port controls using the same historical fit. One independently recalibrated history reuses the certificate without additional risk sampling. Unresolved and adverse-member controls delimit this reuse.

Information Theory.title: On the Subadditivity of Mutual f-Information
Information Theory.summary: We address an open problem raised by Polyanskiy and Wu in their textbook concerning the subadditivity of mutual \(f\)-information. We study two notions of generalized mutual information: mutual \(f\)-information, defined by \(\widetilde{I}_f(X;Y)=D_f(p_{XY}\|p_Xp_Y)\), and variational \((G,f)\)-information, obtained by minimizing an average of transformed \(f\)-divergences. For the first notion, we derive a sufficient condition on \(g(x)=x^2f''(x)\) that guarantees subadditivity under conditionally independent observations. This condition yields explicit families beyond the previously known examples generated by \(x\log x\) and \((x-1)\log x\). Our proof relies on the concavity of a generalized variance functional. For the variational notion, we extend existing sufficient conditions beyond the transforms \(G(x)\in\{x,\log(1+x),-\log(1-x)\}\). Using a comparison inequality for \(G^{-1}(G(A)+G(B))\), we obtain differential criteria for concave and convex transforms. Explicit constructions illustrate the resulting classes of subadditive information measures.

Information Theory.title: Four-Level Quantized Soft Information Aided Hard-Decision Decoder for Product-like Codes
Information Theory.summary: We propose a novel low-complexity soft-aided hard-decision decoding scheme for product-like codes, termed iterative bounded-distance decoding (iBDD) with graded scaled reliability and bit-flipping (GSRF). This scheme operates on four-level quantized soft information. It incorporates a graded scaled reliability rule to assign decoding confidence to the bounded-distance decoding result, and employs a bit-flipping rule based on bit-level and component-code-level reliability. A selective re-decoding rule is designed to further facilitate the error performance while keeping the number of BDD attempts in reasonably low levels. The decoding parameter design of iBDD-GSRF is investigated for product codes and staircase codes, respectively. Simulation results on both codes verify that iBDD-GSRF achieves a gain of more than 0.4 dB over the conventional iBDD, comparable to several existing unquantized soft-aided decoders.

Information Theory.title: Explicit reduced APN permutations: ramification and optimal Galois-ring lifts
Information Theory.summary: Let $m\ge5$ be odd and $q=2^m$. For every odd $r$ with $3\le r<m$ and $\gcd(r,m)=1$ we give the reduced polynomial $P_{m,r}=\mathrm{red}((T_r^3)^{2^{m-2}})$, $T_r=\sum_{i<r}X^{2^i}$, explicitly: it has coefficients in $\mathbb{F}_2$ and exactly $3r-2$ terms, it is an APN permutation of $\mathbb{F}_q$, and its formal derivative $1+X^{2^{r-2}}+X^{2^{m-2}}$ has no zero on $\mathbb{F}_q$ and is two-to-one. We determine the ramification of $P_{m,r}$ as a map of the projective line for all admissible $(m,r)$: there are $2^{m-r}$ finite ramification points, all wild, with index and different exponent $2^{r-2}$, all over the single finite branch value $1$. The $0/1$ lift of $P_{m,r}$ satisfies an identity in $\mathbb{Z}[X]$ that evaluates it over every Galois ring $\mathrm{GR}(2^k,m)$ with $m-1$ squarings, one general multiplication and $r+5$ additions or subtractions. For every quadratic optimal APN permutation $p$ of $\mathbb{F}_q$ (in particular $P_{m,r}$), every $k\ge2$ and every coefficient lift $F$ of $p$ to $\mathrm{GR}(2^k,m)$, we determine the differential rows of $F$ exactly in the unit directions whose residue lies outside the kernel $\{0,ρ\}$ of the linear part of $p'$ (they are the residue rows of $p$; $ρ=1$ for $P_{m,r}$) and in the directions in $2^{k-1}\mathrm{GR}(2^k,m)\setminus\{0\}$ (every nonzero entry equals $2q^{k-1}$). We also give a self-contained proof of the Li--Wang criterion for a Gold function plus a linearised polynomial, which explains why the inner map of $P_{m,r}$ is not a monomial, and record a two-word, two-layer transition that a simple linear layer forbids at the residue level.
Information Theory.comment: 15 pages. Submitted to Finite Fields and Their Applications. Code, Lean 4 formalization and blueprint: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23233173 (version 1.0.1; https://github.com/hirokifukui/residue-apn)

Information Theory.title: Optimal Reduced Representatives of Quadratic APN Permutations in Odd Dimension
Information Theory.summary: The formal derivative of the reduced polynomial representative of a map on a binary finite field depends on the coordinates, although its differential uniformity does not. This matters for lifting permutations to Galois rings: a polynomial over a Galois ring of characteristic a power of two greater than two permutes the ring exactly when its reduction permutes the residue field and the derivative of the reduction has no zero there. We prove that for every odd $n\ge5$, every quadratic almost perfect nonlinear permutation $Q$ of $\mathbb{F}_{2^n}$ admits invertible binary-linear maps $L$ and $A$ such that the derivative of the reduced representative of $L\circ Q\circ A$ has no zero and each of its nonempty fibres has exactly two elements. The range is exact: this fails for $n=3$, as computed earlier, and for even $n$ there are no such permutations. For $n\ge9$, a linearization and a projectively injective cofactor map reduce the problem to counting binary matrices: more than 5% of the invertible inputs $A$ succeed, more than half for $n\ge15$, without any classification. For $n=5,7$ we use two independent classifications and finite certificates. Consequently every such permutation is linearly equivalent to a counterexample to the reduced critical-point conjecture of Bartoli and Stănică that lifts to permutation polynomials of optimal differential uniformity over every Galois ring with this residue field. For odd $n\ge9$ the existence proof is checked in the Lean 4 proof assistant.
Information Theory.comment: 22 pages. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Information Theory. Code, certificates and Lean 4 formalization: https://github.com/hirokifukui/apnlift (Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23055799)

Information Theory.title: Shift-Invariant Permutations with Polynomial Composition: Construction and Algebraic Structure
Information Theory.summary: Shift-invariant permutations of $\mathbb F_2^n$ are particularly attractive in symmetric cryptography because of their regularity and implementation efficiency. Constructing such permutations with an explicit algebraic structure remains a challenging problem. In this paper, we study a family of shift-invariant transformations of $\mathbb F_2^n$ constructed from a recursively defined sequence of mappings $\{γ_j\}_{j\ge 0}$ associated with landscapes. First, we prove that, under an explicit dimension condition relating $n$ to the support of the landscape, the sequence $\{γ_j\}_{j\ge 0}$ has the polynomial composition property if and only if the corresponding landscape is quasi-conserved on $\mathbb F_2^n$ with a nonzero special index. Then, we determine the eventual zero or periodic behavior of $\{γ_j\}_{j\ge0}$, including the exact index at which the sequence either first vanishes or becomes periodic, together with the least eventual period, and establish linear independence until the first linear relation occurs. When the polynomial composition property holds, we establish an explicit isomorphism between the group of permutation elements in the monoid generated by these mappings and the unit group of a quotient ring $\mathbb F_2[z]/\langle p(z)\rangle$, where $p(z)$ is a monomial or a binomial determined by the landscape. This framework reduces the tasks of testing bijectivity, computing iterates, and determining compositional inverses and orders of permutation elements to polynomial computations. Finally, we apply the results to mappings represented by binomials and trinomials in the quotient ring, obtaining explicit criteria and formulas, and tabulate more than one hundred representative constructions of shift-invariant permutations, recovering and unifying several previously studied families.

Information Theory.title: A One-Sided McDiarmid-Type Inequality for Heavy Tails via Reverse KL Tensorization
Information Theory.summary: We revisit McDiarmid's inequality, a central tool in statistical learning theory and algorithm analysis. We show that large deviations above the mean are exponentially unlikely for functions of independent random variables that are almost surely bounded above and satisfy a conditional moment assumption of order $p\in(1,2]$. When $p<2$, the result applies even when the function has infinite variance. Our proof relies on a new tensorization inequality for the Kullback--Leibler divergence, termed reverse KL tensorization, which may be of independent interest. Applications include concentration of the sample mean and median-of-means estimator, and one-sided uniform risk bounds for unbounded losses.

Information Theory.title: Multiplicative Semidefinite Programming Upper Bounds on Quantum No-Signalling-Assisted Zero-Error Capacity
Information Theory.summary: We study zero-error communication and exact simulation of quantum channels assisted by quantum no-signalling correlations. For a channel with Kraus operator space $K$, we introduce a semidefinite programming parameter $Γ(K)$ that is exactly multiplicative under tensor products and upper-bounds $Θ_{\rm NS}(K)$, where $\log_2Θ_{\rm NS}(K)=C_{0,\rm NS}(K)$ and $C_{0,\rm NS}(K)$ denotes the asymptotic quantum no-signalling-assisted zero-error capacity. Among known upper bounds on $Θ_{\rm NS}$ given by semidefinite programs, $Γ$ is the tightest. We also prove that the previously introduced simulation lower bound $Σ^{-}(K)$ is exactly multiplicative and satisfies $Θ_{\rm NS}(K)\leqΓ(K)\leqΣ^{-}(K)\leqΓ(K)^2$. Using this multiplicativity, we show that neither $S_{0,\rm NS}(K)=\log_2Σ^{-}(K)$ nor its regularized extension $S_{0,\rm NS}(K)=\lim\nolimits_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\log_2Σ^{-}(K^{\otimes n})$ holds in general. This answers an open question about the asymptotic simulation cost $S_{0,\rm NS}(K)$. For classical-quantum channels, we obtain sharp bounds. If $r$ is the effective output dimension, then $Θ_{\rm NS}\leqΓ\leq(1+r^{1/2})Θ_{\rm NS}/2$ and $Γ\leqΣ^{-}\leq(1+r^{1/2})Γ/2$. If $k$ is the minimum rank of the output support projections, then $Σ^{-}/Θ_{\rm NS}\leq[(1+r^{1/2})/(1+k^{1/2})]^2$, and this bound is sharp for every $1\leq k\leq r$. Thus, we obtain the sharp bound $S_{0,\rm NS}-C_{0,\rm NS}\leq2\log_2[(1+r^{1/2})/(1+k^{1/2})]$.

Information Theory.title: Superfast Spectral Compressed Sensing with Quadratic Convergence
Information Theory.summary: In this paper, we study the spectral compressed sensing problem of recovering a spectrally sparse signal from linear compressive measurements. Exploiting the low-rank Hankel structure associated with the signal, we formulate a nonconvex fixed-rank optimization problem with a Hankel regularization. We propose a Superfast Iterative Hard Thresholding (SIHT) algorithm, where each iteration consists of a tangent-space least-squares update followed by a fixed-rank hard thresholding projection. SIHT is the first nonconvex algorithm with provable quadratic convergence for spectral compressed sensing. For random Gaussian measurements, it achieves exact recovery in the noiseless case and stable recovery in the noisy case with near-optimal sample complexity. To efficiently implement SIHT, we develop a parameterized conjugate gradient method for solving the least-squares subproblem, endowing SIHT with state-of-the-art computational and memory efficiency. Numerical experiments are provided to validate our results.

Information Theory.title: Direction-Shift Keying for High-Mobility mmWave Communications: Geometry-Based Resilience to Short Channel Coherence Times and Phase Noise
Information Theory.summary: Communication reliability in high-mobility millimeter-wave (mmWave) systems is fundamentally challenged by rapid channel variations, manifested in short channel coherence times, and phase noise, which necessitate frequent channel estimation and phase tracking. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Direction-Shift Keying (DSK), a geometry-based modulation scheme that exploits the relative stability of propagation directions rather than the rapidly varying amplitude and phase of the wireless channel. DSK conveys information through distinguishable directions of arrival (DoAs), enabled by a distributed antenna system (DAS), thereby shifting the communication principle from channel-dependent to geometry-dependent signaling. We first derive the structure of the optimal DSK detector for a mobile device equipped with an arbitrary number of antennas. We then establish the fundamental law governing the temporal stability of propagation directions, termed Direction Coherence Time (DCT), and show that DCT scales as $d/v$, where $d$ is the transmitter--receiver distance and $v$ is the relative velocity. In contrast, conventional Channel Coherence Time (CCT) scales as $λ/v$, where $λ$ denotes the wavelength, revealing a coherence-time advantage on the order of $d/λ$, potentially exceeding four orders of magnitude in mmWave systems. Furthermore, we establish the inherent invariance of DSK to common phase rotations, providing resilience to common oscillator phase noise without explicit phase tracking. Numerical results corroborate the theoretical findings and demonstrate the potential of geometry-based signaling for reliable high-mobility mmWave communications.

Information Theory.title: Efficient Agnostic Learning of Univariate Densities Under Local Differential Privacy
Information Theory.summary: We propose a general framework for non-interactive locally differentially private (LDP) learning of structured univariate distributions that can be approximated by piece-wise polynomials. This gives the first sample-efficient LDP learners for several distribution classes, including mixtures of log-concave distributions, such as Gaussian mixture models (GMMs). These learners also provide agnostic guarantees and are computationally efficient. We also prove a lower bound for learning GMMs under LDP, improving on the standard pure-DP packing lower bounds of Bun et al. [BKSW19]. To obtain our general learning framework, we develop an efficient non-interactive LDP algorithm for synthetic data generation over large domains, which may be of independent interest. We then use it together with a deterministic adaptation of the non-private piecewise polynomial learner of Acharya et al. [ADLS17].

Logic in Computer Science.title: Refusal Is Not Robustness: Measuring Harmful Reachability in Autoregressive Language Models
Logic in Computer Science.summary: LLM safety evaluations via jailbreaking typically index on attack success rate (ASR): whether a generated response violates safeguards. However, ASR only evaluates sampled outputs and provides little information on the underlying generation process. Autoregressive language models define distributions over possible outputs, and a sampled refusal can coexist with substantial probability mass on harmful generation paths. We study this hidden structure through bounded continuation analysis (BCA), which models autoregressive generation as a stochastic process over token prefixes and computes the finite-horizon probability that generation reaches a harmful continuation. BCA constructs a bounded continuation tree, labels terminal continuations with a semantic harm evaluator, and estimates harmful reachability using exact probabilistic model checking. BCA complements ASR by measuring how much harmful behavior remains accessible beneath a sampled safe response. This makes it useful for distinguishing models that look identical under measured ASR values, and allocating red-team effort toward regions of the generation process with greater hidden risk. Across four instruction-tuned LLMs and 100 JailbreakBench behaviors, we show that BCA effectively quantifies hidden harmful behavior and provides a useful signal to guide red teaming.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Decisiveness for countable MDPs and insights for NPLCSs and POMDPs
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
Markov chains and Markov decision processes (MDPs) are well-established probabilistic models. While finite Markov models are well-understood, analysing their infinite counterparts remains a significant challenge. Decisiveness has proved to be an elegant property for countable Markov chains: it is general enough to be satisfied by several natural classes of countable Markov chains, and it guarantees the termination of simple qualitative and approximate quantitative model-checking algorithms.
  In contrast, existing work on the formal analysis of countable MDPs usually relies on ad hoc techniques tailored to specific classes. In this paper, we provide a general framework to analyse countable MDPs (with finitely many enabled actions per state) by extending the notion of decisiveness. Compared to Markov chains, MDPs exhibit an additional nondeterministic choice that can be resolved in an adversarial or cooperative way, leading to multiple natural notions of decisiveness. We show that these notions enable the approximation of supremum reachability and infimum reachability (equivalently, supremum safety) probabilities in countable MDPs using generic approximation schemes.
  We then instantiate our generic approach to two concrete classes of models inducing countable MDPs: nondeterministic probabilistic lossy channel systems (NPLCSs) and partially observable MDPs (POMDPs). This leads to concrete algorithms to compute approximations to supremum safety probabilities in each of these classes.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 49 pages, 14 figures. Extended version of article published in Principles of Formal Quantitative Analysis

Logic in Computer Science.title: Beyond Compilation: Evaluating Faithful Natural-Language-to-Lean Statement Formalization
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Lean verifies that a generated declaration is well typed, but cannot check whether it states what the user intended. We measure how far compilation overstates faithfulness in statement autoformalization without canonical Lean targets. Our criterion requires Lean compilation and agreement of two LLM judges from different model families. On an independent random audit, it agrees with the human majority on 91.5% of cases; it rarely accepts an unfaithful output but rejects some faithful ones. Across eight systems on 227 university-level statements, the gap between compiling and accepted outputs ranges from 1.3 to 29.5 percentage points: our tool-augmented agent compiles 87.2% of the statements, but only 57.7% are accepted. Human review of all the agent's rejections confirms that 23.8 of its 29.5 points are real translation errors. For the gaps of the seven one-shot systems, a two-stage review by Claude Opus 5.5 with Lean and GPT-6.1 Sol, validated on these human labels, finds that 78-100% are real translation errors for six of them. When GPT-5.2, one of the two judges, grades the translations of two models released after it, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5, it accepts 83% of the statements for each, against 21% for one-shot GPT-5.2. For these two models, the same review classifies only 4 of their 54 rejections (7%) as translation errors, so most of their measured gap is judge errors rather than translation errors. This is consistent with these systems erring less while the judge does not: the fewer errors a system makes, the smaller the share of its rejections that are translation errors. Finally, a 2^3 tool ablation of the agent shows that Lean feedback drives most of its compilation gain, and that nearly half of this gain fails the semantic criterion. Code and data are available at https://github.com/grenadeComing/beyond-compilation.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: v4: adds a decomposition of each measured gap into translation errors and other rejections, using a two-stage LLM review validated on human labels, and results for two models released later. 37 pages, 6 figures, 38 tables

Logic in Computer Science.title: A unification of graded and substructural logics
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Type systems which account for resource sensitive computations can generally be split into two styles: First, substructural logics such as Linear Logic which seek to restrict weakening and contraction and reintroduce them in a controlled manner; And second, graded systems which allow weakening and contraction by default, but track the use of variables quantitatively in some algebraic structure -- usually a semiring. We present GRASS (Graded and substructural), a type system which incorporates mechanisms from both of these approaches, thus allowing maximally flexible control over variable usage. Furthermore, GRASS allows grades from an arbitrary collection of grade algebras to coexist in the same system, thus allowing different variables to be controlled with respect to different notions of resource within the same program. We develop the categorical semantics of GRASS, and find that, on the level of categorical semantics, it subsumes multiple established systems such as LNL, Adjoint Logic, and mGL.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: Conference: MFPS XLII; final version; 18 pages, version without appendices

Logic in Computer Science.title: Learning Rational Strategies for Temporal Objectives in Multi-Agent Systems
Logic in Computer Science.summary: We study rational synthesis for stochastic multi-agent systems with unknown dynamics, where each agent is equipped with its own probabilistic temporal objective specified using Probabilistic Linear Temporal Logic on Finite Traces ($\mathsf{PLTL}_f}$). We impose solution concepts (e.g., Nash equilibrium, subgame-perfect equilibrium) as constraints on the joint strategy profile, using payoffs derived from each agent's probability of satisfying its temporal objective. In particular, we formulate per-agent rational synthesis as finding a strategy profile -- if one exists -- such that (i) the designated agent's probabilistic temporal constraint is satisfied, and (ii) the profile represents a stable solution under a chosen solution concept. We give conditional convergence guarantees for tabular Nash-Q learning, certify satisfaction with simultaneous finite-sample confidence bounds, and assess strategic stability with approximate best-response checking. Our approach operates in a stochastic \emph{Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning} (MARL) environment, where model-free learning algorithms attempt to attain extremal satisfaction probabilities for temporal objectives automatically compiled into reward automata. Our approach is empirically validated using 8 general-sum concurrent stochastic games.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Geometric Graph Representations via Compact SAT Encodings
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
We present compact SAT encodings and certifying exact solvers for boxicity and cubicity. The boxicity of a graph is the minimum dimension in which it is the intersection graph of axis-aligned boxes; cubicity is defined analogously using unit cubes. Grid-based formulations face a geometric discretization bottleneck, growing rapidly with the target dimension. We avoid this bottleneck by encoding the total order of interval endpoints in each coordinate. For an $n$-vertex graph and target dimension $d$, our boxicity encoding uses $O(n^2d)$ variables and $O(n^3d)$ clauses, both linear in $d$. Requiring the left- and right-endpoint orders to agree yields a cubicity encoding of the same asymptotic size.
  Satisfying models are decoded into independently checked geometric representations, while unsatisfiable instances used as lower-bound evidence carry mechanically verified DRAT certificates. In a controlled evaluation with 186 trials per encoding on standard and structured graph families, the order encoding solves 96.8% of trials, compared with 71.0% for the known grid formulation, and reduces mean PAR-2 time from 178.21 to 21.70 seconds.
  The pipeline also certifies exact values for several named graphs. We turn one such value into a reusable obstruction by proving that every Kneser graph $K(n,k)$ with $k\ge3$ and $n\ge2k+1$ contains an induced Desargues graph. The resulting lower bound, together with an explicit three-dimensional representation of $K(7,3)$, establishes $\operatorname{boxicity}(K(7,3))=3$. This disproves the conjecture of Caoduro and Sebo that $\operatorname{boxicity}(K(n,k))=n-k$ for all $k\ge3$ and $n\ge2k+1$.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: To appear in ALENEX 2027

Logic in Computer Science.title: Neuro-Relational Programs: Unifying Queries and Neural Computation over Structured Data
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
The conventional approach to deep learning over relational databases applies neural models, such as Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), to a graph representation of the database. Recent approaches instead operate on databases directly, associating tuples with embeddings and extending query mechanisms to jointly process embeddings and relational content. Inspired by these developments, we introduce Neuro-Relational Programs (NRPs), a declarative query language for relational databases whose facts carry numeric vector embeddings. NRPs extend Datalog-style rules with operations that combine, aggregate, and transform embeddings, thereby interleaving relational reasoning and learnable neural components within a single formalism. This yields a general approach to neural computation over relational data: an NRP can be read both as a query plan with trainable components and as a neural architecture with relational structure built in.
  Natural syntactic fragments of NRPs recover existing architectures and query formalisms. Zero-ary NRPs correspond to non-adaptive query algorithms; monadic NRPs generalize GNN-style message passing and precisely capture Deep Homomorphism Networks, a connection that we extend to frontier-guarded NRPs over databases with row-ids. We characterize the expressive power of unrestricted NRPs with ReLU-FFN transformations by FOCQ, an extension of first-order logic with counting interpreted over real-weighted structures, yielding a precise connection with uniform TC$^0$ over ordered databases. Together, these results establish NRPs as a broad declarative framework for querying and neural computation over relational data.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 55 pages; Accepted at PODS 2026

Logic in Computer Science.title: Complete Dynamic Logic of Communicating Hybrid Programs
Logic in Computer Science.summary: This article presents a relatively complete proof calculus for the dynamic logic of communicating hybrid programs dLCHP. Beyond hybrid systems, communicating hybrid programs not only feature mixed discrete and continuous dynamics but also their parallel interactions in parallel hybrid systems. This not only combines the subtleties of hybrid and discrete parallel systems, but parallel hybrid dynamics necessitates that all parallel subsystems synchronize in time and evolve truly simultaneously. To enable compositional reasoning nevertheless, dLCHP combines differential dynamic logic dL with mutual abstraction of subsystems by assumption-commitment (ac) reasoning. The resulting proof calculus preserves the essence of dynamic logic axiomatizations, while revealing-and being driven by-a new modal logic view onto ac-reasoning. The dLCHP proof calculus is shown to be complete relative to $Ω$-FOD, the first-order logic of differential equation properties FOD augmented with communication traces. This confirms that the calculus covers all aspects of parallel hybrid systems, because it lacks no axioms to reduce all their dynamical effects to the assertion logic. Additional axioms for encoding communication traces enable a provably correct equitranslation between $Ω$-FOD and FOD, which reveals the possibility of representational succinctness in parallel hybrid systems proofs. Transitively, this establishes a full proof-theoretical alignment of dLCHP and dL, and shows that reasoning about parallel hybrid systems is exactly as hard as reasoning about hybrid systems, continuous systems, or discrete systems.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: Accepted at JAR

Logic in Computer Science.title: Derivatives for Containers in Univalent Foundations
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
Containers conveniently represent a wide class of inductive data types. Their derivatives compute representations of types of one-hole contexts, useful for implementing tree-traversal algorithms. Derivatives of discrete containers (whose positions have decidable equality) satisfy a universal property with respect to linear morphisms of containers. This induces a well-behaved notion of linear substitution for one-hole contexts.
  Working in Univalent Foundations, we extend the derivative operation to untruncated containers (whose shapes and positions are arbitrary types). We prove that this derivative, defined in terms of a set of isolated positions, satisfies an appropriate universal property in the wild category of untruncated containers and linear morphisms, as well as basic laws with respect to constants, sums and products. A chain rule exists, but is in general non-invertible. In fact, a globally invertible chain rule is inconsistent in the presence of non-set types, and equivalent to a classical principle when restricted to set-truncated containers. We derive a rule for derivatives of least fixpoints from the chain rule, and characterize its invertibility. All of our results are formalized in Cubical Agda.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: revised version addressing reviewer feedback

Logic in Computer Science.title: Bidirectional Elaborators à la Carte
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
Surface syntax in proof assistants like Rocq, Lean, Agda, and Idris is highly implicit, lacking many details that are needed for user-written code to denote precisely defined mathematical objects. Elaboration is an algorithm that accounts for these details by translating surface syntax to an explicit enough core syntax. The reliability and predictability of elaboration relies on several critical properties of the core type system, including decidability of judgemental equality and the injectivity of type constructors; these dependencies are witnessed in a concrete system by explicit calls to conversion checking and weak-head reduction subroutines.
  We introduce a dependently typed monadic domain specific language for the executable specification of correct-by-construction elaboration algorithms that is abstracted from any particular representation of normal forms or algorithm for conversion checking. In particular, we represent a bidirectionally typed surface language for Martin-Löf type theory by shallow embedding in this DSL so that the translation of surface terms into core terms amounts to elementary equational calculation. This translation is correct by construction in the sense that it cannot produce ill-typed terms, and is automatically stable under judgemental equality of core terms and even under substitution; from the latter property, we obtain a new denotational interpretation of the suspension of elaboration problems. Finally, a concrete elaboration algorithm is extracted by algebraic means from a presheaf model of the DSL built out of the bi-initial natural model of Martin-Löf type theory.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: Add further discussion of related work; other minor wording and typographical improvements

Logic in Computer Science.title: Overview and Roadmap of Team Automata
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Team Automata is a formalism for interacting component-based systems proposed in 1997, whereby multiple sending and receiving actions from concurrent automata can synchronise. During the past 25+ years, team automata have been studied and applied in many different contexts, involving 25+ researchers and resulting in 25+ publications. In this paper, we first revisit the specific notion of synchronisation and composition of team automata, relating it to other relevant coordination models, such as Reo, BIP, Contract Automata, Choreography Automata, and Multi-Party Session Types. We then identify several aspects that have recently been investigated for team automata and related models. These include communication properties (which are the properties of interest?), realisability (how to decompose a global model into local components?), tool support (what has been automatised or implemented?), and variability (can a family of concrete product (automata) models be captured concisely?). Our presentation of these aspects provides a snapshot of the most recent trends in research on team automata, and delineates a roadmap for future research, both for team automata and for related formalisms.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Coexponential Exploration in the Clef Programming Language
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Clef was created as a concurrent programming language whose compiler tracks state ownership, waiting computations and request dependencies. We develop a coexponential account of stateful services and their client pools within this design. Delimited continuations retain the computation and resources needed to complete each interaction. These structures give our compiler premises for verifying service composition and preserving it through native lowering to multiple hardware targets. We connect finite actor state transitions to the initial, service and final rules of a coexponential server. A separate operational account relates actor dispatch to single-use continuation frames. We prove state-ownership and reply preservation, give a finite communication-summary analysis, and derive circular-wait exclusion under stated assumptions. A further result identifies when changing service order preserves both state and replies. Our Program Semantic Graph retains these facts through compilation. We are researching reusable proofs to confirm the ownership and communication interfaces, while our BAREWire implementation connects message meaning to its unboxed representation across respective endpoints. A distributed worker example preserves request identity across suspension, reordered replies and boundary conversion. Urschel's growth bounds inform a solver service; a distributed ADM update additionally preserves joint samples, metric evidence and request identity. Our two-category account connects component refinement, reusable proof terms and native realization. Protocols determine the admissible interactions, continuations expose their storage requirements, and retained dependencies support differential compilation. Developers can express ordinary stateful services while the compiler carries the conditions for their correct composition across execution targets.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 36 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Updated for contributions from Karwowski et al. and clarified Padovani's fair-termination result

Logic in Computer Science.title: Fixed-Point Scaffolding in the Clef Programming Language
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Native compilation changes how a program represents values and performs operations from processor to processor. In our view, proofs that justify source-level decisions must remain connected to those changes. We develop fixed-point scaffolding for this continuity in Clef and our Composer compiler. Our Program Semantic Graph retains types, joint constraints and proof dependencies. A thin MLIR middle end witnesses their settled consequences for native CPU, GPU, NPU and FPGA realization. The account connects nanopass traversal with preservation contracts, structural theorems and adjoint interfaces between reasoning modes. Four verification tiers organize automatic inference and reusable domain and system proofs, with probabilistic relations admitted at Tier 4. Established lower-tier facts can directly support richer derivations. We state conditions for composing lowering contracts and assembling compatible program segments, then show how their dependencies govern differential compilation after an edit. A worked foreign-call boundary follows source ranges through argument marshaling, the actual call and return conversion. Current FFI mechanisms bind checking evidence to those witnessed operations. A recent paper from Urschel provides elimination-growth bounds that supply a quantitative example. Reusable premises inform representation and error contracts that retain their sampling, arithmetic and exceptional-path assumptions. A further example admits value-indexed pairing through ordinary MLIR operations, connecting this scaffold to negative and fractional types. Together these constructions explain how a thin middle end can carry the consequences of rich source proofs into unboxed computation graphs. Integrity and efficiency share the same retained evidence. It justifies native realizations and identifies which analyses, proofs and lowered fragments remain reusable during development.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 25 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Updated for contributions from Karwowski et al

Logic in Computer Science.title: Decidable By Construction: Design-Time Verification for Truly Fearless Systems
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Concurrency, parallelism and distributed execution become truly fearless when the compiler tracks wait-for edges, proves multi-threaded work is sound and preserves distributed boundary contracts. In this design, our Composer compiler preserves proofs while lowering Clef directly to native CPU, GPU, NPU and FPGA code, without translation through C or vendor APIs. Our Program Semantic Graph retains the values, relationships and premises that justify BAREWire's unboxed boundary contracts. And C & C++ interfacing is an explicit marshaling boundary, with proofs tied to actual arguments, conversions and returned values. Four verification tiers connect an account of our design. Tier 1 supplies structural inference, founded on principal dimensional types. Tier 2 generates and checks local arithmetic, representation, and computational integrity at the node level. Tier 3 instantiates reusable domain and system lemmas, including distributed proofs supported by Iris, Actris and Aneris. Tiers 1-3 require no developer annotations, with a quotation based lemma library design to extend coverage as use cases expand. Tier 4 admits computational and probabilistic relational proofs, with project annotations identifying the required relations. We extend the same library direction toward recognizing relational constructions from hypergraph structure. A formal composition rule connects arithmetic, ownership, protocol and realization evidence. Our worked distributed reduction preserves one specified result across concurrent workers, reordered arrivals and boundary mappings. Its probabilistic extension carries worker and conversion error with an explicit failure budget. With recent work by Urschel, we show bounds supply a relevant source of reusable proof terms. These constructions make verification a core engineering discipline for truly fearless programs and systems across a variety of hardware targets.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 34 pages, 0 figures, 4 tables. Updated for contributions from Karwowski et al

Logic in Computer Science.title: Layered Monoidal Theories I: Diagrammatic Algebra and Applications
Logic in Computer Science.summary: We develop layered monoidal theories -- a generalisation of monoidal theories combining formal descriptions of a system at different levels of abstraction. Via their representation as string diagrams, monoidal theories provide a graphical formalism to reason algebraically about information flow in models across different fields of science. Layered monoidal theories allow mixing several monoidal theories (together with translations between them) within the same string diagram, while retaining mathematical precision and semantic interpretability. We develop the mathematical foundations of layered monoidal theories, as well as providing several instances of our approach, including digital and electrical circuits, quantum processes, chemical reactions, concurrent processes, and probability theory.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 62 pages, 23 figures, 3 Tables

Logic in Computer Science.title: Model Checking HyperRecHML is Decidable
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
Temporal hyperlogics combine explicit quantification over traces with temporal requirements evaluated over the quantified traces. HyperRecHML is a temporal hyperlogic which allows for arbitrary mixing of trace quantification and the use of fixed points for expressing temporal requirements, which makes it very expressive in comparison to other first-order hyperlogics. HyperRecHML has already been successfully applied in runtime verification, but the decidability of its model checking problem remains open.
  We answer this question positively by providing two main contributions. Firstly, a normalization procedure that allows to reduce arbitrary HyperRecHML formulas to a normal form with restricted nesting of trace quantification and fixed points. Secondly, we provide an automata-based model checking algorithm for formulas of this normal form. The complexity of our algorithm is comparable to similar ones for other hyperlogics, despite the extra expressive power.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Minimal Witness Reinforcement Learning
Logic in Computer Science.summary: ``What are the irreducible conditions that are sufficient to produce an outcome?'' is one of the most common questions that recur across computation and science. Its answers, the minimal sufficient witnesses, are what we mean by explanations, mechanisms and reasons. These problems usually ask for multiple minimal witnesses, yet standard RL methods may reveal only one solution or redundant ones. We formalize this problem as minimal-witness identification and introduce Minimal-Witness Reinforcement Learning (MWRL). MWRL takes the union of the sets certified by successful proposals sampled from the policy and credits each proposal for the coverage the group union would lose without that proposal. This credit assignment, derived directly from the problem definition, unifies the demands for minimality and recovery of alternatives from a single black-box verifier bit. Under this principle, we derive a value iteration planner that recovers the entire family of witnesses and a policy gradient method that can scale to large language models. Across different experimental settings, MWRL recovers most minimal witnesses, while other methods return redundant supersets or a single witness. By making witness families learnable from verifier feedback, MWRL expands the scope of reinforcement learning beyond single-solution optimization. Our code is available at https://github.com/TSUITUENYUE/MWRL.

Multiagent Systems.title: Emergent Discrimination and Polarization in Multi-Agent Systems
Multiagent Systems.summary: We study theoretically how discrimination and polarization can emerge in a population of learning agents. Each agent uses an adaptive linear decision layer to map a language-model embedding of an issue to a binary opinion and maintains an evolving estimate of how much it trusts every other agent. Through pairwise interactions, agents update both their decision weights and trust estimates using an online Bayesian rule derived from teacher-student learning over a noisy channel. In-context-learning experiments with large language models qualitatively reproduce the predicted opinion and trust updates. We then assign each agent one of two arbitrary group labels, A or B, and model group bias by allowing a fraction $f_b$ of agents to shift its perceived agreement with each message by a strength $b$, a bias steering prejudice, depending on whether the sender and receiver share a label. We use order parameters from statistical mechanics to connect these local dynamics to collective states and transitions. Starting from uniformly random initial conditions, simulations reveal a rich phase diagram in the $(b,f_b)$ plane, comprising four collective states: spin-glass frustrated out-group favoritism, nondiscriminatory polarization, discrimination with opinion alignment, and discrimination without opinion alignment. Which state emerges depends on both the strength and prevalence of the bias. These results show how simple local learning dynamics can generate qualitatively distinct forms of polarization and discrimination, underscoring the need for population-level safety analysis of multi-agent systems. They also suggest measurable order parameters for characterizing analogous collective states in human societies.

Multiagent Systems.title: Dynamic Auction Mechanisms in a Closed-Credit Economy: Sequential Slot Reallocation in Air Traffic Management
Multiagent Systems.summary: Indivisible resources allocated in advance may need to be reallocated when capacity reductions make existing assignments infeasible, yet monetary compensation is often impractical or undesirable. We develop a sequential resource reallocation scheme using reusable artificial credits, where agents hold pre-existing resource rights and have heterogeneous marginal valuations over time blocks. Capacity reductions produce fractional endowments, which our closed-credit scheme resolves into indivisible final allocations. We model agents' intertemporal preferences through a predicted-value-to-go function and characterize conditions ensuring that their optimal demand is non-increasing in price. We propose an ascending-auction mechanism that partitions agents into subgroups and uses the minimum subgroup market-clearing price as a common transaction price. We show that the mechanism preserves non-myopic individual rationality and weak nontrader neutrality. Moreover, we establish Pareto efficiency under optimal-demand clearing in the unified market and bound the expected gain from misreporting by the probability that an agent changes the common price. Simulations of airport slot reallocation demonstrate reductions in total modeled delay and cancellation costs relative to a ground-delay baseline.

Multiagent Systems.title: Whose Polarization Is It? Auditing Fairness in Network Polarization Measures
Multiagent Systems.summary: A polarization score is supposed to describe a community, not its surroundings. Yet when a minority community is embedded in a larger network, its measured polarization can rise or fall with the size and structure of the majority around it. We ask whether polarization measures are therefore fair to minorities and develop an audit built around two criteria: measurement invariance (MI), which asks whether otherwise equivalent majorities and minorities receive equivalent scores, and structural exogeneity (SE), which asks whether a minority's score changes when its surrounding majority changes. Resolution sensitivity (RS) is treated as a prerequisite for meaningful fairness assessment. We audit seven polarization measure families spanning the three network-operationalizable dimensions of polarization, introducing Network-Weighted Distance (NWD) to fill an unserved extremeness-separation combination. Across controlled synthetic networks, mechanism-isolating diagnostic topologies, and real political and communication networks, no measure passes all applicable checks. Minorities are systematically scored as more polarized than equivalent majorities. We trace this dependence to two separate channels: majority structure can alter the opinions that opinion-reading measures consume, and, on a different path, opinion-orthogonal structural change can affect the arithmetic of structural measures. Reading opinions is thus double-edged, letting contamination in when structure moves opinions but shielding the score when structure changes and opinions do not. We close with practical guidance for reporting polarization scores without inheriting these biases.

Multiagent Systems.title: Detecting Multi-Agent Collusion Through Multi-Agent Interpretability
Multiagent Systems.summary: Non-verbalised or secret collusion may impose a ceiling on transcript-level monitoring in multi-agent deployments. Internal model activations are known to provide an additional monitoring surface for single-agent phenomena such as deception, but detecting collusion within an unknown subgroup is ultimately a joint inference task over multiple agents. This paper derives collusion detection statistics based on the composite hypothesis testing literature and introduces HELIOS, a multi-agent detection framework for collusion. Using per-agent activation probes as sensors, we then evaluate these principled statistics alongside heuristics on NARCBench, a novel benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collusion detection under environment distribution shift. Across four open-weight models, both our group-level statistics and heuristics transfer zero-shot to NARCBenchs holdout environments. Notably, the best method on every model reaches 0.99 to 1.00 AUROC when transferred from committee deliberations to a steganographic collusion task that unprimed transcript monitors fail to separate. We find empirically that no single statistic or heuristic dominates across tasks, consistent with our analysis that there is no known universally most powerful test for this setting. We then evaluate detector transfer to third-party environments with emergent, rather than instructed, collusion. In one such environment, only 2 of 229 collusive episodes verbalise the coordination in the transcript. We find evidence of partial transfer from NARCBench to these environments, indicating that probes fitted to instructed collusion may not fully capture emergent collusion signals. Overall, we establish multi-agent interpretability as a complementary monitoring technique, while highlighting the need to evaluate detector performance on both emergent and instructed collusion risks.

Multiagent Systems.title: Gossip Agents: Reputation through Opinion Dynamics over Evolving Networks
Multiagent Systems.summary: Sustained cooperation among self-interested learning agents is essential in many shared environments. Reputation systems are among the best-studied mechanisms for promoting such cooperation. Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning approaches, however, typically assume that reputation is either globally available to all agents or derived solely from an agent's own observations, leaving largely unexplored how reputational information propagates between agents. We study gossip, the exchange of information about third parties, as a mechanism for reputation diffusion over dynamic communication networks. Agents form private opinions from limited observations and exchange them with their neighbors following DeGroot opinion dynamics, while the communication network changes as agents interact and move. A tunable broadcast radius controls the reach of information, spanning private reputation, local gossip, and globally shared reputation. We study this framework in two \(n\)-player social dilemmas with distinct network dynamics: a Prisoner's Dilemma with randomly resampled interaction groups and Harvest, where communication neighborhoods emerge from agents' movements. Our results show that the reach of reputational information shapes cooperation in both environments. Moreover, in Harvest, reputation diffusion increases environmental rewards and leads to more peaceful and sustainable behavior.

Multiagent Systems.title: Recursive Organization Improvement: A Modeling Specification for Human--Agent Organizations
Multiagent Systems.summary: Stronger AI agents do not automatically produce better organizations: teams must also learn which work arrangements to retain and when to reconsider them, while those arrangements determine what evidence the team can learn from. We propose a modeling specification for recursive organization improvement and evaluate it through an executable checker, a public-record mapping, and two simulation studies. The specification connects actor-visible histories, organizational memory, decision rights, and the evidence used to retain changes. Study 1 crosses six decision rules, three memory conditions, and three task environments under fixed resource ceilings. In a stationary environment, cumulative evidence raises balanced evaluation's net value per task from 0.452 to 0.480, while selection regret falls from 0.029 to 0.002. After a workflow-ranking reversal, retained evidence delays adaptation. In post hoc acquisition-matched controls, the remaining contribution of program replacement depended on the memory rule: small and uncertain under an eight-round window, positive under cumulative memory after a reversal, and negative under reset evidence. Study 2 models human-agent review with shared errors, copying, and decision rights. It identifies a two-actor case in which public records conceal whether agreement comes from shared errors or copying, and shows how dependence changes the preferred placement of human judgment under a fixed budget. Paid observation can lower decision error while costing more than the deployment gain. Assessments of organizational improvement should track the evidence acquired and retained, using acquisition-matched comparisons to isolate the contribution of evaluator revision.
Multiagent Systems.comment: 23 pages (including references and appendices), 4 figures, 12 tables. Supplementary material: 16 pages, 5 tables (S1-S5)

Multiagent Systems.title: Computational Multi-Agents Society Experiments: Social Modeling Framework Based on Generative Agents
Multiagent Systems.summary: Computational social science has developed descriptive, interpretative, and predictive modeling, but comprehensive modeling combining in-world human intervention with outcome forecasting remains underexplored. Generative agent-based platforms scale populations or reproduce complex scenarios, but researchers typically act through setup, external controls, or post-hoc analysis rather than in-world roles. We introduce Computational Multi-Agent Society Experiments (CMASE), a generative agent-based framework for in-world researcher participation and traceable interventions at runtime. Treating simulation as a simulated ethnographic field, CMASE supports (1) real-time human-computer interaction to study intervention processes; (2) controlled experiments with ethnography-inspired observation, interviewing, and interpretation; and (3) forward exploration of intervention trajectories and downstream responses. CMASE combines LLM-driven perception, memory, and emotion; a composable environment built from texture and area maps; and researcher roles spanning observation, interviewing, participation, and intervention, so that interventions enter as social events rather than exogenous parameters. We replicate two published field studies from different disciplines: urban greenery and social fragmentation, and cooperation in a public goods game, using two substantially different language models. CMASE reproduces reported statistical patterns and provides process-level records for mechanism-oriented interpretation. A controlled comparison shows that embedded social interventions leave observable, auditable processes that parametric manipulation does not. These findings highlight CMASE's methodological value for studying interventions in small- and medium-scale social settings and its interdisciplinary potential. The official code is available at: https://github.com/armihia/CMASE.
Multiagent Systems.comment: Accepted for publication in ACM Transactions on Social Computing (TSC). 36 pages, 6 figures

Multiagent Systems.title: Generalizing Liquid Democracy to multi-agent delegation: A Voting Weight Measure and Equilibrium Analysis
Multiagent Systems.summary: In this study, we propose a generalization of the classic model of liquid democracy that allows fractional delegation of voting weight, while simultaneously allowing for the existence of equilibrium states. Our approach empowers agents to partition and delegate their votes to multiple representatives, all while retaining a fraction of the voting power for themselves. We introduce a penalty mechanism for the length of delegation chains. We discuss the desirable properties of a reasonable generalization of the classic model, and prove that smaller penalty factors bring the model closer to satisfying these properties. In the subsequent section, we explore the presence of equilibrium states in a general delegation game utilizing the proposed voting measure. In contrast to the classical model, we demonstrate that this game exhibits pure strategy Nash equilibria, contingent upon the imposition of a penalty on the length of delegation chains.
