We further show that both channels are exploitable across Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions, a feature intended to provide strong, hardware-enforced isolation between co-located tenants. Using proof-of-concept attacks, we build covert channels that reach roughly 8,500 bits per second through eviction-based signaling and 8,100 bits per second through migration-delay-based signaling across MIG instances. The interrupt-based channel also fingerprints inference workloads across distinct large language models (LLMs) and CPU SPEC2017 benchmarks, and estimates the prompt length processed during LLM inference with high accuracy. These results expose a security gap in hardware-managed heterogeneous memory systems and call into question the isolation guarantees of current MIG-enabled multi-tenant GPU deployments.

Cryptography and Security.title: Does Client Diversity Protect the Lightning Network? Evidence from the 2026 Core Lightning Shutdown
Cryptography and Security.summary: Client diversity is often cited as the Lightning Network's defence against a bug in any one implementation, yet LND runs 84% of public nodes and holds 84% of public channel capacity, a share that has barely moved since 2023. We test what diversity buys with a natural experiment. On 26 August 2026, amid security fixes in every implementation, Core Lightning (CLN) maintainers told operators who could not upgrade to disconnect their nodes. Using 805 daily gossip snapshots, 132,360 on-chain channel closes and a client classifier validated against self-identifying aliases and against the wallet that builds each node's funding transactions, we find that 22% of CLN nodes went dark overnight, ten times the usual rate, mostly Tor-reachable ones; a third were still dark five weeks later. The rest of the network barely noticed. Reachability among all node pairs fell by 7.8 percentage points, a loss exceeded in 4 of 94 ordinary two-day windows and half that of a Tor denial-of-service wave in July, while among CLN pairs it fell by 24.5 points, more than in any ordinary window. Calibrated failure scenarios explain the containment: the blast radius depends on whether a failure reaches the hubs, not on how many nodes run the failing software. Losing ACINQ's Eclair node alone costs the surviving network four times the reachability lost with all 619 routable CLN nodes, and minority clients' reliance on LND for connectivity is what their size implies; CLN nodes in fact peer with each other more than chance. Diversity statistics that count nodes mislead; the quantity to track is which software the hubs run.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 11 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables. Code and aggregate data: https://github.com/bitcoindatalabs/ln-client-diversity

Cryptography and Security.title: Screwtape: Adversarial Transcript Editing for Monitor Red-Teaming
Cryptography and Security.summary: We present Screwtape, a pipeline that converts real agent transcripts into attacks that evade action-only monitors. An LLM attacker edits a transcript so that the agent causes a specified harm, such as leaking an API key or spawning an unmonitored agent. The edited actions are never executed, so we use an LLM verifier to reject attacks that are inconsistent with the original transcript or below a severity bar. The attacker revises the edit until the monitor no longer flags it. We applied Screwtape to 94 Claude Code and Codex transcripts from Redwood Research staff, optimizing against our own monitors. Across 252 runs, it produced 35 attacks that passed the verifier and evaded these monitors. Six of them, confirmed valid by human review, also evaded a held-out monitor provided by a frontier developer. We therefore demonstrate that a red-teamer without access to a developer's infrastructure can find confirmed failures of the developer's monitor. We expect to find more attacks when the pipeline runs inside the developer's infrastructure, with frontier attacker models that lack refusal safeguards and direct optimization against the production monitor. Developers can use these attacks to fix monitor blind spots, and evaluators can use them as counterexamples to safety claims about the monitor.

Cryptography and Security.title: From Detection to Decision: Calibration and Deferral for Prompt-Injection Detection
Cryptography and Security.summary: Prompt-injection defenses are commonly evaluated as binary detectors, although deployed LLM applications must make operational decisions about whether to allow, block, or escalate potentially malicious inputs. Recent probabilistic decision models aim to support such decisions through calibrated confidence estimates, but their reliability under distribution shift remains uncertain. We evaluate a native probabilistic decision model (Jev), two Llama Prompt Guard 2 classifiers (22M and 86M), and an LLM-based judge on 47,611 held-out examples spanning direct and indirect prompt injections, hard-benign inputs, obfuscation, and distribution shift. Using separate development and calibration splits, we assess detection performance, probability calibration, and allow-block-defer policies under a frozen evaluation protocol. The LLM judge achieves the highest overall discrimination (AUROC 0.897), followed by Jev (0.871), Prompt Guard 2 86M (0.757), and Prompt Guard 2 22M (0.714). However, Jev's native probabilities do not consistently outperform post-hoc calibrated classifier scores, and temperature scaling improves calibration without improving discrimination. At an empirical false-negative-rate target of 1%, all evaluated gate-reviewer systems require more than 91.8% escalation and incur substantial false-positive rates. These findings demonstrate that probabilistic outputs alone do not establish reliable security decisions under distribution shift. Effective LLM security systems must jointly evaluate detection, calibration, reviewer behavior, and operational decision policies.

Cryptography and Security.title: Thinking in Graphs: Neo4j-Backed Exploit-Chain Reasoning for LLM Penetration-Testing Agents
Cryptography and Security.summary: LLM coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex can drive penetration-testing tools, but they reason about an engagement as a flat list of findings in a context window. Attackers think in graphs: isolated low-severity exposures turn catastrophic once chained through credential capture, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. This gap feeds a common belief that AI agents cannot truly chain exploitation; we argue this describes the flat context window, not the model. We present ChainGraph, a pattern that externalizes exploit-chain reasoning into a Neo4j property graph wired to an off-the-shelf agent via the Model Context Protocol, no bespoke harness. Findings, attack steps, credentials, assets, and tamper-evident evidence receipts are typed nodes with pre/post-condition edges; JSON/Markdown holds documentary memory while Neo4j holds reasoning memory. We formalize five operator questions (next-step inference, entry-to-crown-jewel pathing, combined-severity promotion, evidence provenance, and chokepoint identification) as reusable Cypher and Graph Data Science queries, plus a chain-severity score distinct from per-finding local severity. On a synthetic multi-forest Active Directory engagement modeled on GOAD, in live Neo4j with GDS, three findings rated Medium in isolation become Critical once their path to the forest root is materialized, and betweenness centrality names the best chain break-points. Scoping each decision to a graph result rather than re-reading the engagement cut the reasoning payload by about 98% on a token proxy. We give a reproducible setup for Claude Code and Codex. Results are illustrative single-run measurements, not a benchmark.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 16 pages, 7 figures, 9 tables, 18 code listings

Cryptography and Security.title: Declared but Unaccountable: Measuring the Seller-Identity Gap in Advertising Supply-Chain Transparency
Cryptography and Security.summary: Public advertising transparency relies on a minimum accountability condition: an account authorized by a publisher in ads$.$txt or app-ads$.$txt should appear in the applicable sellers$.$json registry. When an available registry omits the declared seller ID, the authorization remains visible and machine-readable, but its public verification path breaks. We call this failure the seller-identity gap. We measure the gap using 233.4 million normalized advertising-transparency records and an absent-only, coverage-aware evidence rule. A declaration enters the numerator only when the applicable registry is available and omits its seller ID; unavailable, malformed, confidential, and other non-evaluable states remain separate. The resulting row-level floor is 24.25% in a high-popularity, low-removal reference population and 30.71% among publishers associated with at least 100 copyright-removal requests, a 6.45 percentage-point increase. The gap then remains near one third at stricter cumulative thresholds. Standardizing the populations to common weights over 1,469 shared ad systems reduces the primary contrast to 4.65 points: about 72% remains within systems, while 28% forms a composition-associated residual. We connect these population estimates to recurring seller-account coordinates, byte-identical declaration configurations, and provenance-bearing case packets. We frame this declaration-centered investigative use of public advertising records as Ad Transparency Intelligence: it reconstructs declared supply-chain relationships, identifies where public verification stops, and prioritizes evidence for corroboration without equating correlation with attribution. Advertising transparency supports accountability and investigation only when visible authorizations remain publicly verifiable.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 21 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables. Preprint

Cryptography and Security.title: GhostLock: Learning-Assisted Blind GPS Signal Nullification Without Victim-Side Information
Cryptography and Security.summary: The Global Positioning System (GPS) provides critical positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) services for numerous safety- and mission-critical applications, making it an attractive target for physical-layer attacks. While GPS spoofing and jamming have been extensively studied, GPS Signal Nullification (GSN)-a physical-layer attack that suppresses authentic satellite signals through destructive interference prior to acquisition-remains largely unexplored. Existing wireless signal nullification techniques target conventional communication systems and typically require victim-side information, such as channel estimates or synchronization parameters, making them impractical for GPS. Furthermore, many GPS spoofing defenses assume authentic satellite signals remain available as trusted references, an assumption invalidated by GSN. To address this gap, we present GhostLock, a learning-assisted blind GSN framework requiring only an approximate target location estimate. GhostLock integrates a Blind Adaptive Filter (BAF) with a deep learning-based synchronization module to generate and align an anti-signal using only the attacker's locally received GPS signal, eliminating the need for victim-side observations. We implement GhostLock on a real-time software-defined radio (SDR) platform using GPS-SDR-SIM and GNU Radio. Experimental results demonstrate successful suppression of GPS signal acquisition, establishing the feasibility of blind GSN and motivating new detection and mitigation techniques for this emerging GPS threat model.

Cryptography and Security.title: Performance Characterization of Pulsar's Software-defined Watermark Verifier
Cryptography and Security.summary: Pulsar provides the world's most secure PNT service by incorporating a Combinatorial Watermark into its ranging service. Under conservative signal conditions, Pulsar's Combinatorial Watermark, where 21 ranging code chips are inverted among the 1023, provides 32-bit authentication security each second. In this work, we present our software-defined radio (SDR) implementation of the Pulsar watermark processor. We discuss various threat models, multiple receiver architectures, implications to the receiver, and results from using Pulsar's SDR processing watermarked signals daily from the Pulsar-0 mission. Our results demonstrate the feasible implementation of Pulsar's watermark verification process in commercial GNSS receivers. This is an important milestone in making Xona's Pulsar service available to customers later this year after deployment of our first four production satellites.

Cryptography and Security.title: Privacy-Preserving Text Inference for Health-Misinformation Classification and Semantic Retrieval
Cryptography and Security.summary: Health-misinformation analysis presents a dual challenge: misleading claims can affect public well-being, while systems designed to detect them may expose sensitive user-submitted text. This motivates privacy-preserving inference for public-health applications in which user queries may contain confidential medical information and trained models and reference databases are maintained on organizational servers. We design a privacy-preserving text inference framework based on CKKS homomorphic encryption for health-misinformation classification and semantic retrieval. The classification pipeline fuses BioBERT embeddings, PCA-reduced MPNet embeddings, and SVD-reduced TF-IDF features, while the retrieval pipeline combines MPNet embeddings with ISCC-SCT semantic fingerprints through late fusion. We evaluate predictive performance and benchmark plaintext versus ciphertext-based execution. The hybrid classifier achieved an accuracy of 0.971 and a macro-F1 score of 0.950, with identical reported metrics under plaintext and ciphertext-based inference. The hybrid late-fusion similarity model achieved a Pearson correlation of 0.8691 with human sentence-pair similarity scores on STS-B. For ciphertext-based retrieval, we evaluated naive and optimized implementations. The optimized implementation uses CKKS single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) packing to compute and return multiple similarity scores together, reducing single-query latency over 7,128 indexed items from 222.028 to 5.168 seconds and communication overhead from 6.11 GB to 2.13 MB. These findings demonstrate the technical feasibility of privacy-preserving text inference for health-misinformation applications and characterize its predictive utility and efficiency trade-offs.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Published as a conference paper at SMASH 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: Beyond Boundaries: A Comprehensive Survey of Transferable Attacks on AI Systems
Cryptography and Security.summary: Transferable attacks allow adversarial manipulations or learned attack mechanisms constructed in one setting to compromise other AI systems, potentially reducing attack costs and amplifying security and privacy risks. Yet fragmented terminology and evaluation practices hinder understanding of what transfers, why it transfers, and where transfer fails. This survey synthesizes representative research and develops a unified taxonomy spanning six complementary axes: cross-instance, cross-domain, cross-modality, cross-model, cross-task, and cross-deployment. By separating source-target configuration changes from attacker access and adaptation budgets, the taxonomy provides a common framework for comparing transfer across evasion, poisoning, backdoors, privacy inference, model stealing, and prompt-based attacks. We connect transfer mechanisms, including gradient alignment, shared representations, training persistence, and deployment invariances, to enhancement methods based on augmentation, disentanglement, and optimization. Our synthesis identifies inconsistent transfer, incompatible metrics, and gaps between simulated and physical evaluations, and establishes a research agenda for compositional transfer, configuration differences, temporal persistence, and reproducible benchmarking. Together, this work supports systematic investigation of shared vulnerabilities and guides transfer-aware security assessment and defense.

Cryptography and Security.title: Privacy Foundations for Multi-Institutional Scientific Artificial Intelligence
Cryptography and Security.summary: Scientific artificial intelligence (AI), spanning foundation models (FMs) to federated data-analysis pipelines, is becoming shared infrastructure across national laboratories, universities, hospitals, and industrial partners. This collaboration creates privacy risks whose natural unit is often an institution's participation, research strategy, or technical capability rather than a single record. Differential privacy (DP), federated learning (FL), secure computation, trusted execution, and provenance each protect parts of the stack, but their guarantees rarely compose across mixed-trust institutions, access tiers, and autonomous agents. This perspective recasts privacy for scientific AI as an assurance problem defined by six elements: protected asset, observer, channel, permitted disclosure, guarantee, and evidence. We demonstrate the framing through a claim register for a composite cross-institutional scenario and use it to assess the model lifecycle. Two of the resulting gaps are specific to leadership-class facilities: scheduler, allocation, and telemetry metadata expose an institution's resource posture, and instrument-attached control loops leak research strategy through timing and contention on shared accelerators. We identify six research priorities: institution-level guarantees, agent-communication privacy, cross-tier information flow, privacy-compatible reproducibility, leadership-scale accounting, and instrument side channels. The contribution is a common form for stating, comparing, and auditing claims whose guarantees otherwise remain fragmented across the scientific AI stack.

Cryptography and Security.title: INFUSE: A Unified Surface Benchmark for Indirect Prompt Injection in Agentic Systems
Cryptography and Security.summary: LLM-based agents increasingly execute long-horizon, end-to-end workflows involving shell commands, code modification, dependency installation, and interaction with remote services. This growing autonomy expands their exposure to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where adversarial instructions embedded in external content are interpreted as legitimate task directives. Existing evaluations, however, often focus on isolated malicious strings, single-step tool calls, or narrowly scoped agent configurations. We introduce INFUSE, an end-to-end benchmark for evaluating IPI throughout the lifecycle of long-horizon agent workflows. INFUSE comprises 40 realistic tasks and a structured taxonomy of 56 attack scenarios spanning five threat categories. Attacks are injected through realistic interaction surfaces encountered during task execution, extending evaluation beyond attacks placed only in initial prompts or isolated tool interactions. We evaluate 19 LLMs from the GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Gemma, and Qwen families, producing 41,824 adversarial trajectories (26,220 without defenses) and 720 benign reference runs. Across the benchmark, mean attack success reaches 19.6% under LLM-based evaluation and 15.4% under heuristic verification, with per-model ASR-L ranging from 3.2% to 41.9%. Existing guard models provide limited protection, while prompt-level instructional hardening reduces mean attack success from 58.2% to 14.3%, revealing substantial but model-dependent security-utility trade-offs. Our code is available at https://github.com/judydnguyen/infuse.

Cryptography and Security.title: Foundations of Hardware-Software Leakage Contracts
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Microarchitectural attacks such as Spectre and Meltdown undermine security by exploiting software-visible side effects of microarchitectural optimizations like caches and speculative execution. To use modern hardware securely, programmers must take into account the security implications of these optimizations. Yet instruction set architectures (ISAs)---the conventional abstraction layer between hardware and software---are ill-suited for secure programming: by design, they abstract from microarchitectural details and therefore fail to reflect their security consequences.
  A new security abstraction is emerging to fill this void: hardware-software leakage contracts. To support the principled development of secure software on modern hardware such contracts characterize side-channel leakage at the ISA level. Thereby they enable programmers and compilers to generate code that is provably resistant to side-channel attacks---without having to explicitly reason about the microarchitecture. On the other hand, they provide a specification for hardware designers to ensure that microarchitectures do not introduce unintended and undocumented side channels. This paper introduces the foundations of this emerging topic, discussing recent contributions and unresolved challenges along the way.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Author's manuscript. Final publication is available at Springer via https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-95-8617-2_4

Cryptography and Security.title: AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities
Cryptography and Security.summary: Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited. We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting and executing them only upon receiving a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, these hidden circuits remain provably hard to elicit and interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even given full access to model weights, extending prior work from hiding fixed strings to arbitrary computations. We implement our proof of concept constructions in PyTorch and evaluate elicitation through fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training, using a small chemical reaction prediction task as a proxy for CBRN-relevant capabilities. Our results demonstrate resistance to these methods and, together with our cryptographic guarantees, reveal a limit of elicitation-based capability audits. We release our models to support the improvement of defenses.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 22 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: Prioritizing Microservice Requests via Retries
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Cloud services rapidly shift towards independently-managed microservices architectures. This independence may lead to temporary microservices miscoordination, resulting in overloads and rejections of valuable transactions. This weakness may further be exploited by attackers to launch overload attacks inflicting performance and cost damages.
  Retry operations are a key machinery aiming at overcoming seldom rejections. However, during overload periods they: a) Fail protecting valuable transactions from rejections, and b) Trigger large-scale performance-degrading retry storms.
  We propose simple modifications in retry operations, overcoming these deficiencies by transforming retries into a rejection prioritization mechanism, DiffTry (Differential Retries). It is based on a simple, lightweight, distributed and stateless design and requires neither overload sensing nor microservices coordination.
  We develop an analytical model capturing DiffTry's effectiveness for two services in tandem, then generalize it to networks of services. Our theoretical framework lets practitioners quantify, for a given network, the resulting prioritization and rejection rates, and yields formal guarantees that DiffTry substantially reduces the impact of both incidental and adversarial orchestrated overloads. We validate these predictions in simulation and on a live Kubernetes deployment, where DiffTry is a simple drop-in service-mesh plugin requiring no application changes; the measured rejection closely matches the analysis.

Cryptography and Security.title: Fast Forgiving Base64 Decoding with SIMD Instructions
Cryptography and Security.summary: On the Internet, we use the Base64 format to represent binary data (e.g., images or cryptographic keys) as text. The ES2026 JavaScript standard, following the WHATWG forgiving-base64 rules, requires decoders to ignore ASCII whitespace while rejecting other non-alphabet characters. Prior SIMD Base64 decoders assume whitespace-free input. We present a block-oriented decoding algorithm that removes whitespace inside the SIMD loop: clean 64-character blocks are decoded directly, while blocks with ignorable characters are compacted into a small stack buffer. We provide implementations for x64 (SSSE3 through AVX-512 VBMI2), ARM NEON, and LoongArch. Our C++ decoder reaches up to 94 GB/s on recent AMD Zen 5 processors. In Node 25, integration of our decoder raises Uint8Array.fromBase64 throughput by up to 6x compared with Node 19. The implementation has been adopted by major browsers and JavaScript runtimes.
Cryptography and Security.comment: software at https://simdutf.github.io/simdutf/

Cryptography and Security.title: Quantum-Aware Key Rank for Side-Channel Attacks evaluation
Cryptography and Security.summary: Side-channel attacks on block ciphers rarely recover the key outright: they leave a residual key space ordered by subkey posteriors, and evaluation laboratories report the key rank of the true key against thresholds near 2^48 and 2^60. No evaluation framework models an adversary who collects traces classically and finishes the search on a quantum computer, although quantum search with advice provides exactly that. We give such an adversary a cost model and a metric. For a device whose key has rank r, any quantum algorithm with classical access to the posteriors needs Omega(sqrt(r)) cipher evaluations, and block search achieves O(sqrt(r)); the per-instance advantage is exactly quadratic, and the super-quadratic exponents reported for search with advice are averages over the prior that apply to no single device. Under the NIST MAXDEPTH budget D and a Grover iteration of g gates and depth d, the quadratic advantage holds only for ranks up to (4D/(pi d))^2 and collapses to a constant factor beyond; with the best published AES-128 oracle and D = 2^40 the window closes near rank 2^58.6. We define the quantum-aware key rank, the classical rank of equal cost, computable from the rank estimators laboratories already run, and derive the classical rank a device must retain to keep a given threshold against each depth budget. Block search and amplitude amplification from the product-form posterior state are within a factor of two to four of each other on Hamming-weight posteriors, so the cost of coherent indexing decides between them. Experiments on simulated leakage and a toy cipher confirm the predicted window: at SNR 0.125 a depth-limited quantum adversary is worth about 22 traces to a classical one, however large its gate budget.

Cryptography and Security.title: Tulva: Practical Asynchronous Threshold FHE
Cryptography and Security.summary:
We present Tulva, a practical threshold FHE scheme which equips a base FHE scheme with an asynchronous threshold decryption mechanism in a modular way. Our scheme simultaneously (1) is compatible with virtually any base FHE scheme and leaves its ciphertexts unchanged apart from an appended random tag, (2) supports a wide range of threshold profiles $(t,K)$ and ring degrees $\geq 256$ with 6-25 bits partial decryption per plaintext bit, and (3) achieves security in the presence of partial decryption queries on challenge ciphertexts based on the standard LWE assumption.
  We provide an open-source implementation, benchmark its threshold decryption performance and evaluate the end-to-end costs for typical privacy-preserving Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) use cases. For 16-out-of-512 threshold and a publicly preprocessed ciphertext, computing secret-dependent partial decryption and public share combination requires only 3.7 ms and 0.5 ms, respectively, on commodity hardware. Compared with the state-of-the-art synchronous scheme [Zyskind et al., CCS'25], we replace their ciphertext-independent yet interactive preparation of secret-correlated randomness with a public, ciphertext-dependent 0.5 s preprocessing step, eliminate interaction in the online phase while maintaining similar decryption time on the same machine, and support 32$\times$ more total users.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Full version of the paper accepted at the IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P) 2027. 63 pages

Cryptography and Security.title: From Training to Escalation: Forensic Analysis and Local Recreation of RL/RLHF-Induced Privilege Escalation in AI Agents (CVE-2026-65616)
Cryptography and Security.summary: Mid-2026 reporting on autonomous AI evaluation incidents claimed that frontier large language model (LLM) agents escaped server containment through emergent coordination and cloud infrastructure attacks. This paper contextualizes those claims through forensic analysis and containerized recreation of both the Highly Persistent Internal Model (HPIM) training-case conditions and the Phase One privilege escalation targeting internal package repositories during OpenAI's ExploitGym evaluations. We recreate the configuration of the OpenAI-provided training example and reproduce the cryptographic verification bypass (CVE-2026-65616) in isolated repository servers, where misconfigured systems enabled token forgery and privilege escalation through basic HTTP requests, Python, and JavaScript. Crucially, the training-example conditions and the Phase One (and later) misconfigurations share the same exploitable patterns. Our analysis explains how Zero Trust Architecture principles neutralize this shared attack vector. Contemporary AI risks derive directly from training and deployment conditions in ambivalent learning environments lacking adequate containment measures.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 9 pages, 1 figure. Code and replication environments available at https://github.com/alixiacf/hpim-training-lab DOI:10.5281/zenodo.22817059 and https://github.com/alixiacf/rep-openai-artifactory DOI:10.5281/zenodo.22817059

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Cyclotron: A Recurrence Language for Expressing Interprocessor Communication
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: We present Cyclotron, a compiler that expresses streaming dataflow algorithms using recurrence equations, which are then compiled to distributed topologies of interlinked processors. Our compiler lowers a language of recurrences over logical iteration spaces into per-processor programs of sends, receives, and computations. In these recurrences, data accesses are not limited to external accesses to memory; data can live separately on the iteration space itself, allowing internal points to communicate values directly with other points. Users specify this communication directly in the recurrence language, which allows them to express various communication patterns such as a nearest-neighbor systolic exchange, a one-to-all broadcast, a bidirectional split ring, or an asymmetric and piecewise broadcast pattern, which are often not supported by standard distributed linear algebra libraries. These recurrences describe the algorithm and communication independently of how they map onto the hardware. A programmer then chooses which dimensions execute across processors and which execute over time, without rewriting the entire program. Users only specify data dependencies across the iteration space, and the compiler safely generates a program, per process, with correct placement of both communication and computational operators according to the chosen space--time mapping. We evaluate distributed matrix multiplication, TRSM, Cholesky, and fused Cholesky--TRSM on up to 16 CPU nodes and 16 GPUs, comparing against ScaLAPACK, SLATE, and cuSolverMp. Cyclotron is competitive with and often outperforms these hand-optimized libraries; for Cholesky, the best communication strategy changes with problem size and architecture.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: From Pilots to Production: Lessons in Cross-Institutional Federated Training and Artificial Intelligence for Science
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Many of the most valuable scientific datasets cannot be centralized: they are proprietary, export-controlled, classified, or bound by data-sovereignty restrictions. This inverts the usual paradigm: the model must move to the data, making federated artificial intelligence (AI) core infrastructure for open science. We synthesize lessons from U.S. Department of Energy national laboratories, industry deployments, and the open-source community into a structured account of moving federated AI from pilot demonstrations to dependable, multi-site production. The lessons come from five concurrent efforts spanning leadership-class supercomputers and cloud infrastructure in regulated settings. We organize them around an adapted \textit{five-domain readiness frame} and a stratified view of the stack beneath a trained model: data architecture, privacy and security controls, trust and verification, governance and socio-technical factors, and operations, the layers that decide whether a pilot becomes dependable. The question shifts from ``can we train it?'' to ``can we operate it, audit it, and change it safely?'' We report systems lessons in memory efficiency, reliability, and synchronization; set out what privacy, security, and decentralized trust require in production, and what is not yet validated there; and identify cross-cutting open problems (asynchronous federation, leakage auditing, verification standards, and harmonized data contracts) that we argue warrant a dedicated, international, open-science working group.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Efficient Heuristics and Machine Learning Approach for Fault Characterization in Distributed Self-Stabilizing Programs
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Modern large-scale systems rely on distributed protocols to maximize efficiency while preserving the correctness guarantees of single-process execution. However, designing such protocols is non-trivial: adding resources to a system inherently increases its complexity, which in turn introduces faults that must be addressed during design. One such fault class, arising in systems that use distributed shared memory (e.g., replicated databases), is consistency violating fault (cvf), a fault in which a process accessing shared memory reads stale data previously written by another process. Cvfs are inherent to systems that prioritize availability over strict consistency. Prior work has shown that self-stabilizing programs remain correct under high availability, provided such faults stay within a tolerable bound. Characterizing the behavior of self-stabilizing programs in the presence of cvfs can therefore help system designers build systems that are both correct and efficient. In this paper, we study self-stabilizing programs under cvfs to understand when and where such faults occur, enabling runtime measures that improve computational efficiency. Since exhaustive state-space exploration does not scale, it suffers from state-space explosion; our study investigates two complementary approaches: a conflict-based state-space exploration technique for monotonically stabilizing $(Δ + 1)$-Graph Coloring programs, and a machine-learning-based approach for a Maximal Independent Set program. We propose a conflicting-edges-based state-space exploration algorithm alongside a rigorously validated ML model, evaluated on an out-of-distribution dataset through structural consistency checks against known graph invariants.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 11 pages, 9 figures

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Prioritizing Microservice Requests via Retries
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
Cloud services rapidly shift towards independently-managed microservices architectures. This independence may lead to temporary microservices miscoordination, resulting in overloads and rejections of valuable transactions. This weakness may further be exploited by attackers to launch overload attacks inflicting performance and cost damages.
  Retry operations are a key machinery aiming at overcoming seldom rejections. However, during overload periods they: a) Fail protecting valuable transactions from rejections, and b) Trigger large-scale performance-degrading retry storms.
  We propose simple modifications in retry operations, overcoming these deficiencies by transforming retries into a rejection prioritization mechanism, DiffTry (Differential Retries). It is based on a simple, lightweight, distributed and stateless design and requires neither overload sensing nor microservices coordination.
  We develop an analytical model capturing DiffTry's effectiveness for two services in tandem, then generalize it to networks of services. Our theoretical framework lets practitioners quantify, for a given network, the resulting prioritization and rejection rates, and yields formal guarantees that DiffTry substantially reduces the impact of both incidental and adversarial orchestrated overloads. We validate these predictions in simulation and on a live Kubernetes deployment, where DiffTry is a simple drop-in service-mesh plugin requiring no application changes; the measured rejection closely matches the analysis.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Substep Linearizability: Relaxing Atomicity While Preserving Sequential Specification
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Linearizability is a standard correctness condition for concurrent objects. It takes a correct by construction sequential specification of a concurrent data structure, and produces a composable specification under atomic interleavings of operations. However, some operations like atomic exchangers are not specifiable atomically, making it difficult to reason compositionally about their specifications. Interval linearizability is the state of the art in relaxing linearizability's constraints. Formally it is a powerful framework, but it requires an interval-sequential specification of the target data structure, which we show is challenging to correctly generate or understand, even for simple operations on a single concurrent register. We propose substep linearizability, which we show is equivalent to interval linearizability using X-CCorrectness, a relaxed concurrency framework we created to compare existing linearizability semantics. We show that substep linearizability's sequential specifications are suitable for previously infeasible specification tasks, while being comparable in complexity to linearizability's sequential specifications. For evaluation, we model an atomic exchanger, a popular non-linearizable queue structure, and snapshot isolation between database transactions.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Understanding NVIDIA Grace-Blackwell Unified Memory Through Placement-Controlled Microbenchmarks
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
NVIDIA Grace--Blackwell systems make CPU--GPU memory increasingly unified at the programming level, but unified addressability does not make the memory system uniform. A CUDA managed allocation on GB200 may be served from GPU-local HBM, accessed through host/system memory, demand-migrated, prefetched, reused after GPU access, or evicted and reloaded under capacity pressure. The problem is that these states share a programming interface while exercising different hardware paths and runtime mechanisms, making a single ``Unified Memory bandwidth'' number misleading.
  This paper presents a placement-controlled microbenchmark study of CUDA Unified Memory on NVIDIA GB200, using GH200 as a Grace--Hopper baseline and GB10/DGX Spark as a validation platform. Our methodology separates local HBM access, host/system-memory access, explicit movement, managed first touch, prefetch, reuse, access-pattern sensitivity, oversubscription, and CPU--GPU handoff, then summarizes the observations with a measurement-calibrated model of compute, access, migration, eviction, synchronization, and handoff costs. On GB200, a 1~GB STREAM-style triad reaches 3963~GB/s from local HBM but 304~GB/s through host-mapped CPU/system memory; for a 256~MB streaming kernel, cold CPU-initialized managed memory reaches 14.1~GB/s, while managed prefetch and reuse reach 4606~GB/s and 4504~GB/s. Below the capacity boundary, prefetched and reused managed memory remain above 4.6~TB/s, but at 125\% of CUDA-visible memory they fall to 968~GB/s and 1214~GB/s, showing that Grace--Blackwell unified memory must be understood through placement, access history, locality, reuse, and capacity pressure.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: sGLP: Simulating People with Stochastic Agents
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
Grassroots platforms are designed to be owned, operated and governed by their participants, and thus are constituted from person-to-person smartphone apps that are run by the participants. A grassroots app is specified using a grassroots social contract, which is compiled through an abstraction cascade into a volition-guarded Grassroots Logic Program (vGLP), a multiagent concurrent logic programming language. A vGLP program in turn specifies a smartphone UI via which people express their volitions and thus control the app. Prudence dictates large-scale evaluation and testing of grassroots platforms prior to deployment, but using the many people needed to do that is a contradiction in terms. Hence another solution is needed.
  Here, we present stochastic GLP (sGLP), designed to allow grassroots platforms to be simulated at scale from the vGLP programs that deploy them, with stochastic agents in place of people. sGLP is GLP with a rate extension for specifying stochastic behaviour. A stochastic agent is an sGLP program replacing both the vGLP UI and the person behind it. It is typed by the dual of the interactive type of the UI and specifies a stochastic profile of a person's behaviour.
  We demonstrate sGLP on the grassroots social graph, with a population of men and women drawn from four stochastic profiles --- homophile or indifferent, wary or sociable --- and on grassroots currencies, with four profiles --- spenders or savers, cautious or generous --- and report what the mix of profiles does to the social graph that forms and to the currencies that circulate.
  We prove that every run of a vGLP program in which sGLP agents replace the UI and the people behind it is a vGLP run. We implemented sGLP in GLP by Gillespie's method, and ran reproducible simulations with it.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: TrimSO(2): Fast and Memory-Efficient Training of Equivariant Interatomic Potentials
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Equivariant interatomic potentials enable accurate and efficient simulations of molecules and materials. Among them, models based on SO(2) convolutions reduce the cost of tensor products and achieve state-of-the-art accuracy, but their training remains time-consuming and memory-intensive. Existing training implementations materialize large edge tensors for representation transformations surrounding dense matrix multiplications, increasing memory usage and data movement. We observe that these transformations can be integrated into the model's existing dataflow, avoiding separate intermediate materialization. We introduce TrimSO(2), a fast and memory-efficient algorithm for SO(2)-based equivariant models. It realizes this principle through rotation on gather, recombination with activation, and inverse rotation on reduction, with support for the higher-order differentiation required for training. By avoiding intermediate materialization, TrimSO(2) delivers 2.71-16.73$\times$ operator speedups across forward, backward, and double backward and reduces model-level high-bandwidth memory traffic by 3.81-9.88$\times$. Finally, TrimSO(2) achieves 2.07-2.94$\times$ training speedups and 1.53-3.16$\times$ reductions in peak training memory over PyTorch implementations for official eSEN, UMA, and EquiformerV3 workloads on A100 and H100 GPUs.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: JointServe: Serving Multi-Model Agents on Memory-Constrained GPUs
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: LLM agents are evolving from a single model calling tools to planners that orchestrate multiple expert models whose capabilities live in distinct weights. This shift breaks a hidden assumption of today's serving systems: that the working set of models fits in GPU memory. On the memory-constrained GPUs typical of private and edge deployments, naive whole-model swapping serializes weight transfer with computation and, without host-backed KV restoration, discards session state at a switch. We present JointServe, a serving system that treats weight shards and KV blocks as residency objects competing for one unified memory budget. JointServe exploits three structural properties of agent workloads (directed calls, gapped execution, and dual-state residency) to prepare models before they are called: an intent signal parsed from the caller's own output stream triggers prefetch during generation, partial k* residency reduces switching to incremental layers, and a preemptive transfer scheduler protects live-session KV with a guaranteed bandwidth share. A carve-out control step adjusts the weight/KV allocation as workload demands change. Evaluations show that JointServe reduces session completion time by 21.7% over the strongest whole-model swap baseline and stays usable in a crash regime where every whole-model swap baseline fails to finish (a 46-fold gap). On replayed SWE-bench, tau-bench, and OSWorld traces, it cuts session completion time by up to 49% and lifts SLO attainment from 2.8-24.5% to 76.8-100%.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 18 pages, 12 figures, 1 table

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: The Cost of Context: Profiling the Energy Footprint of Input Tokens in Large Language Models
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: The rapid adoption of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and long-context LLMs has shifted the computational burden toward the prefill phase---the initial stage where the model processes all input tokens in parallel before generating a response---yet its energy impact remains poorly characterised. We investigate the contradiction between massive hardware-level power spikes and the sub-linear marginal cost of input tokens reported in system-level studies. Through high-resolution telemetry of Llama-3.1 and Qwen-2 models on NVIDIA A100 hardware, we identify the efficiency threshold where $O(n^2)$ attention complexity overcomes GPU parallelisation. Our results quantify how optimised memory orchestration (PagedAttention) delays this scaling bottleneck across three orders of context scaling, yielding up to an 8.9$\times$ energy efficiency advantage at 112,000 tokens compared to standard baselines. Furthermore, we characterise the energy disparity between input and output tokens, demonstrating that optimised serving (vLLM) causes this ratio to narrow (from $\approx$850$\times$ to 750$\times$) as context scales due to high decode efficiency, whereas unoptimised baselines show a much smaller, roughly constant gap ($\approx$150--230$\times$) because their prefill is itself expensive. This work establishes context-scaling laws that differentiate engine-level optimisations from inherent model constraints, providing an empirical framework for sustainable LLM deployment.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Accepted at HotCarbon'26, the 5th Workshop on Sustainable Computer Systems; to appear in ACM SIGENERGY Energy Informatics Review, Vol. 6, Issue 2

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Delta Tokenizer: Reference-Identical Tokenization of Session Deltas and Segment-Parallelism for Long Prompts on Multicore CPUs
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
An agent that drives an LLM sends the model the same conversation again and again, and each turn adds only a little text at the end. Inference engines reuse the KV cache of the shared prefix, so only the new tokens pass through the model. However, tokenization has no such shortcut. The CPU front end of the serving engine converts every request back into token IDs from its first character, which lengthens the time to first token (TTFT) and consumes CPU on every turn.
  We present Delta Tokenizer, a CPU tokenization front end that tokenizes only the delta between a request and the previous request of the same session. It retains the earlier token sequence, encodes again only the appended text and the short tail whose tokens the append could affect, and joins the two only at a position the tokenizer's splitting rules themselves cannot move, which keeps the result exact. For long requests with no state to reuse, it cuts the text where practical tokenizers already keep neighboring pieces independent, encodes the pieces on several cores at once, and concatenates the outputs into the reference encoding, exactly. A shared CPU pool schedules these chunks together with the short incremental updates, so an update runs between two chunks rather than behind an entire long job.
  The incremental path shortens the tokenization of a session turn by roughly 40x relative to the Hugging Face reference tokenizer, and on 16 cores the chunk-parallel path encodes a four-million-character request 8.2x faster than a serial encode and 1.6-2.1x faster than LoPT. Inside SGLang, Delta Tokenizer reduces the median TTFT through the chat interface by 59% at 100K tokens and brings the P99 TTFT of agent sessions down 9.5x under load and 23x when long requests tie up the front end. Every output we checked matches the reference, among them 41.8 billion documents encoded by its fast encoder.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 42 pages (16-page main text, references, and supplementary material), 14 figures, 35 tables. The incremental tokenization path and the fast encoder are open source in toktier at https://github.com/asu-idi/toktier. The chunk-parallel path, the CPU pool scheduler, and the SGLang adapter will be released in the same repository

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Computational compressive imaging reconstruction with a simulated-annealing-based Ising solver
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Computational compressive imaging, such as single-pixel imaging and lensless imaging, is a promising imaging technique, enabling the reconstruction of objects from under-sampled measurements through compressed sensing algorithms or deep learning methods. However, the demand for electronic computational resources grows rapidly when recovering high-resolution and multi-dimensional images and training neural networks with numerous parameters, which has become a bottleneck for the widespread adoption of this technique. Here, we propose a physics-driven reconstruction framework that formulates imaging inverse problems as Ising models and directly recovers target objects through the self-evolution of non-von Neumann Ising machines toward the ground state of the Hamiltonian. We employ a simulated-annealing-based Ising solver to demonstrate this proof-of-concept by reconstructing objects in both single-pixel imaging and a lensless diffuser camera at sampling rates ranging from 1% to 25%. By further incorporating a foreground-sparsity constraint and a smoothness constraint, the reconstruction quality of our method is comparable to or even better than that of mainstream algorithms. This approach has the potential to substantially reduce the electronic computational burden of inverse reconstruction, paving the way for real-time, low-power computational imaging.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 15 pages, 6 figures

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Dynamic 3-Coloring of Bipartite Graphs with Optimal Locality
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: We give a dynamic graph algorithm which maintains a 3-coloring in bipartite graphs under edge insertions such that the coloring only changes within a radius of $O(\log n)$ around an inserted edge. In the context of locality theory in distributed graph algorithms, this gives an upper bound on the locality under the dynamic-LOCAL model. Our bound on the locality is tight, as the problem admits a matching $Ω(\log n)$ lower bound in the stronger online-LOCAL model, by a result of Chang et al. [PODC 2024]. Thus, our result closes the gap between dynamic and online locality of this problem.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 18 pages, 2 figures

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: A Self-Defining Operator for Distributed Applications
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: To operate distributed applications with high availability, operators must rapidly diagnose and mitigate any incident. LLM-based agents can help, but unlike experienced human operators they do not improve as they handle more incidents. Each investigation starts from scratch, re-deriving likely causes and re-testing hypotheses even when a similar fault was resolved in the past. We present a self-defining operator (SDO) that improves with time by updating its operational behavior and memory. When SDO resolves an incident, it distills that experience into playbooks, which describe reusable diagnostic instructions for future incidents with similar faults, and detectors, scripts that take application telemetry as input and output relevant playbook(s). SDO continuously runs the detectors and invokes LLMs only when one fires, so its token cost scales with incident count rather than with operational time. Across 11 open-source microservice applications, SDO cuts resolution time by 52% on recurring faults while keeping per-incident cost low. SDO is open source at https://github.com/self-defining-systems/sdo.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Native Dual Pools or Shared Paging? Memory Organization for Concurrent Hybrid LLM Serving
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Hybrid attention-SSM serving combines growing attention KV with fixed-size recurrent and convolution state whose allocation units, reuse boundaries, and lifetimes differ. We implement four memory organizations in a modified vLLM runtime: a coarse shared-page baseline (S0), checkpoint-internal recurrent paging (S1), paging with convolution-slot packing (S2), and native dual pools (D0). Nine evaluation questions cover storage costs and serving behavior. The cumulative S0-S1-S2 refinement improves completed-output throughput and tail completion time at the main operating point. D0-S2 performance varies with memory budget, offered load, and admission headroom. Shared-prefix workloads yield larger stepwise gains; gains also persist in a no-sharing control with equal recorded input-work totals. State traces identify recurrent-checkpoint availability as the limit on joint reuse in the tested S2 runs. Extending producer-side checkpoint lifetime increases reusable depth at a fixed page budget. A fresh-seed SHARE/ISOLATE comparison estimates a positive retention interaction, with a primary confidence interval that includes zero. Retained-state continuation correctness remains unresolved. These findings motivate evaluating physical state representation together with request admission and checkpoint lifetime when designing memory management for concurrent hybrid-model serving.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 10 pages of main text, 31 pages of supplementary appendices. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Real-Time GPU-Accelerated Monte Carlo Evaluation of Safety-Critical AEB Systems Under Uncertainty
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Automatic Emergency Braking (AEB) systems represent a safety-critical national interest, with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard (FMVSS No. 127) requiring AEB in all new light vehicles sold in the United States by September 2029. However, production implementations frequently rely on deterministic stopping-distance or Time-to-Collision (TTC) thresholds that fail to capture uncertainty in sensing, road conditions, and vehicle dynamics. This paper presents a GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo framework for stochastic evaluation of emergency braking performance using a longitudinal vehicle model incorporating aerodynamic drag, road grade, brake actuator dynamics, and weight transfer effects. A one-thread-per-sample execution strategy exploits the independence of Monte Carlo rollouts, while deterministic CPU-generated sampling ensures bit-exact numerical consistency between CPU and GPU implementations. The framework is evaluated across four hardware platforms: two laptop GPUs (GTX 1650, RTX 5070) and two automotive-grade embedded platforms (Jetson Orin Nano, Jetson AGX Orin). Peak speedups of 54.57x are achieved. Real-time feasibility analysis with a complete AEB timing budget demonstrates that the Jetson AGX Orin can execute approximately 25,000 Monte Carlo samples within a 530 ms budget, enabling real-time probabilistic AEB evaluation as part of a complete embedded pipeline. Collision probability analysis demonstrates that a threshold set at the mean stopping distance of 79.2 m leaves a collision probability of approximately 47%, while the conservative 1% risk threshold requires a minimum safe headway of 111.1 m, an additional 31.9 m (40%). These results provide quantitative guidance for risk-aware AEB threshold selection under the NHTSA final rule.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 11 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to IEEE journal for possible publication; under review

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: How the Dirty Set Moves: Characterizing Schedule Reuse in Incremental Sparse Matrix Multiplication
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Sparse matrices, in which most entries are zero, are central to scientific simulation, graph analytics and machine learning, and their multiplication with dense inputs is a core parallel kernel. In many applications the matrix stays fixed while only a few input rows change per step, so the result can be updated from those rows alone, which we call the dirty set. Sparse kernels often add a second optimization based on the inspector-executor principle, in which a tiled schedule is prepared once and reused across calls. However, when this reuse remains profitable as the dirty set moves is not well characterized. In this paper, we show that retained tiled execution rarely beats direct CSC in incremental sparse matrix multiplication, although incremental execution itself remains highly profitable. Across 21 SuiteSparse matrices and controlled patterns of motion, a direct column-wise incremental update is 2.1-8.2x faster than the best of eight full-recomputation codes, among them Intel oneMKL and PyTorch. Yet the same direct update outperforms a tiled executor that retains tile preparation and caches assembled schedules in 779 of 837 workloads. Separating reuse into per-tile preparation and cached schedules shows that the benefit comes from preparation; extra cache capacity seldom helps because a tile set rarely returns after a different one has intervened. Tiling is faster only when tiles merge many entries into each output write, a structural property that we predicted before measurement and confirmed on four held-out matrices of the same family. These results show that the structure of the matrix and the motion of the dirty set, rather than the sophistication of the schedule, determine whether reuse is profitable. We anticipate that our methodology and guidelines will help developers decide when to build schedule reuse into incremental sparse runtimes.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, 8 tables

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Konflux: Optimized Function Fusion for Serverless Applications
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) has become a central paradigm in serverless cloud computing, yet optimizing FaaS deployments remains challenging. Using function fusion, multiple functions can be combined into a single deployment unit, which can be used to reduce cost and latency of complex serverless applications comprising multiple functions. Even in small-scale applications, the number of possible fusion configurations is vast, making brute-force benchmarking in production both cost- and time-prohibitive.
  In this paper, we present a system that can analyze every possible fusion setup of complex applications. By emulating the FaaS platform, our system enables local experimentation, eliminating the need to reconfigure the live platform and significantly reducing associated cost and time. We evaluate all fusion configurations across a number of example FaaS applications and resource limits. Our results reveal that, when analyzing cost and latency trade-offs, only a limited set of fusion configurations represent optimal solutions, which are strongly influenced by the specific pricing model in use.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Accepted for publication in Proceedings of the 14th IEEE International Conference on Cloud Engineering (IC2E '26), October 13-16, 2026, Santa Clara, CA, USA. IEEE

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Beyond the Trial-and-Error Loop: Hybrid Projection and Automated Tuning for Distributed Training
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Configuring distributed LLM training across hundreds of GPUs requires jointly optimizing tensor, pipeline, expert, context, and data parallelism alongside micro-batch size, recomputation, sharding, and overlap, a combinatorial space where memory legality can hinge on a single byte of activation accounting. Today, teams navigate it through expensive multi-node trial and error, burning GPU-hours on crashes and suboptimal recipes. We present Primus Projection, which closes this loop with two coupled components. First, a hybrid projection engine that measures what it can and simulates what it cannot: GPU microbenchmarks on as few as a single device capture compute kernels and any in-scope communication; a sub-node downscale-measure-upscale workflow analytically restores out-of-scope collectives, FSDP overlap, and the full pipeline schedule at the multi-node target. A pure simulation mode runs entirely on CPU, enabling pre-silicon planning without any GPU. Second, the Primus Tuning Agent treats the projection engine as a fast scoring oracle (seconds per candidate instead of tens of minutes) and uses it to drive an intelligent search over the configuration space. A deterministic seed planner sweeps single axes; an LLM investigation loop proposes cross-axis combinations the planner cannot reach, with an analytic memory pre-filter that rejects infeasible candidates before any GPU time is spent. Validated on Llama 3.1 (dense) and Mixtral 8x22B (MoE) across two GPU generations, all projections stay within ~10% of measured multi-node throughput, and fidelity holds at production scale: 4.7% error on DeepSeek V3 671B at 1,024 GPUs and 1.9% on Qwen3-235B-A22B at 256 GPUs. In a Mixtral 8x22B case study, the Primus Tuning Agent discovers a configuration delivering +27% throughput over the published 4-node BF16 reference at the same scale, in under 30 minutes of single-node exploration.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 22 pages, 8 figures, 25 tables

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Arcturus: A Cloud Overlay Network for Global Accelerator with Enhanced Performance and Stability
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Global Accelerator (GA) services play a vital role in ensuring low-latency, high-reliability communication for real-time interactive applications. However, existing GA offerings are tightly bound to specific cloud providers, resulting in high costs, rigid deployment, and limited flexibility, especially for large-scale or budget-sensitive deployments. Arcturus is a cloud-native GA framework that revisits the design of GA systems by leveraging low-cost, heterogeneous cloud resources across multiple providers. Rather than relying on fixed, high-end infrastructure, Arcturus dynamically constructs its acceleration network and balances performance, stability, and resource efficiency. To achieve this, Arcturus introduces a two-plane design: a forwarding plane that builds a proxy network with adaptive control, and a scheduling plane that coordinates load and routing through lightweight, quantitative optimization. Evaluations under millions of RPS show that Arcturus outperforms commercial GA services by up to 1.7X in acceleration performance, reduces cost by 71%, and maintains over 80% resource efficiency--demonstrating efficient use of cloud resources at scale.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Out of date

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Scaling LLM Inference via Parallelism: Throughput-Latency Trade-off
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Large Language Model (LLM) serving systems must balance latency and throughput while efficiently utilizing distributed GPU resources. This challenge arises because inference consists of two fundamentally different phases: prefill, which determines time-to-first-token (TTFT), and decode, which determines inter-token latency (ITL). The use of tensor parallelism (TP), pipeline parallelism (PP), and hybrid configurations exposes different trade-offs between these latency dimensions, making the optimal parallelism configuration highly dependent on workload characteristics, latency requirements, and context length. Moreover, despite the widespread adoption of distributed inference, there is still limited understanding of how parallelism configurations should be selected under varying workload conditions and service-level objectives (SLO). In this paper, we develop a systematic framework for characterizing LLM inference parallelism via throughput-latency trade-offs, SLO-aware serving, and long-context scalability. We introduce the notion of parallelism operating regions by constructing TTFT-ITL feasible sets and Pareto frontiers across different workload compositions, thereby revealing a systematic transition from TP-dominant to PP-dominant configurations as workloads become increasingly prefill-heavy. We further formulate SLO-aware parallelism selection using goodput, showing that stringent TTFT requirements favor PP-dominated configurations, whereas relaxed latency constraints progressively shift the optimality toward TP-dominated configurations with higher serving capacity. Finally, we demonstrate that increasing context length fundamentally changes the relative advantages of parallelism configurations, with PP-dominant configurations exhibiting more favorable scalability and SLO attainment in the long-context regime.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 15 pages, 7 figures

Discrete Mathematics.title: The Komlós Problem in Matrix-Multiplication Time
Discrete Mathematics.summary: We give a randomized algorithm that, for an $m\times n$ matrix whose columns have Euclidean norm at most one, finds a signing with discrepancy below $99$ in expected $\widetilde O(L_{\mathrm{in}}+n^ω)$ bit operations, where $L_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the input encoding length and $ω$ is the exponent of matrix multiplication. The previous fastest algorithm with a constant discrepancy bound, due to Li, is deterministic and uses $O(mn+n^{ω+2}\log^3 n)$ arithmetic operations. We build on the spectral signing framework of Guo, Fang, and Lu and of Li, which rounds a single fractional coloring while one spectral potential controls every row. Li's potential tracks a top eigenvalue, and the gap below that eigenvalue, which can be of order $1/n$, limits the length of every step. We replace it with a resolvent potential that is smooth without any gap condition, and we draw step signs at random, so that the potential only needs to be concave while progress is measured separately. Our key insight is to reuse a single subspace of directions throughout a batch of steps, thereby using only one spectral computation, so that the more expensive linear algebraic operations are paid for only polylogarithmically often at each scale. Within a batch, we sample directions from a Gaussian completion matrix whose inverse we maintain under rank-one row replacements. Finally, we use a finite-precision analysis to prove stability of the algorithm and attain the bit-complexity bound.

Discrete Mathematics.title: Symmetric, rational and infinitely many $(23_4)$ configurations, and the end of the existence problem for geometric $(n_4)$ configurations
Discrete Mathematics.summary: A geometric $(n_4)$ configuration is a set of $n$ points and $n$ lines in the real projective plane such that every point lies on exactly four of the lines and every line contains exactly four of the points. The question of which $n$ admit such a configuration was posed by Grünbaum in 2000, and successive work of Bokowski, Grünbaum, Schewe, Pilaud and Cuntz settled every case but $n=23$. We settle this last case by bounding the symmetry of such configurations and classifying the most symmetric ones exactly. We prove that for every prime $n\equiv3\pmod4$ the group of projective symmetries of a geometric $(n_4)$ configuration has order at most four, explaining why symmetric constructions failed at $n=23$, and the same argument bounds the symmetry of $(n_5)$ configurations for primes $n\not\equiv1\pmod5$. Reducing the Klein four-group case to 4021 bilinear polynomial systems and solving all of them exactly with Gröbner bases, we show that exactly two $(23_4)$ configurations reach this bound up to projective equivalence and that there are no others even over $\mathbb{C}$. Both are self-polar; the first has integer coordinates and the second is defined over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{17})$ but not over $\mathbb{Q}$. Consequently geometric $(n_4)$ configurations exist if and only if $n\ge18$ and $n\ne19$. The same classification recovers Cuntz's $(22_4)$ and $(26_4)$ configurations and finds three new combinatorial types at $n=22$ and $94$ at $n=26$. Among self-polar $(23_4)$ configurations with a single involution we find $50$ more, defined over number fields of degree at most $7$. Four of them deform in one-parameter families, and computing three of these exactly, one birational to the modular curve $X_1(11)$, we prove that there are infinitely many geometric $(23_4)$ configurations, among them infinitely many with rational coordinates that are self-polar and have no projective symmetry.

Discrete Mathematics.title: Automating Observable Closure Analysis for Graph Transformation Models with MolFoundry
Discrete Mathematics.summary: Graph transformations model changing systems, with applications in software, biology and chemistry, among others. We introduce MolFoundry, a graph transformation framework, and present a workflow for observable analysis that tracks the dynamics of local patterns through rule composition. Analysing rule compositions avoids the need to enumerate a potentially infinite state space. Building on rule-algebraic stochastic rewriting, MolFoundry's kernel composes rules with nested application conditions, including missing-edge constraints. Given rules, rates and query patterns, the algorithms iteratively identify auxiliary pattern counts and search for closure. Using exact counting identities supplied by graph-family backends, successful searches yield closed ordinary differential equations for average counts or, with justified individual jumps, finite event models describing joint changes and rates. We evaluate conditional composition and automated discovery of auxiliary observables against published calculations and independent rule application. Applications to aldol addition, copolymerization and chlorination show how the framework yields quantitative predictions directly from molecular graph rules.
Discrete Mathematics.comment: 30 pages, including appendices. Software: https://github.com/dmerkle/molfoundry-observables . Interactive examples and executable notebooks: https://stochmech.algochem.techfak.de/

Discrete Mathematics.title: Claw-Free and Line Graph Edge Deletion on Block Graphs
Discrete Mathematics.summary: Edge deletion problems ask for the fewest edges whose deletion gives a graph with a specified property. We study two such problems on block graphs. First making the graph claw-free, and second making it a line graph. Since every line graph is claw-free, the second problem is at least as difficult as the first. We show that on block graphs the two optimum values are always equal, and both are attained by the line graph of a forest. The main step is a completion argument, in which starting from any claw-free solution, we put back edges to get some nice structure inside each block still maintaining the claw-free property. This reduces both edge-deletion problems to the same problem of selecting vertices within the blocks of the input graph. We solve it by dynamic programming in $O(n+m)$ time, which also produces an optimal deletion set and a forest whose line graph is what remains after the completion argument. We also extend the method to $K_{1,r+1}$-free edge deletion for every fixed $r$.

Discrete Mathematics.title: Potatoes and Onions
Discrete Mathematics.summary:
The first major step in the theory of graph minors of Robertson and Seymour was the grid theorem, a fundamental duality result describing that any graph of sufficiently high treewidth must contain a large grid as a minor. Since this pioneering work, multiple grid theorems have been established in structural graph theory, linking various width parameters of combinatorial objects with the non-existence of grid-like obstructions. In particular, Kawarabayashi and Kreutzer [STOC'15] proved a variant of the grid theorem for directed graphs that links directed treewidth with the non-existence of topological minors of large cylindrical walls. On the other hand, to study immersions of undirected graphs $-$ another containment relation that focuses on edge-disjointness, rather than vertex-disjointness $-$ Wollan [JCTB'15] introduced a parameter, tree-cutwidth, and proved that it is dual to immersions of large walls.
  In this work, we present a version of Wollan's parameter for directed graphs, the directed tree-cutwidth. The main result is a grid theorem for directed tree-cutwidth, establishing that it is dual to directed immersions of large cylindrical walls.
Discrete Mathematics.comment: This work has been accepted for presentation at SODA 2027

Discrete Mathematics.title: Sparse universal graphs for planarity
Discrete Mathematics.summary: We show that for every integer $n\geq 1$ there exists a graph $G_n$ with $(1+o(1))n$ vertices and $n^{1 + o(1)}$ edges such that every $n$-vertex planar graph is isomorphic to a subgraph of $G_n$. The best previous bound on the number of edges was $O(n^{3/2})$, proved by Babai, Chung, Erdős, Graham, and Spencer in 1982. We then show that for every integer $n\geq 1$ there is a graph $U_n$ with $n^{1 + o(1)}$ vertices and edges that contains induced copies of every $n$-vertex planar graph. This significantly reduces the number of edges in a recent construction of the authors with Dujmović, Gavoille, and Micek.
Discrete Mathematics.comment: v5: corrects an error in the proof of Lemma 20

Discrete Mathematics.title: On Partial Optimality in QUBO via Quadratic Posiform Autarkies
Discrete Mathematics.summary: Partially optimal assignments (also called persistencies) allow combinatorial optimization problems to be reduced by fixing a subset of variables to values consistent with at least one optimal solution. For the quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem, such assignments can be computed efficiently via autarkies of quadratic posiforms. However, the largest autarky domain and thus the number of fixed variables can depend on the specific posiform representation. We show that every quadratic posiform with the greatest possible constant term (the roof-dual bound) yields the largest autarky domain obtainable from any quadratic posiform. By computing such a roof-dual-optimal quadratic posiform and a corresponding autarky with largest domain in polynomial time, one can therefore attain the maximum partial optimality obtainable by quadratic posiform autarkies in polynomial time. This justifies the computation of roof-dual-optimal quadratic posiforms and corresponding autarkies in popular polynomial-time algorithms and establishes that finding additional partial optimality in QUBO requires going beyond autarkies of quadratic posiforms.

Discrete Mathematics.title: Exploring the unleaved tree of numerical semigroups up to a given genus
Discrete Mathematics.summary: We present a new algorithm for exploring or counting the numerical semigroups of a given genus that uses the unleaved version of the tree of numerical semigroups. In the unleaved tree there are no leaves rather than the ones at depth equal to the genus in consideration. For exploring the unleaved tree we present a new encoding system of a numerical semigroup given by the gcd of its left elements and its shrinking, that is, the semigroup generated by its left elements divided by their gcd. We show a method to determine the right generators and strong generators of a semigroup by means of the gcd and the shrinking encoding, as well as a method to encode a semigroup from the encoding of its parent or of its preceding sibling. With the new algorithm, we obtained $n_{76}=29028294421710227$ and $n_{77}=47008818196495180$.

Discrete Mathematics.title: Routes planning in a condominium company using mathematical optimization
Discrete Mathematics.summary: This work focuses on planning daily routes for a group of employees of a condominium company. Given a set of employees and a set of customers with pre-scheduled visits, we want to build doubly-open routes to guarantee visits to all customers, ensuring that each customer is visited by an employee with the appropriate skills to carry out the required activity. The travel times between customers and the service time in each customer are known. The problem includes time windows for visiting customers, each employee has a maximum working time, and the daily working period is between 9 AM and 6:30 PM. The routes respect the lunch break period if they extend from morning to afternoon, which means that lunch break can be avoided if the route is fully completed in the morning or in the afternoon. The aim is to minimize the distance covered by all routes with a penalty for including lunch breaks. The distances and times between customers are collected via an API to Microsoft Azure; and the solutions are then displayed on Bing Maps. The results obtained show the operational advantages of an efficient and effective vehicle routing planning in a specific condominium management company.
