High-fidelity simulations resolve geometry-controlled flow but are computationally expensive across large geometry ensembles. Here, we introduce GeONet, a Geometry-Encoded Operator Network that predicts steady-state pressure fields by jointly representing material properties, spatial coordinates, and solid--void geometry. GeONet extends the Branch--Trunk architecture with a dedicated Leaf Network encoding the binary domain mask through multiscale features. The Branch Network represents porosity and permeability, the Trunk Network combines coordinates with local geometric descriptors and random Fourier features, and a gated DeepMixer integrates these representations to predict pressure. GeONet was trained and evaluated using 5,000 PFLOTRAN simulations of heterogeneous Reduced Complexity Platform domains, comprising nearly 30 TB of data. Comparisons with pore-scale Stokes solutions across three geometries yielded Pearson correlations of 0.987--0.991 and $R^2$ values of 0.974--0.982, supporting PFLOTRAN as reference data. Under matched partitions and two-stage hyperparameter optimization, GeONet substantially outperformed a boundary-condition-aware DeepONet baseline. Across three held-out domains, GeONet achieved NRMSE of 0.0381--0.0500, MAPE of 1.76--2.59%, and $R^2$ of 0.9673--0.9822, versus 0.1483--0.2040, 7.81--10.45%, and 0.5658--0.7126 for DeepONet, respectively. On three additional unseen geometries, GeONet achieved NRMSE of 0.0448--0.0676 and $R^2$ of 0.9511--0.9770. These results demonstrate improved accuracy, pressure-range preservation, and cross-geometry generalization through explicit geometry encoding.

Computational Physics.title: A nonequilibrium-capturing unified gas-kinetic scheme I: discrete orthogonal basis construction and expansion on velocity space
Computational Physics.summary: Velocity space discretization is a primary source of computational cost in deterministic methods for multiscale gas flows. A fixed velocity grid often retains redundant kinetic degrees of freedom (DOFs), particularly under near equilibrium conditions. To address this issue, this work develops a nonequilibrium-capturing formulation based on the unified gas kinetic scheme (UGKS), in which the number of kinetic DOFs adapts locally to the degree of nonequilibrium. A discrete orthogonal basis is constructed for numerical implementation, and the velocity distribution function is decomposed into an analytical local equilibrium and a basis expanded nonequilibrium component. The retained, locally adapted DOFs are evolved directly, substantially lowering computational overhead while preserving the discrete conservation of mass, momentum, and energy, as well as accurately capturing nonequilibrium states. The formulation retains the core multiscale coupling of molecular transport and collision inherent to UGKS, providing explicit and implicit schemes for unsteady and steady flows, respectively. Numerical tests across a wide range of flow speeds and rarefaction regimes (from continuum to highly rarefied) demonstrate close agreement with benchmark solutions. For unsteady flows, the explicit scheme achieves speedups of 12.64 to 58.50 over the standard UGKS. In steady state tests, only about $2\%$ of the original kinetic DOFs are required in continuum regions, accelerating each implicit iteration by a factor of 33.87. Even in the most rarefied cases, the scheme captures nonequilibrium behavior using only about $27\%$ of the original DOFs.

Computational Physics.title: High-level, efficient ocean modeling at all scales with Oceananigans
Computational Physics.summary: We describe the user interface, governing equations, and numerical methods underpinning the ocean modeling software called "Oceananigans". Oceananigans development has been led by the Climate Modeling Alliance as part of a larger effort to build a trainable climate model with quantifiable uncertainty. Notably, Oceananigans is written in the Julia programming language, is optimized for GPUs, and can efficiently simulate all scales of ocean motion ranging from millimeter-scale turbulence in a small box to planetary-scale ocean circulation. We argue that this combination of capabilities is enabled by a design that combines a basic, easy-to-optimize, GPU-friendly structured finite volume algorithm exposed behind a high-level, programmable user interface. This design negotiates a dual mandate for highest-possible performance (to support state-of-the-art applications) and enhanced accessibility (to facilitate adoption and development). The dual mandate aims ultimately to accelerate the progress of Earth system science.
Computational Physics.comment: 50 pages; revised exposition, updated examples and references, and corrections to equations and code listings

Computational Physics.title: An implicit multiscale solver for steady kinetic equations based on wave-particle decomposition
Computational Physics.summary: Steady kinetic computations require accurate transport on meshes that do not resolve the mean free path and efficient removal of slowly decaying macroscopic errors. We develop a closed wave-particle decomposition (WPD) and a residual-based implicit solver for this problem. The wave accumulates only the Maxwellian along a local characteristic horizon and is determined by the conservative variables; the particle carries the kinetic complement and collision remainder. Under moment compatibility, the closed system is equivalent to the kinetic equation. For the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook and Shakhov models, a hydrodynamic expansion gives the wave and particle contributions to the Euler and Navier-Stokes fluxes. The implicit iteration couples macroscopic prediction to microscopic correction through a discrete endpoint term and synchronizes the conservative moments after each accepted correction. Its stationary states satisfy the target discrete kinetic equation independently of the iteration controls. Formal analysis gives the smooth fixed-mesh fluid limit. Linear model analysis relates convergence to the horizon-to-relaxation ratio, incomplete macroscopic solves and explicit collision remainders. One- and two-dimensional computations of a normal shock, internal flows and hypersonic external flows test these properties across rarefied and continuum regimes. The results show kinetic fidelity and substantial reductions in iteration counts and wall time relative to the conventional iterative scheme near the continuum limit. Collision-model comparisons and parameter studies support the predicted convergence mechanisms.
Computational Physics.comment: 63 pages, including 44 pages of main text and 19 pages of supplementary material

Computational Physics.title: How deterministic trajectories and their fluctuations underlie allele-frequency statistics in the strong-selection regime
Computational Physics.summary:
We determine statistics of allele-frequency trajectories across replicate populations. Defining $R = 2N_e|s|$ where $N_e$ is the effective population size and $s$ is the additive selection coefficient of a focal allele, we focus on strong selection which corresponds to $R \gg 1$. Strong selection does not require large selection coefficients: in populations of realistic size, it can readily arise from small selection coefficients. Our analysis concerns a biallelic locus over timescales on which mutation can be neglected. Every allele-frequency trajectory belongs to one of two absorbing classes: fixation or loss.
  When $R$ is large, individual allele-frequency trajectories can appear nearly deterministic. This does not imply that an approximation of allele-frequency statistics can be based on a single deterministic trajectory. For a beneficial allele, the deterministic trajectory approaches fixation, yet a non-negligible fraction of stochastic trajectories may be lost. Ignoring trajectories that achieve loss can produce severely erroneous statistics. We address this by conditioning separately on the eventual loss and eventual fixation of the focal allele. This yields an outcome-conditioned representation of a statistic. In the strong-selection regime, we apply a small-noise expansion that reasonably captures transient behaviours of statistics while recovering their exact long-time limits. We illustrate results with numerical examples for the mean allele frequency and its variance.
  The biological interpretation of this work is that, even under strong selection, both trajectory types are of importance. We provide a simple framework for calculating time-dependent allele-frequency statistics relevant to experimental evolution, longitudinal population-genomic data, and the dynamics of alleles driving selective sweeps.

Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.title: Dynamic models with $p$ parameters are identified by $2p+1$ random features
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.summary: A foundational principle in nonlinear dynamics is that the structure of a dynamical system can be recovered from a small number of generic measurements or coordinates. We develop an analogous principle for the identification of dynamic models for time series \textit{with noise}, which builds on previous identification results for noiseless dynamical systems. The noise is allowed to be non-iid, non-Gaussian, and dependent on the state. Our results cover noisily observed differential equations and discrete-time dynamical systems, as well as stochastic models with process noise. We illustrate the utility of this identification principle using a Lorenz-63 model and a Hénon map model, both with observational noise.

Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.title: Estimating dynamic models by matching random features
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.summary: Scientists increasingly express their ideas as dynamic models of complex processes. It is often much easier to simulate these models than to calculate the probability of their generating a particular outcome, making likelihood-based estimation infeasible. Existing likelihood-free approaches rely either on manually chosen summary statistics or on representations learned by neural networks. The former is error-prone and laborious, while the latter is computationally intensive, leaving many scientists in a difficult position. We show that, for a large class of dynamic models, parameters can be estimated by matching a small number of random features of the observed and simulated data. In particular, we show that models with a $p$-dimensional parameter can be identified from just $2p+1$ generic random Fourier features. We introduce two estimators for stationary and nonstationary processes, respectively, and we establish their consistency under mild regularity conditions. More broadly, our results serve as the foundation for a new class of methods for simulation-based inference.

Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.title: Hyperstatistics
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.summary: We propose a general approach, named by us hyperstatistics, to treat complex systems, in which Boltzmann-Gibbs statistics breaks down at the domain level of the system. Hyperstatistics preserves the concavity of the nonadditive $q$-entropy. We obtain analytical closed-form expressions for the here proposed ($q, n$)-generalized Boltzmann factor $B_q^{n}$ considering uniform, $γ$, Log-normal, F, and the $q$-$γ$ probability distribution functions. Remarkably, for all investigated distribution functions, $B_q^{n}$ reduces to a $q$-exponential-type function. To demonstrate the applicability of hyperstatistics, we use a table top experiment of the discharge of a capacitor considering $γ$-distributed relaxation times, the pressure decay over time associated with the pumping of $^4$He lines of a closed cycle cryostat, midrapidity data for $\textit{p}$-Pb collisions at the LHC, as well as data set for acceleration distribution in turbulent systems. Furthermore, we deduce the power-law-like $\textit{universal}$ dielectric response using a $q$-generalized $γ$-distribution function proposed in this work. Hyperstatistics is applicable to systems with inherent non-Boltzmann-Gibbsian statistics at the domain level. We demonstrate that at the domain level hyperstatistics and superstatistics are equivalent, while at the macroscopic level hyperstatistics recovers superstatistics for $q \to 1$ because the Boltzmann-Gibbs character of the domains is restored, as well as Boltzmann-Gibbs statistics for $n \to \infty$.
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.comment: 34 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Supplementary material upon request. This version includes a macroscopic generalized hyperstatistical Boltzmann factor $B_H$

Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.title: Anomaly detection for multijet scenarios
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.summary: Signals of physics beyond the Standard Model continue to resist discovery at the LHC. Recent years have seen the proliferation of new anomaly detection techniques, promising discovery with significantly fewer model assumptions than traditional approaches. Strategies based on weak supervision have been especially successful, but so far were largely limited in scope by their reliance on a resonance manifesting a decay into a pair of jets. In this work, we demonstrate that a well-established idea from jet substructure physics - recursive soft drop - in combination with the CATHODE technique for anomaly detection can be used to simultaneously perform anomaly detection for signals with an arbitrary number of jets in the final state, greatly increasing the scope of such searches.
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables

Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.title: Data-driven reconstruction of spatiotemporal phase dynamics for traveling and oscillating patterns via Bayesian inference
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.summary: Building on the phase reduction theory formulated for reaction-diffusion systems with spatial translational symmetry, we develop a data-driven method that reconstructs the spatiotemporal phase dynamics of traveling and oscillating patterns. Spatiotemporal phase dynamics are described by spatial and temporal phases that represent the position and oscillation of the pattern, respectively. Using Bayesian inference, our method directly reconstructs phase equations from time-series data. When tested on simulation data from coupled Gray-Scott models exhibiting traveling breathers, the method accurately reconstructs the deterministic part of the phase equations in the weak-noise regime, in which the phase dynamics converge to a linearly stable fixed point.
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.comment: 23 pages, 13 figures

Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.title: The BRUIT-FM "open data" noise reduction challenge
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.summary: The BRUIT-FM Challenge asks participants to reduce ''noise'' --- defined as any signal that masks the signal of interest --- on an open dataset of real and synthetic broadband seafloor seismology data. The dataset includes signals from earthquakes, ocean infragravity waves and seafloor currents. It also includes training datasets of synthetic data with reference solutions. Participants are asked to remove or separate these signals to obtain the best earthquake and seafloor compliance signals. The authors will make a first assessment of the submissions, based on noise reduction, signal deformation and ease of use. Participants are invited to a community workshop, in which they will validate the preliminary assessment and collaborate on a community paper describing the results, identifying promising pathways and proposing new directions. The best results will be added to a new version of the dataset, which will persist as a benchmark for future developments.

Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.title: Intrinsic instantaneous coarse-to-fine recoverability in multiscale chaos: The Lorenz-96 system
Data Analysis Statistics and Probability.summary: In multiscale chaotic systems, a central question for closure is how much of an unresolved fine-scale target can be inferred from a simultaneous coarse observation. For a specified observation-target pair, we quantify instantaneous recoverability under the invariant snapshot measure as the fraction of target variance explained by conditioning on the retained coarse variables. Evaluating this quantity across scales produces a scale-resolved recoverability map. Applied to the Lorenz-96 system across a range of forcings, the maps reveal a strongly nonuniform landscape: lower-wavenumber targets have little variance explained by the retained lower modes, while a finite band of higher modes exhibits partial recoverability once the retained scales reach the energetically active intermediate range. Recoverability onset is organized around a reference cutoff at which two retained modes can directly couple to the target through the quadratic nonlinearity, although its precise location depends on attractor statistics. Across the tested forcings, this qualitative onset structure persists while recoverability decreases, leaving a larger fraction of target variance unexplained in more strongly driven regimes. This definition identifies the maximal explained-variance fraction attainable by instantaneous deterministic models under squared loss; the estimated maps provide a scale-dependent diagnostic for closure modeling.

Medical Physics.title: A single radiation hard pixel detector for proton dosimetry, imaging, energy resolution and beam monitoring
Medical Physics.summary: Proton therapy enables highly conformal tumour irradiation by exploiting the Bragg peak. Clinical precision relies on detector systems that provide linearity, spatial resolution, radiation hardness, and, for ultra-high-dose-rate (FLASH) therapy, high dynamic range with sufficient temporal response. No compact all-in-one solution currently fulfils all these requirements. Here, we present pixelated gallium nitride (GaN) arrays as a multifunctional platform. These detectors exhibit high linearity (proton currents from 70 to 1700 pA cm-2) and signal uniformity below 2% across 128 pixels. To probe GaN radiation hardness, we applied cumulative doses up to 6.7 MGy at energies from 25 MeV down to the Bragg-peak regime. Locally deposited dose dictates long-term signal loss, yet devices preserve linearity and spatial response. We demonstrate 0.25 mm effective spatial resolution, validated against radiochromic film. Proton radiography resolves fine tissue structures, with the dose extrapolated to 7 mGy per 1 ms frame in a prospective single-shot configuration. Energy-dependent responses match GATE/Geant4 simulations, and wedge measurements enable Bragg-peak tracking with an energy resolution below 10 keV in an optimised geometry. Real-time ms-scale beam monitoring enables live dose verification.These results establish GaN pixel detectors as a scalable and radiation-hard platform, enabling dosimetry, beam monitoring and energy verification in one device.

Medical Physics.title: Efficient Noise Context-Aware Representation for Low-Dose CT Denoising
Medical Physics.summary: While deep learning-based denoising has become widely adopted in low-dose CT, conventional models use generic architectures designed for natural images, failing to account for non-stationary and spatially correlated CT noise characteristics. To address this, we propose an Efficient Noise COntext-aware REpresentation (ENCORE) framework that explicitly leverages CT noise characteristics and anatomical features. First, we reformulate the noise synthesis procedure based on a realistic noise distribution beyond the conventional Gaussian approximation, establishing a rigorous foundation for training pair generation. Next, we extract local noise power and correlation contexts to guide the denoising process. To fully leverage the potential of noise context, we propose a FlyingConv module, which adaptively changes convolution weights for each local image region. Notably, our approach demonstrates substantial gains in both denoising quality and computational efficiency. Furthermore, manipulating the intensity of the noise context maps at inference time enables zero-shot conditional denoising, allowing for dynamic control over the output image texture. The entire pipeline is available at https://github.com/minwoo-yu/ENCORE.git

Medical Physics.title: Scan-Coil Delay Causes Anisotropic Signal Loss in Fast 4D-STEM
Medical Physics.summary: Fast pixelated detectors are driving 4D-STEM toward microsecond dwell times, a regime in which the finite response of the scan deflection coils becomes comparable to the dwell time itself. Using direct probe imaging and sub-frame diffraction analysis, we document a significant intra-dwell scan-coil delay that systematically smears the recorded signal anisotropically along the fast scan direction, with a settling timescale of several tens of microseconds. We present a phase-correlation-based sub-frame alignment procedure that measures and corrects this smearing, and we assess its impact on focused and defocused 4D-STEM reconstructions over a range of scan step sizes. The correction restores signal across a broad range of spatial frequencies, with the largest gains at the large step sizes required for low-dose biological imaging. Because it operates on existing data with no modification to the microscope, the method offers a practical route to recovering signal that would otherwise be lost to scan-coil delay.

Applications.title: Beyond Match Results: Bayesian Mediation of Ability, Performance, and Winning in Professional Tennis
Applications.summary: Match results measure competitive ability, but they do not explain how ability is expressed during play. Match statistics offer a natural mediator, however performance is usually measured over the same match as the outcome: a full-match statistic uses events that help determine the winner, while a first-set statistic is earlier but rests on fewer service points and still contributes to the result. Comparing the two therefore mixes timing and precision. We develop a Bayesian mediation framework for this problem. Dynamic abilities on hard, clay, and grass courts are estimated from previous seasons only and are linked to both players' service performance, and a Bradley--Terry model relates ability and performance to the match result. A control mediator samples the first set's number of service points from the full match, separating the measurement window from the point count. In 3,820 men's matches, the hard-court mediated share rises from 0.52 with a first-set mediator to 0.95 with a full-match mediator; the point-count contrast accounts for 0.30 of this gap and the window contrast for 0.13. The pattern replicates on the women's tour. Simulations and sensitivity analyzes examine the decomposition and assumptions needed for a causal interpretation.

Applications.title: GeoMix: A Bayesian Framework for Stratigraphic and Geotechnical Inference
Applications.summary: Accurate characterisation of subsea sediments is essential for engineering projects such as offshore wind farms, but the challenging environment and large spatial domains involved make dense geotechnical measurements impractical. Seismic traces offer a cheap, abundant complement, yet their geotechnical interpretation relies on subjective judgement, leading to biased, hard-to-validate predictions of sediment structure. To address this, we introduce GeoMix, a fully Bayesian hierarchical framework for jointly inferring geological stratigraphy and geotechnical properties from seismic and geotechnical data. GeoMix uses a Potts Markov random field to represent spatially coherent geology organised into distinct stratigraphic layers. Labels derived from seismic interpretation are linked to the latent stratigraphy through an observation model that captures elevated uncertainty near transitions between strata. Conditional on the latent stratigraphy, geotechnical properties are modelled using class-specific Gaussian processes, with scalable likelihood evaluation enabled by a grouped Vecchia approximation. Together, these components yield a unified latent-variable model capable of recovering stratigraphy, quantifying uncertainty, and predicting geotechnical properties across large three-dimensional domains. Simulation studies and an application to the IJmuiden Ver offshore wind farm show that GeoMix produces spatially coherent stratigraphic estimates and sediment predictions that are better calibrated and more accurate than existing approaches.
Applications.comment: 72 pages (including 31 pages of manuscript, 36 pages of supplementary material, and 5 pages of references). Includes 21 figures and 6 tables. Supplementary material contains additional methodological details, computational algorithms, and simulation results. Currently under revision

Applications.title: Improving ecological inference and uncertainty quantification from camera trap data through the fusion of AI confidences and manual annotations
Applications.summary: Camera traps have become an important tool in ecological research, enabling large-scale, noninvasive monitoring of wildlife populations and behavior. By automatically recording animals as they pass within view, these devices generate massive image datasets with minimal field effort. This data richness introduces a new bottleneck when translating the images into usable information due to time and effort required for human annotation. Artificial intelligence (AI) has recently been integrated into the workflow to improve efficiency. However, the data procured from AI approaches are of a different nature, necessitating new statistical methods. We develop a new Bayesian hierarchical data-fusion model that combines the strengths of human annotations and AI predictions. The benefits of our approach are an ability to provide uncertainty quantification as well as improved inference and predictive power, which we demonstrate through simulation. We apply our model to an AI analysis of the body condition of white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) from camera trap images from North Carolina to study the relationship between health and their environment. Our analysis derived novel ecological inference compared to a more traditional approach using the same data. We find that bucks in rut have higher (healthier) body condition than other deer and that green, open habitats are correlated with high body condition.

Applications.title: Challenges and Opportunities in Statistical Analyses and Designs for Neuroscience Clinical Trials
Applications.summary: Drug development is a complex, costly, and high-risk process, with neuroscience representing one of the most challenging therapeutic areas due to the complexity of neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders. Neuroscience clinical trials face unique barriers, making the adoption of innovative statistical methods in study design, execution, and analysis especially critical for improving clarity, feasibility, efficiency, and validity in the drug development process. The ASA Biopharmaceutical Section Neuroscience Scientific Working Group (SWG) was formed to advance statistical research and address these distinct challenges. This landscape paper provides an overview of key challenges and opportunities in statistical methods and trial designs for neuroscience, offering insights to guide future research and practice in this evolving field.

Applications.title: A Geometric Framework for the Bayesian Estimation of Joint Environmental Extremes
Applications.summary: Multivariate extreme events tend to have broader impacts on society compared to individual extremes. Flexible and accurate modeling of multivariate extremes is therefore crucial for many practical applications, including risk assessments and mitigation projects. In this work, we introduce a Bayesian modeling framework for bivariate extremes. Our approach utilizes the geometric extremes framework, for which data are decomposed into angular and radial components. The angular distribution is estimated using periodic M-splines, resulting in a natural circular density, while the radial distribution, conditional on the angles, is approximated using Bezier splines. The radial distribution also provides a means of estimating the limit set, the limiting shape of scaled sample clouds that encodes information pertaining to extremal dependence. Our Bayesian approach offers advantages over competing methods, particularly for uncertainty quantification and interpretation. Furthermore, our framework guarantees theoretical properties of limit sets, ensuring validity for inference. Notably, our model can be used to approximate extreme probabilities associated with failure sets in the joint tail, which are useful across many applications. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through numerical experiments and a case study on fire weather in Louisiana, USA, with diagnostics for the latter indicating strong model performance.

Applications.title: The Reach of Treatment Effects: Randomization Inference for Zero-Effect Regions
Applications.summary: A treatment may affect some individuals while leaving others unaffected. We study the reach of treatment effects by asking how large an unaffected covariate region could be. We develop efficient local randomization tests over nearest-neighbour regions to construct a finite-sample valid upper confidence bound for the size of the largest zero-effect region. A small bound provides evidence that treatment effects extend broadly across covariate values by ruling out large zero-effect regions. Under a general outcome model, we characterize how the size of the bound depends on the number of affected units, the size of their treatment effects, and the geometry of the true zero-effect set. We show that, when region size is measured as a sample fraction, the excess of the upper confidence bound over the true size decreases to zero at a minimax optimal rate up to a logarithmic factor. Numerical simulations assess the coverage, power and computational efficiency of our method. Applications to voter-turnout, HIV clinical-trial, and AI-assisted writing data illustrate how our method rules out large zero-effect regions across the covariates of interest.

Applications.title: The Physics Is the Network: Fast, Training-Free Neural Emulation
Applications.summary: Neural emulation need not require learning a substitute for known physics. We investigate PolyNets that couple a continuous-time neural representation of polynomial dynamics with a simple recurrent network for discrete-time integration. When the governing coefficients are known, the resulting tensor graph requires no training and preserves the prescribed numerical scheme while enabling efficient hardware execution and parallel simulation. Using the one-dimensional Korteweg-de Vries equation, we compare PolyNet with CPU and GPU finite-difference Runge-Kutta solvers and three trained neural models: a state-map emulator, a physics-informed predictor, and a learned-tendency integrator. Analytical soliton solutions provide a reference for amplitude and phase errors across grid resolutions, 10^6 dispersively scaled time steps, ensembles of up to 10^4 trajectories, and varying initial amplitudes. PolyNet achieves accuracy comparable to the numerical solvers, including at amplitudes outside the learned models' training conditions. It combines this fidelity with high GPU throughput, approximately constant over the tested resolution range, and favorable ensemble scaling.

Applications.title: Probabilistic AI models outperform numerical weather prediction models on record breaking heat extremes
Applications.summary: AI weather prediction (AIWP) models have emerged as a key complement to physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) models, and now often outperform them on aggregate skill. Yet, several studies report that physics-based models still forecast extreme events better, in particular record-breaking extremes, based on the evaluation of deterministic forecasts. Here we evaluate heat extreme forecasts from probabilistic AIWP models over global land and show that they clearly outperform the ECMWF IFS ensemble, both raw and post-processed, including for record-breaking events, in all regions and at all lead times considered. AIWP models better forecast the occurrence and intensity of extremes, are better calibrated in the tail and miss fewer records. Station observations confirm these results. We argue that many reported AIWP limitations stem from unsuitable verification choices, specifically comparing deterministic forecasts that target different quantities. Instead, a fair evaluation of extremes necessitates probabilistic verification.

Applications.title: Propensity score with factor loadings: evaluating the effect of the Paris Agreement on the returns of European stocks
Applications.summary: Factor models for longitudinal data, where policy adoption is unconfounded with respect to a low-dimensional set of latent factor loadings, have become increasingly popular for causal inference. Most existing approaches, however, rely on a causal finite-sample approach or computationally intensive methods, limiting their applicability and external validity. In this paper, we propose a novel method for panel causal inference within a super-population framework, based on inverse propensity score weighting, where the propensity score is a function of latent factor loadings. The approach relaxes the traditional restrictive assumptions of causal panel methods, while offering advantages in terms of causal interpretability, policy relevance, and computational efficiency. Under standard assumptions, we develop a three-step estimation procedure for the ATT and derive its large-sample properties using M-estimation theory. Simulation results show that the proposed estimator remains reliable across a variety of designs, including settings with misspecified factor structure and weakly dependent errors. We apply the method to assess the causal effect of the Paris Agreement - a policy aimed at fostering the transition to a low-carbon economy - on European stock returns. Our empirical results suggest a statistically significant and negative short-run effect on the stock returns of firms that demonstrate a strong commitment to sustainability.

Applications.title: The long shadow of pandemic: Understanding the lingering effects of cause-specific mortality shocks
Applications.summary: In the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, empirical data have revealed that large-scale health crises not only cause immediate disruptions in mortality dynamics but also have persistent effects that may last for several years. Existing mortality models largely assume that mortality shocks are transitory and overlook how their effects can be long-lasting and heterogeneous across age groups and causes of death. In response to this limitation, we propose a novel stochastic mortality model that captures age- and cause-specific long-lasting effects of mortality jumps through a gamma-density-like decay function, estimated via a customized conditional maximum likelihood algorithm. Applying the model to recent U.S. mortality data, we reveal divergent persistence patterns across demographic groups and provide key insights into the tail risk profiles of life insurance and annuity products. Our scenario-based analyses further show that neglecting persistent shock effects can lead to suboptimal hedging, while the proposed model enables what-if testing to analyze such effects under potential future health crises.
Applications.comment: Mortality shocks, Long-lasting pandemic effects, Stochastic mortality modeling, Cause-specific mortality, Natural hedging

Applications.title: Principal stratification with continuous treatments and continuous post-treatment variables
Applications.summary: Principal stratification (PS) is a commonly used approach for understanding the mechanisms through which a treatment affects an outcome. The goal of this work is to extend the PS framework to studies with continuous treatments, which introduces a number of both challenges and opportunities in terms of defining causal effects and performing inference. This manuscript provides multiple key methodological contributions: 1) we introduce principal causal estimands for continuous treatments that provide insights into different causal mechanisms, 2) we show that nonparametric identification is possible under a principal ignorability assumption, but only under a restrictive assumption on the joint distribution of potential mediators, which can be dropped under certain parametric assumptions, 3) we utilize nonparametric Bayesian models for the joint distribution of the potential mediating variables to mitigate issues from model misspecification, and 4) we provide theoretical justification for utilizing an outcome model to identify the joint distribution of the potential mediating variables, and show that this is only possible if a principal ignorability assumption is violated. Lastly, we illustrate our methodology by applying it to a novel study of the relationship between the economy and arrest rates, and how this is potentially mediated by police capacity.

Applications.title: Beyond Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Accelerators: Directed Evidence for Adaptive Sustainability Portfolios
Applications.summary: Governments and development partners often seek Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) "accelerators" whose progress can propagate gains across human well-being, institutions, resources, and environmental priorities. Such claims require evidence on direction, timing, robustness, and trade-offs, not only network connectivity. We map directed SDG interdependence using a balanced panel of 114 countries observed annually from 2000 to 2024. Because the goal series are persistent, trending, and cross-sectionally dependent, we combine Dumitrescu-Hurlin panel Granger non-causality tests on first-differenced series with false-discovery control across 272 directed goal pairs, and panel local projections with Driscoll-Kraay standard errors for 31 theory-derived indicator linkages. We find 84 directed linkages after correction: 40 synergies and 44 trade-offs. This dense structure does not support a universal accelerator. Driver-receiver rankings are fragile across lag orders, centrality metrics, bootstrap resampling, and alternative dependence controls; only peace and strong institutions as a net receiver and poverty reduction as an effect-size-weighted driver are distinguishable in the bootstrap screen. Two local-projection pathways are supported, both leading to lower child mortality, and the education-child-health association is corroborated in independent World Development Indicators data across 183 countries. The policy implication is not to abandon SDG integration, but to replace fixed global accelerator rankings with adaptive portfolios built around supported, time-lagged linkages and monitored constituent indicators.
Applications.comment: 28 pages, 5 figures; supplementary information (Tables S1-S9, Figures S1-S2) included as ancillary file. Code and data: see Open Research statement in the paper

Applications.title: Predicting future insurance markets: Simulation of technology adoption paths with a Bayesian Bass model
Applications.summary: Technological progress can give rise to new loss exposures or reduce existing risks. In either case, it strongly affects insurance companies' existing lines of business. As the magnitude of such effects is often closely connected to the innovation's market penetration, reliably predicting its adoption process is vital in enabling insurers to adapt their business strategy accordingly. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel combination of contributions from the domain of innovation diffusion. Our methodology generates adoption scenarios that holistically account for different sources of uncertainty, offers a structured way to incorporate expert judgment and insights from pre-existing technologies, and updates its predictions as new information on the technology's diffusion becomes available. Its modular nature ensures that components can be easily replaced by suitable alternatives. Using publicly accessible data on privately-owned battery electric vehicles in Germany, the application of our approach for predicting changes to insurance losses and for supporting insurers' sustainability strategies is visualized in a motor insurance case study.

Applications.title: Discrete p-Fold Directional Models for Binned Orientation Data with Applications to Sand-Grain Orientations and Urban Street Networks
Applications.summary: Discrete directional data exhibiting p-fold rotational symmetry, where directions separated by integer multiples of 2π/p are equivalent, arise in various applications but are often modeled using continuous distributions. In this article, we develop two general methods for constructing distributions for such data: symmetrization and folding of discrete circular distributions, and wrapping of discrete linear distributions. Particular models arising from these constructions are studied, together with their properties and estimation methods. For axial sand-grain orientation data, the proposed models are compared with discretized continuous axial distributions, whose category probabilities require numerical integration. The proposed models attain smaller Akaike information criterion values among the models considered while allowing direct likelihood evaluation without numerical integration. The framework is also applied to binned Manhattan street-orientation data, demonstrating its applicability to higher-order rotational structures, specifically the 4-fold case.

Applications.title: What If They Took the Shot? A Hierarchical Bayesian Framework for Counterfactual Expected Goals
Applications.summary: How would the probability of scoring change if a different player took the same shot? Although expected goals models describe the difficulty of scoring opportunities, comparing players on identical chances requires accounting for uncertainty in their estimated conversion probabilities. We address this question through a hierarchical Bayesian framework that evaluates alternative shooters under the same observed circumstances. Using 35,700 eligible shots from four leagues during the 2015/16 season, we compare a contextual benchmark with a primary player-intercept model and a provisional extension that allows player differences to vary with shooting conditions. Paired posterior draws preserve shared uncertainty when individual probability differences are aggregated across opportunities. Chronological validation demonstrates improved predictive performance relative to a constant-rate baseline, but introducing player effects provides negligible additional gains. Controlled single-seed experiments show that greater information per player improves estimation accuracy and narrows uncertainty intervals, although distinguishing small differences remains difficult and confident conclusions about near-null effects can become more frequent. Applications involving Giroud--Vardy and Berardi--Sansone similarly yield estimated differences that are small relative to their posterior uncertainty. These findings highlight an important distinction between predicting the outcome of a shot and establishing whether one player would be more likely to convert it. The proposed framework makes this distinction explicit by evaluating alternative shooters on fixed recorded opportunities while accounting for their contextual exposure. The resulting comparisons concern conditional conversion rather than the causal consequences of replacing a player in a match.

Applications.title: A New Perspective on Cumulative Residual Rényi Entropy
Applications.summary: This paper introduces a new cumulative residual Rényi entropy (CRRE), which addresses limitations of the existing cumulative residual Rényi entropy. The conventional measure suffers from two primary drawbacks: its failure to converge to the cumulative residual entropy (CRE) as the order parameter approaches unity, and its lack of guaranteed positivity. Our proposed CRRE resolves these issues, offering a theoretically consistent and always nonnegative measure of uncertainty in residual lifetimes. We explore its mathematical properties, including its relationship with existing information measures. Furthermore, the concept is extended to its dynamic version, and its time-dependent characteristics are investigated. A non-parametric estimator of the proposed CRRE is developed, its almost sure convergence is established, and is validated through Monte Carlo simulation. The effectiveness of CRRE as a tool for quantifying uncertainty is confirmed through its application in chaotic theory and financial data.

Applications.title: Simulation Based Inference of a Simple Neural Network Structure
Applications.summary: Neurophysiologists are nowadays able to record from a large number of extracellular electrodes and to extract, from the raw data, the sequences of action potentials or spikes generated by many neurons. Unfortunately these ''many neurons'' still represent only a tiny fraction of the neuronal population that constitutes the network. Using association statistics such as the estimation of the cross-correlation functions, they are trying to infer the structure of the network formed by the recorded neurons. But this inference is compromised by the tremendous under-sampling of the neuronal population. We propose to focus instead on simple spike train statistics, like the empirical spikes frequency, or the interspike interval distribution. Their sampling distributions can be estimated by simulations, and, given a few observed spike train statistics, they provide enough information to infer the structure of the underlying network. We show that, on a ''toy model'', our method gives significantly better results than the sub-network reconstruction method with regards to the inference of the connection probability of the original network.

Applications.title: Longitudinal Brain Aging in Covariance Space: Temporally Calibrated Bayesian Inference for Adaptive Covariance Operators
Applications.summary: Functional brain aging is often characterized by differences between people of different ages, although aging unfolds within individuals. This distinction is especially important for functional connectivity, where the direction of covariance change may evolve across adulthood. We introduce a Bayesian longitudinal covariance-operator framework that models each visit covariance as a latent positive-definite state informed by repeated resting-state fMRI runs. The approach calibrates run-level information for temporal dependence and replicate variability, separates within-person aging from between-person age differences, and uses an adaptive tangent representation to learn the low-dimensional structure of longitudinal change without relying on pooled covariance variation. The longitudinal operator varies smoothly in magnitude and orientation with age, while exact Fréchet derivatives translate the fitted trajectory to the covariance scale. This framework allows us to examine how brain covariance organization changes within individuals, whether longitudinal aging follows the population age gradient, and which functional systems contribute to their divergence. In the Dallas Lifespan Brain Study, within-person covariance aging differs substantially from the cross-sectional age gradient through early and middle adulthood, with the discrepancy diminishing later in life. Covariance reorganization is strongest around midlife, and the longitudinal signal is concentrated in a few coordinated directions, with most off-diagonal change occurring between functional systems. These findings demonstrate that population-level signatures of brain aging do not necessarily reflect individual aging trajectories and highlight the importance of modeling longitudinal covariance change directly.
Applications.comment: 32 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Supplementary materials: 8 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Includes theoretical results, technical details, and a simulation study

Applications.title: Learning Checklists to Reduce Lottery Effects in Scientific Peer Review
Applications.summary: Reviewer lottery error describes error due to a small set of peer reviews attending to only some of the issues with a paper that a larger pool of eligible reviewers would raise. We show this error can be reduced by surfacing a checklist of criticisms learned from a historical review corpus. Our approach generates a tree of checklists representing coarsenings of the atomic review claim space, then selects the coarsening that maximizes a theoretically-motivated measure of correlated agreement among reviewers. We realize this approach with an LLM-assisted pipeline and test it on NeurIPS 2021 and ICLR 2022 review data. In simulated review with LLM reviewers, the learned checklist reduces the mean squared error (MSE) of a three reviewer committee by 58% on NeurIPS and 21% on ICLR, and on both venues the checklist with the highest correlated agreement has the lowest error for committees of three or more. In a human study with 20 participants, the learned NeurIPS checklist lowers the MSE of a paper ranking, measured against the NeurIPS 2021 order, from 0.48 to 0.22.

Machine Learning.title: On the Last-Iterate Convergence of Clipped Gradient Methods
Machine Learning.summary: In stochastic (strongly) convex optimization, establishing last-iterate convergence guarantees for first-order methods has recently garnered increasing attention, as this not only deepens the theoretical understanding of these algorithms but also aligns more closely with practice. Notably, people have demonstrated that one of the most famous, simple, and popular methods, Stochastic Gradient Descent ($\mathtt{SGD}$), provably achieves last-iterate convergence. However, the existing results may have limited applicability, since they typically rely on strong conditions on the gradient noise (e.g., an exponentially decaying tail) rather than the more realistic heavy-tailed noise. Unfortunately, when faced with heavy-tailed noise, $\mathtt{SGD}$ is known to exhibit undesirable behavior or even fail to converge. To address the challenge of heavy-tailed noise, people have proposed $\mathtt{Clipped}\text{-}\mathtt{SGD}$, an algorithm that combines $\mathtt{SGD}$ with a simple mechanism, gradient clipping. Although $\mathtt{Clipped}\text{-}\mathtt{SGD}$ performs well in practice, its last-iterate convergence property remains highly underexplored. In this work, we prove the first optimal last-iterate rates in high probability for $\mathtt{Clipped}\text{-}\mathtt{SGD}$ under heavy-tailed noise, thereby closing a gap in the literature.

Machine Learning.title: Acceleration and its Limits in Gaussian Variational Inference
Machine Learning.summary: We study whether the classical momentum-based acceleration that improves the condition-number dependence of gradient descent from $κ$ to $\sqrtκ$ for strongly convex, smooth objectives extends to Gaussian variational inference (GVI) for strongly log-concave, log-smooth target distributions. With exact Gaussian expectations, a convex composite formulation of GVI yields the classical accelerated $\sqrtκ$ convergence rate. However, when only pointwise derivatives are available, we construct a family of strongly log-concave targets for which any randomized algorithm requires $κ^{1-o(1)}$ queries to achieve a fixed objective accuracy, even when the initial objective gap is bounded independently of $κ$. Thus curvature bounds alone cannot guarantee uniform accelerated total-query complexity. We then ask which additional structure permits acceleration and give positive examples: under a Hessian-Lipschitz assumption, variance-reduced stochastic methods yield accelerated guarantees when the Hessian variation is sufficiently small. Finally, experiments on real datasets show substantial empirical speedups from acceleration across a broad range of methods.

Machine Learning.title: Failure Is the Mother of Success: Recovering Supervision with Grounding Hindsight
Machine Learning.summary: When every rollout for a problem fails, GRPO receives neither a successful exemplar nor a nonzero group-relative advantage, so it learns nothing from exactly the problems it most needs to learn. The failed reasoning can nevertheless suggest what to try next. We present Replay-Selected Hindsight Distillation (RSHD), which turns failed attempts into an additional, tested source of supervision during GRPO training. The policy writes a corrective note about each failed attempt without seeing a reference answer or solution, then re-solves the problem with the note in context. A note is admitted only if its replays succeed more often than the original group did, after screening for notes that state the answer, and an admitted replay is distilled into the plain-prompt policy. Because admission is decided by fresh successes rather than by the failed rollout itself, the procedure can recover supervision from groups in which every attempt failed, and it applies equally to failures in mixed groups. Only the policy is trained, the only judge is the outcome verifier, and deployment requires no notes or extra inference. Across model families and sizes and two training domains, RSHD consistently improves over GRPO on in-domain benchmarks, and the gains carry over to out-of-domain evaluation sets.

Machine Learning.title: Halve-Then-Greedy: Adaptive Sampling for Posterior Success with Near-Optimal Instance Dependence
Machine Learning.summary: We study fixed-budget adaptive experimentation aimed at maximizing the probability of obtaining sufficient posterior evidence that a recommended design's mean performance exceeds a target. Unlike best-arm identification, this objective does not require finding the best design. For Gaussian bandits with a Gaussian prior, we propose \emph{Halve-Then-Greedy} (HTG), which combines a large initial balanced allocation, successive halving, and posterior-greedy sampling. We prove instance-dependent, finite-budget exponential bounds on posterior-failure probability that capture both separation from unfavorable arms and the presence of multiple favorable arms. On one-positive-arm families, we establish an asymptotic sample-complexity lower bound that HTG matches up to a logarithmic factor. We further analyze uniform sampling and sequential halving, revealing regimes where they require more samples than HTG by linear and logarithmic factors, respectively. Simulations illustrate HTG's sample-efficiency advantages and their dependence on instance structure.

Machine Learning.title: PAC-Causal Learnability: From Identification to Finite-Sample Guarantees
Machine Learning.summary: Causal identification asks whether a causal target can be recovered from the observational distribution in an idealized infinite-data setting. In practice, only finite samples are available, and identifiability alone does not determine how much data are needed for reliable estimation. We introduce Probably Approximately Correct Causal (PACC) learnability, which formalizes uniform accuracy-confidence guarantees over a causal model class. From a PAC-learning perspective, we ask how many samples are sufficient to estimate a causal target to accuracy $ε$ with probability at least $1-δ$. We show that PACC sample complexity is shaped by three recurring factors: causal identification strength, target complexity, and nuisance complexity, and derive a general sufficient bound linking them to finite-sample causal learning. We illustrate the framework through self-controlled case series, instrumental variables, and propensity-score-based estimation, showing how distinct causal methods can be analyzed within a common framework.

Machine Learning.title: A Model Ensemble-Based Post-Processing Framework for Fairness-Aware Prediction
Machine Learning.summary: Striking an optimal balance between predictive performance and fairness continues to be a fundamental challenge in machine learning. In this work, we propose a post-processing framework that facilitates fairness-aware prediction by leveraging model ensembling. Designed to operate independently of any specific model internals, our approach is widely applicable across various learning tasks, model architectures, and fairness definitions. Through extensive experiments spanning classification, regression, and survival analysis, we demonstrate that the framework effectively enhances fairness while maintaining, or only minimally affecting, predictive accuracy.

Machine Learning.title: Two-Stage Score Estimation for Group-Specific Diffusion Models
Machine Learning.summary: Generative modeling across related distributions raises a question: how can shared structure support accurate generation for a target distribution with limited observations? We develop a statistical framework for diffusion transfer that analyzes a shared pooled score together with a target-specific offset. Under Besov regularity of the pooled density and a stable hierarchical composition model for the offset, we derive convergence rates that separate the costs of learning these components and identify when a simpler offset yields a faster risk-bound rate than separate fitting. Under suitable boundary and regularity assumptions, we prove that the offset remains bounded and jointly regular as diffusion time approaches zero. These results allow the lower time cutoff to vanish polynomially and provide total-variation guarantees for diffusion models as density estimators. Synthetic simulations and image benchmarks provide a proof of concept for the framework.

Machine Learning.title: Nonconvex Composite Functional Constraints via First-Order Augmented Lagrangian Methods under Local Regularity
Machine Learning.summary: We study nonasymptotic convergence of primal-dual methods for a class of nonconvex constrained optimization problems under local multiplier regularity. Both the objective and functional inequality constraints are compositions of convex Lipschitz outer functions with smooth nonlinear mappings. Unlike existing analyses requiring regularity globally or along the entire iterate sequence, we impose multiplier regularity only near the feasible set. Using an auxiliary minimax problem with a compact dual set, we derive Lyapunov estimates that identify nearly feasible iterates under feasible initialization and a sufficiently large penalty, without assuming multiplier boundedness. Local regularity then bounds the associated multipliers and makes dual truncation inactive, yielding approximate KKT certificates for the original problem. The smoothed prox-linear augmented Lagrangian method with dual regularization yields an $O(K^{-1/3})$ KKT residual rate. Without regularization, piecewise linear outer functions and additional local structural assumptions yield a local dual error bound and the sharper $O(K^{-1/2})$ rate.

Machine Learning.title: Ranked Right, Sized Wrong: Ensemble Spread Fails Silently at Streamflow Extremes
Machine Learning.summary: Deep learning models, particularly Long Short-Term Memory networks, are increasingly used for operational streamflow forecasting, with ensemble spread providing a signal of predictive uncertainty. As climate change increases the frequency of hydroclimatic extremes, these models will increasingly operate under flow conditions that are rare in their historical records. We therefore evaluate whether ensemble spread remains informative under increasing flows, examining both its magnitude relative to error and its ability to rank errors. Prediction error is approximately $2\times$ the corrected spread at ordinary flows and up to $4\times$ at the highest flows, with the discrepancy increasing with flow (log-log slope $1.30$, 95% CI: $[1.20,1.41]$). Under-dispersion is strongest in observed extreme flows beyond the training record, reaching an $18\times$ discrepancy. This is pervasive and not explainable by conditional mean bias. Area Under the Sparsification Error, a standard distribution-free metric of uncertainty ranking, describing how well a model knows when it is uncertain, indicates near-oracle ranking for ensemble spread ($0.071$), yet ordering by predicted discharge alone nearly matches it. Informative uncertainty ranking can coexist with severe under-dispersion. In deployment, error ranking cannot be verified, yet the spread is available, and it is relied on as the uncertainty signal under increasingly extreme conditions, while systematically understating risk, most severely for the extreme events that matter most.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at the Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning workshop at NeurIPS 2026. 13 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23142989

Machine Learning.title: Near-Exponential Convergence Rates for kNN Classification based on Boltzmann Margin
Machine Learning.summary: Convergence-rate analysis for classifiers is often conducted under either Tsybakov margin or Massart margin. The former is a relatively weak condition that typically yields polynomial rates, while the latter is substantially stronger but can guarantee exponential rates. In this paper, we introduce a new condition, called Boltzmann margin, that bridges the gap between these two regimes. It is weaker than Massart margin, generally stronger than Tsybakov margin, and can imply many of their properties under suitable conditions. We apply Boltzmann margin to the analysis of kNN classifiers and establish the first near-exponential convergence rates for kNN classification. We also present extensions of the main results and provide numerical evidence supporting the main theoretical implications.
Machine Learning.comment: Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI)

Machine Learning.title: Sign Betting for Misspecified Regression: Variance Adaptivity and Optimal Approximation
Machine Learning.summary: We study bounded regression under model misspecification, evaluating a function $f$ by its $L_1(P_X)$ distance to the conditional mean $η(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]$, rather than the standard $L_2(P_X)$. This $L_1$ metric is natural for downstream decision problems such as bandits and reinforcement learning. We analyze the min--max estimator of Baraud & Maillard (2025), which we call \emph{sign-betting regression}. Our main results show that sign-betting regression achieves high-probability $L_1$ oracle inequalities under misspecification. Under realizability, our bound adapts to the average conditional variance and recovers the variance-adaptive rate of Li et al. (2026). We further characterize the optimal universal approximation factor for proper learning by showing that sign betting achieves factor 3, while no proper learner can satisfy a distribution-free, high-probability $L_1$ oracle inequality with a universal approximation factor strictly below 3. We extend the upper-bound analysis beyond finite classes and complement the theory with experiments in synthetic and real-world model-selection tasks.

Machine Learning.title: Formal Bayesian Transfer Learning via the Total Risk Prior
Machine Learning.summary: Existing methods for transfer learning struggle to deal with situations where the source datasets are limited and not guaranteed to be well-aligned with the target dataset. A typical strategy is to use the empirical loss minimizer on the source data as a prior mean for the target parameters. We propose using a risk minimizer conditional on source parameters instead. This allows us to construct a joint posterior for all parameters from the source and target datasets. As a consequence, we benefit from full Bayesian uncertainty quantification and can perform model averaging via Gibbs sampling over indicator variables governing the inclusion of each source dataset. We show how a particular instantiation of our prior leads to a Bayesian Lasso in a transformed coordinate system and describe connections between the Maximum a Posteriori estimate associated with our approach and the Trans-Lasso method. We find that the MAP estimator MSE-dominates the Trans-Lasso in the normal means setting when there is no regularization on the source datasets. Finally, we perform numerical experiments finding that our approach provides superior predictive performance relative to frequentist and Bayesian baselines on a genetics application, particularly when the source data are limited.

Machine Learning.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent: A Nonlinear Time Series Perspective
Machine Learning.summary: This paper investigates the statistical behavior of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with constant step size under the framework of iterated random functions. Compared to previous studies establishing the convergence of SGD in probability measure, e.g., Wasserstein distance, our approach directly provides the convergence in Euclidean distance by showing the Geometric Moment Contraction (GMC) of SGD. This new convergence can address the non-stationarity of SGD due to fixed initial points and can provide a more refined asymptotic analysis of SGD. Specifically, we prove quenched central limit theorem, invariance principle and $α$-stable convergence for averaged SGD (ASGD) regardless of initialization. Furthermore, we provide a novel perspective to understand the impact of step sizes in SGD by studying its derivative with respect to the step size. The existence of stationary solutions for the derivative processes is shown, enabling the use of interpolation to recover the full-trajectory of SGD. Subsequently, we utilize multiple step sizes and show an enhanced Richardson-Romberg extrapolation with improved bias representation, which brings ASGD estimates closer to the global optimum. Finally, we propose a new online inference method and a bias-reduced variant for the extrapolated ASGD. Empirical confidence intervals are constructed and the coverage probabilities approach the nominal level as $n$ grows.

Machine Learning.title: Flexible Doubly Robust Proximal Causal Inference for Censored Outcomes
Machine Learning.summary: Estimating causal effects on right-censored time-to-event outcomes is challenging under unmeasured confounding. Proximal causal inference addresses unmeasured confounding through proxy variables, but existing proximal survival methods rely largely on restrictive parametric bridge models. We introduce Proximal Survival Bridge learning (PSB), a flexible doubly robust proximal framework for censored outcomes. Building on existing proximal identification of treatment-specific survival curves, the framework yields outcome-bridge (OB), treatment-bridge (TB), and doubly robust (DR) estimators, with two flexible bridge learners: PSB-K, a kernel estimator with a low-rank time decomposition, and PSB-N, a neural estimator trained by a projected maximum-moment-restriction loss. Unlike existing flexible proximal learners for scalar outcomes, PSB directly handles censoring and survival-curve targets. On a standard SEM benchmark, a proximal semi-synthetic ACTG study, and the real-world Framingham study, PSB-K performs strongest on SEM and ACTG, whereas PSB-N is the most stable on Framingham. Additional results with modern causal survival baselines, weakened or invalid proxies, and heavier censoring assess robustness across challenging settings.

Machine Learning.title: A Mixture-of-Experts Framework for Multi-Stream Quickest Change Detection
Machine Learning.summary: A Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework is proposed for quickest change detection (QCD) where there are multiple experts, and each expert produces a sequence of statistics for change detection. A change is declared when a weighted sum of these statistics crosses a threshold. This framework is then applied to the problem of multi-stream QCD to obtain a family of powerful algorithms that outperform the best known algorithms in the literature. In the multi-stream QCD problem, a decision-maker observes multiple streams of observations. At the change point, the distribution of an unknown subset of the streams changes. The optimal algorithm based on a generalized likelihood ratio is computationally expensive. One of the most computationally and performance-efficient algorithms in the literature is the rank-weighted sum (RWS) scheme based on Shiryaev-Roberts statistics. It is shown in the paper that the MoE-based QCD algorithm for multi-stream data outperforms the RWS scheme. This is demonstrated through simulation results on real-valued Gaussian mean shift data and high-dimensional data from Gaussian--Bernoulli Restricted Boltzmann Machines (GB-RBMs).

Machine Learning.title: A Greedy PDE Router for Blending Neural Operators and Classical Methods
Machine Learning.summary: When solving PDEs, classical numerical solvers are often computationally expensive, while machine learning methods can suffer from spectral bias, failing to capture high-frequency components. Designing an optimal hybrid iterative solver--where, at each iteration, a solver is selected from an ensemble of solvers to leverage their complementary strengths--poses a challenging combinatorial problem. While greedy selection is desirable for its constant-factor approximation guarantee to the optimal solution under Lipschitz assumptions, it requires knowledge of the true error at each step, which is unavailable in practice. We address this by proposing an approximate greedy router that efficiently mimics a greedy approach to solver selection. Empirical results on the Poisson, convection-diffusion, and anisotropic diffusion equations show that our method consistently reduces time-to-solution relative to single-solver baselines and existing hybrid approaches such as HINTS.

Machine Learning.title: A Distribution-to-Distribution Neural Probabilistic Forecasting Framework for Dynamical Systems
Machine Learning.summary: Probabilistic forecasts provide a principled representation of forecast uncertainty through predictive distributions. Directly propagating predictive distributions with conventional physical models requires solving distributional evolution equations, a task well-known to be computationally prohibitive for high-dimensional nonlinear systems. Consequently, multi-step predictive distributions are commonly approximated using ensembles or sampled trajectories. A novel distribution-to-distribution (D2D) neural probabilistic forecasting framework is proposed with compatible distributional encoding and decoding interfaces around a replaceable neural forecasting module. Kernel mean embeddings represent input distributions, while mixture density networks parameterise outputs, enabling recursive multi-step forecasting in distributional form. The framework is demonstrated on the Lorenz63 system. Results show that the D2D model captures nontrivial distributional evolution, produces skillful probabilistic forecasts without explicit ensemble simulation, and remains competitive with a naively initialised perfect-model benchmark. This provides proof-of-concept evidence that predictive distributions can be recursively propagated through a neural forecasting model and evaluated in terms of probabilistic forecast performance.

Machine Learning.title: Complete or Sparse: A Tale of Two Identifiabilities
Machine Learning.summary: Understanding when neural networks learn interpretable representations is central to mechanistic interpretability. We study this through identifiability: when can supervised learning recover the true latent variables underlying the data? We introduce two data generating processes distinguished by their causal direction where either labels cause latents (generative) or latents cause labels (discriminative). When the representation has at least as many dimensions as the latent space, we prove that the optimal encoders are linear in the latents. Conversely, when dimensions are insufficient, identifiability generically fails and encoders become nonlinear. We then show that additional constraints yield recovery of individual latent variables, not just linear mixtures. In the generative setting, non-negative activations and energy efficiency force each neuron to encode exactly one latent, providing a precise account of selective grandmother cell-like responses. In the discriminative setting, when latents are sparse and the true measurement matrix satisfies the spark condition, the learned encoder inherits compressed sensing structure, enabling sparse dictionary learning to perfectly recover individual latents. This constitutes, to our knowledge, the first identifiability result for undercomplete nonlinear independent component analysis. Our framework unifies nonlinear ICA, compressed sensing, and neural network interpretability, delineating exactly when representations transition from nonlinear distortions to linear representations and, under additional constraints or steps, to clean, axis-aligned codes. Theoretical predictions are validated on synthetic benchmarks and on activations drawn from vision models, large language models, and macaque inferotemporal cortex.

Machine Learning.title: Optimal Condition for Initialization Variance in Deep Neural Networks: An SGD Dynamics Perspective
Machine Learning.summary: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD), one of the most fundamental optimization algorithms in machine learning (ML), can be recast through a continuous-time approximation as a Fokker-Planck equation for Langevin dynamics, a viewpoint that has motivated many theoretical studies. Within this framework, we study the relationship between the quasi-stationary distribution derived from this equation and the initial distribution through the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. As the quasi-steady-state distribution depends on the expected cost function, the KL divergence eventually reveals the connection between the expected cost function and the initialization distribution. By applying this to deep neural network models (DNNs), we can express the bounds of the expected loss function explicitly in terms of the initialization parameters. Then, by minimizing this bound, we obtain an optimal condition of the initialization variance in the Gaussian case. This result provides a concrete mathematical criterion, rather than a heuristic approach, to select the scale of weight initialization in DNNs. In addition, we experimentally confirm our theoretical results by using the classical SGD to train fully connected neural networks on the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets. The result shows that if the variance of the initialization distribution satisfies our theoretical optimal condition, then the corresponding DNN model always achieves lower final training loss and higher test accuracy than the conventional He-normal initialization. Our work thus supplies a mathematically grounded indicator that guides the choice of initialization variance and clarifies its physical meaning of the dynamics of parameters in DNNs.

Machine Learning.title: Computational and Statistical Hardness of Calibration Distance
Machine Learning.summary:
The distance from calibration, introduced by Błasiok, Gopalan, Hu, and Nakkiran (STOC 2023), has recently emerged as a central measure of miscalibration for probabilistic predictors. We study the fundamental problems of computing and estimating this quantity, given either an exact description of the data distribution or only sample access to it.
  We give an efficient algorithm that exactly computes the calibration distance when the distribution has a uniform marginal and noiseless labels, which improves the $O(1/\sqrt{|\mathcal{X}|})$ additive approximation of Qiao and Zheng (COLT 2024) for this special case. Perhaps surprisingly, the problem becomes $\mathsf{NP}$-hard when either of the two assumptions is removed. We extend our algorithm to a polynomial-time approximation scheme for the general case.
  For the estimation problem, we show that $Θ(1/ε^3)$ samples are sufficient and necessary for the empirical calibration distance to be upper bounded by the true distance plus $ε$. In contrast, a polynomial dependence on the domain size -- incurred by the learning-based baseline -- is unavoidable for two-sided estimation.
  Our positive results are based on simple sparsifications of both the distribution and the target predictor, which significantly reduce the search space for computation and lead to stronger concentration for the estimation problem. To prove the hardness results, we introduce new techniques for certifying lower bounds on the calibration distance -- a problem that is hard in general due to its $\textsf{co-NP}$-completeness.
Machine Learning.comment: To appear at SODA 2027. v2 added figures for visualizing the NP-hardness reduction

Machine Learning.title: LASER: Latent Space Adjoint Matching for Support-Constrained Entropy-Regularized Offline RL
Machine Learning.summary: While offline reinforcement learning (RL) enables policy optimization from static datasets without costly online interaction, it remains bottlenecked by the risk of executing out-of-distribution (OOD) actions. Recent approaches mitigate this by learning a behavior-cloning policy through flow matching and then performing RL within its constrained latent space. However, naively optimizing the latent policy can easily cause the policy to collapse into a brittle mode or exploit sharp artifacts of the learned critic. In this work, we find that entropy regularization is essential in latent-space RL for addressing these challenges. We introduce LASER, a novel offline RL algorithm that applies latent-space adjoint matching to achieve entropy-regularized latent-space RL with expressive flow policies while avoiding backpropagation through time. Through comprehensive experiments on 40 challenging OGBench tasks with varying dataset qualities, we show that LASER achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, LASER uses fixed method-specific hyperparameters across all tasks and outperforms the evaluated baselines, including those with task- and dataset-specific tuning, which highlights the robust applicability of LASER. Project website: https://mit-realm.github.io/laser/.

Machine Learning.title: Selection-Safe Conformal Early Exit: Distribution-Free Coverage under Adaptive Depth
Machine Learning.summary: Calibrating a conformal prediction set at each early exit does not preserve coverage once a data-dependent exit is selected. We construct one terminal path score from prefix maxima, calibrate a single split-conformal quantile, and return nested prefix sets that all contain the valid terminal set. The guarantee is selection-safe without an alpha/L correction and holds simultaneously for every post-calibration label-free stopping policy that preserves terminal-set containment. We also bound the efficiency cost of the path maximum by the empirical tail of the early-over-terminal score excess. Across eight encoder task-backbone cells, pathwise selection attains macro coverage 0.901 versus 0.814 for naive layerwise selection, with average set size 1.41 and latency fraction 0.71. On CIFAR-100 with a 24-exit ViT-L/16 (n_cal=500), first-eligible stopping at budget b=4 attains coverage 0.902, set size 2.76, and latency fraction 0.57, and the same calibration supports deployment-time budget changes without refitting.
