In controlled ablations with declared ground truth on emulated and physical cells, OpenPLC and ARM and RISC-V boards, a check on a replica always left an unprotected interval: a pause written from a few to over 100ms after submission escaped it. Only a check in the scan of a software controller, either a controller-local interlock or the version-conditional command, closed the interval for the state that controller owns; only the version-conditional command also refused commands after a pause that had been undone. A global version revoked up to every valid command under unrelated updates. Versions scoped to what the intent reads, or to the truth of its predicates, did not; with continuous signals on the variables the intent reads, only the latter avoided false revocations, though it burdens the store as predicates accumulate. On one embedded-board core, XAIR validated 148-168 intents/s.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 46 pages, 6 figures, 11 tables

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: QwenGyre: An Elastic Reinforcement Learning Framework for Training xLong-Horizon Agents
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly undertake extreme-long (xlong) horizon tasks, where a single execution can span hours, hundreds of model--environment interactions, and nearly 1M tokens per rollout. Applying online reinforcement learning (RL) to such executions poses two fundamental challenges: (1) severe execution variance and prolonged rollout delays cause massive GPU idling; and (2) complex non-linear branching generates massive trajectory redundancy, crippling training efficiency. To address these, we presents QwenGyre, an end-to-end framework for xlong-horizon online RL. QwenGyre elastically reallocates GPUs between rollout and training without interrupting live executions, while its trajectory processor reconstructs branching histories, scores partial progress, and deduplicates redundant paths to bound training costs. Scaled to our flagship model, Qwen~3.8 2.4T, with 700K tokens per rollout, QwenGyre yields a 6.0% absolute gain on NL2RepoBench (52.5% $\to$ 58.5%) in 48 steps. Across our evaluations on diverse domains of training datasets, QwenGyre delivers up to $1.85\times$ and $1.78\times$ speedups over Colocate and Async, respectively.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Unsupervised Head Network Personalization for Split Computing via Federated Learning
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Split Computing (SC) is a distributed inference method designed for balancing computational load and reducing latency by partitioning a neural network into head and tail networks and deploying them across both a mobile device and a server, respectively. Due to the limited bandwidth and computational power of mobile devices, the head network is often replaced with a neural network that requires lower computational and communication resources. However, it is challenging to prepare a sufficient quantity and quality of labeled data on the mobile device side for training the replacement head network. Furthermore, the data prepared by mobile users often contains sensitive privacy information, making data aggregation difficult. In this paper, we propose a data-efficient head network training method for SC. This method utilizes federated learning and knowledge distillation to train the head network using a small amount of non-IID and unlabeled data from mobile devices, ensuring that the training datasets are not exposed. Moreover, by introducing personalization, we enhance the accuracy to levels comparable to or exceeding those of existing methods. The experimental evaluations demonstrate that, despite data constraints imposed only on our method, it achieves accuracy comparable to the baselines. Furthermore, it significantly reduces the communication requirements by 95% on mobile devices, with only a 3-5 percentage point drop in accuracy from the original model.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 12 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Benchmarking CPU, GPU, and ML Power-Flow Solvers from 14 to 70,000 Buses
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Learned surrogates for power-flow (PF) computation are usually motivated by speed, compared against a single CPU-based baseline. We show this comparison is fragile: across 7 open-source CPU-based solvers evaluated on identical inputs, throughput varies by roughly 2.5-3 orders of magnitude, so the choice of baseline alone can flip the conclusion. We build a benchmark spanning 9 physics-based solvers: 7 CPU-based and 2 GPU-based, including a new batched GPU solver, gumsim2grid - and 3 published ML surrogates, evaluated under a shared, independently implemented KCL-mismatch check across 15 grids from 14 to 70,000 buses. On the PF task itself, a sufficiently parallelized CPU solver or gpusim2grid matches or exceeds the throughput of the ML surrogates we test while remaining orders of magnitude more accurate; we find no evidence that these GNN-style surrogates are yet competitive for PF specifically, though prior work reports genuine gains on related but more combinatorial tasks such as optimal power flow or power grid control. Beyond this finding, we hope the benchmark suite, code and reference evaluator released at https://github.com/Grid2op/gpusim2grid helps close a broader reproducibility gap in this space, where batched GPU-based PF solvers are rarely open-sourced or evaluated against a common set of baselines.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Online Continual Learning on Intel Loihi 2 via a Co-designed Spiking Neural Network
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Edge AI must adapt to new classes and shifting data within a tight power budget, but online continual learning (learning from each sample before the next arrives) is where conventional processors are least efficient: each small update pays a full dispatch at full power. We present CLP-SNN, a spiking architecture that recasts the Continually Learning Prototypes (CLP) algorithm as event-driven neural dynamics: a self-normalizing local rule replaces CLP's global renormalization, prototype allocation becomes novelty-triggered neurogenesis, and correctness-modulated plasticity becomes reward-gated per-neuron metaplasticity. Deployed on Intel Loihi 2 as the first online continual learner on that chip, rehearsal-free CLP-SNN matches Replay and SLDA on OpenLORIS at 1-shot; at 25-shot, it stays within 0.8 percentage points of Replay and 6.2 points below covariance-based SLDA. Each prediction-and-update step on extracted features completes on-chip in 0.33 ms at 0.05 mJ, 7.3x lower latency and 341x lower energy than Replay on a Jetson Orin Nano.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: NVIDIA Spectrum-X: Hardware-Accelerated Multiplane Networking for Large-Scale AI Training
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: As distributed model training scales to span hundreds of thousands of GPUs, scale-out networks face unprecedented performance and efficiency demands. NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet has been designed from the ground up to achieve predictable and stable network performance with high utilization and low latency. This paper presents the Spectrum-X multiplane architecture, which replaces hierarchical depth with topological parallelism, and introduces hardware-accelerated load balancing in NICs and switches as the key architectural approach to provide fast reaction to highly dynamic network conditions at the microsecond timescales that AI training workloads demand. We describe the motivation, design principles, evaluation methodology and performance on state-of-the-art benchmarks, as well as the lessons we learned from deploying and debugging Spectrum-X networks in large-scale systems. Our evaluation highlights production-grade AI infrastructure performance across four core dimensions: 98% of the theoretical line rate with low jitter-free latency; strong cross-tenant isolation for concurrent workloads; robust, capacity-proportional bisection bandwidth and 7% latency increase for 10% fabric link failures; and rapid reaction to host and fabric link flaps during LLM training workloads.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Evaluating Runtime Prediction and Conservative Walltime Policies in HPC Systems
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Efficient use of large-scale supercomputing systems depends on accurate runtime estimation and walltime selection. To avoid premature termination, users often overestimate walltime, leading to poor resource utilization and reduced scheduling efficiency. This paper presents a predictor-agnostic framework for safe walltime recommendation in production HPC environments. Rather than proposing a new runtime prediction model, the primary contribution is the SAFE decision layer, which converts predicted runtimes into conservative bounded walltime recommendations suitable for deployment. Runtime prediction is therefore treated as a modular component within the proposed framework. We evaluate the approach using large-scale production job histories from the Fugaku and NREL Eagle supercomputers, comprising approximately 24M and 11M jobs, respectively. Runtime prediction performance is first evaluated using representative predictors, including linear regression, neural networks, and a neural ensemble. The proposed SAFE framework is then evaluated using the NN ensemble predictor. Experimental results indicate that similarity-aware prediction substantially improves runtime estimation for workloads similar to previous executions. When combined with the proposed conservative walltime recommendation policies, these improvements enable walltime gap reductions of approximately 20 - 26% while maintaining job termination rates below 1% across both systems.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: OpenAgenet / OAN Yellow Paper: Technical Architecture for Trust-Governed Resource Identity and Discovery
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: This yellow paper describes the technical architecture of OpenAgenet / OAN. OAN is a protocol-neutral trust layer for open Agent interconnection and discoverable AI resource products. It specifies the role architecture, did:oan identity objects, registration workflow, governance-backed Root lifecycle enforcement, Root-verified package model, authorization-aware Discovery, Root-issued infrastructure authorization VCs, signed trusted invocation, Root's trust, data-distribution, and semantic-governance hub responsibilities, verification requirements, state transitions, security properties, implementation boundaries, and deployment considerations. The design is intended to support heterogeneous Agent frameworks and interaction protocols, including MCP, A2A, ANP-like systems, domain-specific Agent protocols, Skills, MCP Servers, and Tool/API resources. OAN does not define the entire business conversation among Agents or the native protocol of every resource; it defines how resource identities become admissible, discoverable, verifiable, and safe to approach before protocol-specific interaction begins, and how defined profiles carry that identity into protected protocol interaction.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Constrained Federated Reinforcement Learning for Secure Offloading in Vehicular Edge Computing
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Vehicular Edge Computing (VEC) reduces latency for computation-intensive vehicular applications by offloading tasks to roadside edge servers. Real vehicular workloads, however, consist of dependent subtasks with stringent reliability needs, while the cross-region collaborative learning used to adapt offloading policies must stay robust to heterogeneous data and secure over open wireless channels. We propose CRAFT, a Constrained Reinforcement-based Adaptive Federated Task Offloading framework that casts Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)-structured offloading and resource allocation as a Constrained Markov Decision Process. CRAFT couples centralized-critic policy learning with Lagrangian relaxation to explicitly regulate the long-term task-completion constraint, and uses two-tier federated aggregation with proximal regularization to jointly mitigate non-Independent and Identically Distributed (non-IID) drift and stabilize constraint adaptation. Confidentiality and integrity for federated parameter exchange are provided by post-quantum homomorphic encryption and lattice-based signatures with modest amortized overhead. On a Virtual Machine-based testbed over a realistic Melbourne Central Business District network with real computation kernels, CRAFT cuts weighted cost by up to 42% over state-of-the-art baselines, maintains a completion rate of around 96%, and adds 6.4% security overhead.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: A mechanism for collective foraging: percolating recruitment cascades coupled to a maximum-entropy
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Foraging recruitment is a contagion: an agent that finds a resource triggers a linear-threshold cascade, the model built for rumour and adoption spread on social networks, now embedded in space. Because activation is degree-normalized, the same rule that spreads the cascade also stifles it as neighbourhoods crowd, so the swarm aggregates on a resource and then releases to explore again. The cascade runs on the communication network, but acting on it moves agents in physical space, and that motion rewires the network: network and space are one coupled system, and this feedback, not any tuning, makes the coordination self-limiting. Because recruitment chains along the graph rather than reaching near neighbours alone, whether a discovery stays local or spans the swarm is a question of percolation. The swarm holds itself in a cascade window that is locally near-critical though globally subcritical, a self-organized, self-limiting drive-release cycle, sandpile-like but non-conservative. Nothing is tuned, yet behaviours that foraging biology documents separately emerge together: recruitment to discoveries, marginal-value patch-leaving, and Levy search with a switch to local exploitation. These follow from one least-committal principle, the resource field and the search both as maximum entropy, with Levy search matched to the field's sparsity and recruitment to its clustering, so active-matter order and optimal foraging appear as one system seen in two domains. The gains are real but conditional: up to 7.6x the harvest of solitary search when resources are sparse and clustered, shrinking to nothing when search is already easy. That sparse, clustered field is also the generic one, because resources almost inevitably aggregate, so one untuned rule should recur widely.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 48 pages, 19 figures (10 main + 9 SI), 2 tables, Code and data: https://github.com/galenwilkerson/collective-foraging-cascades

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: DIFFLET: A Fast Inference Engine for Diffusion Transformer Models on AWS Trainium
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: On AWS Trainium2, every component of a diffusion model runs as a program compiled ahead of time for fixed shapes, while pipelines differ across models, prompt lengths across requests, and caching decisions across denoising steps. We present Difflet, a serving engine in which five model pipelines share one compilation backend, joint attention is split across cores by attention head, and a host controller decides at each denoising step whether to run the denoiser or reuse its earlier output. A small probe program computes the caching signal on the device and returns one number per step, and a resident model process keeps every program loaded across requests. Across five image and video model families, fused attention accelerates denoiser steps by 1.2-4.3x over the same framework using PyTorch/XLA attention, and at 32.8k visual tokens it is the only attention that compiles. On four of the five models, resident serving is 1.5-3.4x faster than standalone runs that reload weights from a warm file cache for each generation.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Learning-Theoretic Foundation for General Coded Computing: The Adversarial Setting
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
Adversarial workers pose a severe challenge in distributed computing systems by returning corrupted outputs that can substantially distort the recovered computations. Coded computing addresses this threat by introducing redundancy across worker assignments. Existing exact and approximate coded-computing methods typically handle adversarial outputs by explicitly locating and correcting or removing erroneous evaluations, which adds significant computational overhead at the master node. Moreover, existing analyses do not characterize how the recovery error scales with the number of workers and the adversarial budget.
  In this paper, we develop an adversarially robust extension of general coded computing (GCC), a learning-theoretic approximate coded-computing framework that designs the encoder and decoder by minimizing an upper bound on the end-to-end recovery error. Rather than identifying corrupted workers, the proposed method uses smoothness regularization to limit the influence of their outputs. The resulting encoder and decoder can be implemented using smoothing splines with linear master-side complexity. We derive a non-asymptotic bound on the worst-case end-to-end approximation error by decomposing it into three components: (1) the encoder approximation error, (2) the decoder reconstruction error under fully honest results, and (3) the adversarial perturbation error. For maximum of $q\geq 1$ adversarial workers among $N$ workers results in a worst-case error of order $\mathcal{O}((q/N)^{6/5})$ with appropriate selection of smoothness parameter, demonstrating that the approximation error vanishes asymptotically whenever the number of adversaries grows sublinearly with the network size. Experiments on scalar computation and neural-network inference are consistent with the predicted convergence behavior.

Discrete Mathematics.title: Hull Games of Induced Path Convexities in Graphs
Discrete Mathematics.summary: In 1984, Frank Harary introduced the first convexity games in graphs, all of them based on the geodesic convexity, which is the graph convexity related to shortest paths. In 2024, Araújo et al. obtained the first PSPACE-hardness proofs on some of these geodesic games and generalized them to any graph convexity. In this paper, we investigate convexity games on several known induced path convexities: the monophonic $\mathrm{m}$-convexity and the $\ell_k$-convexities, based on induced paths and on induced paths of size at most $k$. We prove that the hull games $\mathrm{CHG}_{\mathrm{m}}$, $\mathrm{CHG}_{\ell_k}$ and their misère variants are PSPACE-complete for every $k\ge2$ even in graphs with diameter at most 3. We also use the Sprague-Grundy Theory to obtain a polynomial time algorithm to decide the winner of the games $\mathrm{CHG}_{\mathrm{m}}$ and $\mathrm{CHG}_{\ell_k}$ for any $k\ge2$ in disjoint unions of paths and cycles. For $k\ge3$ odd, we prove that Alice (1st player) wins $\mathrm{CHG}_{\ell_k}$ in the path $P_n$ if and only if $n$ is odd and she wins in the cycle $C_n$ if and only if $n=3$ or $n=α\cdot (k+1)-1$ with $α\ge2$. For $k\ge2$ even, the only periodic nimber sequences of $\mathrm{CHG}_{\ell_k}$ obtained through extensive computational testing occurred for $k=2^h-4$ with $h\ge3$, e.g, $k\in\{4,12,28,60,\ldots\}$. In this case ($k=2^h-4$ with $h\ge3$), we prove that the nimber sequences of $\mathrm{CHG}_{\ell_k}$ in $P_n$ and in $C_n$ are periodic and Alice loses (resp. wins) in $P_n$ (resp. $C_n$) with $n>k$ only when $n=3k+4$ (resp. $n\in\{2k+1,5k+3\}$). Finally, we show that, for $k=2$, the game $\mathrm{CHG}_{\ell_2}$ in paths $P_n$ is closely related to the classical game Couples-are-Forever of J. H. Conway: it is still an open problem if the nimber sequence is periodic or not and Alice loses only for 12 values of $n$ up to $100$ million.

Discrete Mathematics.title: There is no $8$-regular $K_3$-irregular graph
Discrete Mathematics.summary: A graph is $K_3$-irregular if its vertices belong to pairwise distinct numbers of triangles. We prove that no $8$-regular $K_3$-irregular graph exists, settling the last unresolved case. Following the initial discovery of such graphs for regularities $r \in \{10,11,12\}$ (Stevanović et al., 2024), our previous work (Hak et al., 2025) showed that no such graphs exist for $r \le 7$, provided the first example for $r=9$, and proved that any $8$-regular candidate must have between $17$ and $22$ vertices. We exclude these possible orders for $r=8$ by combining careful analysis of triangle degrees with integer linear programming techniques. Meanwhile, a recent construction (Zhang, 2026) established that regular $K_3$-irregular graphs do exist for all $r \ge 9$. Together with our results, this establishes that an $r$-regular $K_3$-irregular graph exists if and only if $r\geq 9$.
Discrete Mathematics.comment: Updated version, properly adressed range {1..20} for n=20. Any comments are welcome

Discrete Mathematics.title: ARRIVAL in cube-root subexponential time
Discrete Mathematics.summary:
In the ARRIVAL problem, a token travels through a switch digraph: at every vertex, it leaves along one of two out-arcs, and the two are used alternately. The question is which of two terminals the token reaches first. ARRIVAL lies in $\mathsf{NP} \cap \mathsf{coNP}$, but no polynomial-time algorithm is known.The fastest known algorithms turn some vertices into terminals and search for consistent guesses of the numbers of tokens that these vertices send out. The first, due to Gärtner et al. [ICALP 2021], searches all vertices at once with an algorithm for fixed points of monotone maps, and the second, due to Haslebacher [ICALP 2025], searches one vertex at a time by binary search. Both search for a fixed point of the same map, which returns how many tokens arrive at the guessed vertices.
  We guess the vertices in blocks of $k$, between these two extremes, which needs a search in $k$ dimensions with few evaluations of this map. To do so, we build on the connection between ARRIVAL and $\ell_1$-contractions established in the second of these works. We search with $\ell_1$-centerpoints of the remaining guesses, which are guaranteed to exist by Haslebacher et al. [FOCS 2025], and which we approximate deterministically. In order to prove our results, we show how to find the least fixed points of maps from $\{0, \ldots, N\}^k$ to itself that have unit increments.
  For ARRIVAL on $n$-vertex switch digraphs, this gives run time $2^{\mathcal{O}(n^{1/3} \cdot \log^{2/3} n)}$, improving the previous time bound of $n^{\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n})}$. We work with the more general \garrival problem, with many tokens and several terminals, and solve it in the same time when there are at most $2^n$ tokens.

Discrete Mathematics.title: Isolation of non-triangle cycles in graphs
Discrete Mathematics.summary: Given a set $\mathcal{F}$ of graphs, we call a copy of a graph in $\mathcal{F}$ an $\mathcal{F}$-graph. The $\mathcal{F}$-isolation number of a graph $G$, denoted by $ι(G, \mathcal{F})$, is the size of a smallest set $D$ of vertices of $G$ such that the closed neighbourhood $N[D]$ of $D$ intersects the vertex sets of the $\mathcal{F}$-graphs contained by $G$ (equivalently, $G-N[D]$ contains no $\mathcal{F}$-graph). Let $\mathcal{C}$ be the set of cycles, and let $\mathcal{C}'$ be the set of non-triangle cycles (that is, cycles of length at least $4$). Let $G$ be a connected graph having exactly $n$ vertices and $m$ edges. The first author proved that $ι(G,\mathcal{C}) \leq n/4$ if $G$ is not a triangle. Bartolo and the authors determined a set $\mathcal{E}_4$ of nine graphs such that $ι(G,\{C_4\}) \leq n/5$ if $G$ is not an $\mathcal{E}_4$-graph. Chen and Cui recently strengthened this result by proving that $ι(G, \mathcal{C}') \leq n/5$ if $G$ is not an $\mathcal{E}_4$-graph. This had been proved by Zhang and Wu for the case where $G$ contains no triangle. Various authors proved that $ι(G,\mathcal{C}) \leq (m+1)/5$ if $G$ is not a triangle. We prove that $ι(G,\mathcal{C}') \leq (m+1)/6$ if $G$ is not a $4$-cycle. Zhang and Wu established this for the case where $G$ contains no triangle. Our result yields the inequality $ι(G,\{C_4\}) \leq (m+1)/6$ of Wei, Zhang and Zhao. These bounds are attained by infinitely many (non-isomorphic) graphs. The proof of our inequality hinges on also determining the graphs attaining the bound.

Discrete Mathematics.title: Multi-Capacity Online Assortment Optimization with Consecutive Stays under Markov Chain Choice
Discrete Mathematics.summary:
We study online assortment optimization under Markov chain choice and independent Bernoulli arrivals, with each period's request type known in advance. Each product may have multiple interchangeable physical copies, and each booking reserves consecutive service slots on a single copy. Customers choose among products, while the platform assigns purchases to feasible copies. We develop a sales-based relaxation that upper-bounds the optimal online revenue and use it to design a policy with two components: independent sampling and purchase--update coupling. We generate independent copy proposals and make a product eligible whenever at least one of its copies proposes. A general revenue-extraction bound for random candidate sets with independent product inclusions shows that optimizing over eligible products recovers at least half of each period's relaxation revenue benchmark in expectation. A purchase--update coupling reproduces the interval flows through independent virtual copy updates while preserving physical feasibility. Under general Markov chain choice, the policy uses a random gate to make the coupling feasible: it offers the selected assortment with probability \(1-1/e\) and the empty assortment otherwise. No gate is needed under multinomial logit (MNL) choice.
  The resulting policies achieve approximation ratios of \((1-1/e)/2\) and \(1/2\), respectively, relative to the optimal nonanticipative online policy, independently of product capacities. In the single-copy MNL setting, our policy improves the guarantee of \citet{huwu2026} from \(0.271\) to \(1/2\) under the same arrival convention. The \(1/2\) static extraction factor and the \(1-1/e\) uniform scalar-gate factor are separately sharp, and the \(1/2\) MNL guarantee is tight for the proposed policy.

Discrete Mathematics.title: Metric Dimension is NP-complete on Graphs of Treewidth Two
Discrete Mathematics.summary: The metric dimension of a connected graph is the least number of vertices whose distance vectors distinguish all vertices. We show that deciding whether the metric dimension of a graph is at most a given integer is NP-complete on graphs of treewidth at most two, and even on two-connected two-terminal series-parallel graphs of pathwidth at most five. As the problem is polynomial on trees, the graphs of treewidth one, this settles the treewidth threshold of its hardness, which was known to lie between two and twenty-four. The reduction is from satisfiability of formulas in which every literal occurs at most twice. To such a formula with $n$ clauses and $r$ variables it associates a two-terminal series-parallel graph $G_\varphi$ with $O((n+r)^2)$ vertices and pathwidth at most five, whose metric dimension is $2(n+r)+7$ if the formula is satisfiable and $2(n+r)+8$ otherwise.
Discrete Mathematics.comment: v3: NP-completeness extended to two-connected two-terminal series-parallel graphs of pathwidth at most five; v2: open questions corrected. 86 pages, 5 figures

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The Optimal Sampler for Diverse TSP Solutions: Characterization, Limits, and Learning
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We address the Diverse Traveling Salesman Problem (D-TSP) that seeks a set of $k$ distinct TSP tours. Each selected tour must not exceed a prescribed multiple of the optimal tour length, while the maximum pairwise Jaccard similarity within the selected set is minimized. This formulation is important for applications requiring both solution quality and fault tolerance, such as logistics planning, robotics, and strategic patrolling. We propose a novel hybrid framework that decomposes D-TSP into a sampling stage and a selection stage. The selection stage is a max-min dispersion problem, for which any approximation better than a factor of two is NP-hard; we therefore focus on the sampling stage. Our contributions are both theoretical and empirical. Theoretically, we give two end-to-end guarantees for the optimal sampling distribution, from two perspectives: including an optimal set in the sampled pool, or having at least $k$ mutually distant tours in the pool. The second reduces the number of samples from exponential to linear in $k$, at the cost of weakening the benchmark from the best $k$ tours to the best $βk$ for some $β> 1$. For practical use, we prove that a pipeline that samples spanning trees and then converts to tours does not hurt the quality of the pool in principle. Empirically, both objectives are learnable, and our experiments not only validate the analysis but also outperform the baselines on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, by a single trained model with no fine-tuning.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Solving problems in RDV Graphs faster and easier
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In interval graphs and many generalizations thereof, problems such as Matching, Independent Set, and Dominating Set can be solved with simple greedy algorithms in linear (i.e., $O(m+n)$) time. However, it is sometimes possible to improve on this runtime if a suitable representation as intersection graph is given; for example it is possible to find a minimum dominating set in an interval graph in $O(n)$ time. We study RDV graphs, a generalization of interval graphs, namely, the intersection graphs of directed paths in a rooted tree. It was known that the above three problems can be solved in $O(n\log n)$ time if a suitably small representation is given. In this paper, we reduce the runtime to $O(n)$. Furthermore, while the previous results used non-trivial operations such as range-minimum queries and ray-shooting queries, we need nothing more complicated than lists and (for Matching) a Union-Find data structure.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Amplified Pruning and Path Selectors for Deterministic Radio Gossiping
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study deterministic gossiping in unknown strongly connected directed radio networks with $n$ vertices, $m$ arcs, and distinct identifiers in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, where $N=n^{\mathcal O(1)}$. Messages are unrestricted; collision detection is unavailable. Our protocol combines amplified reception certificates, adaptive pruning, and permutation selectors. Each pruning iteration costs $\mathcal O(n\log^2n\log\log n)$ rounds. A two-step quadratic contraction limits each receiver and each class of identical closed in-neighborhoods to $\mathcal O(\log\log n)$ qualifying selections. Under an explicit degree-concentration condition, our protocol takes $\mathcal O(m\log^2n(\log\log n)^2)$ rounds. For directed regular graphs with common in- and out-degree $Δ$, our strategy achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n\sqrtΔ,n^2/Δ\})$, extending the identifier range of Wu and Chrobak and improving their high-degree bound. At completion entry, let $a\ge1$ count original sources not yet credited as globally disseminated. Permutation selectors reduce our balanced completion budget by a factor of $\log^{2/3}(a+1)$ relative to interleaved path selectors. Our geometric protocol attains $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(k^2+nτ+\min\{u^2,(nu)^{2/3}\})$ for an original path cover of scale $k$, weight $τ$, and $u$ exceptions. Every graph also admits $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n^{4/3},N+(mn)^{3/5}\})$ rounds. Only $n,N$ are inputs. Within the stated graph classes and identifier ranges, these results answer the polynomial-identifier and average-degree questions of Wu and Chrobak. The unrestricted general-graph cases remain open.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Dynamic k-center clustering with lifetimes
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The $k$-center problem is a fundamental clustering variant with applications in learning systems and data summarization. In several real-world scenarios, the dataset to be clustered is not static, but evolves over time, as new data points arrive and old ones become stale. To account for dynamicity, the $k$-center problem has been mainly studied under the sliding window setting, where only the $N$ most recent points are considered non-stale, or the fully dynamic setting, where arbitrary sequences of point arrivals and deletions without prior notice may occur. In this paper, we introduce the dynamic setting with lifetimes, which bridges the two aforementioned classical settings by still allowing arbitrary arrivals and deletions, but making the deletion time of each point known upon its arrival. Under this new setting, we devise a deterministic $(2+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm with $\tilde{O}(k/\varepsilon)$ amortized update time and memory usage linear in the number of currently active points. Moreover, we develop a deterministic $(6+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm that, under tame update sequences, has $\tilde{O}(k/\varepsilon)$ worst-case update time and heavily sublinear working memory.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A minimum witness for the 3/2 configuration-linear-program gap in two-weight graph balancing, unique at its size
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Restricted assignment minimizes makespan, the busiest machine's load, when each job has one size and a set of allowed machines. Its tightest studied relaxation is the configuration linear program, which fractionally gives each machine whole job sets that fit. Its integrality gap, the worst-case ratio of integral optimum to relaxation value, is open in general. On two-weight graph balancing (sizes 1 and 2, each job allowed on at most two machines) the gap is known: Jansen, Land, and Maack (2016) give both bounds. Their Table 1 instance attains 3/2, and their Corollary 11 bound of 2-s/b for sizes s < b matches it at {1,2}. We ask how small such an instance, a witness, can be. We give a six-job witness I* on the complete graph on four machines: unit jobs form a cycle through all four, and two weight-2 jobs take the remaining edges. I* has integral optimum 3 against relaxation value 2, one job fewer than the smallest earlier witness of this class. We prove I* minimum and unique at its size, on any number of machines: no instance with at most five jobs reaches gap 3/2, and at six jobs I* is the only witness, up to relabeling machines and adding unusable machines. At seven jobs uniqueness fails: we classify all thirteen witnesses, including the Jansen-Land-Maack instance. Eight jobs give 154, nine 1,662. At least four machines are necessary. Kartak et al. (2015) classified the extremal non-round-up instances of the same relaxation in one-dimensional cutting stock for small demand; the Discussion relates them. Recognizing witnesses at relaxation value 2, shared by all ours, is coNP-complete, so no min-max characterization with polynomially checkable conditions exists unless NP = coNP. Every feasibility decision behind the exhaustive claims was made twice, in floating-point and exact rational arithmetic, with identical results. We accept the pipeline's negatives only after it rediscovers I*.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 37 pages, 12 figures, 1 table. v3: corrects the infeasibility-verdict count behind the six-machine sweep (4,228,054, not 4,231,347), a false remark on the vertex hypothesis and two internal contradictions; the coNP consequence is stated precisely; exploratory LP bounds are labelled numerical; overstatements narrowed. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/SKX86

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The 11/6 supremum of the Wang-Sitters rounding scheme for graph balancing
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Wang and Sitters' 11/6-approximation for graph balancing (each job allowed on at most two machines) is not one algorithm but a set of permitted executions. Step 1 may return any feasible solution of the fractional relaxation. Step 3 may match remaining jobs to the rounding's slots in many ways. We determine exactly what that latitude permits: ratios arbitrarily close to 11/6, none reaching it, so 11/6 is the least constant bounding every permitted run. We then determine the worst-case guarantee, against the optimum itself, as a function of the big-job threshold beta, the fractional share at or above which Step 2 assigns a job. On Wang and Sitters' own range 1/2 < beta < 1 the guarantee is exactly max{3/2 + beta/2, 5/2 - beta}. We extend the same eligibility rule to 0 < beta <= 1/2, outside the range they state. There a big job's two shares can both reach the threshold, so Step 2 acquires a third choice. We determine it too: exactly 3/2 + (1-beta)floor(1/beta), hence unbounded as beta falls. The worst-case ratio is therefore known at every threshold in (0,1), and attained at none. Consequently 2/3 is the unique optimal threshold, and the guarantee jumps at one half and again at every threshold 1/k below it, rather than degrading smoothly. A companion note examines changes that leave the constant unchanged.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 43 pages, 9 figures. v3: the beta < 1/2 seven-machine witness is certified in exact rational arithmetic; the strict-rule endpoint at beta = 1/2 is argued in full; the computational status cites the companion's NP-hardness of best-matching selection for a supplied fractional solution; smaller corrections. Companion to arXiv:2609.10004. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/SKX86

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Minimum-makespan completion and vertex selection leave the Wang-Sitters constant at 11/6
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Wang and Sitters' rounding scheme for graph balancing (each job allowed on at most two machines) keeps the makespan, the busiest machine's load, within 11/6 of the optimum, and a companion note shows that no smaller constant holds. One suspected cause is Step 3's freedom to match leftover jobs to slots in any valid way. We show that removing that freedom does not improve the constant. An idealized oracle that always picks the valid matching with the smallest makespan still has worst-case constant exactly 11/6 against the optimum. Both natural 7/4 bounds for it, against the relaxation's target and against the optimum, are false. Requiring Step 1 to return a vertex (corner) of the relaxation does not help when that vertex is chosen adversarially. The loss therefore does not come from Step 3's freedom alone. We also prove a reduction confining every overload above 7/4 to two shapes, give a seven-machine instance on which the natural two-phase repair fails, and prove a strict 7/4 bound on the generalized three-path family.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 52 pages, 11 figures. v2: new results: where the cut-term bound 3/2+1/(r+1) is attained on the three-path family (correcting v1), and strong NP-completeness of completing a supplied fractional solution with two slots per machine (polynomial with one); corrects two complexity remarks and smaller misstatements. Companion to arXiv:2609.03890. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/SKX86

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Computing Lewis Weights to High Precision by Fixed-Point Iteration
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The $\ell_p$-Lewis weights of a matrix are defined by a fixed-point equation. For $p<4$, Cohen and Peng [CP15] showed that iterating an equivalent rearrangement of this equation computes Lewis weights to high precision; for $p\geq4$, prior high-precision methods instead use optimization-based approaches. We show that the direct Lewis fixed-point iteration, appearing in the thesis of Lee [Lee16], computes Lewis weights to high precision for every $p>2$.
  For a matrix $\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ partitioned into row blocks $\mathbf{A}_{[1]},\ldots,\mathbf{A}_{[k]}$, we compute, for $p>2$, coordinatewise $\varepsilon$-approximate $\ell_p$ block Lewis weights in $O\left(p\log\frac{p\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^k\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A}_{[i]})}}{\varepsilon}\right)$ rounds of exact leverage-score-vector computations. For ordinary Lewis weights, this becomes $O\left(p\log\frac{p\sqrt{m}}{\varepsilon}\right)$, improving the $O\left(p^2\log(m/\varepsilon)\right)$ bound of Gribling, Sidford, and Zhang [GSZ26] for $p\geq4$. Our guarantees also extend to approximate leverage-score computations.
  Our main observation is that each direct Lewis update contracts the KL divergence to the true weights by a factor of $1-\frac{2}{p}$. We also give an alternate explanation of this contraction through volume sampling and entropic independence. Synthetic experiments closely match our predicted local contraction rates and iteration counts grow approximately linearly with $p$; real-data experiments illustrate the information-concentration tradeoff of finite-$p$ block Lewis designs.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 25 pages, 8 figures; v2 primarily adds Theorem 1.5, concurrent work citation, and code for experiments

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Birthday Estimators Are Uniformly Optimal for Renyi Entropy
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Collisions are a basic probe of unknown distributions, used for testing and for counting substructures in graphs, and they underlie Rényi entropy, a fundamental measure of uncertainty with applications in cryptography, machine learning, physics, and biology. Motivated by this, we study the natural birthday estimator.
  We prove Bernstein-type concentration for it and show that it is minimax optimal, uniformly and jointly in alphabet size, order, accuracy, and confidence, with no sample splitting, clipping, or median aggregation.
  This, in particular, settles the sample complexity of integer-order Rényi entropy estimation up to absolute constants in all regimes, closing the gap between the best known upper and lower bounds.
  Our concentration bound rests on a sensitivity analysis of collision count, and the matching lower bound on a sharp analysis of detecting a hidden spike in a plateau distribution.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Dynamic Distances Without Matrix Inverse
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the fully dynamic exact distance problem in unweighted directed graphs, where the graph undergoes edge insertions and deletions, and the distance between two query vertices must be reported. Under the combinatorial Boolean matrix multiplication conjecture, any subquadratic-time algorithm for this problem must use algebraic techniques. All prior work uses the polynomial matrix inverse as its algebraic tool, but within subquadratic time, this technique can only maintain distances up to a small-polynomial hop bound. So larger distances must be reassembled from short-range pieces by a combinatorial layer. This hybrid algebraic-combinatorial construction has led to a substantial slowdown for dynamic distances compared to other dynamic graph problems relying on algebraic techniques.
  We give the first subquadratic-time dynamic distance algorithm built on dynamically maintaining a different algebraic object than the matrix inverse. By maintaining the Frobenius form $A=KCK^{-1}$ of a dynamic generic (i.e., cyclic) matrix $A$, we can query all the powers $A^\ell = K C^\ell K^{-1}$ efficiently. For adjacency matrix~$A$, the smallest $\ell$ with $(A^\ell)_{s,t}\neq 0$ is the $st$-distance in the associated graph. So, unlike dynamic matrix inverse, we get distance information directly without hop truncation, and we no longer need to perform any combinatorial reassembly. This purely algebraic approach to dynamic distances leads to the fastest dynamic distance algorithm with $O(n^{1.58})$ update time.
  The earlier use of the Frobenius form maintained the dense change of basis $K$ explicitly and required $\tilde O (n^2)$ time per update [KS23]. Our key observation is that this change of basis is highly structured, which lets us maintain it implicitly. This gives the first subquadratic dynamic algorithm for the Frobenius normal form and characteristic polynomial for generic matrices.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Diverse Schedules for Makespan Minimization on Unrelated Machines
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study makespan minimization on unrelated machines with the additional goal of constructing diverse schedules: Instead of outputting a single schedule, we seek a collection of schedules with provable makespan guarantees and substantially different job assignments. Committing to a single schedule in advance may be undesirable. Processing times may be uncertain, and constraints or domain knowledge may emerge later, so $k$ schedules of similar quality offer meaningful alternatives. We measure pairwise diversity by the weighted Hamming distance between job assignments and study the two standard objectives in the diverse-solutions literature: max-sum diversity, which maximizes the total pairwise distance between schedules, and max-min diversity, which maximizes the smallest pairwise distance.
  For the max-sum objective, we show that optimal diversity can be achieved in polynomial time without sacrificing the classic makespan approximation factor. For every feasible makespan target $T$, we can compute $k$ schedules of makespan at most $2T$ whose max-sum diversity is optimal among all $k$ schedules of makespan at most $T$. Therefore, we match the classic factor-$2$ makespan guarantee of Lenstra, Shmoys, and Tardos (Math. Prog., 1990) and preserve optimal diversity.
  For the max-min objective, we show that the diversity problem is inherently harder. Namely, we show that, even without makespan constraints, deciding whether three schedules of given pairwise diversity exist is NP-hard. We complete this with two complementary bicriteria approximation algorithms for every fixed $k$ and $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$. The first preserves almost all of the optimal max-min diversity with makespan at most $(3\lceil12/\varepsilon\rceil+1)T$. The second keeps the makespan arbitrarily close to the classic $2$ guarantee while achieving a $\frac{1}{2}(1-\varepsilon)$ fraction of the optimal max-min diversity.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Shortened version of the abstract to comply with arxiv's character limit

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Improved Approximation for Unsplittable Capacitated Vehicle Routing Using Quota Trees
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In the Unsplittable Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (UCVRP), we are given a set $V$ of $n$ clients with normalized demands $d_v \in (0,1]$, a depot $r$, a unit vehicle capacity, and symmetric metric travel costs $c$ on $V \cup \{r\}$. We seek a collection of routes of minimum total cost that start and end at $r$, serve each client's entire demand on a single route, and respect the unit capacity constraint $\sum_{v \in V(R)} d_v \le 1$ on every route $R$, where $V(R)$ denotes the clients served by $R$. This models deliveries from a common depot in which each customer's order must be delivered in a single trip.
  UCVRP generalizes the metric traveling salesman problem (TSP) and is therefore NP-hard. Capacity constraints add a packing difficulty: when all clients are colocated away from the depot, minimizing the route cost is equivalent to minimizing the number of bins in bin packing. Consequently, UCVRP admits no polynomial-time approximation ratio below $3/2$ unless $\textbf{P=NP}$ (Grandoni, Mathieu, and Zhou, 2023). The classical $3.5$-approximation has been improved through several recent advances; in particular, Zhao and Xiao (2026) recently obtained a $(2+\ln 2+\varepsilon)$-approximation.
  In this paper, we give a deterministic $(5/2+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm running in $n^{O(1/\varepsilon)}$ time for every rational $0<\varepsilon\le1/9$, applicable to general capacity and arbitrary positive demands. Our algorithm uses local search to select routes through one client with large demand and clients with small demands. It constructs candidate routes using endpoint quota trees after rounding demands and creating vertex copies. We combine these routes with those obtained by matching and set packing, keeping their client sets disjoint. The remaining clients are served by partitioning a tour constructed using weighted graphic matroid parity.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The Complexity of Weak Partition Connectivity in Hedgegraphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We prove that deciding whether the weak partition connectivity (WPC) of an unweighted hedgegraph is at most a given integer is NP-complete, resolving an open question about its computational complexity. Hardness holds even for connected full-support split systems, where each hedge consists of two nonempty, vertex-disjoint hyperedges covering all vertices. We also obtain hardness on connected edge-colored simple graphs in which each color class is a spanning forest with exactly two nontrivial trees. On both classes, exact computation of fractional WPC is NP-hard, whereas hedge connectivity is computable exactly in polynomial time. A binary matrix formulation yields the reduction and a deterministic polynomial-time exact algorithm under a linear intersection condition on row supports after normalization and column compression. In particular, both integer and fractional WPC are computable in polynomial time when these supports have size at most two, whereas NP-hardness holds already when their size is bounded by three. For every fixed $b$, we give deterministic and randomized efficient polynomial-time approximation schemes on hedgegraphs in which each hedge has at most $b$ connected components, counting isolated vertices. Both schemes return one partition that simultaneously approximates integer and fractional WPC. Unless $\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}$, neither objective admits a deterministic FPTAS, even on the two hard instance classes.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Approximating Prize-Collecting TSP below 1.556
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The prize-collecting traveling salesperson problem is a variant of the metric traveling salesperson problem in which vertices may be left unvisited by paying their associated penalties. The objective is to minimize the length of the tour plus the total penalty of the unvisited vertices. Blauth, Klein, and Nägele gave the previously best-known LP-relative $1.599$-approximation. Their algorithm constructs tours by applying a splitting-off preprocessing to an LP solution, decomposing the resulting solution into trees, pruning them, and performing parity correction. We improve the LP-relative approximation ratio to $1.55576$. Our main contribution is a new bound on the cost of parity correction that exploits parity information revealed by further pruning in the analysis. This bound makes the splitting-off preprocessing unnecessary, so the improvement is achieved by a simpler version of their algorithm. The stated factor follows from a numerical parameter search with exact verification, while an elementary analysis already yields an LP-relative $1.56$-approximation.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Near-Optimal Bounds for Testing Residual-String Equality and Parenthesis Languages
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Residual-String Equality, denoted $\texttt{ResStringEq}$, is the property consisting of all pairs of strings over $\{0,1,*\}$ that are equal after deleting all `$*$' symbols from them. This property was first introduced by Fischer, Magniez, and Starikovskaya (SODA 2018), who used it to show a lower bound on testing the $\texttt{Dyck}$ languages, where $\texttt{Dyck}_m$ is the language consisting of balanced sequences of parentheses over $m$ parenthesis types. They showed that testing $\texttt{ResStringEq}$ on inputs of length $n$ requires $Ω(n^{1/5})$ queries, and presented a reduction from testing $\texttt{ResStringEq}$ to testing $\texttt{Dyck}_m$ for any $m \geq 2$. Furthermore, they showed that $\texttt{Dyck}_m$ can be tested with $O(n^{2/5+δ})$ queries for every constant proximity parameter, where $δ>0$ is an arbitrarily small constant.
  In this work, we nearly close the gap, by showing that testing $\texttt{ResStringEq}$, and hence $\texttt{Dyck}_m$ (for any $m\geq 2$), requires $Ω(n^{2/5})$ queries. We also show a stronger lower bound of $Ω(\sqrt{n})$ for testers that make non-adaptive queries. We establish that the $Ω(\sqrt{n})$ bound is nearly tight, by presenting a non-adaptive tester for $\texttt{ResStringEq}$ that uses $O(n^{1/2+δ})$ queries for an arbitrarily small constant $δ>0$. Furthermore, we extend this non-adaptive tester to the $\texttt{Dyck}$ languages, with the same query complexity. Finally, we improve the dependence on the proximity parameter $ε$ in the tester of Fischer, Magniez, and Starikovskaya, reducing it from $O(1/ε)^{\mathrm{poly}(1/δ)}$ to $O(1/ε)^{O(\log(1/δ))}$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Output-linear time enumeration of potential maximal cliques
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
First defined by Bouchitté and Todinca, Potential Maximal Cliques (PMC) are a well studied notion in graph theory due to its numerous applications. The PMCs of an undirected graph $G$ are defined as the maximal cliques of the minimal triangulations of $G$. Their number can be exponential in the size of the graph. PMCs were crucial in the design of a polynomial-time algorithm which solves Maximum Weight Independent Set on $P_6$-free graphs (Grzesik, Klimošová, Pilipczuk, Pilipczuk, 2020). They also play a central role in the proposal of a polynomial-time algorithm to solve Largest Induced Subgraph of treewidth $\le t$ (Fomin, Todinca, Villanger, 2013).
  Last but not least, certainly one of the main application of PMCs is the existence of an exact dynamic-programming algorithm to determine the treewidth of a graph (Fomin, Kratsch, Todinca, Villanger, 2008) which uses its list of PMCs as an input. In fact, the enumeration of PMCs stands as the bottleneck for the computation of treewidth with this method: the PMC-enumeration step takes output-quadratic time (Bouchitté, Todinca, 2002) while the dynamic-programming one takes a time linear in the number of PMCs. This two-step procedure was proven to be among the most performing approaches in practice to determine treewidth.
  Answering a longstanding open question, we propose an algorithm to enumerate PMCs in output-linear time, i.e. a running time linear in the number of PMCs. This offers nice perspectives not only from the theoretical viewpoint - better running time for the PMC-based methods determining treewidth, for Minimum Fill-In and Largest Induced Subgraph of treewidth $\le t$ - but also from the practical side, with the possibility to propose top-performance implementation.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: This paper was accepted at SODA 2027. 54 pages, 18 figures

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: ARRIVAL in cube-root subexponential time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In the ARRIVAL problem, a token travels through a switch digraph: at every vertex, it leaves along one of two out-arcs, and the two are used alternately. The question is which of two terminals the token reaches first. ARRIVAL lies in $\mathsf{NP} \cap \mathsf{coNP}$, but no polynomial-time algorithm is known.The fastest known algorithms turn some vertices into terminals and search for consistent guesses of the numbers of tokens that these vertices send out. The first, due to Gärtner et al. [ICALP 2021], searches all vertices at once with an algorithm for fixed points of monotone maps, and the second, due to Haslebacher [ICALP 2025], searches one vertex at a time by binary search. Both search for a fixed point of the same map, which returns how many tokens arrive at the guessed vertices.
  We guess the vertices in blocks of $k$, between these two extremes, which needs a search in $k$ dimensions with few evaluations of this map. To do so, we build on the connection between ARRIVAL and $\ell_1$-contractions established in the second of these works. We search with $\ell_1$-centerpoints of the remaining guesses, which are guaranteed to exist by Haslebacher et al. [FOCS 2025], and which we approximate deterministically. In order to prove our results, we show how to find the least fixed points of maps from $\{0, \ldots, N\}^k$ to itself that have unit increments.
  For ARRIVAL on $n$-vertex switch digraphs, this gives run time $2^{\mathcal{O}(n^{1/3} \cdot \log^{2/3} n)}$, improving the previous time bound of $n^{\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n})}$. We work with the more general \garrival problem, with many tokens and several terminals, and solve it in the same time when there are at most $2^n$ tokens.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Subjective Valuations Make It Hard to be Fair: The Complexity of Resource Allocation to Groups of Agents
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the parameterized complexity of finding an EF1 allocation of indivisible items in the group-sharing setting, which has received increasing attention in recent years. There, items are not allocated to individual agents but rather to one of two (or possibly more) groups, and agents within that group all share the assigned items. We consider both the "fixed" (EF1-Fix) and "variable" (EF1-Var) group cases, where in the former the assignments of agents to groups are prescribed. While both are NP-hard in the classical sense, we show that their algorithmic behavior differs significantly from the parameterized perspective. As our main results, we:
  (1) prove that both cases are NP-hard even when the number of agents is a small constant;
  (2) circumvent this hardness by establishing fixed-parameter tractability for EF1-Var w.r.t. the number of "subjective" items, that is, items which are viewed as chores or goods by different agents---but rule out an analogous result for EF1-Fix; and
  (3) establish fixed-parameter tractability for EF1-Fix w.r.t. the number of item types, but link the existence of an analogous fixed-parameter algorithm for EF1-Var to a fundamental open question in the setting of Integer Linear Programming.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Practical and Space-Efficient LZ77 and LZ Pre-Compression via String Synchronizing Sets
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The Lempel-Ziv (LZ77) factorization decomposes a text into the least possible number $z$ of phrases that each refer to an earlier occurrence. It is this phrase count, rather than the encoded size, that governs the size of LZ-based compressed indexes, and computing a factorization with few phrases is a time and space bottleneck in their construction. In practice, computing LZ77 quickly typically requires the suffix array. In theory, the exact LZ77 factorization, and a 3-approximation of it, can be computed more space-efficiently without the full suffix array [SPIRE 2023]. These algorithms have remained unimplemented, because two of their components resist a direct implementation: a lookup table that degenerates to patterns of length at most two for realistic inputs, and an orthogonal range reporting data structure that is impractical. We replace both, fine-tune every remaining stage, and obtain the first practical implementation, which runs in space close to the text rather than to the suffix array. On one thread, our 3-approximation factorizes 12-19x faster than the classical LPF algorithm while using 14x less memory; on 32 threads, even our exact algorithm is 1.4-2.9x faster than parallel LPF, at 9x less memory. In practice the approximation ratio stays far below 3. As a side result, passing only the perfect phrases of our 3-approximation to a downstream compressor yields a precompressor that is on par with the state of the art [Dinklage, SEA 2026] in compression ratio, and better in memory consumption and parallel throughput.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 17 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Full version of the ALENEX 2027 paper

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Assortment optimization given basket shopping behavior using the Ising model
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In markets where customers tend to purchase baskets of products rather than single products, assortment optimization is a major challenge for retailers. Removing a product from a retailer's assortment can result in a severe drop in aggregate demand if this product is a complement to other products. Therefore, accounting for the complementarity effect is essential when making assortment decisions. In this paper, we develop an analytical framework designed to address this problem. We model customers' choices using the binary Ising model, which is a special case of a Markov random field. This model captures pairwise demand dependencies as well as the individual attractiveness of each product, with binary variables indicating whether products are included in the purchased basket. For estimation, we utilize existing methods developed for the spin formulation of the Ising model and then apply a parameter transformation to express the fitted model in the binary form used for assortment optimization. We show that the assortment optimization problem under the Ising model is NP-hard. We also provide multiple theoretical insights into the structure of the optimal assortments based on the graphical representation of the Ising model, and propose several heuristic algorithms that can be used to obtain high-quality solutions to the assortment optimization problem. Our numerical analysis demonstrates that the developed simulated annealing procedure leads to an expected profit gain of 15% compared to offering an unoptimized assortment (where all products are included) and around 5% compared to using a revenue-ordered heuristic algorithm.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Splitting Planar Necklaces with Few Straight Cuts
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In the classical necklace splitting problem, beads of different colors lie on a line, and the goal is to divide them among $k$ agents using as few cuts as possible so that every agent receives the same number of beads of each color. We study the planar analog in which a cut is a full straight line and the objective is minimizing the number of lines: $m$ points colored red and blue must be separated by straight-line cuts into regions that can be allocated to $k$ agents so that each agent receives the same number of points of each color. Projection to a line gives $2(k-1)$ cuts, and $k-1$ are sometimes necessary; we give algorithms, static and dynamic, that provably close part of this gap. We develop several approaches that capitalize on the extra degree of freedom: a ``star'' search that produces solutions with as few as $\lceil \frac{k}{2} \rceil$ cuts and never more than $k$ whenever a fair contiguous circular partition exists, with further guarantees for evenly spaced input, and a general algorithm that produces at most $k + \log_2(k+1) - 2$ cuts in $Θ(m \log k)$ time, built on a one-dimensional necklace splitting subroutine that requires no presorting. We then adapt the general algorithm to a dynamic setting, maintaining exact fairness and the cut bound under arbitrary relocation of points, with expected update time that scales with the total distance moved.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Improved Approximation and Hardness Results for the Monitoring Edge-Geodetic Set Problem
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the \emph{Monitoring Edge-Geodetic Set} problem (MEG-Set), which asks for a minimum-cardinality set $M$ of vertices of an undirected graph $G$ of $n$ vertices such that every edge of $G$ belongs to all shortest paths between some pair of vertices in $M$.
  We present new approximation and hardness results for MEG-Set. On the positive side, we design a deterministic polynomial-time $O(n^{1/3}\log^{2/3}n)$-approximation algorithm, improving upon the previously best-known $O(\sqrt{n\log n})$ approximation ratio. On the negative side, for every constant $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, we prove that the problem admits no polynomial-time $\big(2^{\log^{1-\varepsilon} n}\big)$-approximation algorithm, unless $\mathsf{NP}\subseteq \mathsf{DTIME}(n^{\operatorname{polylog} n})$. This substantially improves upon the previously known logarithmic inapproximability bound. We also prove that \megset is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard on planar $2$-degenerate graphs, whereas $\mathsf{NP}$-hardness was previously known for $1$-apex $2$-degenerate graphs.
  We conclude by observing a connection between monitoring edge-geodetic sets and subsetwise distance preservers, i.e., subgraphs that preserve distances between all pairs of vertices in $S\subseteq V(G)$. Specifically, we show that any upper bound on the size of the latter yields a lower bound on the size of the former.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Improved Online Load Balancing in the Two-Norm
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study the online load balancing problem on unrelated machines, with the objective of minimizing the square of the $\ell_2$ norm of the loads on the machines. The greedy algorithm of Awerbuch et al. (STOC'95) is optimal for deterministic algorithms and achieves a competitive ratio of $3 + 2 \sqrt{2} \approx 5.828$, and an improved $5$-competitive randomized algorithm based on independent rounding has been shown by Caragiannis (SODA'08). In this work, we present the first algorithm breaking the barrier of $5$ on the competitive ratio, achieving a bound of $5-c$ for some $c \geq 0.0157$. To obtain this result, we use a new primal-dual framework to analyze this problem based on a natural semidefinite programming relaxation, together with an online implementation of a correlated randomized rounding procedure of Im and Shadloo (SODA'20). This novel primal-dual framework also yields new, simple and unified proofs of the competitive ratio of the $(3 + 2 \sqrt{2})$-competitive greedy algorithm, the $5$-competitive randomized independent rounding algorithm, and that of a new $4$-competitive optimal fractional algorithm. We also provide lower bounds showing that the previous best randomized algorithm is optimal among independent rounding algorithms, that our new fractional algorithm is optimal, and that a simple greedy algorithm is optimal for the closely related online scheduling problem $R || \sum w_j C_j$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: An Exact Polynomial-Time Algorithm for the Minimum Shared-Power Edge Cut Problem
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The Minimum Shared-Power Edge Cut (MSPEC) problem seeks to disconnect two designated terminals with minimum total power by assigning powers to graph vertices and deleting every edge for which the sum of the powers at its endpoints reaches its edge weight. Previous work gave a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme for this problem, while its exact computational complexity remained open. We prove that general MSPEC with nonnegative edge weights can be solved exactly in polynomial time. Specifically, we first use linear programming duality for each fixed cut to reformulate MSPEC as minimizing the maximum terminal-relaxed matching weight over all $s$-$t$ cuts. Then, we construct a terminal-copy extended graph that transforms the maximum-weight matching model with unconstrained terminal capacities for a fixed cut into an equivalent ordinary maximum-weight matching model. Next, we extend the submodularity of the unweighted maximum-matching cut function to nonnegative edge weights and prove that the restriction obtained by fixing the terminal copies on prescribed sides remains submodular. Consequently, MSPEC reduces to exact submodular function minimization. Once an optimal cut is obtained, a corresponding optimal power assignment can be recovered. This result resolves the open question concerning the exact computational complexity of general MSPEC.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A 2/3-Approximation Algorithm for the Residual Maximum Matching Problem in General Graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The residual maximum matching problem asks for a maximum matching whose deletion leaves a graph with the largest possible matching number. For unweighted graphs, previous work provides a $1/2$-approximation guarantee in general graphs and a $2/3$ guarantee in graphs with a perfect matching. We present a $2/3$-approximation algorithm running in $O(n^5)$ time, extending the latter guarantee to general graphs. The algorithm improves the residual matching number through single-edge exchanges involving free vertices. We prove that, for any maximum matching that admits no further improvement by such exchanges, the residual matching number is at least $2/3$ of the optimum, and we give an example showing that this bound is tight.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: An Analytic 0.48-Approximation for Non-Monotone k-Submodular Maximization under a Matroid Constraint
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We give a randomized polynomial-time $0.48$-approximation for maximizing a nonnegative non-monotone $k$-submodular function under a matroid constraint, for every $k\ge2$. The algorithm combines a top-two label rule with a nested-chain potential and maximum-weight matroid bases. Its analysis reduces the approximation guarantee to a one-dimensional time allocation: a uniform local lower bound leads to a linear differential equation, concavity closes the remaining interval, and two elementary budgets complete the proof. A strict saving in the time budget absorbs sampling and discretization errors, yielding the exact $0.48$ guarantee in the value-oracle model.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 22 pages, 1 figure, 1 table; author list updated to include Wenguo Yang

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: FPTAS for Polygonal Multi-Robot Motion Planning
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study multi-robot motion planning in a polygonal environment with polygonal robots. The setting of the problem consists of a polygonal domain $\mathcal{W}$ with $n$ vertices and $k$ robots $R_1,\dots,R_k$ translating in $\mathcal{W}$ each of which is represented by a polygon of constant complexity. Given a source configuration $\mathbf{s}$ and a target configuration $\mathbf{t}$ of the robots in $\mathcal{W}$, the goal of the problem is to find a collision-free motion plan from $\mathbf{s}$ to $\mathbf{t}$ that is shortest with respect to some cost function. We present the first fully polynomial-time approximation schemes (FPTAS) for motion planning with any fixed number $k$ of robots, under the min-sum objective, the min-max objective, and the min-makespan objective. Here, the min-sum variant aims to minimize the total traveling distance of all robots, the min-max variant aims to minimize the maximum traveling distance of a single robot, and the min-makespan variant aims to minimize the total time cost under the assumption that all robots move with a maximum speed $1$. The algorithm directly generalizes to the problem in any fixed dimension $d$, with a polytope environment and polytope robots. Our result settles an open question of Agarwal, Halperin, Sharir, Steiger [SODA'24] and Agarwal, Holmgren, Steiger [SODA'26], who gave an FPTAS for $k=2$ unit-square robots and a bicriteria-approximation algorithm for a fixed number $k$ of unit-square or unit-disk robots, respectively. Compared to the previous results, our algorithm is substantially simpler.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Algorithms for Computing Longest Unbordered Factors on Run-Length Encoded Strings
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: A border of a string is a non-empty proper prefix of the string that is also a suffix. A string is called unbordered if it has no border. The longest unbordered factor is a fundamental notion in stringology, closely related to string periodicity. This paper addresses the longest unbordered factor problem: given a string of length $n$, the goal is to compute its longest factor that is unbordered. While recent work has achieved subquadratic and near-linear time algorithms for this problem, the best known worst-case time complexity remains $O(n \log n)$ [Kociumaka et al., ISAAC 2018]. In this paper, we investigate the problem in the context of compressed string processing, focusing specifically on run-length encoded (RLE) strings. We first present a simple yet crucial structural observation relating unbordered factors and RLE-compressed strings. Building on this, we propose an algorithm that solves the problem in $O(m^{1.5} \log^2 m)$ time and $O(m \log^2 m)$ space, where $m$ is the size of the RLE-compressed input string. Furthermore, we propose another algorithm for the problem that runs in average $O(m \log^2 m)$ time and $O(m\log m)$ space: The average-case bound holds under an exponent-bounded random-input model, in which the input is chosen uniformly from the strings of RLE size $m$ whose run exponents are at most a given bound $E\geq 2$. Our approaches extend key ideas from [Gawrychowski et al., SPIRE 2015] to the RLE setting through new combinatorial insights. When the RLE size $m$ is sufficiently small compared to $n$, our algorithms achieve linear-time behavior in $n$, potentially leading to improved performance over existing methods in such cases.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Accepted for Theory of Computing Systems

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: ${\varepsilon}$-Cost Sharding: Scaling Hypergraph-Based Data Structures to Trillions of Keys
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We describe a simple and yet very scalable implementation of static functions (VFunc) and of static filters (VFilter) based on hypergraphs. We introduce the idea of $\varepsilon$-cost sharding, which allows us to build structures that can manage trillions of keys, at the same time increasing memory locality in hypergraph-based constructions. Contrarily to the commonly used HEM sharding method, $\varepsilon$-cost sharding does not require to store of additional information, and does not introduce dependencies in the computation chain; its only cost is that of few arithmetical instructions, and of a relative increase $\varepsilon$ in space usage. We apply $\varepsilon$-cost sharding to the classical MWHC construction, but we obtain the best result by combining Dietzfelbinger and Walzer's fuse graphs for large shards with lazy Gaussian elimination for small shards. We obtain large structures with an overhead of 10.5% with respect to the information-theoretical lower bound and with a query time that is a few nanoseconds away from the query time of the non-sharded version, which is the fastest currently available within the same space bounds. Besides comparing our structures with a non-sharded version, we contrast its tradeoffs with bumped ribbon constructions, a space-saving alternative to hypergraph-based static functions and filters, which provide optimum space consumption but slow construction and query time (though construction can be parallelized very efficiently). We build offline a trillion-key filter using commodity hardware in just 60 ns/key. Finally, we show that $\varepsilon$-cost sharding and fuse graphs carry over with no effort to data structures that reduce to static functions, such as monotone minimal perfect hash functions and compressed static functions.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Improved rapid phase ordering for Ising dynamics on random regular graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study Glauber dynamics for the Ising model on random $d$-regular graphs with $n$ vertices at low temperature, in the regime $β\geq C/d$ where $C,d$ are sufficiently large constants. In this regime, the full mixing time is exponential in $n$, because of the bottleneck between the two dominant phases: configurations with a majority of plus spins and configurations with a majority of minus spins. We show that, for sufficiently large $d$, if the dynamics is initialized with an excess of at least $ε_{C,d} n$ plus spins over minus spins, then it quasi-equilibrates in time $O(\log n)$ to the Gibbs measure conditioned on positive magnetization. In addition, the required bias $ε_{C,d}$ can be chosen so that $ε_{C,d}\to 0$ as $d,C\to\infty$.
  Previous bound of \cite{GSS25+} in the Ising and large-$d$ setting required $β\gtrsim (\log d)/d$. A key difficulty is that, even from the all-plus initialization, one must control the propagation of negative information in spacetime in a low-temperature model with strong local correlations. We address this by developing a new bootstrap approach to proving subcriticality of disagreement clusters under the grand coupling.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Cascade: GPU-Accelerated Out-of-Core Suffix Array Construction for LLM Corpora
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Suffix arrays power deduplication, contamination testing, and training data attribution over the corpora used to train large language models, and must be rebuilt for every new corpus or tokenizer. However, constructing them at scale is slow. infini-gram's indexing pipeline takes about two days to process 1.4 trillion tokens on its authors' 128-core CPU server. GPU-accelerated constructors are an order of magnitude faster, but their working sets must fit in GPU memory. Partitioning the corpus only moves this limit to host memory. Sorting the suffixes of one partition needs the ranks of suffixes in other partitions, which existing designs keep in a corpus-wide rank table that must stay in memory.
  We present Cascade, a GPU-accelerated out-of-core suffix-array constructor. Its partitions each own a fixed, contiguous range of the final suffix array, so the GPU sorts them independently and never merges them. Cascade then replaces the rank table with streamed rank exchange. Ranks are sent directly to the partitions that need them, and an invariant makes partition-local ranks sufficient for every comparison. With no rank table, intermediate data spills across GPU memory, host memory, and SSD as the corpus grows, and host memory only needs to hold the text.
  On seven corpora of 8-238 billion tokens, Cascade builds suffix arrays on a single GPU server 3.0-8.2x faster end to end than infini-gram's pipeline, and its construction is 6.3-11.4x faster than libsais's. It indexes the 198-billion-token C4 corpus and the 238-billion-token Pile in 23 and 37 minutes end to end, both of which exceed libsais's host-memory capacity on the same server. A batched query engine over the index reproduces infini-gram's counts at median speedups of 10.8-32.6x, with the index in GPU memory, host memory, or on SSD.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Shaving Logs via Large Sieve Inequality: Faster Algorithms for Sparse Convolution and More
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
