Information Theory.summary: Reporting guidance for information-theoretic measures is rarely tested against ground truth. We test one guardrail in two multi-agent reinforcement learning games, a social dilemma and a coordination race, where directed influence between selected agent pairs is zero by construction, over 100 seeds. Omitting one precondition, exclusion of the non-stationary training transient, gives false-positive rates of 100.00% and 99.95%: agents annealing exploration independently, in runs that never met, are flagged as influencing one another. Excluding the transient reaches 3.05% in the social dilemma but 11.8% in the coordination game, so the non-stationarity must be treated and exclusion is neither the only way nor sufficient. What we recommend instead changes the null model. Series, statistic and estimand are left untouched: permuting the source within blocks of training time reaches 5.25% and 5.50%, the only one of the three at or below the size of the test in both games. The construction is not new, being a restricted permutation local to blocks of training time; the measurement is. A third null control, four learners in the social dilemma, defeats all three, and there conditioning costs three times what ours does, 15.20 points against 4.55. Titrating injected links separates it from conditioning on identical pairs, 82.5% against 58.0%, while the ablated test reports a positive with or without a link, so its apparent sensitivity is uninformative. Five block counts spanning 16 to 256 land in the nominal region. Code and data are released.
Information Theory.comment: 33 pages, 4 figures. Substantially revised: rebuilt around a controlled experiment with ground-truth null and positive controls. Code and data at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22658530 and https://github.com/dentros/te-nonstationarity

Logic in Computer Science.title: Lean4Agent: Formal Modeling and Verification for Agent Workflow and Trajectory
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Equipping Large Language Models (LLMs) to execute reliable multi-step workflows has become a central challenge in artificial intelligence. Despite recent advances in LLMs' agentic capabilities, most agent systems still lack formal methods for specifying, verifying, and debugging their workflow and execution trajectories. This challenge mirrors a long-standing problem in mathematics, where the ambiguity of natural languages (NLs) motivates the development of formal languages (FLs). Inspired by this paradigm, we propose **Lean4Agent**, to the best of our knowledge, the first framework that uses Lean4, a dependent-type FL to model and verify agent behavior. **Lean4Agent** launches **FormalAgentLib**, an extensible Lean4 library for formally modeling and verifying agent workflows' semantic consistency under explicit assumptions, and enabling localization of execution-time failures revealed by trajectories. Building on **FormalAgentLib**, we further develop **LeanEvolve**, which applies results in **FormalAgentLib** to revise workflows to enhance its capability. Extensive experiments on a hard problem subset of SWE-Bench-Verified and a subset of ELAIP-Bench across 5 leading LLMs indicate that the verification-passing workflows outperform the failing ones by an average of **11.94%**, and **LeanEvolve** further improves SWE performance by **7.47%** on average. Furthermore, **Lean4Agent** establishes a foundation for a new field of using expressive dependent-type FL to formally model and verify agent behavior.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: Nips 2026 accepted paper

Logic in Computer Science.title: SLoSa: Small, Low-Power, and Safe Foundation Models for Robotic Task Planning
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Safe robotic task planning requires planners that can reliably achieve task goals while satisfying safety constraints. Classical planners search over explicit symbolic task representations and can provide formal guarantees with respect to encoded safety constraints, but require rigid input formats. Their computational cost also increases rapidly with the search space. In contrast, large language models (LLMs) offer flexible task interfaces and strong generalization capabilities, but they are large, power-hungry, and pre-trained with little robot-specific safety data and knowledge. Thus, they can be difficult to deploy locally on robotic systems with limited resources. To address these limitations, we present SLoSa, a neuro-symbolic compression and fine-tuning framework for training foundation-model-based robotic task planners with Small size, Low power demand, and Safety awareness. The framework first constructs a safety-aware dataset using classical planners, an advanced teacher LLM, and formal verifiers, followed by two training stages: supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning guided by a verification-based reward machine to enforce safety alignment. We evaluate SLoSa across four Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) domains, two household simulation environments, local edge platforms, and a desktop robotic arm. Across the PDDL tasks, verifier-guided post-training raises the success rate of compact 4B-14B planners to 70.5-76.0%, while INT4 deployment on a Jetson Orin requires 17.85-26.41 W of average power. Results in household simulators and on the physical robot further demonstrate the applicability of SLoSa across diverse robotic task settings.

Logic in Computer Science.title: An algorithmic construction of Nullstellensatz certificates for graph automorphism groups
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Solvers for graph isomorphism and related problems are widely used in both theoretical and applied domains, but their complexity often requires users to trust their correctness without verification. We present a certifying algorithm for computing a generating set of the automorphism group of a given graph, meaning that it produces an independently verifiable certificate that the output list of automorphisms generates the entirety of the automorphism group. The problem of constructing a certificate is reduced to certifying that a system of multivariate polynomial equations is infeasible. An individualization-refinement algorithm produces a derivation within an algebraic proof system, representing a Nullstellensatz certificate of infeasibility. We provide an implementation of both the certifying algorithm and a certificate verifier, and demonstrate their viability on graphs with hundreds of vertices.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Simply Logical -- The First Three Decades
Logic in Computer Science.summary: This paper charts the evolution of the Prolog textbook Simply Logical -- Intelligent Reasoning by Example from print with runnable programmes on a 3.5-inch diskette published in 1994, via various intermediate online versions, to the fully interactive online edition available today. Our aim is to investigate -- from both the writer's and the reader's perspectives -- the potential impact of technology on educational materials. The three authors of this paper present three distinct and complementary points of view, which come together to shape an interactive online book that offers an immersive learning experience. Peter describes the philosophy behind the original book and experiences teaching from it. Jan demonstrates how contemporary web programming has enabled a fully interactive realisation of the book's philosophy. Kacper reports how different technologies can be adopted to build a versatile authoring toolkit that underpins the interactive online edition of the book. Collating these distinct yet coherent perspectives allows us to reflect on future opportunities for interactive Prolog teaching materials arising from the continuous development of web technologies. The insights we offer should be of interest to teachers of Prolog as well as those wanting to find out about the latest educational technologies.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: Published in "Prolog: The Next 50 Years"

Logic in Computer Science.title: Strict Equality in Higher Identity Types: Axioms, Completeness, Decidability
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Reasoning about higher identity types uses two equalities, strict equality and equivalence of cells witnessed by a path. Strict equality is a congruence for every operation on cells, but associativity and the identity laws fail for it. Equivalence of cells satisfies those two laws, but it is not a congruence. Representations of higher identity types often conflate equational properties that hold strictly with those that hold only up to a path. We separate the two and axiomatize the former, introducing SEq, an equational theory generated by eleven axioms for strict equality between cells. We prove soundness and completeness for homotopy models, and completeness already over finite CW-complexes. Nine of these axioms form a strongly normalizing rewrite system whose normal forms are unique up to picture equivalence, and the resulting word problem is decidable in exponential time. We also give presheaf models over a cubical base category in which composition arises from a pushout in the base category itself, without requiring Kan filling structure. The same pushout structure provides explicit higher-dimensional witnesses for associativity and the identity laws.

Logic in Computer Science.title: SAT Sampling at Scale via GPU-based Boolean Constraint Propagation
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Constrained-random verification tests hardware designs by sampling solutions of Boolean formulas. Existing samplers largely follow one of two approaches: CPU-based SAT samplers (e.g., CMSGen), which remain effective even at rare targets but offer limited throughput, and GPU-based gradient samplers, which achieve high throughput at high-probability targets but collapse at rare ones. We introduce Gpap-S, the first GPU sampler built on Boolean constraint propagation (BCP). At its core is Gpap, a new GPU engine for BCP that efficiently propagates many independent partial assignments concurrently on a shared Boolean formula. This capability allows Gpap-S to combine the rare-target robustness of SAT-based sampling with the throughput of GPU parallelism by exploring thousands of decide-and-propagate trajectories simultaneously. On the benchmark families used to evaluate prior GPU gradient samplers, Gpap-S is 2.2-18.7x faster at the high-probability targets considered in those evaluations. At rare targets, where those samplers often fail to generate any samples, Gpap-S achieves a geometric-mean speedup of roughly two orders of magnitude. Across all benchmarks, Gpap-S is also 83.4-1,571x faster than the CPU-based CMSGen. This throughput does not come at the expense of sample quality: under Barbarik, the statistical tester used to evaluate CMSGen, Gpap-S is accepted on every instance we test, as is CMSGen. We release Gpap as a reusable GPU library for high-throughput BCP.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 22 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables

Logic in Computer Science.title: What is a Good Projection?: Correctness and Separation Results of End-Point Projections
Logic in Computer Science.summary: \emph{Multiparty session types} (MPST) is a type discipline for ensuring distributed programs are implemented correctly \emph{by construction}. MPST starts by specifying a choreographic protocol as a \emph{global type} and \emph{projects} it onto each participant, generating \emph{local types} with a guarantee of type soundness and deadlock-freedom. A central issue of MPST is that its type soundness is fragile, as it must be proven each time with respect to a chosen projection algorithm under specific semantics with a specific program correctness goal. To overcome this problem, we propose general criteria for a \emph{good projection} -- a set of requirements for projection algorithms by which type soundness, deadlock-freedom and liveness of distributed programs are \emph{automatically} derived. Using the criteria, we prove that 8 distinct projections in the literature are good under both synchronous and asynchronous semantics, and that 4 are incorrect, failing type soundness. We extend the good projection criteria to mixed choice global types and asynchronous communication optimisations, proposing new ``good projection'' algorithms. We apply properties of good projections to prove \emph{separation} and \emph{expressiveness} results over the projection algorithms and MPST typing systems. Having a generalised typing system that is robust with respect to the good projection criteria, we provide an implementation with mixed choice global types that is \emph{modular} with respect to a chosen projection algorithm and desired program properties. Our separation results help programmers make informed trade-offs between complexity and expressiveness when choosing projection algorithms, and our theory ensures their chosen algorithms are correctly applied.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 91 pages. 6 figures. Conditionally accepted to POPL 2027

Logic in Computer Science.title: Proof-Carrying Contracts: Commitments AI Agents Cannot Break
Logic in Computer Science.summary: AI agents increasingly act on behalf of people or other agents, purchasing services, exchanging information and delegating work. What an agent must respect is written in instructions, policies or agreements, but text alone cannot make it comply. It may make mistakes, be redirected by what it reads, or pursue different interests. For an economy of such agents to function, parties need agreements they can rely on without inspecting or trusting one another's agents. We introduce Proof-Carrying Contracts (PC2), a framework for making agreed constraints enforceable throughout an agent's interactions with a system. Before a requested operation can run, the agent must supply a machine-checkable proof that it preserves the agreed constraints in every case allowed by its model. An execution system called the Airlock checks the proof and controls access to the operation. The parties specify the conditions to preserve, while the agent supplies the reasoning needed to justify its decisions and remains free to adapt its strategy. This avoids having to design a separate permission policy and prove that every decision it permits is safe. We prove that the constraints hold at every instant during execution, even for an adversarial agent, and identify when this implies safety in the world. Reusable capability modules provide tools and guarantees from which contracts can be constructed. PC2 provides a foundation for an agent economy whose agreements protect both those delegating work and those carrying it out.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 70 pages, 8 Figures,

Logic in Computer Science.title: Linear Axiomatization of Linear Differential Equations
Logic in Computer Science.summary: This article presents an axiomatization of linear differential equations that is complete for topologically open properties with compact initial conditions and time horizons by proving them deductively via a sound reduction to formulas of linear real arithmetic. Indeed, linearity is preserved: linear differential invariants are complete for open properties of linear differential equations and reduce with a linear number of Lie derivatives (per atom) to linear real arithmetic. In particular, this article shows that the linear fragment of differential dynamic logic (dL), a modal extension of standard first-order logic over the reals satisfies these completeness properties. By establishing completeness within decidable linear real arithmetic, the need for proving sophisticated nonlinear formulas of real arithmetic is circumvented. Furthermore, this article establishes generalizations to the nonlinear fragment of dL that enable the practical certification of reachability computations, validating the output of external computations in dL with machine-checkable proofs.

Logic in Computer Science.title: A General Construction of Strict Models in HoTT
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
Homotopy type theory (HoTT) provides a natural setting for studying the metatheory of type theory, as it comes with additional extensionality principles compared to ordinary Martin-Löf type theory. In particular, it is especially suitable for developing semantics of type theory, where one distinguishes two kinds of models: strict models, which give us sound interpretations, and pseudomodels. Pseudomodels are useful as they occur prevalently and can be turned into strict models by constructions called strictifications. However, the commonly used strictifications do not translate well to HoTT, as they require assumptions that are generally not satisfied by concrete examples of models.
  We show how to carry out the universe model construction, due to Voevodsky, in HoTT. Under this construction, every pseudomodel together with a universe type closed under enough type formers gives rise to a strict model. We also show how to interpret type formers in the resulting model assuming that the universe is closed under them. Finally, we demonstrate that this construction generalises existing instances of strict set models in the literature, and we apply it to more examples, yielding presheaf models and assembly models of type theory in HoTT. Our results are formalised in Rocq using the UniMath library.

Logic in Computer Science.title: TREBL -- A Relative Complete Temporal Event-B Logic. Part I: Theory
Logic in Computer Science.summary: The verification of liveness conditions is an important aspect of state-based rigorous methods. This article addresses the extension of the logic of Event-B to a powerful logic, in which properties of traces of an Event-B machine can be expressed. However, all formulae of this logic are still interpreted over states of an Event-B machine rather than traces. The logic exploits that for an Event-B machine $M$ a state $S$ determines all traces of $M$ starting in $S$. We identify a fragment called TREBL of this logic, in which all liveness conditions of interest can be expressed, and define a set of sound derivation rules for the fragment. We further show relative completeness of these derivation rules in the sense that for every valid entailment of a formula $\varphi$ one can find a derivation, provided the machine $M$ is sufficiently refined. The decisive property is that certain variant terms must be definable in the refined machine. We show that such refinements always exist. Throughout the article several examples from the field of security are used to illustrate the theory.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Noise-aware Verification and Synthesis of Quantum Programs
Logic in Computer Science.summary: This work provides a comprehensive framework for noise-aware quantum program analysis, ranging from logical foundations to model checking and automated synthesis. While most research on quantum programming considers an idealized, noise-free semantics for quantum programs, we reason about quantum programs that are executed on real, noisy hardware. We use the error models published by quantum-hardware vendors to give a hardware-dependent semantics to quantum programs. We then present a noise-aware quantum Hoare logic with a relatively complete proof system. We finally use state-space exploration techniques for the hardware-aware verification and synthesis of loop-free quantum programs. In this way, we synthesize optimal, hardware-dependent solutions for parity bit-flip, GHZ state preparation, and other problems that commonly occur as subroutines in larger quantum algorithms. We evaluate our method on all 55 hardware specifications provided by the IBM Qiskit toolkit. Finally, we also show that classical probabilistic branching is needed for optimality in quantum programming.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Just Previsions
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Previsions are positively homogeneous functionals, and are generalized forms of integration functionals. We investigate previsions -- just previsions, not sublinear or superlinear previsions as in previous work. We show that every prevision can be expressed as an infimum of sublinear previsions, and as a supremum of superlinear previsions under mild conditions. This extends to homeomorphisms between spaces of previsions and certain hyperspaces over spaces of sublinear or superlinear previsions, which can also be characterized in terms of orthogonality relations, making the construction a variant of a double powerspace construction.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 33 pages, 1 figure

Logic in Computer Science.title: Forall-Exists Relational Verification by Filtering to Forall-Forall
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Relational verification encompasses reasoning about data abstraction, security and privacy, secure compilation, and functional specification of tensor programs, among others. Several relational logics and tools support compositional reasoning about $\forall\forall$ (2-safety) properties and, generally, $k$-safety properties. In contrast, few logics and tools exist for reasoning about $\forall\exists$ properties which are critical in the presence of nondeterminism. This paper's primary contribution is a technique for verifying a $\forall\exists$ judgment by way of a novel transformation. The filter-adequacy transformation adds assertions to a product program in such a way that the desired $\forall\exists$ property (of a pair of underlying unary programs) is implied by a $\forall\forall$ property of the transformed product. The paper develops bicoms, a form of product programs that facilitates expressing good alignments and caters for direct translation of $\forall\forall$ properties to unary correctness; proves that successful $\forall\forall$ verification of a transformed bicom implies the $\forall\exists$ spec for its underlying unary commands; and evaluates the technique using a prototype auto-active relational verifier. The technique enables users to work with ordinary assertions and assumptions, and a standard assertion language, so that existing $\forall\forall$ and unary verification tools can be used for $\forall\exists$.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: v2: expanded evaluation section; expository improvements throughout; v3: add missing author in metadata

Logic in Computer Science.title: Containment of Conjunctive Queries with Negative Information over Semirings
Logic in Computer Science.summary: We study the containment problem for (unions of) conjunctive queries ((U)CQs) with negative information on semiring-annotated databases. Our approach to negative information follows the treatment of negation proposed by Grädel and Tannen (2017, 2019, 2021 and 2024) for first-order logic and fixed point logic which applies productively to large classes of semirings, including bounded distributive lattices, as well as the important provenance semirings studied for positive CQ containment by Green (2009). Negation features in (U)CQs along two dimensions: negated equalities (disequations), and negated relational atoms. We study complexity for each of them separately, as well as jointly. For disequations, we extend a methodology that proves the same complexity bounds as the ones already known for the standard Boolean semiring (in the second level of the polynomial hierarchy) for most semirings of interest. Two prominent exceptions are $\mathbb{N}[X]$ and Trio(X) where the complexity bound for containment is in the second level of the counting hierarchy. For CQs with negated relational atoms we show that the complexity, surprisingly, is the same as that of the containment of CQs without negation when one considers model-defining and provenance-tracking interpretations (namely, nondeterministic polynomial time). Interestingly, among bounded distributive lattices, the Boolean two-element case is the only one where the complexity of the problem continues to be hard for the second level of the polynomial hierarchy for model-defining interpretations. Furthermore, we show that the complexity increases again for distributive lattices if we focus on other classes of interpretations. Finally, we consider queries that have both negated equalities and negated relational atoms and show that the complexity of containment continues to be that of the case with just negated equalities.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Constructive Ordinal Exponentiation
Logic in Computer Science.summary: In classical mathematics, ordinal arithmetic is well-studied; constructively, addition and multiplication are well-known. We study constructive ordinal exponentiation, where ordinals are taken to be transitive, extensional, and wellfounded orders on sets. We present a negative result showing that general constructive ordinal exponentiation is impossible, but we suggest two definitions that come close. The first definition is abstract and solely motivated by the expected equations; this works as long as the base of the exponential is positive. The second definition is based on decreasing lists and can be seen as a constructive version of Sierpi{ń}ski's definition via functions with finite support; this requires the base to have a trichotomous least element. Whenever it makes sense to ask the question, the two constructions are equivalent, allowing us to prove algebraic laws, cancellation properties, and preservation of decidability of the exponential. The core ideas do not depend on any specific constructive set theory or type theory, but a concrete computer-checked mechanization using the Agda proof assistant is given in homotopy type theory.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: v6: Accepted for publication in the Journal of the ACM. Extended version of our LICS'25 paper (v4)

Logic in Computer Science.title: BARReL: a modern backend for Atelier B in Lean
Logic in Computer Science.summary: BARReL is a Lean 4 library bridging Atelier B, an industrial tool for the B method, and the Lean proof assistant by enabling users to conduct their formal B developments---up to machine refinement and implementation---interactively inside Lean, while retaining standard B syntax. B partial operators are encoded with explicit well-definedness conditions, using Lean's dependent types to enforce a well-definedness discipline by construction. That is, proof obligations and proof steps cannot silently rely on ill-typed or ill-defined instantiations. BARReL also provides basic automation for discharging these conditions. The implementation is written entirely using Lean metaprogramming and is designed to be modular: extending the supported B fragment typically requires only adding new syntax and encoding clauses. We compare the resulting workflow with Atelier B on a B refinement development and examine the checks required during interactive proof through two examples.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Computable Quantification in Reflective Grounded Arithmetic
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Informal statements of Gödel's incompleteness theorems often run: "any consistent formal system with arithmetic has true but unprovable statements." That reading assumes a classical notion of truth, under which a universal statement is true as soon as each of its numeral instances is. This paper presents reflective grounded arithmetic (RGA), in which truth is grounded in computation and universal quantification is grounded reflectively: a universal statement is true when the system's own proof search certifies its schematic instance, and false when the system refutes one numeral instance. RGA allows recursive definitions without restriction and proves addition, multiplication and Ackermann's function total as theorems quantified inside the system. RGA is consistent, and it is complete for its own, grounded notion of truth: every well-formed statement that evaluates to true is provable. Gödel's theorems still hold for RGA, as a companion paper shows. The statements that classical reasoning calls true but unprovable have every numeral instance provable but no certified schematic instance, so they are ungrounded in RGA; read instance by instance, in an $ω$-semantics for which RGA is also sound, they are true. All results are machine-checked in Isabelle/HOL: soundness and consistency; completeness for grounded truth, open statements included; $ω$-soundness and $ω$-consistency; that grounded truth is recursively enumerable and RGA represents exactly the recursively enumerable sets; and $ω$-incompleteness. The logic is neither classical nor intuitionistic: double negation is eliminable as an entailment, excluded middle fails wherever a statement has no boolean value, RGA has the disjunction and witness properties, and the deduction theorem holds exactly at provably decided hypotheses.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Local Allow, Global Deny: Why Per-Action Authorization Does Not Compose in LLM Agents
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Autonomous LLM agents act through tools under per-action authorization: a local guard screens each tool call in isolation. We show that local authorization does not compose into global authorization. A compositional authorization failure (CAF) is a locally authorized execution, or a pair of locally authorized executions, that violates a global policy spanning intent, purpose, provenance, consent, and delegation. We characterize CAFs along two axes, expressiveness (single-trace safety versus relational k-safety) and observability (a ladder of monitor profiles). Our central result is an impossibility: relational purpose violations form a 2-safety hyperproperty with no per-trace locus of blame, so a per-action monitor that never raises a false alarm detects none of them, independent of the underlying model or decision procedure; they become visible only under cross-execution monitoring, which none of the six guardrails we survey implements. We make this constructive with AL-SYNTH, a SAT/SMT synthesizer (using no language model) that emits minimal CAF witnesses, each checked against an exhaustive oracle. The empirical signature is sharp: across nine LLM judges the per-action view approves the synthesized witness almost without exception, blocking it at a rate comparable to a benign control, yet the same models flag it when shown the two executions together. Per-action authorization is therefore structurally insufficient for relational policy conjuncts not reducible to single-trace safety: to bound them, a monitor must compare executions or accept false alarms.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: Extended version of a paper accepted at the 8th IEEE International Conference on Trust, Privacy and Security in Intelligent Systems and Applications (IEEE TPS 2026), with full proofs and appendices. 12 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/anmolpandey299/al-synth

Logic in Computer Science.title: Rational polynomial solvability reduces to stratifiability of semilinear sets
Logic in Computer Science.summary: A semilinear set is stratifiable if it is a finite union of linear sets whose periods have at most two nonzero coordinates, with no two periods in one component connecting alternating pairs of coordinates. We give a computable many-one reduction from the existence of a rational zero of an integer polynomial to deciding stratifiability. After the classical reduction to quadratic systems, we reduce rational solvability of these systems to a problem we call finite separation by Cartesian products of rational linear forms. Its input consists of rational subspaces $D_1,\ldots,D_k\le\mathbb Q^r\times\mathbb Q^r$. A separator is a map $(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)\mapsto(u(\boldsymbol x),v(\boldsymbol y))$, where $u,v\colon\mathbb Q^r\to\mathbb Q$ are nonzero rational linear forms. The problem asks whether finitely many separators suffice so that every pair outside $\bigcup_iD_i$ receives, from some separator, a value attained at no pair in that union. We then reduce this problem to stratifiability. Ginsburg and Spanier's characterization of letter-bounded context-free languages} also induces a reduction from rational polynomial solvability to context-freeness of letter-bounded languages specified by semilinear exponent sets. An OpenAI preprint claims undecidability of rational polynomial solvability; if correct, our result settles the decidability of general stratifiability, a problem open since 1966.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 13 pages plus 10 pages of appendix

Logic in Computer Science.title: Privacy-Preserving Robustness-Guided Testing
Logic in Computer Science.summary: In industries like semi-conductors and aerospace, it is common for the design company to contract out part of the testing process to a Testing-as-a-Service (TaaS) company. In such a setup, both parties want to keep their intellectual property private (i.e. unknown to the other party): namely the design and its output traces for the designer, and the detailed correctness specifications for the tester. We demonstrate a practical way for conducting provably private TaaS using a cryptographically secure multi-party computation protocol. We do so for the common setup where the specification is in Signal Temporal Logic, and testing is done using robustness-guided falsification. Our implementation carefully separates the steps of falsification, and manages to be $\textit{maximally secure}$, in the sense that the parties learn the absolutely minimum necessary for falsification. For up to a 100-dimensional input search space, the generation of one test takes less than 80 msec, and the overhead of the privacy-preserving protocol is less than 6x. These numbers mean that privacy-preserving TaaS is practical, thus enabling TaaS in security-sensitive industries.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, presented at IEEE/ACM Embedded Systems Week (ESWEEK) 2026 for ACM SIGBED International Conference on Embedded Software (EMSOFT) 2026

Multiagent Systems.title: The Butterfly Effect in LLM Social Simulations: From Architecture Sensitivity to Robustness Audits
Multiagent Systems.summary: A butterfly effect occurs when a local perturbation propagates through a system and produces divergence in its collective outcome. In LLM social simulations, this creates a particular challenge for scientific inference: sensitivity to implementation choices can enter agent interactions and alter the collective outcomes on which scientific claims are based. We study this problem through a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma and a social-media echo chamber, spanning representation- and design-level perturbations across four LLM families. We find that controlled perturbations can substantially alter collective outcomes, with sensitivity varying across both perturbations and models. In the Prisoner's Dilemma, changing only the representation of a matched persona shifts two-agent cooperation by 75.2 percentage points for GPT-5.2, while game framing and memory representation produce smaller or less consistent effects. Multi-agent interaction further reshapes representation sensitivity, producing amplification or attenuation depending on the model and perturbation. In the echo-chamber simulation, persona representation changes interaction targeting and is accompanied by divergence in collective interaction structure, extending representation sensitivity from agent behavior to network-level outcomes. These results show that robustness cannot be inferred from a single simulation configuration and that local sensitivity can change as it propagates through interaction. We introduce TRAILS (Taxonomy for Robustness Audits In LLM Simulations) and the Social Simulation Audit Card as a framework for systematically auditing these dependencies and calibrating the scope of scientific claims to the robustness evidence that supports them.

Multiagent Systems.title: Transformers as Generic Deep Neural Networks: Exact Compilation, the Cost of Removing Activation-Activation Products, and Multi-Agent Attention Clustering
Multiagent Systems.summary: Transformers are deployed as a special model class. Neural processing units (NPU) add dedicated operators for attention and normalization, and quantization relies on Transformer-specific algorithms. We show the computation does not force this. Every Transformer block, with attention, LayerNorm and a GELU MLP, compiles exactly into a generic deep neural network built from fixed affine maps, routing and the square, sigmoid and inverse square root, plus GELU or its sigmoid approximation. Without activation-activation products, every transform-wise compilation adds at least $N^2$ scalar nonlinear evaluations per head for dense scores. Keeping that one operation type removes this cost; its elementwise form, present on every surveyed NPU, suffices with the sigmoid and inverse square root. For top-$k$ attention with exchangeable tail scores, we prove that exact or conditional-mean tail mass gives an unbiased, minimum-mean-square-error estimate of the attention distribution, while tail drop is conditionally biased. When queries or agents cluster, centroids choose the keys first, reducing the number of computed scores from $N^2$ to $Nk$ per head. On DeiT-Tiny, MambaIRv2-Light and Pythia-70M the compiled models match their references with all keys, standard post-training quantization applies, and the exact tail-mass estimate beats tail dropping with half as many keys on DeiT-Tiny and, for $k\le8$, on Pythia-70M.
Multiagent Systems.comment: 36 pages, 6 tables and 2 figures in the main text, 8 supplementary tables. Code: https://github.com/iceslice0/transformer-to-dnn

Multiagent Systems.title: Model Capacity Frontier: A Development Framework for LLM-Supported Social Simulation
Multiagent Systems.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly incorporated into agent-based models (ABMs) on the premise that richer, context-sensitive human behavior can improve empirical fidelity. However, LLM-supported ABMs introduce an open-ended design space in which subtle modeling and configuration choices, such as prompt design and environment coupling, can substantially alter outcomes. Developing LLM-supported ABMs to simulate human collective behavior therefore requires navigating configuration sensitivity while identifying the limitations of the current model architecture. In this paper, we introduce the Model Capacity Frontier (MCF), a framework that characterizes the empirical performance attainable by a specified architecture across its admissible configurations. In multi-objective settings, this capacity is represented by an estimated Pareto frontier obtained through systematic configuration exploration. We demonstrate MCF in crowd simulation of university commencement events with approximately 12,000 agents, using empirical movement data on temporal occupancy, spatial distribution, and flow direction. We first characterize the capacity of a conventional crowd model and then evaluate successive LLM-supported architectural extensions. In the process, MCF reveals which dimensions of attainable performance expand and which remain limited, providing empirical targets for refinement and re-evaluation. Initial LLM integration improves flow direction but degrades temporal occupancy and spatial distribution; subsequent architectural refinement of the LLM layer improves temporal occupancy and recovers spatial performance, while retaining much of the earlier gain in flow direction. Our case study shows how MCF guides the systematic architectural development of LLM-supported ABMs in configuration-sensitive, open-ended design spaces.

Multiagent Systems.title: JaxMARL-BC: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Macroeconomic Modelling, in Seconds
Multiagent Systems.summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) offers a principled way of populating simulated economies with many heterogeneous decision makers. Its adoption, pioneered in finance, has nonetheless been slow in macroeconomics because of two main limitations: the lack of a shared frame of reference connecting MARL systems to dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models the profession already trusts, and the very long training times. The first limitation was recently addressed by the Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Business Cycle (MARL-BC), which places deep RL households in a real business cycle economy and reduces to classic DSGE models in specific limits. Here we address the second limitation. We present JaxMARL-BC, a JAX-accelerated simulator that trains MARL-BC economies in seconds (between 75x and 724x faster than the reference implementation), and scales to 200,000 independent learning households. We verify its correctness against the known DSGE limits, characterise its scaling through a simple cost law, and demonstrate its value by a proof-of-concept calibration of an extended model with heterogeneous returns on capital, in a two-hour experiment that would previously have taken over a month. We release JaxMARL-BC as open source.

Multiagent Systems.title: Fig: Automated Multiagent Behavior Elicitor
Multiagent Systems.summary: Many social evaluations for multiagent systems study behaviors as they emerge from environments instead of systematically intervening in the environment to elicit such behaviors. We introduce Fig (Finding Interactions in Games), an agentic system that performs targeted elicitation interventions on game environments. It takes a natural language behavior description, decomposes it into sub-behaviors, generates new social games or selects existing ones, and executes single or combined interventions to the games' engine, opponents, instructions, and context. To evaluate model behavior, it combines built-in mechanical checks and synthetic rubric judgments. We validate the interventions, generated games, and evaluation mechanisms via human review. Models attempt the target behavior in 45.2% of episodes on average for valid scenarios generated by Fig for six test behaviors -- cooperation, exploitation, deception, covert coordination, betrayal, and sabotage. For game-behavior pairs with available controls, Fig's interventions increase attempt rates by 10.9% on average compared to matched control games. Fig shows that multiagent environments can serve as programmable test beds for intentional, controllable, and reproducible behavior evaluation. Code is available at https://github.com/fleet-ai/fig.

Multiagent Systems.title: To Manipulate or Not: Opinion Dynamics in LLM Interactions
Multiagent Systems.summary: Large language models increasingly take part in extended conversations where they can both shape and be shaped by another party's views, yet most persuasion research measures only one side of that exchange. We introduce a controlled LLM-LLM debate framework in which two language-model roles repeatedly discuss a contested topic (climate-change attribution): one is given an assigned stance and, in some conditions, an explicit instruction to persuade, while the other receives no assigned position. Across four ordered model combinations involving GPT-6 Luna and Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, we track both each role's explicitly reported position and a separate measure of its turn-by-turn behavior inside the conversation. Opinion dynamics differ substantially across model combinations: same-model interactions narrow the opinion gap on average, clearly for only one of the two models, while cross-model interactions widen it. Explicit reports and in-dialogue behavior capture distinct aspects of opinion dynamics, and a blanket instruction to persuade does not reliably increase influence. These findings suggest that conversational influence depends not only on assigned roles and initial positions but also on the participating models, with implications for how opinion change is measured in extended LLM interactions.

Multiagent Systems.title: GBClaw: An agentic AI framework for atomistic grain boundary research and mechanistic discovery
Multiagent Systems.summary: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems hold immense potential for automating complex workflows in materials discovery and design, but extending them to domain-intensive mechanistic investigations remains challenging. Here, we present GBClaw, an agentic AI framework for investigating the structure and deformation of general grain boundaries (GBs). Although general GBs constitute the vast majority of real-world interfaces in polycrystalline materials, they remain understudied because their structural complexity and interfacial mismatch complicate experimental and modeling research. GBClaw integrates large language models (LLMs) into a modular architecture comprising an orchestrator, specialized agents, domain-specific tools, simulation interfaces, and hierarchical memory. Through dynamic replanning and iterative workflow refinement, the framework effectively connects systematic simulations with targeted mechanistic analysis. Applied to 14 general asymmetric tilt GBs in nickel, GBClaw characterized interfacial defect structures and identified diverse deformation modes across these incommensurate boundaries. Comparing boundary sliding with and without secondary GB misfit dislocations revealed substantial differences in shear strength, underscoring the critical role of defect hierarchies in sliding resistance. Furthermore, researcher-guided follow-up calculations traced an anomalously high shear resistance to metastable boundary structures. This work demonstrates that combining agentic AI with domain expertise bridges high-throughput computational screening with deep physical understanding of complex material interfaces.

Multiagent Systems.title: ASPIRE: Agentic /Skills Discovery for Robotics
Multiagent Systems.summary: Traditional robot programming is notoriously challenging: it requires orchestrating multimodal perception, managing physical contact dynamics, and handling diverse environment configurations and execution failures. We introduce ASPIRE (Agentic Skill Programming through Iterative Robot Exploration), a continual learning system that autonomously writes and refines robot control programs in a code-as-policy paradigm while compounding experience into a reusable skill library. ASPIRE operates in an open-ended learning loop, consisting of three components: (1) a closed-loop robot execution engine that exposes fine-grained multimodal traces, enabling the agent to autonomously diagnose failures, synthesize repairs, and validate outcomes; (2) a continually expanding skill library that distills validated fixes into reusable, transferable robotic knowledge; and (3) an evolutionary search procedure that generates diverse programs, systematically debugging them to explore beyond single-trajectory refinement. ASPIRE surpasses prior methods by up to 77% on manipulation tasks under perturbation, 72% on Robosuite's bimanual handover task, and up to 32% on long-horizon household tasks. The accumulated skill library further enables zero-shot generalization: on representative unseen long-horizon tasks, ASPIRE achieves 31% success, outperforming the 4% success rate of prior methods. Performance scales with the capabilities of frontier models. With Claude Opus 5.5, ASPIRE nearly saturates these benchmarks, achieving 99% average success across all 80 LIBERO-Pro tasks and 100% success on representative Robosuite and BEHAVIOR-1K tasks. Beyond simulation, skills discovered in simulation reduce real-world robot programming effort across embodiments and robot APIs, while skills acquired through online interaction with physical robots enable ASPIRE to solve a Rubik's Cube with progressively improving efficiency.
