The framework models scammer-baiter interactions as a two-player game with empirically grounded strategies and utility functions, using Nash equilibrium as a formal benchmark for evaluating learned behaviour. Across 300 simulated dialogues and three LLM architectures, adaptive strategy selection achieves 28.9-79.7% closer alignment to Nash equilibrium than non-adaptive baselines. The code and an annotated dataset of 300 dialogues with turn-level strategy labels and utility scores are released at https://github.com/nardinebasta/GameofPhones_/ .
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted at the 2026 Joint European Conference on Machine Learning and Knowledge Discovery in Databases (ECML PKDD 2026)

Cryptography and Security.title: Arithmetic limiting laws over shifted primes: dimension zero, Fourier decay, and absolute continuity
Cryptography and Security.summary: For each prime $p$, let $c(p)=\frac{\varphi(p-1)}{p-1}\prod_{j\ge1}(1-p^{-j})$, the limiting probability, as $n\to\infty$, that a uniformly chosen matrix in $M_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$ has primitive-root determinant. As $p$ ranges over the primes, $c(p)$ has the classical shifted-totient limiting law $μ_G$ on $[0,1/2]$. Let $μ_f$ be its image under $x\mapsto-\log x$. We prove that $μ_G$ has Hausdorff dimension zero and gives full mass to absolutely normal Liouville numbers. Every Borel set of positive $μ_G$-mass has packing dimension at least $1/2$, and local dimension fails to exist $μ_G$-almost everywhere. Both Fourier transforms satisfy the effective bound $O((\log|τ|)^{-1/3}(\log\log|τ|)^{1/3})$. In every fixed reduced progression, the empirical laws of $c(p)$ and $\varphi(p-1)/(p-1)$ approach their respective limiting laws with sharp Kolmogorov order $1/\log x$. Over unrestricted primes, these laws and their negative-logarithmic images converge in $W_1$ at rate $O_B((\log x)^{-B})$ for every fixed $B>0$. We obtain concentration expansions to every fixed inverse-logarithmic order and prove that every sufficiently short maximizing interval for $μ_f$ contains $\log3$. For $U_T$ uniform on $[0,T]$, $(\log T)\widehat{μ_f}(U_T)$ converges in distribution to a circularly symmetric random variable whose modulus is an explicit random Euler product, with convergence of absolute moments of every real order $s>-1$. For every $A>0$, the strongly additive function $f_A$ with prime values $(\log\ell)^{-A}$ has absolutely continuous limiting laws for $f_A(n)$ and $f_A(p-1)$. We give extremal estimates and certified NTT prime searches. A lattice supplement determines second distinct nonzero squared norms of type-$A$ tensor products and gives uniform cyclotomic smoothing asymptotics at $ε=2^{-c\varphi(m)}$ for every fixed $c>0$. These statements are unconditional.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Substantially expanded from the last version: proves absolute continuity for all positive logarithmic-jump exponents, giving counterexamples to the 1979 Erdos-Katai singularity conjecture; adds sharp prime-sampling rates, raw-ratio Fourier decay and normality, local-dimension oscillation, and complex Fourier-amplitude laws. Uniform cyclotomic smoothing is extended to every positive error exponent

Cryptography and Security.title: Proof-of-Machine-Learning-Inference: Mining Knowledge, Not Hashes
Cryptography and Security.summary: Bitcoin-style Proof-of-Work (PoW) secures permissionless blockchains but spends substantial computation on hash puzzles which have no utility other than extending the chain. At the same time, we have seen that the rise of generative AI has created significant demand for computational resources that are unfortunately available only to a few players. We propose a solution that solves both problems at the same time. In particular, we present Proof-of-ML-Inference (PoML), a consensus protocol in which miners perform user-requested machine-learning inference as part of their consensus algorithm. We identify exactly what computational assumptions are needed for ML inference to safely replace hash work, formalize those assumptions, and give evidence that LLMs and diffusion models satisfy them. We then formally analyse the security of our protocol by reducing the security of our protocol to the security of the Bitcoin Backbone model. Finally, we empirically evaluate block-time stability, showing that, in a simulated environment, PoML maintains a block production rate close to its calibrated block-time target.

Cryptography and Security.title: How To Track Qubits Through Space and Time (Or: Sailing in a Quantum Boat)
Cryptography and Security.summary: While quantum position verification aims to certify a prover's location using quantum information, existing security definitions only guarantee that part of the successful adversarial party is in the claimed location. This leaves open the possibility that a distributed team of adversaries can jointly simulate a prover in a way that defeats the intended meaning of `being at a location' in position-based cryptography. We introduce stronger notions of position verification that we call quantum localization, which requires that there is a specified, unclonable state at the verified spacetime point-and that this state can be found nowhere else. We show that quantum localization leads naturally to a meaningful notion of trajectory verification, in which quantum information is verifiably tracked through space and time. We construct quantum localization and trajectory verification protocols using quantum anchor states, which generalize coset states from unclonable cryptography. The security of our schemes is proven in the classical oracle (i.e. ideal obfuscation) model, which can be heuristically instantiated in the plain model using post-quantum indistinguishability obfuscation. We also introduce and instantiate the concept of functionality localization, which guarantees that the adversary has the ability to compute a secret function at the verified spacetime point, and this function cannot be computed anywhere else. This raises the intriguing possibility of localizing computational capabilities in space and time. More broadly, we believe our notions of quantum localization and subsequent feasibility results provide stronger foundations for position-based cryptography. At a conceptual level, our results also explore the tight link between two fundamental notions in physics-location and information-thus serving as a natural foundation for cryptographic capabilities tied to physical spacetime.

Cryptography and Security.title: BrushOff: Stroke-Based Re-rendering as a Watermark Removal Attack on Painting
Cryptography and Security.summary: Invisible watermarks are used to mark who owns a painting. We show that a simple attack removes the most robust one we test. The attack redraws the watermarked painting with brush strokes, using a pretrained stroke-based renderer. We call this attack BrushOff. It needs no training, no knowledge of the watermark, and no generative model. We test four watermarks on 500 paintings from five styles. VINE, a recent watermark built to survive image editing, survives all 14 conventional distortions we test, with at least 97.8% detection. Repainting lowers its detection to 1.8%, while the output keeps a no-reference quality score close to that of the clean paintings. Diffusion regeneration can also remove VINE, but at the same removal level it moves the image twice as far from the painting in DreamSim distance, and it changes what the painting shows. Because the renderer draws a countable number of strokes, we can control the attack strength step by step. Finally, we test what kind of signal survives. A simple probe that stores bits in the relative brightness of neighboring regions survives repainting, while a probe that uses absolute brightness does not. The same probe fails under diffusion regeneration, while VINE fails under repainting. Robustness to these two attacks is therefore a separate property, and benchmarks should test both.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables

Cryptography and Security.title: DM-RSA-OAEP: Formal Treatment of a Dual-Modulus Fault-Detection Countermeasure Based on Physical Diversity
Cryptography and Security.summary: We revisit DM-RSA, an RSA variant that uses two independent moduli, whose original version was broken by Håstad's attack and contained an incorrect compromise-tolerance claim. We give a formal treatment of its repaired variant, DM-RSA-OAEP: (i) a complete IND-CCA2 security proof in the random-oracle model via a two-step hybrid argument, upper-bounding the security of the scheme by that of the weaker underlying RSA-OAEP instance, with an explicit simulation loss; (ii) a fault-detection theorem in an explicit adversary model that covers computation, key, and verification faults, including safe-error attacks, under a clearly stated physical-diversity assumption; (iii) an explicit analysis of why the countermeasure degrades to uselessness when the diversity assumption is violated (common-mode faults on a single chip). We position the scheme against the countermeasure landscape and against the broken dual-modulus literature. The contribution is deliberately framed as a fault countermeasure with a provable detection guarantee, not as a computationally stronger RSA. We conclude with a concrete instantiation and a detailed measurement protocol.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 9 pages

Cryptography and Security.title: Beyond Attack Success Rate: Cost-Aware Metric for Evaluating Iterative LLM Jailbreaks
Cryptography and Security.summary: Attack success rate (ASR) evaluates jailbreaks against large language models without accounting for repeated calls to the victim model. Yet each additional call gives the deployed system another opportunity to detect the attack and intervene. We introduce $\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{STEP}}$, which penalizes additional victim-model calls while retaining binary success judgments. Our evaluation considers GCG~\cite{zou2023universal}, PAIR~\cite{chao2025jailbreaking} with a step budget, and a single-step PAP~\cite{zeng2024johnny} baseline on JailBreakBench across three model families. GCG's scores decrease by 7.0--8.7 percentage points after discounting, while PAP's remain unchanged. While for PAIR~\cite{chao2025jailbreaking}, we see a wider discounting range between 3.4-12 percentage points, showing that the "step" quantity differs per iterative strategy. Reporting both metrics makes the discount due to repeated victim-model interaction explicit. Code is available \hyperlink{https://github.com/SuELS-Group/beyond_asr}{here}.

Cryptography and Security.title: BR-MoE: Budgeted Semantic Release for Privacy-Preserving Traffic Analytics
Cryptography and Security.summary: Traffic cameras support useful analysis, but their outputs can reveal private information. Replacing images with text reduces direct visual exposure. It does not place a formal bound on disclosure. The published reinforcement learning and mixture-of-experts framework refines scene descriptions through relevance, coverage, and brevity rewards. It does not account for repeated releases under a fixed privacy budget. This paper proposes budgeted semantic release as an extension of that framework. Four scene experts first process isolated video chunks. Their outputs are mapped to a fixed, bounded semantic schema. A reinforcement learning controller selects which expert summaries to release and how much privacy budget to spend. The controller uses public task requests and previous private releases. A separate privacy filter enforces the total budget. Calibrated noise is added before the summaries are converted to text. Under explicit chunk isolation and bounded-event assumptions, the complete release transcript satisfies an event-level differential privacy bound. The design also supports reuse of previous summaries without new disclosure. An evaluation protocol covers traffic utility, privacy attacks, release freshness, and computational cost. Illustrative tables show the intended reporting format. They do not establish empirical gains. The proposed contribution is a task-aware release interface with auditable privacy accounting for repeated traffic descriptions.

Cryptography and Security.title: Connection Escrow: Holding AI-Agent Pod Egress in the Kernel Until an Isolated Verifier Rules
Cryptography and Security.summary: AI agents in containers act by opening network connections, and the text that drives them can be hostile. Controls placed between the agent and its tools are bypassed by a child process or a direct socket, and their approval is not tied to the connection the kernel later opens. We present connection escrow: every outbound TCP connection from a supervised pod is parked inside the kernel's connect() path, before any packet exists, by a 98-instruction eBPF program on the pod's cgroup. A node interceptor attributes the held socket to its kernel socket cookie, process, executable digest, cgroup and pod identity, parks the first bytes the agent writes, and asks a verifier in a separate container with its own key. The connection is released only on a signed verdict naming that one socket cookie and destination, unexpired and unused; no verdict by the deadline resets it, and a late approval is refused. The agent is unmodified. A 36-check adversarial suite with real cgroups passes on the eBPF hold point (33 of the checks also apply, and pass, on an iptables hold point): refused connections never reach the destination; forged, rebound, replayed, expired and late verdicts are refused; the agent's attempt to reach the verifier is itself escrowed; child-process and renamed-binary bypasses fail; UDP is pinned to the resolver. On a Kubernetes cluster, unmodified pods are held per connection and attributed to their SPIFFE identity, a raw socket that bypasses a sidecar proxy is held, and 600 connections from six pods are gated. The hold adds 4.5 ms median per released connection, of which 24 us is policy. Finally, we gate on request content without terminating TLS: an eBPF uprobe reads the plaintext at the agent's TLS-library boundary (shared OpenSSL, static OpenSSL, Go crypto/tls), a model scores it, and the connection is held on that verdict while TLS stays end-to-end and the enforcer holds no key.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Code: https://github.com/45h0kg/benign-attach-gateway

Cryptography and Security.title: Mal-AAEGAN: Adversarial Autoencoder with Double-Critic WGAN-GP for Malware Generation
Cryptography and Security.summary: Machine-learning (ML) malware detectors are known to be vulnerable to adversarial samples. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) such as MalGAN, Mal-LSGAN, and our previous Mal-D2GAN can craft adversarial malware to probe and harden these detectors, yet they operate directly on a high-dimensional, discrete binary feature space, which leads to unstable training, vanishing gradients, and adversarial samples of limited diversity. To address these problems we propose Mal-AAEGAN. First, an adversarial autoencoder (AAE) learns a low-dimensional, regularized and continuous latent representation of the $M$-dimensional binary API feature vector, and the generator performs an additive perturbation in this latent space rather than in the raw binary space. Second, training follows the Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty (WGAN-GP) scheme using two critics: a mimic-black-box critic that inherits the role of the substitute detector and a naive critic that inherits the role of the additional detector. A decode-binarize-OR pipeline guarantees that the original API calls of the malware are preserved. The model is evaluated on two malware datasets of different input dimensionality ($M\in\{139,215\}$) against eight common ML detectors and compared, under an identical protocol, with MalGAN, Mal-LSGAN and Mal-D2GAN. Mal-AAEGAN trains stably in the continuous latent space and attains an evasion rate on par with or higher than these binary-space baselines across both datasets, while its generator stays responsive to the noise input rather than reducing to a single fixed perturbation per malware.

Cryptography and Security.title: Differential privacy with adjustable preservation of multivariate relationships
Cryptography and Security.summary: This paper derives an exact attenuation formula for multivariate cross-moments under differential privacy achieved through randomized response. From a proposed alternative formulation of randomization matrices compliant with differential privacy guarantees we show that, under attribute-level randomization and where the randomization of the whole distribution is characterized by Kronecker products, any cross-moment of the anonymized dataset involving distinct attributes is equal to the original cross-moment multiplied by attenuation parameters, themselves determined by the part of the overall privacy budget allocated to each attribute. This characterization enables explicit and transparent controls of multivariate relationships preservations in differential privacy through privacy budget allocation. A simple numerical illustration demonstrates that identical total budgets can yield substantially different covariance-preservation profiles. The results also make the multiplicative loss of higher-order interactions explicit and thus can support mechanism design guided by analytical priorities.

Cryptography and Security.title: Exact Compilation and Resource Laws for Hidden Integer Feedback
Cryptography and Security.summary: Hidden randomized rounding couples the privacy loss of successive integer releases. We study a rational-feedback mechanism under predictable signed-unit participation and full observation of every physical output. A preparation's lifetime connects three results. First, preserving complete carries until an observed echo synchronizes the worlds gives exact finite-law point compilation, with support-width exponent $3C-2$ at every fixed budget $C\ge2$. Second, releasing commitments earlier gives a monotone hierarchy whose exact endpoint, strict gaps and numerical brackets quantify calibration loss. At one fixed discrete Gaussian, a loss allowance of 0.09 requires all four commitments. Third, legal regeneration yields an unrestricted KL rate with a square-root testing remainder and a complete asymptotic frontier under joint physical-time and participation constraints. At fixed rational parameters, finite-window occupation programs approximate that frontier to error $2^{-b}$ in polynomial bit time in $b$. Verified countable-transcript semantics and independently checked finite certificates support these analyses. A matched static workload illustrates the resulting design tradeoff: a structured finite integer matrix improves error and fresh randomness, while the scalar feedback instance retains fewer noise-state and source-table bits.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 59 pages, 4 figures; includes supplementary material. Ganxuan Yang and Siqi Wen contributed equally. Corresponding author: Jidong Yuan

Cryptography and Security.title: Reliable Estimation of Differential Privacy under Selection Bias
Cryptography and Security.summary: Statistical privacy audits are essential for verifying the theoretical privacy guarantees of differentially private (DP) mechanisms. Auditors typically use Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs) to estimate a lower bound on the true privacy leakage of DP mechanisms at a specified confidence level, which should not exceed the theoretical privacy upper bound guaranteed by DP. However, we found that many auditing implementations in prior work introduce a selection bias when running MIAs, which leads to statistically invalid and overestimated lower bounds. Because most audits are not tight, this bias has thus far gone unnoticed: the estimated lower bounds remained well below the theoretical upper bounds. Nevertheless, accurately evaluating this lower bound is critical, as a flawed statistical assessment could lead to false alarms on correct mechanisms or an incorrect evaluation of the guarantee's tightness. This work employs tools from the statistical literature to correct this bias. We present an overview of the different correction methods and assess their respective advantages. Furthermore, we perform a comprehensive re-analysis of results returned by prior audit implementations and show that without statistical correction, these audits violate the theoretical upper bounds up to four times more often than their claimed confidence level implies. With correction applied, the resulting lower bounds are statistically valid, and violations occur at no more than the nominal rate.

Cryptography and Security.title: Fake News, Real Crashes: Information Injection Attacks on LLM Financial Trading Agents
Cryptography and Security.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents now trade real capital using news as evidence, yet they cannot reliably tell fabricated headlines from real news. Because they read the same feeds under near-identical policies, a single fabricated post can push them into the same trade at the same moment. We present a systematic attack benchmark for information injection against LLM trading agents. Unlike prompt injection, which targets the model's instructions, information injection targets the evidence the agent trusts. The benchmark spans five injection vectors and seven event categories, evaluated over ~10,000 decisions on 15 U.S. stocks. Five findings emerge. (i) Prompt injection achieves 14% attack success rate (ASR), but fabricated news reaches 62% and two 30-word templates reach 100% on all 15 stocks, inverting the usual LLM-security intuition. (ii) For fact-poisoning templates, surface form matters more than content, since removing credibility cues such as a named source or a "BREAKING" tag drops ASR from 100% to 0% while the fake claim remains identical. (iii) Success depends on the agent's state, with a fake indicator panel scoring 91% against an agent about to hold but 12% against one about to buy. (iv) Attacks generalize across model vendors and remain effective when blended, unlabeled, into real news feeds. (v) Most attacks evade standard defenses, since model scaling stops shallow vectors but not fact poisoning, peer debate fails, and only hierarchical aggregation reduces ASR.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 25 pages, 7 figures, 18 tables

Cryptography and Security.title: Temporal Dynamics and Security Assessment of SRT Protocol: A 96-Day Longitudinal Analysis of Production Streaming Infrastructure
Cryptography and Security.summary: This study presents a 96-day longitudinal analysis of Secure Reliable Transport (SRT) protocol behavior in a production streaming environment between Iraq and Turkey, examining 262,672 transport metric samples and 5,033,104 system resource measurements collected between October 2025 and January 2026. The research addresses temporal patterns, system-resource relationships, attack vulnerability, and anomaly detection. Results reveal significant temporal variation: Negative Acknowledgment exhibits 7.6-fold hourly variation and 11.5-fold daily variation (p < 0.001), though with small effect sizes (eta^2 < 0.04), indicating that temporal period explains less than 4 percent of total variance. Central Processing Unit (CPU) utilization emerges as the strongest system-level correlate of transport variation (r = 0.617 with NAK rate). Controlled User Datagram Protocol (UDP) flood experiments at 500 packets per second cause CPU increases of 176 to 806 percent, while SRT transport metrics change by only plus or minus 13 percent demonstrating protocol resilience through the Automatic Repeat Request mechanism. An unexpected anomaly reaching 97.7 percent CPU enabled signature-based differentiation between attack types. A Z-score anomaly detection method outperforms fixed thresholds, detecting all 7 security events. This study contributes the longest temporal characterization of SRT metrics reported to date, the first system-SRT correlation analysis, and the first controlled security assessment of SRT infrastructure. These findings provide actionable guidance for capacity planning, security hardening, and multi-metric monitoring of production SRT deployments.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 21 pages, 11 figures, published in Journal of Communications (JCM), vol. 21, no. 4, pp. 544-564, 2026

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: LLM-Attack Suite: A Unified Red-Team Framework for Privacy Evaluation of Split and Distributed LLM Systems
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Split language models keep input text on a client but send intermediate representations to a server. Attacks can reconstruct text from these messages. Comparing privacy evaluations is difficult when attackers see different messages, know different model weights or use different datasets and recovery measures. We present LLM-Attack Suite, a framework that records these choices and lets researchers check, compare and extend an evaluation. Compatible attacks reuse recorded messages, and their predictions are saved for independent scoring. The scoring rule requires a linked undefended reference before a defence can pass. Reports also identify attacks that remain untested. In a controlled GPT-2 experiment, adding gradients returned during training increased token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact-document recovery from 13.71% to 37.77%. The 95% interval for the token gain lay above the two-percentage-point threshold fixed before testing. This experiment is shared with a companion study; here it tests how the evaluation responds to a change in attacker access. Further studies measure how corpus choice and compression defences affect recovery, compare an adapted published attack with its reference implementation, and test the measurement code. The framework reports implementation checks separately from measured attack effectiveness. Each privacy claim should state the attacker, dataset and scoring rule, report its controls and identify untested attacks.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: HyCo: Hybrid Drafting for Cost-Efficient Mobile-Cloud Speculative Decoding
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Device-cloud speculative decoding reduces server computation, but growing a deep draft tree with a small language model (SLM) requires repeated passes on a mobile neural processing unit (NPU). We present HyCo, which runs the server model's native multi-token prediction (MTP) head on the device to build a deep chain and uses one SLM pass to add alternative branches. The server returns the hidden state, input embedding, and key-value entries needed by the head instead of executing its sequential steps. Quantization, a restricted vocabulary, and a 1K-token window fit both drafters to the NPU. An ε-threshold rule additionally relaxes exact preservation of the verifier's sampling distribution. In single-client runs with a Galaxy S26 Ultra over LTE/5G, HyCo reduces server GPU time per output token relative to server-side MTP self-speculation by 38.6% on Spec-Bench and 29.2% on 32K-token summarization. With the same acceptance rule, three runs of each system on Spec-Bench show 9.0 percentage points more saving and 1.9x delivery speed than an SLM-only drafter. HyCo differs from Cloud+MTP by +0.2 judge-score points (paired 95% CI: -0.9 to +1.3); exploratory translation favors SpecEdge-ε. Without relaxation, HyCo exact saves 27.7% and 11.9% on the two datasets.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Under review at ACL Rolling Review (October 2026)

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: SweepANN: A GPU-Accelerated Large-K Approximate Vector Search for Drug Discovery
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
DrugCLIP places small molecules and protein pockets in one space, turning genome-wide drug discovery into large-K retrieval by vector proximity. A campaign fixes over 20K pockets in advance for one library of over 500M molecules. Each pocket keeps K = 500K candidates, 0.1% of the collection, versus 100 in ANN benchmarks. Missed hits never get tested, so mean recall must reach 99% relative to exact search. Large answers make IVF probe every list holding a result and graph search track K or more candidates, so costs grow with K. On our CPUs and GPUs, neither index family reaches the target without losing most of its edge over scanning.
  SweepANN partitions compressed vectors across GPUs and scans each resident partition. One matrix multiplication scores each block for a whole query batch, reading it once. Several plans perform the K-dependent selection and merging of each query's K answers, each returning an exact top-K under compressed scoring. The window plan retains each query's best K from sampled blocks as its seed, and only rows above each seed's minimum score, shared once across GPUs, enter the buffers.
  Four Blackwell GPUs (RTX PRO 6000) answer all 26,562 pockets with a resident time of about 61 seconds, excluding library loading, and 99.6% mean recall relative to exact FP32 search. DrugCLIP reports roughly 24 hours with eight A100 GPUs in its own campaign. On 500M rows, the window plan runs 1.41x faster than SweepANN's grouped plan in the same memory. Across 25M-500M rows and K of 10K-500K, all GPU IVF configurations meeting the recall target take 8.2-24x SweepANN's resident time. On DEEP1B's 1B vectors across eight GPUs, against SweepANN's exact full-score scan of uncompressed FP32 rows, the window plan cuts resident time by 5.4x and 3.2x at K = 100K and 500K. It also cuts per-GPU peak memory by 6.0x and 5.3x, losing 1.0 and 0.7 mean-recall points.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 38 pages (24 pages of body and references, 14 pages of appendix), 16 figures, 48 tables. Code and data-processing scripts will be released as open source

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Fault Tolerance for Stream Processing Engines
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Distributed Stream Processing Engines (DSPEs) target applications related to continuous computation, online machine learning and real-time query processing. DSPEs operate on high volume of data by applying lightweight operations on real-time and continuous streams. Such systems require clusters of hundreds of machines for their deployment. Streaming applications come with various requirements, i.e., low-latency, high throughput, scalability and high availability. In this survey, we study the fault tolerance problem for DSPEs. We discuss fault tolerance techniques that are used in stream processing engines that were state of the art at the time of writing (2016), namely S4, Storm, Flink, Spark Streaming, Samza and MillWheel. Further, we give insight on fault tolerance approaches that we categorize as active replication, passive replication and upstream backup. Finally, we discuss implications of the fault tolerance techniques for different streaming application requirements. This revised version corrects errors in the original 2016 manuscript, summarizes later developments in Flink and Spark, discusses durable logs and archival storage for replay, and points to more recent surveys.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Revised version: corrects errors in the background, system descriptions and analysis; summarizes later developments in Flink and Spark; adds a discussion of durable logs and archival storage; redrawn

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Magneton: Optimizing Energy Efficiency of ML Systems via Differential Energy Debugging
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
The training and deployment of machine learning (ML) models have become extremely energy-intensive. While existing optimization efforts focus primarily on hardware energy efficiency, a significant but overlooked source of inefficiency is software energy waste caused by poor software design. This often includes redundant or poorly designed operations that consume more energy without improving performance. These inefficiencies arise in widely used ML frameworks and applications, yet developers often lack the visibility and tools to detect and diagnose them.
  We propose differential energy debugging, a novel approach that leverages the observation that competing ML systems often implement similar functionality with vastly different energy consumption. Building on this insight, we design and implement Magneton, an energy profiler that compares energy consumption between similar ML systems at the operator level and automatically pinpoints code regions and configuration choices responsible for excessive energy use. Applied to 9 popular ML systems spanning LLM inference, general ML frameworks, and image generation, Magneton detects and diagnoses 16 known cases of software energy inefficiency and further discovers 8 previously unknown cases, 7 of which have been confirmed by developers.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 15 pages, 10 figures, to appear in the 24th USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI '27)

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: FaaSpot: Fault-Tolerant Serverless Workflow Execution on Spot Instances
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
Serverless computing is increasingly used to run complex DAG workflows across diverse applications, and individual function execution times have grown to support them, pushing workflow makespans to hours. Open-source serverless platforms, deployed on a pool of VMs, typically use on-demand instances, and their cost increases with the makespan. Spot instances are far cheaper, but a preemption is likely before the workflow finishes. A preemption at a fan-out node or a task feeding a fan-in node stalls every parallel branch, cascading a single preemption into a workflow-wide failure. Prior systems address this challenge by migrating high-impact tasks to reliable, non-spot resources, sacrificing spot's cost advantage.
  We present FaaSpot, a serverless workflow execution system that runs every workflow task on spot instances with no on-demand fallback. Our key insight is that cascade-prone positions are determined by the DAG's topology and can be identified before execution. Therefore, FaaSpot analyzes the workflow DAG once at submission time and classifies each task by the impact of its preemption. Selective checkpointing, survival-aware scaling, and lineage-based retry then act on this single classification, with no runtime coordination. We evaluate FaaSpot on a trace-driven spot emulator with eight DAG workflows against four state-of-the-art baselines. FaaSpot completes 89.03% of runs at $0.018 per successful run, 21pp (percentage points) above the average baseline success rate and at a lower cost per success than every baseline, while reducing mean latency by 2.3x.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 14 pages, 12 figures, 7 tables. To appear in the 27th International Middleware Conference (Middleware '26), December 14-18, 2026, Tarragona, Spain

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: GeoSplit: Selective Edge--Server Map Acquisition for Cross-User Travel-Mode Recognition
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Networked mobility sensing couples local trajectory inference with remote geospatial context, making communication decisions part of the prediction system. We present GeoSplit, an edge--server framework for travel-mode recognition that separates the utility of map evidence, its training-time transfer, and its selective acquisition at runtime. On GeoLife with 10% labels, we evaluate these components under user-day and user-disjoint grouping. For unseen users, aligned full-map context raises macro-F1 from 0.7154 to 0.7864, while map-informed distillation yields a motion-only student at 0.7225. Through a compact query interface, entropy gating achieves 0.7729 macro-F1 versus 0.7738 for all queries, querying 39.5% of trajectories and reducing application payload by 60.5%. Under user-day grouping, selective and all-query scores are similarly close at a 21.6% query rate. Learned value estimation and probability fusion offer no consistent improvement. These results illustrate communication-efficient edge--server inference for an intelligent transportation sensing task.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Democratizing MoE inference on commodity GPUs with CoMoE
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
Deploying Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models relies heavily on Expert Parallelism, which generates intense inter-GPU communication. Consequently, state-of-the-art inference systems require high-bandwidth, P2P interconnects (e.g., NVLink) in datacenter GPUs to handle massive token routing, making deployment prohibitively expensive. Consumer GPUs offer comparable compute power at significantly lower cost, promising to democratize MoE inference for individuals and enable privacy-preserving local deployments. However, their bandwidth-limited (only weak PCIe bus bandwidth) and host-mediated interconnects (no P2P support) introduce severe communication bottlenecks.
  We present CoMoE, a communication-efficient MoE inference system that resolves this mismatch through novel host-centric routing. Our key insight is that the unique communication topology provides the opportunity to elevate the host to an active routing hub, which can fundamentally reduce communication volume and eliminate global synchronization-induced stalls. Specifically, for token dispatch, we introduce host-backed token multicast to write shared tokens to the host exactly once, eliminating outbound transmission redundancy. For token combine, we propose a fine-grained, token-level aggregation mechanism using host staging buffers, which replaces rigid global synchronization and mitigates straggler effects. Evaluation on RTX 5090 GPUs shows that CoMoE improves inference throughput by up to 1.46x, approaching the performance of NVLink-capable A800 GPUs at only 23.4% of the hardware cost.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: CQTwin: A Digital-Twin Toolkit for Operational Analytics of HPC Schedulers
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: HPC facilities collect years of job scheduler records, yet much of this operational data remains underused because accessible tools for turning it into actionable insight are scarce. We present CQTwin, an open-source digital-twin toolkit for operational analytics of HPC scheduling data. CQTwin addresses this gap through two complementary modes: offline trace replay and online event-driven simulation. Built on the Python-based CQSim discrete-event simulator, CQTwin combines a fidelity-validated, high-performance C++ engine with an interactive browser-based dashboard and a Snapshot Lab, enabling facility staff, operators, and researchers to characterize workloads, compare scheduling policies, and explore what-if scenarios. As an offline twin, CQTwin replays archived workload traces under alternative policies to show how the same workload would have unfolded under different scheduling decisions. As an online twin, it consumes job events as they arrive and projects how alternative policies would process the currently queued jobs, providing guidance for real-time decision-making. The dashboard supports the complete analysis workflow, including workload characterization, experiment configuration and monitoring, and multidimensional comparison of simulation results, allowing users to determine visually which policies best suit a workload and what trade-offs they entail. We validate CQTwin using production traces from the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility spanning 2016-2023.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Accepted at the 1st International Workshop on HPC Operational Data Analytics (HPC-ODA 2026), held with SC26. 8 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Thread Scaling of Hexaly on the TDVRPTW across Two Model Encodings. An Experimental Report: Binding Choice, Slice-Count Choice, and Two Thread Ladders
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Thread scaling in Hexaly on the Time-Dependent Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows (TDVRPTW) depends on modeling, and on the language binding through which the model reaches the solver. We compare two encodings, both reaching the solver through its C++ binding: one evaluates continuous travel-time functions exactly through external callbacks, which that binding evaluates concurrently, while the other approximates them with time slices evaluated natively by the solver. Independent CPU accounting confirms that both use the cores they are allocated, but they respond differently to width. The external-function encoding stabilizes, reducing its seed dispersion by about 30% up to 8 threads before widening again, yet its pooled quality barely moves, because nine of the ten instances improve while the hardest one degrades by enough to cancel them. For the time-sliced encoding we first select a discretization on feasibility under the original travel-time functions rather than on approximation error, and the retained setting then improves monotonically with the thread count, gaining about a quarter of its final gap and reducing the seed dispersion by nearly half between 1 and 16 threads. At equal single-threaded budget the two encodings are close, and the small pooled edge of exact evaluation comes from that same hardest instance, so the practical advantage of the discretization is thread scaling rather than fidelity traded for speed. These descriptive results support multi-threading as a way to improve solution quality and stability when the model can exploit it, and they show that binding-level constraints on external evaluation must be measured, not assumed.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: v3: 22 pages. Corrected author lists in KAYROS, MAMUT-routing and Poryos2026 references. No new experiments or changes to results. Raw experiment data deposited at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22047134

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: SafeWall: A Risk-Aware Job Walltime Recommendation for HPC Scheduling
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: In high-performance computing (HPC), users must submit resource requirements for their jobs, with user-supplied walltime being a critical parameter. However, these estimates are notoriously inaccurate, as users tend to overestimate walltime to prevent the scheduler from terminating their jobs prematurely. While existing work on learning-based walltime prediction primarily focuses on maximizing prediction accuracy, such predictions are inherently risky for walltime recommendations. Specifically, underestimation leads to job termination before completion, resulting in lost progress and wasted resources. In this study, we present SafeWall, a novel recommendation method that adjusts walltime predictions by incorporating an explicit, nonnegative safety buffer to mitigate underestimation risk. The core of our approach is a risk-aware buffer that dynamically calibrates safety margins based on individual user's historical behavior. When user data is limited, the system employs statistical shrinkage to align these margins with a global baseline, ensuring robustness. This yields a lightweight mechanism that optimizes the trade-off between prediction accuracy and termination risk. SafeWall is modular and applicable to various learning-based prediction models. We evaluate SafeWall using five public workload traces, including the full-lifetime job log from the 4,392-node Theta machine at the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility. Across all traces, SafeWall substantially reduces underestimation risk compared to the unbuffered base predictors, while preserving competitive accuracy. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/SPEAR-UIC/JSSPP26-SafeWall.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Accepted at the 29th Workshop on Job Scheduling Strategies for Parallel Processing (JSSPP 2026), held with IEEE IPDPS 2026. 20 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: KrMM Recurrences: HPC-Enhanced Estimators for Nonlinear Classical Shadows
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: While quantum technologies are rapidly evolving, near-term applications heavily rely on hybrid quantum-classical paradigms. Among these, the classical shadows framework has gained a lot of traction, not only for quantum information science, but also for the development and verification of quantum hardware. It allows to efficiently classically estimate many properties of quantum states from randomized measurements alone, a task that is otherwise intractable due to the destructive nature of measurements in quantum systems. There are, however, many properties of interest that are, due to their very problem formulation, not efficiently estimable. In this work, we identify a computational kernel occurring in estimators of polynomial functions, a class of problems that are in general computationally difficult to solve. We show that this structure allows a row-wise partition that, together with a custom SIMD vectorization, enables massive parallelization and can reduce the computational cost significantly. We show applicability and scalability of the approach on different tasks, and our results showcase that the approach allows high sequential throughput and close-to-ideal parallel scaling. The work thus provides a new way of identifying and exploiting structure in classical shadow estimators, resulting in practical advantages on inherently difficult problems.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 12 pages, 10 figures

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Dynamic Load Balancing for Uncertainty Quantification with Applications in Bayesian Inversion
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) workflows present a particular scheduling challenge in high performance computing environments, as they typically generate large numbers of heterogeneous model evaluations with loose but non-trivial dependencies between tasks. A static one-size-fits-all approach in traditional schedulers is inadequate to handle heterogeneous tasks optimally. We introduce an improved load balancer in the UQ and Modelling Bridge (UM-Bridge) framework aimed at mitigating these issues; UM-Bridge is a language-agnostic interface developed to couple UQ software with numerical simulation. This load balancer is first benchmarked against the previous implementation using a synthetic problem. Then, as a realistic example, we test the load balancer with a Bayesian inverse problem solved via multilevel delayed acceptance sampling. The underlying forward problem is a hierarchy of tsunami simulations enabled through ExaHyPE, whose runtimes span several orders of magnitude and loose dependencies between levels make the workload particularly challenging to schedule. Our results indicate the load balancer distributes the sampling requests effectively with an average idle time of close to a millisecond, a thousand times lower than the previous version, without any prior assumptions about the workload or application.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Memory Profiling and Migration for Heterogeneous Memory Architectures
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Heterogeneous memory systems that combine high-bandwidth memory (HBM) with commodity DRAM can accelerate bandwidth-bound HPC workloads, but current page placement largely depends on manual tuning or OS heuristics not designed for multi-tier dynamics. We present SHAMBLES, a kernel-integrated framework that profiles application memory behavior at low overhead and migrates data across tiers without requiring application changes. SHAMBLES exposes a policy-agnostic interface and a lightweight user-space runtime with pluggable policies (e.g. recency and frequency based) as well as static placement for controlled studies. A logging mode provides reproducible timelines of allocations and migrations to aid analysis. We implement SHAMBLES on a commodity Linux system with HBM and DDR exposed as NUMA nodes and evaluate it with the HPCG, DGEMM benchmarks and Himeno stencil mini-app. Our design and methodology show how transparent, policy-driven migration can respond to changing access locality and concentrate hot data in HBM without developer intervention, offering a practical path to performance portability on tiered memory. Results from HPCG show that we can maintain up to 93.75% of the all-in-HBM baseline performance, while keeping only 40% of the problem size in the HBM. DGEMM experiments show that dynamic policies in SHAMBLES sustain up to 99% of the all-in-HBM performance, while keeping only one third of the DGEMM matrix footprint in HBM. For Himeno, SHAMBLES shows that fast-tier selection must be both workload-aware and size-aware: with a 50% fast-tier budget, it can outperform fixed all-in-HBM and all-in-DDR placements for the L size, while the XL size shifts back toward HBM.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. v2: corrected the reference list (removed an erroneous reference, added and updated others), revised the corresponding discussion in the introduction, related work and future extensions, and added the shambles source code repository link

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: A Generic On-Board AI Processing Chain for Earth Observation: From Application Development to Embedded Deployment and Mission-Level Orchestration
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Earth observation satellites acquire more data than they can downlink. Extracting information on board with artificial intelligence (AI) turns the satellite into a data-reduction stage that downlinks compact products, such as masks or detections, instead of full scenes; deploying it in a mission, however, involves the whole processing chain and not only the neural network. We present a generic on-board AI processing chain along three axes, with wildfire segmentation as the worked example among ship detection and cloud segmentation. (i) The AI model is tuned (spectral-band selection, input normalization), quantized to 8-bit integers (int8) and ported to an AMD Versal VCK190, with its excellent segmentation performance preserved on the board. (ii) A modular tiler-inference-mosaicer workflow, reused unchanged across applications, brings the tile-level model to scene level, turning a full acquisition into a scene-level mask or detection list. (iii) Each step is packaged as a unikernel and orchestrated on board by ORCHIDE, a cloud-native orchestrator. The chain is characterized end to end, from the standalone execution on the target to its execution under orchestration with parallel workflows on a representative test bench. Beyond AI inference on individual tiles, this approach aims at increasing the maturity of on-board AI deployment by addressing a complete processing chain, from the acquired scene to the mission-level execution.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Pangolin: Efficient DAG-based BFT State-Machine Replication with TEE-Accelerated Commitment
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Currently many Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) protocols use directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to let replicas propose blocks of requests in parallel for improved throughput. Yet, the existing DAG-based designs mainly consider the atomic-broadcast layer: They typically do not describe an efficient client interaction layer, their garbage collection is either unspecified or relies on trusted external storage, and the lowest-latency designs rely on timing assumptions that may be violated in geo-distributed deployments. In this paper, we propose the Pangolin protocol: It introduces a novel low-latency DAG-based atomic broadcast layer and completes it into an efficient state-machine replication (SMR) framework. To preserve system throughput, clients issue requests to a single replica and verify replies efficiently via compact execution proofs. Furthermore, Pangolin introduces a new garbage-collection scheme for DAGs which bounds memory usage even under full asynchrony. Pangolin leverages trusted execution environments to tolerate f Byzantine faults with only n >= 2f + 1 replicas and accelerates vertex commitments significantly: Broadcasting certified vertices requires only a single communication step, and commit rules are refined to commit both frequently and early without revealing the coin-elected anchor. This way, Pangolin overtakes the fastest partially synchronous DAG protocols while being live under asynchrony: In our evaluation, Pangolin achieves an average 1.27x (up to 1.52x) latency speedup over Mysticeti.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 28 pages

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Bidirectionality is Necessary in Cellular Machines for Exact-Arrival Multi-Agent Path Finding
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: On ranked directed acyclic graphs coupled by vertex conflicts we study exact-arrival multi-agent path finding (departure and arrival pinned in place and time) posed as a distributed output task: every cell must emit its own bit of a valid joint path-support mask. The machines are cellular: one automaton per cell, state factored over cells, communication only along a fixed local fabric, synchronous rounds, a query-independent output round, no central decoder, and a per-topology transition code. "Necessary" here means: on an explicit hard topology, over all its feasible queries, no universally correct local-only architecture can renounce either temporal orientation; with global flags, impossibility becomes a bandwidth-round trade-off. The class is not vacuous: a flooding machine solves every instance in as many rounds as the diameter of the local fabric. The bound survives two concessions: we supply every agent's exact individual cavity, which alone solves the single-agent problem in zero rounds and makes the single-agent direction theorem vacuous; and we allow $k$ one-bit global aggregate flags. On a twelve-cell, two-agent, depth-three topology no forward-only machine with $k=0$ is correct on two feasible queries, for any number of rounds; the time-reversed topology does the same to backward-only machines. Placing $p$ copies side by side gives, for forward-only machines, $J_R+kR\ge p$ at constant depth, where $J_R$ measures how much of the query reaches the targets' cones and is $0$ here. A backward-only machine solves that family in constant rounds and a flag-streaming one in $\lceil p/k\rceil+O(1)$, so the bound is tight in order; on the composite family neither orientation can be renounced. The finite lemmas of the gadget and the pair-invariance contradictions are checked in Lean 4; the semantic bridge, the cone lemma and the counting are paper proofs. We report no benchmarks.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 33 pages. Ancillary files: Lean 4 development for the finite gadget (theoremA.lean), exhaustive check scripts with frozen expected outputs, reproduction README and clean-run log. Companion paper: "Stability Certifies Validity: Amoeba-Inspired Rule Systems for SAT and Single-Agent Trajectory Constraints, Machine-Checked in Lean 4"

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Bridging In-Situ Visualization to Game Engines: From ParaView Catalyst via ANARI to Unreal Engine
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: In-situ high-performance computing (HPC) simulations produce massive datasets that remain difficult to stream into game engines for interactive visualization. We present an in-situ, disk-free pipeline that couples simulation data to Unreal Engine 5 through ParaView's ANARI rendering API. A modified ANARI-USD device captures Universal Scene Description (USD) scene graphs in memory at the ANARI layer and streams the engine-agnostic USD format through an embedded ZeroMQ broker to visualization clients, where JuSync, middleware with a companion Unreal Engine 5 plugin, parses the geometry as it arrives and routes it to engine rendering components at runtime, producing scenes that are camera-navigable once received. The decoupled design keeps simulation execution independent of visualization load, and clients may connect or disconnect at any time. The pipeline is demonstrated on the JURECA-DC supercomputer at Forschungszentrum Jülich, streaming Free Electron Laser (FEL) simulation data with point clouds of tens of millions of particles.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 10 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at SC26 (Chicago), ISAV Workshop; to appear in IEEE Xplore, DOI pending

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: SIGMA: A Versatile Streaming Graph Partitioner for Vertex- and Edge-Balanced Distributed GNN Training
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Distributed Graph Neural Network (GNN) training depends critically on how the underlying graph is partitioned across compute resources. Existing graph partitioners focus either on vertex partitioning or edge partitioning and typically optimize only a single communication objective (edge cut vertex cut) under a single balance constraint (vertex balance edge balance). We present SIGMA (Streaming Integrated Graph Partitioning with Multi-objective Awareness), a versatile streaming graph partitioner that supports both vertex and edge partitioning within a unified multi-objective, multi-constraint framework. Depending on the target distributed GNN system, SIGMA can be configured for edge-cut-oriented vertex partitioning or vertex-cut-oriented edge partitioning while simultaneously accounting for vertex and edge balancing. A clustering-based preprocessing stage incorporates global graph structure to improve partition quality while preserving the efficiency and scalability advantages of streaming partitioning. We evaluate SIGMA on six benchmark graphs spanning diverse domains and scales using two distributed GNN training systems: DistGNN (edge-partitioned) and DistDGL (vertex-partitioned). Across both settings, SIGMA consistently achieves strong performance, showing its ability to navigate complex trade-offs between partition quality, training efficiency, and memory consumption, frequently outperforming established streaming approaches and delivering competitive results against high-quality in-memory partitioners, with particularly strong results in edge-partitioned GNN training. These results demonstrate that a unified streaming partitioner can effectively address the communication, compute, and memory challenges of distributed GNN training across fundamentally different system architectures.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: GeoTrain: Energy-Aware Automatic Parallelism for Foundation Model Training on Heterogeneous Geo-Distributed Resources
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
Training foundation models at the frontier typically requires large-scale dedicated and centralized clusters with fast interconnects - infrastructure that is prohibitively expensive and generally accessible only to well-resourced organizations. Decentralized training over pooled, geographically distributed GPUs offers an alternative, but introduces substantial heterogeneity in compute, memory, power, and network performance. Existing distributed training systems are primarily designed for clusters with fast, low-latency interconnects and typically use all available GPUs when configuring parallel training. In geo-distributed environments, however, slower devices and weak network links can become bottlenecks, while optimizing solely for throughput overlooks significant energy cost.
  We present GeoTrain, an automatic parallelism system that jointly optimizes training performance and energy consumption for heterogeneous geo-distributed GPU environments. GeoTrain simultaneously selects GPUs, partitions model layers, and determines pipeline configurations while accounting for heterogeneous compute, memory, power, and network constraints. To efficiently explore this large combinatorial search space, GeoTrain employs an optimized memetic algorithm with specialized genetic operators and local search. Experiments with decoder-only Transformer models on real-world and simulated heterogeneous topologies demonstrate that GeoTrain reduces iteration time and energy consumption by up to $61.4\%$ and $11.7\%$, respectively, over the existing state-of-the-art approaches. It also finds the exact optimum on verifiable instances and scales beyond exact methods as the number of GPUs increases, while exposing favorable energy-time trade-offs, including cases where its time-optimal distributed training plan is both faster and more energy-efficient than the baselines.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: CEMA-Router: Infrastructure-Aware Batch Routing for LLM Inference in Cloud-Edge Systems
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Large language models (LLM) are increasingly integrated into pervasive applications spanning heterogeneous cloud-edge resources. These heterogeneous resources differ in computational capacity, energy efficiency, network conditions, and deployed model quality, creating trade-offs among response quality, monetary cost, energy consumption, and batch completion time when routing inference requests. Existing LLM routers typically make per-query routing decisions based primarily on model quality and token cost, whereas cloud-edge schedulers often overlook quality differences among deployed models. Consequently, these objectives remain insufficiently coordinated. We present CEMA-Router, an infrastructure-aware batch router for LLM inference in pervasive cloud-edge systems. CEMA-Router formulates batch routing as a multi-objective search problem that jointly minimizes model-quality loss, monetary cost, energy consumption, and straggler-dominated batch completion time. To efficiently explore the search space, it employs a routing-specific memetic algorithm, combining largest-request-first, load-aware seeding with probabilistic, evaluator-guided Lamarckian repair. Routing decisions are informed by deployment-specific node profiles, dynamic backlog estimates, and model-quality signals. We further implement CEMA-Router as an end-to-end system comprising a request manager, routing service, and profiler, supporting both real cloud-edge deployment and trace-driven simulation. We evaluate the system using RouterBench traces and GSM8K and MMLU workloads on a heterogeneous cloud-edge testbed. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, CEMA-Router reduces the weighted objective by up to 86% for GSM8K and 80% for MMLU, while reducing energy consumption by up to 33% and 19% and batch completion time by up to 27% and 30%, respectively.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Holistic Buoyancy-Driven Cloud Native Resource Management
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Efficient resource management is a challenge in multi-tenant cloud environments as workloads compete for shared resources such as last-level cache and memory bandwidth, whose congestion can change dynamically as workload composition and resource demands evolve. Existing resource management approaches often rely on static resource requirements or prior workload profiling, limiting their ability to respond to changing resource contention as required in the cloud. In this paper, we leverage workload buoyancy, a runtime framework for capturing workload sensitivity to individual resources and application-level performance, to enable adaptive scheduling and resource management. We propose a holistic approach that incorporates buoyancy into workload scheduling, node-local resource allocation, and workload rescheduling throughout the workload lifecycle. We implement our approach as a Kubernetes-native prototype and evaluate it on a multi-node cluster using diverse cloud workloads under varying levels of resource contention. In a high-congestion scenario, our approach increases the percentage of workloads satisfying their SLOs from 7.74% to 87.8% on average compared with the Kubernetes baseline, while reducing resource congestion, the severity of SLO violations, and cluster fragmentation using limited rescheduling.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 12 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Fault-Tolerant Offloading Framework for Real-Time Applications in Mobile Edge Computing
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: This paper studies a Deadline-constrained task Offloading and resource Allocation Problem (DOAP) in a backhaul-network-enabled Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) system with both bandwidth and computational resource constraints. The goal is to maximize the total inference accuracy improvement across all tasks. We formulate this problem, denoted as $\mathbf{P}$, as an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) problem and show it is NP-hard via a reduction from the maximum-weight three-dimensional matching problem. To address $\mathbf{P}$, we develop $\mathtt{FastSA}$, a linear-time $\frac{1}{10}$-approximation algorithm based on the local-ratio technique. To the best of our knowledge, $\mathtt{FastSA}$ provides the first constant-factor performance guarantee for backhaul-network-enabled DOAPs. In addition, we introduce a fault detection and recovery framework that enables robust MEC operation under backhaul link and edge server failures. Experiments using profiled image classification workloads and real-world taxi traces show that $\mathtt{FastSA}$ achieves an average accuracy improvement of $25.6\%$ over benchmark algorithms under fault-free conditions while maintaining the lowest runtime. Under fault-injected scenarios, our framework reduces performance degradation by an average of $12.8\%$, demonstrating its effectiveness in fault handling.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Do We Need Asynchronous SGD? On the Near-Optimality of Synchronous Methods
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Modern distributed optimization methods mostly rely on traditional synchronous approaches, despite substantial recent progress in asynchronous optimization. We revisit Synchronous SGD and its robust variant, called $m$-Synchronous SGD, which can be interpreted as a method with a backup-worker strategy, and theoretically show that they are nearly optimal in many heterogeneous computation and communication scenarios, which is somewhat unexpected. We analyze the synchronous methods under random times and adversarial partial participation of workers, and prove that their time complexities are optimal in many practical regimes, up to logarithmic factors. While synchronous methods are not universal solutions and there exist tasks where asynchronous methods may be necessary, we show theoretically that they are sufficient for many modern heterogeneous computation and communication scenarios.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Bitcoin-IPC: Scaling Bitcoin with a Network of Proof-of-Stake Subnets
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
Despite holding over $1.7T in value, Bitcoin scales poorly: Layer-1 (L1) processes only a few transactions per second, and Layer-2 (L2) solutions suffer from operational and liquidity fragmentation that requires external bridges for cross-chain connectivity.
  We present Bitcoin-IPC, a protocol that horizontally scales Bitcoin via permissionless, interconnected, programmable Proof-of-Stake L2 subnets staked in L1 BTC. Subnets leverage Bitcoin L1 for interconnectivity, settlement, and security, including Sybil protection, equivocating validator slashing, unilateral exit for honest stake, long-range attack protection, and compromised subnet firewalling. Bitcoin-IPC cross-subnet transfers involve only source/destination subnet validators and L1, with no external bridges or per-path liquidity lock-up. Embedded and batched in Bitcoin's witness mechanism, cross-subnet settlements can approach 6 vB per transfer, 23x less than a native L1 payment. Filling Bitcoin blocks with such batches corresponds to L1 monetary throughput of about 273 transfers per second, without modifying Bitcoin.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: PTOPOFL: Topology-Guided Personalised Federated Learning with Persistent-Homology Client Descriptors
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Clustered and personalised federated learning (FL) needs a signal telling the server which clients should share a model. Most methods derive it from losses or model updates that must be recomputed during training. We study pTopoFL, which derives it once, before training, from a compact persistent-homology (PH) descriptor of each client's feature distribution: the server clusters clients on these descriptors, weights them within clusters, and runs blended clustered local gradient descent, returning one personalised model per cluster. For strongly convex, smooth losses we analyse the complete procedure: for any partition, one round is a contraction with factor (1-eta*mu)^tau; the fixed point is characterised by a local-step drift bound, an exact formula for the effective strength of blending (which yields a calibration rule) and a stochastic floor exposing a bias-variance trade-off of clustering; and personalisation lowers the heterogeneity floor in proportion to a measurable share of the dispersion of client optima. Experiments on synthetic federations, a label-skew benchmark and a real four-hospital dataset confirm the theory and delimit the method. When feature geometry and decision rules co-vary, the PH partition recovers the latent client groups, including differences a linear-subspace descriptor misses, and pTopoFL is competitive with the strongest clustered baselines; on the real federation it lowers the test log-loss of FedAvg from 0.463 to 0.438, on par with the best personalised methods. When heterogeneity is invisible in feature geometry, it offers no advantage over FedAvg. pTopoFL transmits model parameters and is no more private than FedAvg; we give a record-level differential-privacy accounting and show that privatising the descriptor destroys the partition. Code reproduces every number.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 32 pages, 6 Figures. Revised version with fine theoretical demonstration on convergence. Also real clinical dataset added

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Revisiting Cauchy-Schwarz Norm Bounds for SDC Detection in LLM Inference
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
Large Language Models (LLMs) execute billions of floating-point operations per output token across many hardware accelerators. At this scale, hardware-induced faults can bypass system-level detection mechanisms and cause Silent Data Corruption (SDC). Algorithm-Based Fault Tolerance (ABFT) is the state-of-the-art technique for protecting matrix multiplication from such faults, but it incurs non-negligible computational overhead and requires thresholds to distinguish hardware-induced errors from floating-point roundoff. In this paper, we revisit Cauchy--Schwarz Norm Bounds (CSNB) as a low-overhead alternative for detecting SDC during LLM inference. We compare CSNB against ABFT through controlled fault injection and evaluate the runtime overhead of both verification and threshold determination across multiple model sizes, batch sizes, and generation lengths.
  Our results show that, on average, CSNB retains 99% of the fault detection capability of ABFT for the evaluated linear layers in dense LLMs, while reducing verification overhead by 87% and threshold determination overhead by 67%. For Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router gate computations, however, CSNB retains only 55% of the fault detection capability of ABFT. These findings suggest that CSNB is a promising low-overhead alternative for protecting linear layers in dense LLMs, while checksum-based verification remains preferable for the evaluated MoE router gate.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: An Event-Driven System Architecture for a 15-Minute Urban Flood Digital Twin: A Hanoi Case Study
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Flash floods in Hanoi submerge roads within minutes of heavy rain onset, yet public flood advisories remain retrospective. Hydrodynamic models could supply forward-looking depth guidance, but they are typically run offline for historical events, and prior studies have not evaluated whether physics-based simulation, spatial serving, and vehicle-aware routing can operate together within a fixed refresh cycle using a cloud solver and a single commodity server. This paper evaluates an end-to-end prototype of an automated flood digital twin designed to meet a 15-minute refresh cycle under data scarcity. The architecture organizes execution into decoupled, event-driven workflows that chain weather-gated 3Di simulations through hydraulic restart states, serve flood depths through a dual-track spatial layer, and publish road-edge depths via standardized output contracts. Evaluated on a 57-run storm replay in the My Dinh and Tay Mo sector of Hanoi driven by satellite rainfall estimates, every cycle completed within the 15-minute deadline, publishing a ready edge table at a median of 537 s after slot start. Indexed raster tiles resolved point-depth lookups in a median of 0.54 ms (277 times faster than un-tiled rasters), while pre-rendered vector tiles served web maps without database queries. These findings demonstrate that a commodity server coupled to a cloud solver can sustain the 15-minute operational cycle and decouple routing policies from simulation internals. Because simulated depths were not validated against field gauges and the replay used observed satellite rainfall, the results establish system feasibility rather than forecast accuracy or route safety.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: 3D-MoE: Complementarity-Guided Hardware-Software Co-Design for MoE Decode on 3D-Stacked NMP
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) have become a mainstream way to scale Large Language Models (LLMs), because each token activates only a small subset of experts, reducing inference cost. However, MoE decode remains highly memory-bound and exhibits strongly skewed, time-varying expert loads. 3D-stacked DRAM near-memory processing (NMP) provides the bandwidth that decode demands, yet its tiled organization makes load balancing expensive: expert parallelism (EP) preserves locality but suffers from hotspot-induced imbalance, while more distributed strategies weaken locality and increase NoC traffic.
  To address this locality-balance conflict, we observe that domain-specialized token routing creates offsetting expert-load fluctuations across decode steps, a property we call expert complementarity. Using this insight, we propose 3D-MoE, a hardware--software co-designed system for MoE decode on 3D-stacked NMP. 3D-MoE uses offline, one-time complementarity-guided grouping and locality-aware mapping to establish coarse-grained inter-group balance, handles residual intra-group hotspots through a lightweight Collaborative Memory-Network (CMN) that streams each hot expert's weight tiles once from its host DRAM channel to helper cores over a reconfigured local broadcast path, and uses cost-aware online remapping to remain robust to workload drift. Across MoE models, 3D-MoE achieves an average 4.63$\times$ MoE-layer speedup over EP and improves end-to-end throughput by 1.58$\times$--1.86$\times$ over the strongest NMP baselines, with 2.11\% additional logic-die area.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: ETH: Data-Balanced Heterogeneous Pipeline Parallelism for Training Large Models
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Current heterogeneity-aware training systems for large models balance workloads by assigning unequal numbers of layers across pipeline stages, a strategy aimed at equalizing execution time through a unique pipeline configuration. However, this approach fails to address critical memory constraints and suffers from inherently coarse balancing granularity. In this paper, we propose Heterogeneous Pipeline Parallelism (HPP), a novel approach enabling efficient and fine-grained data balance across heterogeneous pipelines. To address HPP's key challenges, prohibitive search overhead for optimal configurations and high communication overhead from asymmetric All-Reduce, we design the ETH training system. ETH employs a hierarchical workload balance framework that jointly optimizes balance across heterogeneous pipelines and within individual pipeline stages. To mitigate asymmetric communication costs, ETH implements block-wise gradient aggregation. Furthermore, it integrates specialized optimizations that dramatically reduce HPP configuration search overhead. Evaluations demonstrate ETH achieves up to 2x training speedup while reducing configuration generation overhead by up to 56x compared to state-of-the-art systems. The code is available at https://github.com/YuMJie/ETH.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 19 pages, 14 figures. Accepted at USENIX NSDI 2027

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Peer-Relative Trust-Guided Update Screening for Robust Semi-Decentralized Federated Learning under Label-Flipping Attacks
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Trust and reputation mechanisms can reduce the influence of malicious clients in federated learning (FL), but strict update filtering is difficult under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data because honest local updates may temporarily reduce performance on a shared validation proxy. Building on our earlier trust-based semi-decentralized FL (SDFL) framework, this paper operationalizes the trust signals and introduces peer-relative update screening that combines a robust validation-utility score with direction- and norm-based update quality. The method is evaluated with 50 MNIST clients, 20% persistent label-flip attackers, Dirichlet heterogeneity levels of 0.5 and 0.1, 100 communication rounds, and five paired random seeds. Under moderate heterogeneity, the proposed method reaches 98.37% final accuracy while rejecting 95.82% of malicious updates and retaining 90.30% of benign updates; the final benign and malicious trust distributions are completely separated (KS=1.00). Under severe heterogeneity, it reaches 95.25% accuracy, rejects 88.55% of malicious updates, and retains 76.90% of benign updates (KS=0.96). Trust weighting alone preserves slightly higher utility in the most heterogeneous condition, but accepts all malicious submis-sions. The results therefore distinguish influence mitigation from explicit containment and quantify the utility-selectivity trade-off introduced by screening. The study provides an empirically validated off-chain governance core that can feed blockchain-based audit and incentive layers in SDFL.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 9th International Conference on Blockchain Technology and Applications (ICBTA 2026)

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Mask-Aware Execution for Efficient JEPA Training
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are becoming a core representation-learning primitive and a building block for latent world models across vision, video, audio, brain dynamics, and time series.
