On Gset instances G14, G23, G60, and G64, the sparse model achieves mean refined approximation ratios of $0.9828$, $0.9926$, $0.9781$, and $0.9369$, respectively, with $80.4\%$-$89.3\%$ fewer parameters than the complete Walsh representation. The trained coefficients are transferred without retraining to quantum circuits. Statevector simulations of the four Gset instances achieve fidelities above $0.99994$ and preserve all correlator signs. Separately, a seven-qubit experiment on a $15$-vertex graph executed on IBM quantum hardware achieves a correlator-sign agreement of $0.927\pm0.049$ relative to the corresponding noiseless circuit. These results demonstrate the potential of sparse Walsh-PCE for large-instance quantum-inspired MaxCut optimization while validating the transfer of classically trained parameters to quantum hardware.

Emerging Technologies.title: Gradient-Based Optimization Enables Scalable Fault-Tolerant Quantum Gate Synthesis
Emerging Technologies.summary: We develop a numerical approach to optimizing a quantum circuit over a discrete gate set by using gradient descent to tune $R_Z$ angles to a solution where many $R_Z$ gates can be rounded to a Clifford or $T$ gate without introducing further synthesis error. Through benchmarking, we show that our approach is able to match state-of-the-art techniques for multi-qubit Clifford + $T$ circuit synthesis, and is able to find circuits for unitaries that previous approaches fail to find solutions for. Our approach can adapt to any discrete gate set, which we demonstrate using the Clifford + $T$ + $\sqrt T$ gate set.
Emerging Technologies.comment: 10 pages 3 figures and tables

Graphics.title: Walk in Envelopes: Efficient Branching Walk-on-Spheres via Certified Solution Bounds
Graphics.summary: Branching Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) solves semilinear PDEs without meshes, but its computational cost grows sharply near critical branching rates. We introduce Walk in Envelopes (WiE), which uses certified solution bounds to transform branching diffusion rather than prune existing trees. The transformation suppresses reproduction, introduces controlled termination, and preserves unbiasedness with an envelope-dependent variance bound. We realize the transformed process through exact rejection sampling using standard screened WoS kernels, supported by certified spline envelopes and adaptive sampling, and further prove that suitable harmonic envelopes yield bounded expected reproduction counts even as conventional BBM diverges.

Graphics.title: Balancing Image Compression and Generation with Bootstrapped Tokenization
Graphics.summary: Despite progress in image tokenization, standard methods encode redundant information by mixing all granularities within each token, thus redundancy persists between tokens. The mix of information of different granularity also complicates the training of generators. This paper introduces SelfBootTok, a method that resolves this by cleanly decomposing information into global and local token groups. Through self-bootstrapped learning, the model predicts local details exclusively from global tokens, shifting the burden of visual details from the generator to the tokenizer. Consequently, our generator is far more efficient, requiring only global tokens and reducing computation by approximately 40%, while delivering superior reconstruction and generation. Moreover, this paradigm scales elegantly: by leveraging more data or parameters to self-supervise local representation learning, SelfBootTok achieves a new state-of-the-art gFID score of 1.56 using only 64 tokens.

Graphics.title: OUGS: Active View Selection via Object-aware Uncertainty Estimation in 3DGS
Graphics.summary: Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have achieved state-of-the-art results for novel view synthesis. However, efficiently capturing high-fidelity reconstructions of specific objects within complex scenes remains a significant challenge. A key limitation of existing active reconstruction methods is their reliance on scene-level uncertainty metrics, which are often biased by irrelevant background clutter and lead to inefficient view selection for object-centric tasks. We present OUGS, a novel framework that addresses this challenge with a more principled, physically-grounded uncertainty formulation for 3DGS. Our core innovation is to derive uncertainty directly from the explicit physical parameters of the 3D Gaussian primitives (e.g., position, scale, rotation). By propagating the covariance of these parameters through the rendering Jacobian, we establish a highly interpretable uncertainty model. This foundation allows us to then seamlessly integrate semantic segmentation masks to produce a targeted, object-aware uncertainty score that effectively disentangles the object from its environment. This allows for a more effective active view selection strategy that prioritizes views critical to improving object fidelity. Experimental evaluations on public datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the efficiency of the 3DGS reconstruction process and achieves higher quality for targeted objects compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, while also serving as a robust uncertainty estimator for the global scene.
Graphics.comment: 12 pages. Updated author manuscript corresponding to the Eurographics 2026 / Computer Graphics Forum publication

Graphics.title: CrossTL: Hub-Based Translation of GPU Programs and the Preservation of Source Rules
Graphics.summary: GPU programs are written in vendor languages that disagree about integer overflow, division by zero, NaN handling, floating-point contraction, data layout and dispatch, so a translated program can compile and still compute something else. We describe CrossTL, an open-source translator that routes ten GPU source languages to eleven targets through CrossGL, a textual hub language, with repository-scale porting, contracts that loaders check, and native parity tests. We define faithful translation as refinement up to rejection under a compile configuration, and test whether a hub that records each source rule and lowers it through one per-target table keeps rules that a syntax-only hub loses. On an internally pre-registered suite of 66 hazard kernels in six languages, run on an Apple GPU through Metal, MoltenVK and WebGPU and on CPU implementations of Vulkan, OpenGL and an emulated Direct3D 12, SPIRV-Cross, naga, Tint, Slang and CrossTL each lose some source rule, and outcomes change with Metal's math mode and between two Vulkan implementations. A rule-carrying prototype of the hub removes 34 of 39 divergences on the rules it carries, against 14 for local fixes to four SPIR-V defects, and refuses where WGSL cannot express a rule. The registered hypothesis that it keeps every rule fails: MoltenVK, a non-conformant Vulkan layer, drops a rule that correct SPIR-V carries natively. On 2,585 programs written by third parties, 31% of CrossTL's translations are usable, established translators produce valid output significantly more often in 31 of 39 comparisons, and carrying the rules changes no target's accepted share by more than 0.2 points. Recording each operation's source rule suffices for the rules tested but is not necessary: one strongest rule would keep them too, at about nine times as many rewrites and 58 more refusals on the corpus.
Graphics.comment: 57 pages (30 main text). Replication package in the ancillary files

Graphics.title: PhysLDM: Latent Diffusion for High-Fidelity Deformable Simulation
Graphics.summary: Neural simulation of high-fidelity deformable bodies is a foundational challenge in computer graphics and physical AI. Long-horizon prediction for high-resolution 3D volumetric meshes is hard: autoregressive methods are prone to error accumulation, while direct multi-frame prediction at native resolution is computationally prohibitive. This motivates a compact spatiotemporal latent representation, which is largely unexplored for mesh-based volumetric physics. Meanwhile, it remains unclear whether deterministic regression or generative diffusion is the more suitable predictive paradigm. To address these coupled challenges, we introduce PhysLDM, a unified latent-diffusion paradigm for one-shot deformable simulation. Its core is a holistic spatiotemporal VAE that avoids the "staircase" artifacts of standard temporal compression (e.g., video VAEs), achieving ~2.48 mm reconstruction precision on meter-scale scenes at up to 78x token compression. Based on this reliable latent space, we systematically compare regression and diffusion methods. Our experiments uncover a key modeling insight: complex deformable dynamics are often chaotic, and in this regime deterministic regression tends to produce non-physical averages, whereas diffusion better models their distribution. Accordingly, we employ a latent diffusion model that effectively learns from chaotic data to generate physically plausible trajectories. Trained purely kinematically on an Objaverse-scale dataset, a single PhysLDM generalizes zero-shot to unseen OOD datasets. Its differentiability further enables efficient solution of inverse problems and higher-order design optimization. To our knowledge, PhysLDM is the first high-fidelity spatiotemporal autoencoder and latent-diffusion paradigm for volumetric deformable dynamics, offering a scalable and robust approach to neural simulation. Project Page: https://yucrazing.github.io/physldm/

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Breaking the 1/3 Barrier for Approximate Nash Equilibria in Symmetric Bimatrix Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We give the first unconditional family of polynomial-time algorithms that breaks the $1/3$ approximation barrier for symmetric bimatrix games. For every fixed $δ>0$, an algorithm in this family computes a symmetric $(1-1/\sqrt{2}+δ)$-approximate Nash equilibrium, improving on the previous best guarantee of $(1/3+δ)$ due to Kontogiannis and Spirakis [2011].

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Polynomial Algorithms for Simultaneous Share-Based and Envy-Based Guarantees
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study the simultaneous achievement of share-based and envy-based fairness in the allocation of indivisible goods with nonnegative additive valuations. The AnyPrice share (APS) is a strengthening of the maximin share (MMS). A polynomial-time algorithm is known to guarantee a $2n/(3n-1)$ approximation of APS, but without an accompanying envy-based guarantee. Separately, allocations simultaneously satisfying minimum EFX share (MXS) and envy-freeness up to one less-preferred good (EFL), and subsequently the stronger requirement of residual maximin share (RMMS) together with EFL, have been shown to exist. However, the known constructions do not provide pseudopolynomial-time guarantees.
  We develop algorithms that combine these share-based and envy-based fairness requirements. First, for every $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, we give an algorithm that computes an allocation satisfying exact EFL, $(1-\varepsilon)$-MXS, and $2n/(3n-1)$-APS. Its running time is polynomial in the binary input length and $1/\varepsilon$. Thus, we match the previously established polynomial-time APS approximation while simultaneously guaranteeing exact EFL and an arbitrarily close approximation to MXS.
  Second, we provide a pseudopolynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously guarantees exact MXS, exact EFL, and $2n/(3n-1)$-APS. Third, for every fixed number of agents, we obtain a pseudopolynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously achieves exact RMMS and exact EFL.
  Finally, we establish that computing a numerical threshold between MXS and RMMS is weakly NP-hard, even for additive valuations. This identifies a computational barrier to extending our polynomial-time approach to exact MXS through independently computed residual-valid share thresholds.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Online Fair Division under an Oblivious Adversary
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study online fair division, where indivisible goods arrive one at a time and must be allocated immediately and irrevocably among $n\ge2$ agents. Against an oblivious adversary that fixes the input in advance, we ask what fairness guarantees randomized online algorithms can achieve. We present the Deficit Allocation (DA) algorithm, which improves the previously known high-probability approximation to PROP1 from inverse-logarithmic to inverse-doubly-logarithmic in $n/δ$, where $δ$ is the failure probability. DA does not require $δ$ as input. With probability at least $1-δ$, a refined variant achieves an arbitrarily close approximation to proportionality when no single item is too valuable relative to an agent's proportional share; without any restriction on item values, it obtains an arbitrarily close approximation to PROP$k$ for $k$ doubly logarithmic in $n/δ$. For $n2^{-2n}\leδ\le1/2$, our bounds on the approximation factor and $k$ are asymptotically tight for the stronger fractional benchmark that divides each item equally among the agents who value it positively. We also prove that algorithms that use only which agents value each item positively, but not by how much, cannot improve upon the logarithmic dependence of uniformly random allocation. However, other fairness notions admit weaker guarantees. For EF1, every randomized online algorithm has an input on which any positive approximation succeeds with probability at most $e^{-Ω(n)}$. For EFX, this probability is at most $1/n!$ with only $n+1$ items, tight within a factor of $(n+1)/2$; for MMS, it can be at most $5/6$. Finally, allocating each item uniformly among the agents who value it positively gives, with probability at least $1-δ$, an arbitrarily close approximation to EF$k$ for $k$ logarithmic in $n/δ$, and this dependence is necessary for this rule.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: How Do People Evaluate Non-Ideal Budgets? Evidence from Pairwise Comparisons
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Budget aggregation allows citizens to express their ideal budget allocations, which a predetermined rule combines into a collective allocation. Existing theoretical work on budget-aggregation rules often relies on assumptions about how voters evaluate allocations that differ from their ideals, yet these assumptions have received little empirical validation. We present a framework for testing hypotheses about voters' utility functions through pairwise comparisons. Our modular, open-source polling system elicits participants' ideal allocations and presents carefully generated pairs of non-ideal alternatives. Different pair-generation algorithms enable tests of specific utility models and general preference properties. We conducted over 60 polls, yielding over 3,000 valid participant-poll observations. Our results show that most choices are inconsistent with common utility models, including $\ell_1$, $\ell_2$, and Leontief. Participants also frequently violate sign and issue symmetry, evaluating increases and decreases differently and assigning different importance to deviations across issues. In contrast, more general properties, including star-shapedness, single-peakedness, and peak-linearity, receive greater empirical support. These findings suggest that standard symmetric distance-based models incompletely capture budget-allocation preferences and motivate further evaluation of more flexible utility models for practical budget aggregation.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: MMS Allocation for Chores with Item Disposals
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Web platforms organize collective work, including content review and community maintenance, that imposes heterogeneous effort costs on participants. Fairly distributing these burdens while leaving as few tasks unassigned as possible is a natural objective for the design of such platforms. We study this through the maximin share (MMS) allocation problem with chore disposals under nonnegative additive costs. Our goal is to minimize the number of unassigned chores while guaranteeing every agent her MMS benchmark from the original instance. We prove that, for every instance with $n \ge 4$ agents, at most $n-3$ chore disposals suffice. We improve the bound of $2m/11+n$ disposals established by Barman et al. (2025), where $m$ is the number of chores, and eliminate the dependence on $m$. For four agents, we obtain a tight bound: one disposal always suffices, whereas known instances admit no complete MMS allocation (Ezra and Garbuz, 2026). We also prove the same result for goods: $n-3$ duplications suffice to ensure MMS.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Strategy recovery for Mean-Payoff Games is as hard as solving them from scratch
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Mean-Payoff Games (MPGs) form an interesting family of deterministic, infinite-duration, zero-sum, turn-based games played by two players on a finite weighted directed graph. The goal of the players is to minimize, respectively maximize, the $\textit{limiting average}$ of the costs of the edges on an infinite path constructed by the two players. The complexity of solving MPGs is a long-standing open question. The decision problem associated with these games is known to be in $\text{NP}\cap \text{co-NP}$, and even $\text{UP}\cap \text{co-UP}$, yet the problem is not known to be in $\text{P}$. This is one of the simplest combinatorial problems with such a status.
  A full solution of an MPG gives the $\textit{value}$ of each vertex of the game, along with a pair of $\textit{optimal strategies}$ for the two players. (Each player has a succinct $\textit{positional}$ optimal strategy.) The problem of finding optimal strategies for the players given the values of all vertices is known as the $\textit{strategy recovery}$ problem. We describe a simple reduction from the problem of solving MPGs to the strategy recovery problem for MPGs. This shows that the strategy recovery problem for MPGs is essentially as hard as solving MPGs from scratch, i.e., without knowing the values. The reduction uses simple $\textit{game transformations}$ and simple $\textit{self-reducibility}$ and $\textit{peeling}$ arguments. This answers a question of Andersson and Miltersen. Mamino obtained a similar result for $\textit{stochastic}$ games with a limiting average objective, but his technique does not extend to deterministic games such as MPGs. We go one step further and show that finding an optimal strategy for one of the players of an MPG remains hard even if an optimal strategy of the second player, and hence all the values, are known.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Non-Monetary Mechanisms for Stochastic Scheduling via Sampled Pairwise Externality Compensation
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: How can a shared resource be allocated without money when agents have private, stochastic demands that can be queued for a while, and may behave strategically, or even adversarially? We introduce a paradigm for non-monetary online resource allocation called Sampled Pairwise Externality Compensator (SPEC). Our objective is to guarantee each agent a large fraction of its ideal utility: an individual benchmark corresponding to serving the highest-valued fraction of its demand permitted by an equal share of capacity. We seek guarantees that hold regardless of other agents' behavior, including potentially adversarial and collusive behavior. Our approach builds on the idea of pairwise externality compensation, making it computationally efficient by replacing exact calculations of future externalities with sampled estimates. The central insight is that local mixing, exploited through coupled simulations, allows these estimates to be computed efficiently while preserving robust utility guarantees. In our main technical contribution, we instantiate SPEC in a stochastic scheduling model in which agents receive jobs with private values, unserved jobs persist across periods subject to random expiration, and a single server processes at most one job per period. Our mechanism gives each agent a simple strategy that achieves the optimal worst-case fraction of ideal utility available to a fully informed planner, up to a sublinear additive loss in total utility. We also show that this fraction approaches $1$ in the long-horizon limit as the expiration probability vanishes: sufficiently persistent jobs allow each agent to secure nearly its full ideal utility. The mechanism runs in $O(n^2)$ expected amortized time per period, where $n$ is the number of agents; significantly, the expected amortized computational overhead per period is independent of the time horizon $T$.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Test-Time Compute Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Test-time compute has emerged as a promising strategy to enhance the reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs). However, this strategy has in turn increased how much users pay cloud-based providers offering LLM-as-a-service, since providers charge users for the amount of test-time compute they use to generate an output. In our work, we show that the market of LLM-as-a-service is socially inefficient: providers have a financial incentive to increase the amount of test-time compute, even if this increase contributes little to the quality of the outputs. To address this inefficiency, we introduce a reverse second-price auction mechanism where providers bid their offered price and (expected) quality for the opportunity to serve a user, and users pay proportionally to the marginal value generated by the winning provider relative to the second-highest bidder. To illustrate and complement our theoretical results, we conduct experiments with multiple instruct models from the $\texttt{Llama}$ and $\texttt{Qwen}$ families, as well as reasoning models distilled from $\texttt{DeepSeek-R1}$, on math and science benchmark datasets.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Improved Approximation and Tight Competition for Simple Auctions
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study simple auctions for one additive buyer whose values for $m$ items are independent. Write $\mathrm{REV}$ for optimal revenue, $\mathrm{SREV}$ and $\mathrm{BREV}$ for the revenues from separate selling and grand bundling, and $\mathrm{BSPA}_2$ for grand-bundle second-price revenue with two independent bidders. For independent regular items, we prove $\mathrm{REV}\le\mathrm{BSPA}_2\le2\mathrm{BREV}$. This establishes tight approximation and competition guarantees for bundling under regularity and answers an open question from Beyhaghi et al. (EC 2025). For general independent items, we prove $\mathrm{REV} \le \mathrm{SREV} + \frac{π^2}{6}\mathrm{BREV} \le 2.645 \max\{\mathrm{SREV}, \mathrm{BREV}\}$. This improves the previous approximation factors of $6$ from Babaioff, Immorlica, Lucier, and Weinberg (FOCS 2014, JACM 2020) and $5.2$ from Ma and Simchi-Levi (AISTATS 2021). On the lower bound side, we construct an instance in which prices for three disjoint bundles earn more than $2.11\max\{\mathrm{SREV},\mathrm{BREV}\}$, improving the previous lower bound of $2$ from Rubinstein (ITCS 2016). We also show that exact recovery of one buyer's optimal revenue by the better of separate selling and bundling requires $Θ(\log m)$ bidders in the worst case.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Voice-Based AI Feedback in Higher Education: A Field Study on Quality and Actionability
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Student feedback is a critical input for continuous improvement in higher education, yet traditional end-of-semester written surveys suffer from low response rates, superficial answers, satisficing, and limited actionability. Voice-based conversational AI agents can conduct structured interviews at scale, asking open-ended questions and probing follow-ups, and may capture richer qualitative feedback than written instruments. This research proposal asks what characteristics, depth, and strategic value feedback collected through voice-based conversational AI agents has in higher education, and whether such agents elicit detailed, honest, and actionable feedback that can support instructional improvement and institutional learning. Drawing on survey-mode-effects research, the Computers As Social Actors (CASA) paradigm, and dynamic capabilities theory, we develop three hypotheses on elaboration, social presence and disclosure, and actionability. A completed technical pilot at the Technical University of Munich established the feasibility of telephone-based AI interviews; the main field study is planned for the "Advanced Leadership Communication" course at MIT Sloan with approximately 60 students, using a convergent mixed-methods design and a four-dimensional coding framework for actionability (specificity, thematic richness, constructive orientation, contextual depth). The study extends CASA theory to evaluative educational settings, characterizes voice-based AI as a distinct feedback modality, and links micro-level feedback quality to institutional sensing capabilities.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 9 pages. Research proposal accepted, following double-blind peer review, for presentation at the 46th Annual Conference of the Strategic Management Society (SMS), Berlin, October 17-20, 2026

Human-Computer Interaction.title: AI-Mediated Employee Voice and Performance: Disentangling Informational and Affective Pathways
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Employee voice -- the discretionary expression of ideas, concerns, and suggestions intended to improve organizational functioning -- creates value inside firms, yet organizations increasingly replace or augment human-led listening with AI-enabled systems that collect, analyze, and route employee input at scale. Whether algorithmic listening replicates the value-creation mechanisms of human voice, and whether it alters the pathways through which voice translates into performance, remains an open question. This research proposal theorizes that traditional voice bundles two distinct functions, knowledge extraction and relational signaling, and that AI mediation may decouple them: strengthening the informational pathway (implemented improvement measures) while weakening the affective pathway (the experience of being heard). We propose a randomized field intervention at a global strategy consulting firm, covering approximately 2,000 client-facing consultants, that varies the form of listening across three conditions -- no structured voice, human-led survey-based voice, and AI-enabled conversational voice -- and links weekly team survey data to longitudinal performance ratings. A dual-mediation model is tested in which voice affects performance through (1) implemented process improvements and (2) affective well-being. The study extends voice theory to knowledge-intensive professional services, disentangles the micro-mechanisms of voice, and provides causal evidence on whether AI can serve as an effective listener.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 10 pages, 1 figure. Research proposal accepted, following double-blind peer review, for presentation at the 46th Annual Conference of the Strategic Management Society (SMS), Berlin, October 17-20, 2026

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Figures as Interfaces: Toward LLM-Native Artifacts for Scientific Discovery
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming scientific workflows, not only through their generative capabilities but also through their emerging ability to use tools, reason about data, and coordinate complex analytical tasks. Yet in most human-AI collaborations, the primary outputs, figures, are still treated as static visual summaries: once rendered, they are handled by both humans and multimodal LLMs as images to be re-interpreted from pixels or captions. The emergent capabilities of LLMs open an opportunity to fundamentally rethink this paradigm. In this paper, we introduce the concept of LLM-native figures: data-driven artifacts that are simultaneously human-legible and machine-addressable. Unlike traditional plots, each artifact embeds complete provenance: the data subset, analytical operations and code, and visualization specification used to generate it. As a result, an LLM can "see through" the figure--tracing selections back to their sources, generating code to extend analyses, and orchestrating new visualizations through natural-language instructions or direct manipulation. We implement this concept through a hybrid language-visual interface that integrates LLM agents with a bidirectional mapping between figures and underlying data. Using the science of science domain as a testbed, we demonstrate that LLM-native figures can accelerate discovery, improve reproducibility, and make reasoning transparent across agents and users. More broadly, this work establishes a general framework for embedding provenance, interactivity, and explainability into the artifacts of modern research, redefining the figure not as an end product, but as an interface for discovery. For more details, please refer to the demo video available at www.llm-native-figure.com.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: When Interpretations Persist: Downstream Influence in Gaze-Aware Assistants
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: AI assistants may carry forward not only observations but also interpretations of what a person is doing or may do next across time. Once retained, these interpretations become context for later predictions and system-triggered outputs. We study whether this representation step changes later behavior in gaze-aware streaming assistance. Holding retrieved events, their order, and the target input fixed, we find that Free-form Interpretation amplifies historical influence in both directions: correct histories produce more helpful changes and wrong histories more harmful changes. Unsupported and broader interpretations about activity or future behavior are associated with greater harmful influence. Evidence-Bounded Interpretation preserves distinctions between observation, inference, uncertainty, and temporal scope, reducing unsupported and overcertain content and lowering wrong-source harmful influence while retaining most helpful influence. The same effect structure appears with a second model. These findings identify persistent interpretation as a consequential design choice for history-aware human-AI systems.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 25 pages, including references and appendix

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Simulating Infant Senses with Age-Tuned Networks
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: What a newborn sees, hears and feels, and how this changes month by month, has been measured sense by sense, with different methods and in different units. We bring these measurements together for the first two years of life and ask whether small neural networks tuned to a given age can turn them into a quick, inspectable simulation of sensory perception. Each sense's immaturity is written as a fixed, age-indexed filter on the input, and a small prediction network learns behind it over the first year. The filters alone reproduce the order in which the senses mature, by construction. The networks add what filters cannot: in vision they extract far less than their input allows at early stages (at the newborn stage a toy's position cannot be read out, $R^2 = 0.00$, against 0.57 for a network trained directly on the same input), and a critical period and perceptual narrowing emerge without being built in; in hearing they track what their input allows. The same filters drive the Baby Senses Lab, a free website that shows a user's own images and sounds as a baby of a chosen age might sense them. It is a research and teaching tool, not a diagnostic test.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 21 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Code and website: https://github.com/pikulsomesh/developmental-world-models and https://pikulsomesh.github.io/developmental-world-models/

Human-Computer Interaction.title: UnexpectedParrots: Iterating Behavioral Experiment Design with In-Silico Simulations
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Running behavioral experiments is expensive, slow, and prone to design flaws, often detectable after collecting data. We introduce UnexpectedParrots to iteratively refine behavioral study designs before a researcher recruits costly human participants. UnexpectedParrots relies on reasoning traces in addition to responses from LLM participants to uncover diagnostic critiques of structural errors and missed opportunities in existing study designs. When evaluated against a human-pilot or a no-simulation design-only baseline, UnexpectedParrots adds most value, producing unique, high-quality critiques. In a moderated user study with 12 proficient researchers, we find UnexpectedParrots useful, time-saving, and thought-provoking. Critiques provided by UnexpectedParrots often converge on issues researchers identify only during independent human pilots or additional formative interviews, even when the fidelity of the simulated populations remains questionable. Our users deem UnexpectedParrots useful not only as a tool to conduct early pilot studies and identify errors but also as an ideation tool to expand one's research horizon.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: The Double-Edged Sword of Open-Ended Interaction: How LLM-Driven NPCs Affect Players' Cognitive Load and Gaming Experience
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: This study examines how large language model-driven non-player characters (LLM-NPCs) affect players' cognitive load and gaming experience, with a particular focus on the underlying psychological mechanisms, differences across task scenarios, and the role of individual traits. Conducting a randomized between-subject experiment (N=130) in a self-developed game prototype "Campus Culture Week", we compared player interactions with LLM-NPCs and traditional pre-scripted NPCs across multiple interactive modules. The results showed that the LLM-NPC condition, which combined free-form natural-language input with LLM-generated responses, produced higher cognitive load than preset-option scripted NPC interaction (p < .001), with expressive effort and response uncertainty as significant mediating pathways. However, LLM-NPCs did not yield a statistically significant improvement in overall gaming experience (p = .195); while they positively influenced players' perceived autonomy, they exerted a negative influence on system usability and trust. The effects of LLM-NPCs also significantly varied across task scenarios (p < .001), with stronger increases in cognitive load in more open-ended modules such as content creation and relationship building. The influence of individual differences was generally limited, with no robust associations remaining after correction for multiple comparisons. This study provides empirical evidence for understanding the "double-edged sword" effect of LLM-NPCs on player experience, and highlights the importance of scenario-sensitive and user-sensitive design in intelligent NPC systems.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Under review at IEEE Transactions on Games

Human-Computer Interaction.title: It's Complicated: Factors Influencing the Effectiveness of LLM-Generated Feedback in a Live Programming Course
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: We report on three iterations of an LLM-generated feedback system deployed in a live web development course, spanning three underlying models and three feedback formats. We ask how feedback presence and its characteristics (length, complexity, format) relate to student performance, whether prior feedback exposure is associated with final-project performance, and how performance changes after first exposure. Feedback was associated with more favorable immediate outcomes in several comparisons, but the pattern varied by outcome and period. In pooled models, longer feedback was associated with lower next-submission correctness, more remaining attempts, and longer resubmission time. Prior same-part feedback was associated with lower final-project solve probability. Student-level comparisons found differences on final-project steps begun before exposure, while within-student changes across steps were uncertain. These comparisons do not identify the causal effect of feedback. Changes on standard exercises were more favorable among exposed students, but the groups' different course-stage splits limit causal interpretation. Bounded message length and student choice of format are directions for experimental evaluation. Our final-project analysis captures follow-up performance rather than directly measuring learning or understanding.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: OUGS: Active View Selection via Object-aware Uncertainty Estimation in 3DGS
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have achieved state-of-the-art results for novel view synthesis. However, efficiently capturing high-fidelity reconstructions of specific objects within complex scenes remains a significant challenge. A key limitation of existing active reconstruction methods is their reliance on scene-level uncertainty metrics, which are often biased by irrelevant background clutter and lead to inefficient view selection for object-centric tasks. We present OUGS, a novel framework that addresses this challenge with a more principled, physically-grounded uncertainty formulation for 3DGS. Our core innovation is to derive uncertainty directly from the explicit physical parameters of the 3D Gaussian primitives (e.g., position, scale, rotation). By propagating the covariance of these parameters through the rendering Jacobian, we establish a highly interpretable uncertainty model. This foundation allows us to then seamlessly integrate semantic segmentation masks to produce a targeted, object-aware uncertainty score that effectively disentangles the object from its environment. This allows for a more effective active view selection strategy that prioritizes views critical to improving object fidelity. Experimental evaluations on public datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the efficiency of the 3DGS reconstruction process and achieves higher quality for targeted objects compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, while also serving as a robust uncertainty estimator for the global scene.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 12 pages. Updated author manuscript corresponding to the Eurographics 2026 / Computer Graphics Forum publication

Human-Computer Interaction.title: EditPPT: Structured Execution and Evaluation for Reliable Slide Editing
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Reliable slide editing requires precise modifications to intended objects while preserving the rest of the presentation. We argue that slide editing is a problem of structured, constrained modification rather than open-ended code generation. Despite the complexity of real presentations, editing requests can largely be decomposed into the objects to change, the operations to apply, and the state to preserve. This perspective guides both evaluation and execution. For evaluation, we introduce DeckEdit-Bench, 183 editing tasks on 28 human-authored decks whose target and preserved objects are annotated at the shape level, so that intended and unintended changes are scored mostly by deterministic rules. For execution, we present EditPPT, a multi-agent framework that resolves targets before editing, restricts each specialist to a subset of 37 predefined tools, and validates each edit for instruction fulfillment and preservation, correcting or rolling back failed ones. Across five backbone models, EditPPT reaches 66.7-74.9% Task Success while keeping Preservation above 97%. Even with an open 27B model and no task-specific fine-tuning, it approaches Claude Code with Sonnet 5 in Task Success while better preserving the original deck. These results suggest that constraining how edits are executed, not only model scale, makes slide editing more reliable.

Information Theory.title: On the Information Bottleneck for Stable Variables
Information Theory.summary: We consider a generalization of the Gaussian information bottleneck problem to jointly stable variables $X$ and $Y$. Specifically, for $X = Y + A$, where $A$ is stable and independent of $Y$, we find optimal stable linear encoders of the form $T = kX + N$, with $N$ stable and independent of $X$. We characterize the linear stable information bottleneck in closed-form and its critical value. Furthermore, we show that, except for the Gaussian case, such stochastic linear encoders are strictly suboptimal, while becoming asymptotically optimal at large compression rates. Our linear solution recovers the Gaussian information bottleneck for jointly Gaussian variables as a special case.

Information Theory.title: From Formulation to Articulation: Considerations for AI-Assisted Research in Information Theory
Information Theory.summary: Recent advances in artificial intelligence have contributed to several information-theoretic results through genuinely different modes: a language model may suggest a proof, participate in an extended mathematical dialogue, coordinate computation, or operate as one component of a search harness. Treating all of these as "AI-discovered mathematics" obscures distinctions that matter for scientific reliability, attribution, and reproducibility. This article examines a set of recent cases through a four-stage pipeline: how the problem was formulated; how AI participated in finding a solution; how the resulting analytical and computational claims were verified; and how machine-generated outputs were translated into mathematical exposition for human understanding. Based on these cases, we recommend that research publications (1) disclose the nature and extent of AI assistance at each stage, (2) report verification of analytical reasoning separately from certification of numerical computations, and (3) place more emphasis on articulating the underlying ideas, techniques, and interpretations.

Information Theory.title: Can Quantum Entanglement Increase the Capacity of a Classical Relay Channel?
Information Theory.summary: We show positive and negative results on classical relay channels with entanglement assistance, revealing a sharp contrast between strictly causal and causal relay encoding. First, we consider van der Meulen's setting of a unit-delay relay, with strictly causal encoding. We show that the standard cutset upper bound continues to hold with entanglement assistance, and deduce that entanglement does not increase the capacity for several classes of relay channels. Second, we consider a zero-delay relay, where the encoding is causal. We present an example in which entanglement enables rates that exceed the cutset upper bound by at least 12.5%. Namely, entanglement shared between the source and relay significantly increases the capacity of a classical zero-delay relay channel.

Information Theory.title: Universal Distributed Feature Extraction Complementary to Side Information via H-Score
Information Theory.summary: This paper considers a distributed estimation system where edge nodes transmit averaged features to a center node for parameter estimation. A key challenge arises when the center node possesses auxiliary side information: how to design local extractors that are universally optimal for any downstream task, while avoiding redundancy with the side information. To tackle this problem, we orthogonally decompose the joint function space and demonstrate in the weak-dependence regime that the modal decomposition of the canonical dependence kernel's conditional-additive component yields optimal, task-independent features. We construct a distributed nested H-score to learn this decomposition and show that, under a limited feature budget, the mean-squared error (MSE) gap to the best task-specific features is determined solely by the task's alignment with the discarded, least informative modes, and vanishes to leading order for every square-integrable task once the budget is sufficient.

Information Theory.title: LiftDiff: Guided Discrete Diffusion for Quantum Code Construction
Information Theory.summary: The realization of fault-tolerant quantum computation relies on Quantum Error-Correcting Codes (QECC). Of particular interest are codes that combine a high encoding rate with sufficient distance. Existing algebraic constructions, such as lifted product (LP) codes, build a large quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) code from a classical base matrix. In this work we introduce LiftDiff, a generative approach to the discovery of QECC. A discrete denoising diffusion model is trained to generate base matrices over the group algebra $\mathbb{F}_2[\mathbb{Z}_\ell]$, which are then expanded into LP codes. The reverse diffusion process is guided by an energy function that evaluates quantum code properties, including girth, degree, sparsity and decoding performance, steering the sampler toward matrices that yield LP codes with favorable parameters. Our method discovers codes with parameters such as $[[169,13,11]]$, $[[143,15,9]]$, and $[[260,24,10]]$, including a $[[247,19,14]]$ code that achieves the highest ${kd^2}/{n}$ among the baselines. Moreover, several discovered codes outperform the Gross code across a broad range of the tested physical error rates under both code-capacity and circuit-level noise.

Information Theory.title: Pre-Query Retention with Bounded Bit and Word Retrieval
Information Theory.summary: An agent can retain information before receiving a future question and later retrieve evidence from an archive. Evaluating this arrangement requires accounting for both retained information and the width of each retrieval response. Decision-tree capacity bounds describe individual sets of distinguishable records, but a memory writer must encode every possible record before the query is known. We study fixed-length retention beside an immutable binary archive, with a worst-case limit on raw bit or word reads. We characterize feasible one-bit-read memory cells and construct encoders that partition the complete record space. Supporting pairwise exclusive disjunction and conjunction with one bit read is equivalent to supporting every Boolean query. For multiple reads, we combine explicit encoders with decision-tree counting and an entropy converse. The word-read bounds differ by at most two retained bits when the read budget is at most half the archive length. Under an explicit condition on word width and archive length, raw-word caching attains the exact optimum among all writers. A related condition preserves this optimum under positive average error. Exhaustive checks validate the implementations. In a matched dialogue-agent study, a categorical sufficient statistic preserves source decisions with less storage and lower decoding latency than the universal encoder. A catalogue-specific index reduces private state further and requires additional shared storage. The results characterize how response width and future query structure determine retention requirements.
Information Theory.comment: 24 pages, 4 figures. Complete proofs and experimental details included. Both authors contributed equally

Information Theory.title: Dimension-free comparison inequalities between $f$-divergences for Gaussian location mixtures
Information Theory.summary: We establish dimension-free comparison inequalities between the Kullback-Leibler (KL) and $χ^2$-divergences and the squared Hellinger distance for Gaussian location mixtures with compactly supported mixing distributions. We show that both divergences are bounded by the squared Hellinger distance up to constants depending only on the radius of the support, independently of the ambient dimension and the number of mixture components. These results resolve an open question raised by \cite{jia2023entropic} and strengthen existing comparison inequalities. Our proof relies on a Gaussian interpolation argument that relates the derivatives of these divergences to differences between posterior means.

Information Theory.title: A Self-Coupling Gaussian Extremal Inequality for Information-Constrained Optimal Transport with Applications to Rate-Distortion-Perception
Information Theory.summary: How much mutual information is needed to achieve a target correlation between two copies of a prescribed distribution? We prove a sharp Gaussian extremal inequality for this self-coupling problem: among distributions with a fixed mean and covariance, the Gaussian has the greatest minimum information cost for meeting a positive semidefinite cross-covariance target. The inequality is strict for non-Gaussian distributions when the target is positive definite. The proof uses a midpoint gluing construction. Two Ornstein--Uhlenbeck half-bridges, each started from the prescribed endpoint law, meet at a common intermediate distribution and are joined by conditional gluing. Changing the Gaussian reference then turns the resulting relative-entropy bound into the desired extremal inequality. As a first application, scaling one endpoint of the self-coupling establishes Gaussian extremality for rate-distortion-perception with unlimited common randomness, under quadratic distortion and squared Wasserstein-2 perception measures. We also establish an analogous result for finite common randomness, where the problem involves two mutual information constraints associated with an auxiliary random variable. In that setting, we retain an intermediate observation on one half-bridge and balance the two information budgets simultaneously using the Poincaré-Miranda theorem.
Information Theory.comment: 31 pages. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Information Theory

Information Theory.title: Convergence of Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models: A Rényi Divergence Perspective
Information Theory.summary: Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) have emerged as a powerful framework for generative modeling by transforming standard Gaussian inputs into outputs that approximate a target distribution. While DDPMs have been proved to converge in total variation, KL divergence, and Wasserstein distance, these discrepancy measures share a fundamental limitation of being insensitive to distributional mismatch in low-probability regions. To address this, we adopt the stronger Rényi divergence as the discrepancy measure. Leveraging a Girsanov-type change-of-measure argument, we establish the first Rényi characterization of DDPMs to the best of our knowledge, showing that the total error decomposes into a mixing error, a discretization error, and a score estimation error. We assume the target distribution is sub-Gaussian and characterize the score error via the cumulant generating function, relaxing both the log-Sobolev-inequality and $L^\infty$-score-error conditions used in prior Rényi divergence analyses of inexact Langevin Monte Carlo, a score-based sampling algorithm closely related to DDPM. Our results also establish an iteration complexity for achieving $ε$-accuracy in $α$-Rényi divergence that is asymptotically proportional to $α^3/ε$. Finally, by extending our analysis, we establish the first Rényi divergence convergence guarantee for critically damped DDPMs, a kinetic variant governed by critically damped Langevin dynamics. Similar to existing characterizations of critically damped DDPMs, this result shares the structural scaling of standard DDPMs, differing by at most a logarithmic factor in the mixing error exponent, and supports the conjecture that critically damped DDPMs do not yield a theoretical improvement.

Information Theory.title: Polynomially larger deletion codes by linear hashing of substring counts
Information Theory.summary: We reduce the leading redundancy coefficient for binary codes correcting any fixed number $t\ge2$ of deletions from $2t$ to $2t-1$. This is the first improvement to that coefficient since Levenshtein's 1965 bound. More generally, over every fixed alphabet of size $q\ge2$, codes of length $n$ correcting any combination of at most $t$ insertions, deletions and substitutions exist with redundancy $(2t-1)\log_q n+O_t(\log_q\log_q n)$. For two deletions, the upper-bound coefficient drops from $4$ to $3$, halving the gap to the lower-bound coefficient $2$. The leading coefficient $2t-1$ also holds for $t$ bounded substring edits, where both the removed and inserted strings have bounded length. The proof combines random binary linear hashing of substring counts with a two-colouring argument. A linear dependence among differences of substring-count vectors forces their local changes to overlap, and this overlap lowers the redundancy coefficient from $2t$ to $2t-1$. The result provides an edit-distance analogue of Varshamov's 1957 bound in the Hamming metric, both in the leading redundancy coefficient and in the role of linear independence in the proof.
Information Theory.comment: Extended to arbitrary fixed alphabets, mixed edits, and bounded substring edits; simplified proof using binary linear hashing

Logic in Computer Science.title: Neutrosophic Graph Rewriting as a Computational Model
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Graphs, which are made up of points connected by lines, are used to represent relationships between objects. They are useful for solving problems in computer science, logistics, biology, and other fields, including social networks and the internet. Neutrosophic graphs are graphs whose points and lines are characterized by membership, indeterminacy, and non-membership degrees. In the simplest case, only lines are characterized by these degrees. The process by which we transform one graph to another is called graph rewriting. It has been shown that graph rewriting can be described mathematically by pushouts, which are category-theoretic structures. It has also been shown that fuzzy graphs have this property, and here we prove that neutrosophic graph rewriting can be described by pushouts in a certain category. By providing a fuzzy version of category theory, it is possible to define fuzzy categorical structures and thus to define neutrosophic graph rewriting in a more suitable manner. Since graph rewriting is actually a model of computation, neutrosophic graphs are a neutrosophic model of computation. A hypergraph is a generalization of a conventional graph. It allows a single "hyperline" to connect many points, which is different from regular graph lines that only connect two points. Neutrosophic hypergraphs can be used to reformulate Wolfram's models, which are supposed to be a mathematical model of reality.

Logic in Computer Science.title: A Common Ancestor of PDL, Conjunctive Queries, and Unary Negation First-order Logic
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
We introduce and study UCPDL+, a family of expressive logics rooted in Propositional Dynamic Logic (PDL) with converse (CPDL) and universal modality (UCPDL). In terms of expressive power, UCPDL+ strictly contains PDL extended with intersection and converse (a.k.a. ICPDL), as well as Conjunctive Queries (CQ), Conjunctive Regular Path Queries (CRPQ), or some known extensions thereof (Regular Queries and CQPDL). Further, it is equivalent to the extension of the unary-negation fragment of first-order logic (UNFO) with unary transitive closure, denoted by UNTC, which in turn strictly contains a previously studied extension of UNFO with regular expressions known as UNFO$^{reg}$.

We investigate the expressive power, indistinguishability via bisimulations, satisfiability, and model checking for UCPDL+ and CPDL+. We argue that natural subclasses of CPDL+ can be defined in terms of the tree-width of the underlying graphs of the formulas. We show that the class of CPDL+ formulas of tree-width 2 is equivalent to ICPDL, and that it also coincides with CPDL+ formulas of tree-width 1. However, beyond tree-width 2, incrementing the tree-width strictly increases the expressive power. We characterize the expressive power for every class of fixed tree-width formulas in terms of a bisimulation game with pebbles. Based on this characterization, we show that CPDL+ has a tree-like model property. We prove that the satisfiability problem for UCPDL+ is decidable in 2ExpTime, coinciding with the complexity of ICPDL. As a consequence, the satisfiability problem for UNTC is shown to be 2ExpTime-complete as well. We also exhibit classes for which satisfiability is reduced to ExpTime.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Studying proof data with proof theory: the case of AI-generated mathematics
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
I present a method for analyzing large collections of formally verified mathematical proofs (e.g. OpenAI's) grounded in
  some historical and philosophical musings on mathematics in the age of AI. Many of the quantities involved, such as
  the size of a proof term or the number of redundant steps, are already computed by work on improving
  automated provers, where they serve as targets. My aim is to turn them into measurements of proofs themselves:
  compared against a reference library and against each proof's own cut-free form, checked against theorems they
  must obey, and controlled for how the proofs were compiled. With these instruments, I measure how (much)
  machine-generated mathematics diverges from human mathematics, and find that AI-written formal proofs realize far less of the logical
  compression available to them than human mathematicians do (31% against 73% in mathlib, and 55% against 86%
  on proofs that call no automation). These figures are broadly in line with reports from those who build provers and
  proof-improvement tools that AI-written proofs are often longer than they need to be.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Taming Cyclic Dependencies in Stabilization-Based String Constraint Solving
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Word equations with cyclic variable dependencies pose a challenge to SMT string solvers. In stabilization-based procedures, such dependencies can trigger repeated refinement of regular-language assignments without reaching stability. We present Z3-Noodler-C, an extension of Z3-Noodler, combining equality-aware stabilization with dedicated loop reasoning. We introduce equality predicates to retain relevant equations as single stability obligations, and extend stabilization with equality-aware substitution and adapted concatenation-eliminating refinement to expose cyclic dependencies as overlapping variable bindings. Dedicated loop reasoning rules then exploit the periodic structure of these bindings, avoiding certain infinite derivations. We evaluate Z3-Noodler-C against Z3-Noodler, cvc5 and OSTRICH2. On 64 systematically generated, syntactically simple instances involving cyclic dependencies and regular constraints, our solver solves all instances, compared with only 20 solved for the best baseline. On equation-oriented instances from SMT-LIB'25, Z3-Noodler-C achieves the highest coverage, solving 20 more instances than Z3-Noodler while maintaining competitive aggregate CPU time.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Learning Rational Strategies for Temporal Objectives in Multi-Agent Systems
Logic in Computer Science.summary: We study rational synthesis for stochastic multi-agent systems with unknown dynamics, where each agent is equipped with its own probabilistic temporal objective specified using Probabilistic Linear Temporal Logic on Finite Traces ($\mathsf{PLTL}_f}$). We impose solution concepts (e.g., Nash equilibrium, subgame-perfect equilibrium) as constraints on the joint strategy profile, using payoffs derived from each agent's probability of satisfying its temporal objective. In particular, we formulate per-agent rational synthesis as finding a strategy profile -- if one exists -- such that (i) the designated agent's probabilistic temporal constraint is satisfied, and (ii) the profile represents a stable solution under a chosen solution concept. We give conditional convergence guarantees for tabular Nash-Q learning, certify satisfaction with simultaneous finite-sample confidence bounds, and assess strategic stability with approximate best-response checking. Our approach operates in a stochastic \emph{Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning} (MARL) environment, where model-free learning algorithms attempt to attain extremal satisfaction probabilities for temporal objectives automatically compiled into reward automata. Our approach is empirically validated using 8 general-sum concurrent stochastic games.

Logic in Computer Science.title: A sound pure type system with ranks as sorts and Type-in-Type
Logic in Computer Science.summary: We present a dependently typed pure type system that contains a circular axiom $s : s$ for a certain sort $s$ and is nonetheless strongly normalizing. Girard's paradox is avoided because our sorts are not closed under a $Π$-former: function types are placed in sorts according to their rank. Turns out that this system has a unique set of characteristics: it has similar normalization behaviour as STLC (so complexity of normalization is TOWER-complete) while at the same time allowing non-uniform representation of arbitrary elementary recursive functions; furthermore, it has a nontrivial set-theoretical model in ZF+GCH and allows to carry out nontrivial proof developments. Base normalization proof is surprisingly simple (modulo general metatheoretical properties of pure type systems) and has been fully formalized in vanilla Rocq (formerly Coq) without additional axioms.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 28 pages, 3 figures, supplementary material to be found at http://github.com/TurtlePU/pts-rk

Multiagent Systems.title: Belief Coevolution in a Social Network of Generalist and Specialist Large Language Models: A Controlled Study
Multiagent Systems.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent environments. However, the processes by which beliefs form and propagate among interacting LLMs remain poorly understood. We introduce CoevolveSim, a framework for studying belief diffusion within networked LLM populations. CoevolveSim allows us to isolate and study three factors: domain specialization, social-role assignment, and social network structure. Within this framework, generalist and specialist LLM agents exchange and revise beliefs. In each round, an LLM agent observes a summary of its neighbors' beliefs before updating its own. We find that persona-style role assignment reshapes individual belief revision but has little effect on population-level consensus. In contrast, introducing finetuned specialist LLMs produces a large change in consensus and is accompanied by persistent asymmetries in outgoing influence. We further show that an opinion-dynamics surrogate combining individual persistence with population-level belief composition reproduces consensus with high fidelity in every scenario, whereas predicting individual final-round beliefs in heterogeneous LLM populations additionally benefits from agent identity.
Multiagent Systems.comment: 37 pages (9 pages of main text), 8 figures, 18 tables

Multiagent Systems.title: Reward and Behavioral Measures of LLM Coordination in Dining Philosophers
Multiagent Systems.summary: Does high reward indicate productive coordination among language-model agents sharing resources? We examine this question in dining philosophers, where instances of the same model must acquire shared forks to eat. We evaluate seven model conditions across 630 episodes at five, ten, and fifteen philosophers, measuring scalar reward, deadlock, and meal throughput. At five philosophers, Mistral-Small 24B receives mean reward 0.827 while producing no meals. The reward decomposition explains this mismatch: avoiding deadlock earns a bonus without requiring meal production. To assess a policy trained with this reward, we compare the final checkpoint from a single Qwen3-14B group relative policy optimization (GRPO) training run with its base model. At five philosophers, the trained model has lower throughput (0.008 versus 0.020) and a higher deadlock rate in point estimates. Differences in mean episode reward are not statistically significant at any evaluated philosopher count. These findings show that the evaluated reward can assign high scores without task progress and support reporting behavioral measures alongside reward when comparing models and evaluating fine-tuned policies.

Multiagent Systems.title: Large Language Models over Networks: Collaborative Intelligence under Resource Constraints
Multiagent Systems.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming society, powering applications from smartphone assistants to autonomous driving. Yet cloud-based LLM services alone cannot serve a growing class of applications, including those operating under intermittent connectivity, sub-second latency budgets, data-residency constraints, or sustained high-volume inference. On-device deployment is in turn constrained by limited computation and memory. No single endpoint can deliver high-quality service across this spectrum. This article focuses on collaborative intelligence, a paradigm in which multiple independent LLMs distributed across device and cloud endpoints collaborate at the task level through natural language or structured messages. Such collaboration strives for superior response quality under heterogeneous resource constraints spanning computation, memory, communication, and cost across network tiers. We present collaborative inference along two complementary and composable dimensions: vertical device-cloud collaboration and horizontal multi-agent collaboration, which can be combined into hybrid topologies in practice. We then examine learning to collaborate, addressing the training of routing policies and the development of cooperative capabilities among LLMs. Finally, we identify open research challenges including scaling under resource heterogeneity and trustworthy collaborative intelligence.

Multiagent Systems.title: Can Trustless Agents Be Trusted? An Empirical Study of the ERC-8004 Decentralized AI Agent Ecosystem
Multiagent Systems.summary:
As autonomous AI agents increasingly transact across organizational boundaries, a fundamental trust challenge emerges: how can an agent assess whether an unknown counterpart is trustworthy? The ERC-8004 protocol addresses this challenge with the first permissionless trust layer for AI agent economies, built around three on-chain registries for Identity, Reputation, and Validation. Despite its rapid adoption, the protocol has not been studied empirically, leaving it unclear whether the information it records provides a trustworthy basis for decision-making. To address this gap, we present the first empirical study of ERC-8004 across three chains: Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain (BSC), and Base, covering the period from protocol deployment through May 13, 2026. We crawl on-chain Identity and Reputation events, off-chain files, and x402 payment transactions.
  On the identity side, we find that most registrations are placeholders rather than active agents, with only a small fraction (3%, 4%, and 15% across Ethereum, BSC, and Base) exposing a valid ERC-8004 registration file with at least one live service endpoint. On the reputation side, we show that the Registry, as currently deployed, cannot function as a trust signal: values are not commensurable, feedback records are rarely grounded in verifiable interactions, and reputation can be manipulated at minimal cost. Consistent with these design weaknesses, we find that a substantial fraction of reviewers (73.5%, 59.2%, and 90.6% across Ethereum, BSC, and Base) exhibit coordinated Sybil behavior. After removing Sybil-flagged feedback, 15.8%, 77.9%, and 86.8% of rated agents, respectively, are left with no valid feedback. We then turn these findings into concrete recommendations for future revisions of ERC-8004. Our study yields actionable protocol-design implications and establishes an empirical baseline for research on AI agent markets.

Multiagent Systems.title: Learning Rational Strategies for Temporal Objectives in Multi-Agent Systems
Multiagent Systems.summary: We study rational synthesis for stochastic multi-agent systems with unknown dynamics, where each agent is equipped with its own probabilistic temporal objective specified using Probabilistic Linear Temporal Logic on Finite Traces ($\mathsf{PLTL}_f}$). We impose solution concepts (e.g., Nash equilibrium, subgame-perfect equilibrium) as constraints on the joint strategy profile, using payoffs derived from each agent's probability of satisfying its temporal objective. In particular, we formulate per-agent rational synthesis as finding a strategy profile -- if one exists -- such that (i) the designated agent's probabilistic temporal constraint is satisfied, and (ii) the profile represents a stable solution under a chosen solution concept. We give conditional convergence guarantees for tabular Nash-Q learning, certify satisfaction with simultaneous finite-sample confidence bounds, and assess strategic stability with approximate best-response checking. Our approach operates in a stochastic \emph{Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning} (MARL) environment, where model-free learning algorithms attempt to attain extremal satisfaction probabilities for temporal objectives automatically compiled into reward automata. Our approach is empirically validated using 8 general-sum concurrent stochastic games.

Multiagent Systems.title: Explore or Confirm? LLM Agents Misallocate Measurements Under Noise
Multiagent Systems.summary: As model reasoning gets cheaper, the physical experiment becomes the slow and costly step in discovery. Each experiment returns a noisy reading: a high value can mean a good candidate or a lucky draw. With a fixed budget, an AI agent must keep choosing between exploring a new candidate and confirming a promising one by re-testing it. We measure that choice in Wellocate, a simulated assay campaign with known true values. It is built on a generated landscape and on two real protein datasets, GB1 and PhoQ, scrambled so no model can answer from memory. We test five language models as minimal agents, with no tools and no memory beyond the history in each prompt. They misallocate in both directions. Three over-confirm, spending most of the budget re-testing. On the generated landscape one under-confirms, trusting single readings, and there every model ends with a worse final pick than a basic scripted strategy. Each failure has its own cause. The over-confirmers run short of new candidates worth trying: a list of untried candidates cuts their re-testing and, on real protein data, makes two of them pick much better. A running summary of their readings or a description of the landscape changes it by at most five percentage points. For the under-confirmer, re-testing its top candidates in a final round, replayed on its own campaigns, recovers only about a quarter of what it loses by picking the wrong candidate. This suggests confirmation has to run through the whole campaign. We release Wellocate as a benchmark and reinforcement-learning environment with frozen splits and scripted baselines. With it, anyone can measure how an agent splits its budget before trusting it with real experiments, and train agents to split it better. Code, data and the environment are available at https://github.com/Xstendyl/wellocate.
Multiagent Systems.comment: 38 pages, 12 figures. Code, data and environment: https://github.com/Xstendyl/wellocate

Multiagent Systems.title: Scam Town: Can Scam Education Spread Like a Vaccine?
Multiagent Systems.summary: Most older adults who hear a warning about scams hear it from someone they know: a relative, a neighbour, or a friend who was targeted. Yet research on scam prevention almost always studies one person at a time. We ask whether scam awareness can spread through a community and protect it the way a vaccine does, since a warning protects whoever hears it and can be passed on. To find out, we built Scam Town, a simulated community in which a large language model plays each resident. Scam centres phone the residents, and after a call a resident can warn the people they know. Word of mouth helped, but it did not take off on its own: each warning led to fewer than one more, so a community cannot count on warnings "going viral". Across 80 simulated towns, everyday talk cut the number of people scammed by roughly a fifth. The largest gains came when an official warning, from a bank, a senior centre, or an agency, reached most of a town and residents then talked about it: in simulation (a combination we did not test live) the two together cut scams by about half. Protection was greatest when warnings reached the people scammers actually call, who here were older residents. Because our residents are language-model stand-ins rather than real people, we treat these findings as predictions to test with people, not as proof. They point to a simple recipe for scam education: give people a clear story they can retell, design campaigns to be passed along, and reach first those most likely to be called.

Multiagent Systems.title: KernelClaw: A Multi-Agent Framework for GPU Kernel Optimization with Dual-Memory Mechanisms
Multiagent Systems.summary: Improving GPU kernel efficiency is crucial for efficient AI systems. Recent work has explored leveraging large language models (LLMs) for GPU kernel generation and optimization. However, existing LLM-based kernel optimization pipelines typically rely on opaque, implicitly learned heuristics within the LLMs to determine optimization strategies. This leads to inefficient trial-and-error and weakly interpretable optimizations. Our key insight is to replace implicit heuristics with expert optimization knowledge that is aware of task trajectories. Specifically, we present KernelClaw, a multi-agent framework with a dual-level memory architecture. KernelClaw operates by coordinating agents with long-term memory of reusable expert knowledge and short-term memory to prevent repetitive backtracking. On KernelBench Levels 1-3, KernelClaw achieves a 100% success rate and average speedups of 6.98x, 7.89x, and 1.94x over Torch Eager on Levels 1, 2, and 3, respectively, outperforming prior baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/0satan0/KernelMem/.

Multiagent Systems.title: Open-Ended Video Game Glitch Detection with Agentic Reasoning and Temporal Grounding
Multiagent Systems.summary: Open-ended video game glitch detection aims to identify glitches in gameplay videos, describe them in natural language, and localize when they occur. Unlike conventional game glitch understanding tasks which have largely been framed as image-level recognition or closed-form question answering, this task requires reasoning about game-specific dynamics such as mechanics, physics, rendering, animation, and expected state transitions directly over continuous gameplay videos and distinguishing true glitches from unusual but valid in-game events. To support this task, we introduce VideoGlitchBench, the first benchmark for open-ended video game glitch detection with temporal localization. VideoGlitchBench contains 5,238 gameplay videos from 120 games, each annotated with detailed glitch descriptions and precise temporal spans, enabling unified evaluation of semantic understanding and temporal grounding. We further propose GliDe, an agentic framework with three key components: a game-aware contextual memory for informed reasoning, a debate-based reflector for multi-perspective glitch detection and verification, and an event-level grounding module that recovers complete glitch intervals from fragmented temporal evidence. We also design a task-specific evaluation protocol that jointly measures semantic fidelity and temporal accuracy. Experiments show that this task remains highly challenging for current multimodal models, while GliDe achieves substantially stronger performance than corresponding vanilla model baselines.

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: Let Them Sleep: Recursive Self-Pruning Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Agents that run for a long time have a memory problem, and it is not the one most systems optimize for. Storing every trace and retrieving the nearest neighbors works early and quietly stops working later: the store fills up with failures the agent then repeats, and with facts that were true fifty turns ago. RSPM (Recursive Self-Pruning Memory) borrows the fix biology already found. At intervals the agent sleeps. It clusters its recent failures, distills each cluster into a short rule, and deletes the raw episodes it just learned from. Rules decay unless something reinforces them, and rules that recur across many contexts get promoted into general ones. We tested this on three settings with little in common: a difficulty-calibrated SWE-bench simulation, temporal consistency across 12 conversational benchmarks, and long-horizon QA on LoCoMo-10. All three improve, by 9.1, 11.9, and 7.6 points respectively. More interestingly, the two studies that instrument the store itself converge on nearly the same operating point without being tuned toward it: roughly 93% fewer retry loops and roughly 30% fewer stored entries. That hints that knowing what to forget is a general property of agent memory rather than a benchmark-specific trick.
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.comment: Baylearn2026 paper accepted for Oral Presentation

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: A Unified Physics-Informed Neural Network for Modeling Coupled Electro- and Elastodynamic Wave Propagation Using Three-Stage Loss Optimization
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks present a novel approach in SciML that integrates physical laws in the form of partial differential equations directly into the NN through soft constraints in the loss function. This work studies the application of PINNs to solve a one dimensional coupled electro-elastodynamic system modeling linear piezoelectricity in stress-charge form, governed by elastodynamic and electrodynamic equations. Our simulation employs a feedforward architecture, mapping space-time coordinates to mechanical displacement and electric potential. Our PINN model achieved global relative L2 errors of 2.34 and 4.87 percent for displacement and electric potential respectively. The results validate PINNs as effective mesh free solvers for coupled time-dependent PDE systems, though challenges remain regarding error accumulation and stiffness in coupled eigenvalue systems.
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.comment: We are withdrawing this preprint due to critical flaws discovered in the underlying simulation code that compromise the final conclusions leading to gravely misleading implications for future work.

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: Small-scale neural simulation of Caenorhabditis elegans on Loihi-2 using NeuroML2Loihi
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Neural simulation is an essential methodology for studying biological nervous systems, but it remains limited by the computational costs of repeatedly updating neural and synaptic states over many timesteps. Neuromorphic hardware is a promising substrate for this class of workloads because such devices combine event-driven execution, localized memory, and spike-based communication. However, neuromorphic \textit{software} remains comparatively fragmented and difficult to integrate with the model-description standards used by the computational neuroscience community.
