Built on a pretrained motion prior, the policy uses task and phase dependent observation masks to select information relevant to the current interaction goals. We introduce a goal-conditioned loco-manipulation curriculum that combines partial reference guidance for precision with exploration from varied initial states while allowing goal-directed execution beyond the demonstrated trajectories. We further introduce a cross-task curriculum that jointly trains individual skills and selected task sequences, preserving physical states across task boundaries and maintaining grasps during subsequent scene interactions. Together, these support sequential task execution and simultaneous scene interaction with object manipulation. We evaluate sitting, standing, climbing, stair traversal, and goal-directed manipulation, together with sequential execution and with random different conditions. Additionally, we demonstrate skill compositions in indoor environments, illustrating their integration within the same control formulation.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Auctions Meet Bandits: An Empirical Analysis
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Sponsored search positions are typically allocated through real-time auctions, where the outcomes depend on advertisers' quality-adjusted bids - the product of their bids and quality scores. Although quality scoring helps promote ads with higher conversion outcomes, setting these scores for new advertisers in any given market is challenging, leading to the cold-start problem. To address this, platforms incorporate multi-armed bandit algorithms in auctions to balance exploration and exploitation. However, little is known about the optimal exploration strategies in such auction environments. We utilize data from a leading Asian mobile app store that places sponsored ads for keywords. The platform employs a Thompson Sampling algorithm within a second-price auction to learn quality scores and allocate a single sponsored position for each keyword. We empirically quantify the gains from optimizing exploration under this combined auction-bandit model and show that this problem differs substantially from the canonical bandit problem. Drawing on these empirical insights, we propose a customized exploration strategy in which the platform adjusts the exploration levels for each keyword according to its characteristics. We derive the Pareto frontier for revenue and efficiency and provide actionable policies, demonstrating substantial gains for the platform on both metrics when using a tailored exploration approach.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Learning Market Competition in Shared Spectrum: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: This paper investigates market competition among wireless service providers (SPs) that serve customers using shared spectrum. Prior work has analyzed such markets through models of competition with congestible resources, capturing both the congestion-sensitive nature of wireless spectrum and the effects of spectrum sharing on service quality. These models typically assume that the market demand function is known, enabling SPs to optimize pricing or quantity decisions under either Bertrand or Cournot competition. In contrast, we consider a setting in which the demand function is initially unknown and must be learned over time. We model this learning process using multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), allowing competing SPs to learn market dynamics while adapting their competitive strategies. Although MARL has shown strong performance in a variety of economic settings, recent work has demonstrated that it can also give rise to tacit collusion among self-interested agents. We therefore examine whether similar collusive behavior emerges in shared-spectrum markets and how its prevalence depends on the mode of competition (price versus quantity) and the choice of MARL algorithm. Our results provide insight into the interaction between learning dynamics, market structure, and spectrum sharing, with implications for both wireless market design and the deployment of learning-enabled decision-making systems.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Cooperation Without Shared Rewards via Reciprocal Q-Augmentation
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: General-sum games are more challenging than fully cooperative or adversarial settings because agents may deceive or exploit one another. Achieving high social welfare requires sustained cooperation, while a single defection can drive agents toward a welfare suboptimal Nash equilibrium. Moreover, assuming access to other agents' rewards or internal states is often unrealistic and implicitly introduces additional cooperation into the setting. To address this issue, we introduce \textit{Reciprocal Q-Augmentation} (RQA), a method that uses a latent-variable opponent model to augment the Q-function with estimates of how one's actions affects other agents. RQA allows agents to learn both cooperative and defective policies using only their own Q-function. We show that, in social dilemmas, agents that all follow the cooperative policy of RQA learn to cooperate faster and reach higher levels of cooperation than fully cooperative algorithms. Moreover, a single RQA agent that switches appropriately between its cooperative and defecting policies can induce cooperation in agents trained with standard RL algorithms, which would otherwise end up defecting. We evaluate our approach on the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma, Iterated Traveler's Dilemma, Iterated Stag Hunt, and \texttt{CleanUp-Lite}. Our experiments show that the algorithms implementing RQA outperforms fully cooperative methods with shared rewards and enables cooperation with algorithms that otherwise fail to reach high social welfare.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Strategic Origins of Network Structure
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: The structure and dynamics of complex networks are intimately linked. Despite immense progress in statistically characterizing these systems, a generalized mechanistic framework explaining why specific mesoscale structures emerge remains elusive. Here we introduce the game-graph equilibrium, the stable rest point of a payoff-driven partner-choice dynamic, analogous to a Nash equilibrium. This reveals network structure as the fossilized record of strategic interaction. We prove analytically that two-type games have exactly four network topologies, which are their exhaustive thermodynamic phases: assortative, disassortative, and two core-peripheries. This result generalizes to $K^K$ topological classes for $K$-type interactions. Furthermore, four distinct Nash equilibria produce core-periphery topologies, yet their payoffs reveal whether the underlying dynamic is cooperative or exploitative. To recover the generating dynamics from observed networks, we develop mechanistic inference by constraining a block model to lie on a low-dimensional, game-theoretic manifold. Applied to real-world networks, the model yields interpretable quantities, distinguishes states that look identical to conventional methods, predicts network topologies it has never seen without retraining, and controls its own complexity without hand-tuned penalties. Networks such as international trade are well described by the model despite the hard constraint, suggesting that real-world systems are organized by payoff-driven partner choice. Our framework resolves a foundational ambiguity by offering a precise, mechanistic definition of communities: strategic equivalence.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: A Geometric Analysis of Gains from Trade
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We provide a geometric proof that the random proposer mechanism is a $4$-approximation to the first-best gains from trade in bilateral exchange. We then refine this geometric analysis to recover the $3.147$-approximation guarantee previously established by Fei (2022).

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Competition and Diversity in Generative AI
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Recent evidence, both in the lab and in the wild, suggests that the use of generative artificial intelligence reduces the diversity of content produced. The use of the same or similar AI models appears to lead to more homogeneous behavior. Our work begins with the observation that there is a force pushing in the opposite direction: competition. When producers compete with one another (e.g., for customers or attention), they are incentivized to create novel or unique content. We explore the impact competition has on both content diversity and overall social welfare. Through a formal game-theoretic model, we show that competitive markets select for diverse AI models, mitigating monoculture. We further show that a generative AI model that performs well in isolation (i.e., according to a benchmark) may fail to provide value in a competitive market. Our results highlight the importance of evaluating generative AI models across the breadth of their output distributions, particularly when they will be deployed in competitive environments. We validate our results empirically by using language models to play Scattergories, a word game in which players are rewarded for answers that are both correct and unique. Overall, our results suggest that homogenization due to generative AI is unlikely to persist in competitive markets, and instead, competition in downstream markets may drive diversification in AI model development.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Multi-agent Assortment Optimization in Sequential Matching Markets
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Motivated by the challenges faced by choice-based matching platforms, in this work, we study a generalization of the foundational model introduced by Ashlagi et al. (2022). Specifically, this model consists of two sides (e.g., customers and suppliers) who have preferences over the opposite side in the form of discrete choice models. A matching is realized through a two-step process where the platform's decision is to initially present to each agent on one side an assortment of users of the opposite side. The ultimate goal of the platform is to maximize the total expected revenue collected from the matching. Due to the computational complexity of this problem, we focus on the design of approximation algorithms with constant-factor guarantees for the constrained version of the problem under general choice preferences. First, to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to draw connections with the literature of submodular optimization and show that one-sided choice-oblivious approaches perform arbitrarily bad. Second, we show that, for the general setting, there exists a two-sided choice-aware randomized algorithm that achieves a (1-1/e)-approximation factor, which is the best possible. Third, we design an algorithm that is asymptotically optimal when one side follows the well-known multinomial-logit (MNL) choice model under the small probability regime. Fourth, we provide a simple and effective algorithm with a 1/4-approximation guarantee for the unconstrained setting with both sides following MNL models. Finally, we assess the performance of our proposed methods with a detailed computational study and discuss several extensions.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Optimizing Social Utility in Sequential Experiments
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Regulatory approval of products in high-stakes domains such as drug development requires statistical evidence of safety and efficacy through large-scale randomized controlled trials. However, the high financial cost of these trials may deter developers who lack absolute certainty in their product's efficacy, ultimately stifling the development of `moonshot' products that could offer high social utility. To address this inefficiency, in this paper, we introduce a statistical protocol for experimentation where the product developer (the agent) conducts a randomized controlled trial sequentially and the regulator (the principal) partially subsidizes its cost. By modeling the protocol using a belief Markov decision process, we show that the agent's optimal strategy can be found efficiently using dynamic programming. Further, we show that the social utility is a piecewise linear and convex function over the subsidy level the principal selects, and thus the socially optimal subsidy can also be found efficiently using divide-and-conquer. Simulation experiments using publicly available data on antibiotic development and approval demonstrate that our statistical protocol can be used to increase social utility by more than $35$$\%$ relative to standard, non-sequential protocols.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Tree Plurality Veto: Voting in Few Rounds with Efficient Communication and Low Metric Distortion
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We consider the metric distortion framework for voting, where $n$ voters and $m$ candidates are embedded in an unknown metric space. A voting rule selects a candidate using only voters' ordinal preferences, and its distortion is the worst-case ratio between the social cost of the selected candidate and the minimum social cost. We study how round complexity trades off against total communication in deterministic voting protocols with low distortion. Deterministic rules can achieve the optimal distortion of $3$ in one round by eliciting complete rankings using $Θ(nm\log m)$ bits, while a direct sequential implementation of PluralityVeto achieves the same distortion using only $O(n\log m)$ bits but requires $Θ(n)$ rounds.
  Our main result is TreePluralityVeto, a deterministic voting protocol that, for every $r\ge 2$, achieves distortion at most $2r-1$ using at most $r$ rounds and $O(n\log m+n s^{1/(r-1)}\log s)$ bits of total communication, where $s = \min\{n, m\}$. The protocol runs PluralityVeto on a hierarchical partition of the voters, collecting restricted rankings in parallel at each level. The branching factor controls the tradeoff between rounds and communication, and a matching-based analysis shows that each level increases the distortion bound by at most $2$.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Congestion Games with Heterogeneous Valuations: An Optimal Transport Approach
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: In emerging urban mobility and logistics applications, such as advanced air mobility, electric vehicle charging, and shared service systems, agents with heterogeneous valuations choose among multiple outcomes while sharing congested resources. Existing congestion game and resource-allocation models, however, typically restrict either the structure of heterogeneous outcome preferences or the form of congestion externalities. We introduce a nonatomic congestion game framework in which agents have multidimensional heterogeneous valuations over a finite set of outcomes, with the population represented by a measure over the valuation space. We show that, although there is a continuum of heterogeneous agents, both Nash equilibria and social optima admit finite-dimensional characterizations. Nash equilibria are characterized by aggregate flows and outcome-level threshold vectors, while social optima admit a semi-discrete optimal transport formulation characterized by aggregate flows and strategy-level Kantorovich dual potentials. For separable utilities and latency functions $\ell_e$ such that $x\mapsto x\ell_e(x)$ is convex for every resource $e$, the social welfare problem becomes a convex optimization problem, and we characterize social optima through marginal congestion costs and capacity-dual prices. Our results provide a geometric characterization of congestion games with multidimensional heterogeneous valuations and connect nonatomic congestion games with semi-discrete optimal transport.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Envy-Free Chore Allocation with Unit Subsidies under Negative Dichotomous Valuations
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study the allocation of indivisible chores with subsidies under negative dichotomous valuations, where the marginal disutility of every chore is either zero or one. This is the chore analogue of the dichotomous goods model of Barman et al. (2022), for which a subsidy of at most one unit per agent is known to suffice for envy-freeness.
  Our main contribution is to show that the same optimal guarantee holds for chores under no structural assumption beyond binary marginals. For every instance with negative dichotomous valuations, there exists a complete allocation $\mathcal{A}$ and a subsidy vector $p\in\{0,1\}^n$ with $\sum_{i\in N} p_i\le n-1$ such that $(\mathcal{A},p)$ is envy-free. Moreover, $\mathcal{A}$ is EF1 even before subsidies are paid. The subsidy bound is tight, and both the allocation and the subsidies can be computed in polynomial time in the value-oracle model. Unlike in the corresponding goods setting, a natural incremental extension approach does not work for chores. Our proof instead exploits key properties of an envy-free partial allocation and its associated equality graph to complete the allocation and determine which agents require subsidies.
  As a further extension of the main theorem, we establish the same optimal unit-subsidy guarantee for objective mixed instances with signed binary marginals, where every item is a good for all agents or a chore for all agents; these valuations need not be additive. The key step is to prove that the goods-side extension argument of Barman et al.~\cite{BKNS22} remains valid even when the previously allocated bundles contain chores. Finally, even for negative dichotomous chore valuations, we show that the unit-subsidy guarantee cannot, in general, be maintained if Pareto optimality is also required.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Revised version: Added a unit-subsidy guarantee for objective mixed instances with signed binary marginals, along with additional results on Pareto optimality. Presentation and proofs revised

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Human-AI Productivity Paradoxes: Modeling the Interplay of Skill, Effort, and AI Assistance
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools are rapidly adopted in the workplace and in education, yet the empirical evidence on AI's impact remains mixed across different operating contexts. We propose a model of human-AI interaction to better understand and analyze several mechanisms by which AI affects productivity. In our setting, human agents with varying skill levels exert utility-maximizing effort to produce certain task outcomes with AI assistance. We find that incorporating endogeneity in skill development or AI unreliability can induce a productivity paradox: increased levels of AI assistance may degrade productivity, leading to potentially significant shortfalls. We construct interpretable measures that characterize when the productivity paradox occurs. Moreover, we examine the long-term distributional effect of AI on skill, and demonstrate that skill polarization can emerge in steady state. We identify an effort-skill non-monotonicity condition under which skill polarization emerges.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Spherical-Design Oracles for Zeroth-Order Optimisation: Deterministic, Variance-Free Gradient Estimation
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: In this work, we develop a zeroth-order (ZO) method that estimates the gradient with minimal bias and variance. Instead of the random directions often used in the ZO literature, we consider central differences with directions given by a fixed spherical $t$-design, a finite point set that integrates every polynomial of degree at most $t$ exactly. The oracle is deterministic and thus does not induce any variance.We also propose a general finite difference method in the higher-order-smoothness regime and show the bias of both finite difference methods. We then show the convergence of the proposed ZO method via the input-to-state stability concept. Numerical experiments show the superiority of our proposed method over the existing random ZO methods.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: How a Cooperative-Override Circuit Suppresses Nash Play in Large Language Models
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: On the named Prisoner's Dilemma under direct prompting, three larger instruction-tuned models, Llama-3-70B, Qwen2.5-32B, and Qwen2.5-72B, lock at full cooperation, the metric's maximum distance from Nash with zero variance across replicates, while Llama-3-8B plays near-Nash. Opening the models, a logit-lens analysis finds a distributed cooperative override. Intermediate readouts lean toward the Nash action through roughly three quarters of network depth before a late surge toward cooperation, and the final layer settles the contest. The size of that final correction, not the surge, rank-matches chain-of-thought behavior across scale and two architectures. In the 8B the override is a single causally controllable direction in the residual stream; steering it dials the decision, and clamping its component at one position of one layer moves the choice strictly monotonically, Spearman rho = 1.000, with generation fluent. The circuit is lexical. It survives name removal and payoff rescaling but disengages when Cooperate and Defect are replaced with neutral labels, and on 48 payoff-random games with neutral surfaces no model locks cooperative on any dilemma or shows general equilibrium competence. In mixed-model populations a single Nash-playing agent collapses cooperation contagiously. What suppresses Nash play in large language models is a word-triggered circuit rather than missing competence, and it can be measured, bounded, and controlled.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: v3: major revision. Title changed (previously "What Suppresses Nash Equilibrium Play in Large Language Models? Mechanistic Evidence and Causal Control"). Main text rewritten at 12 pages; mechanistic campaign re-run under a seeded, hash-verified protocol; new 48-game payoff-random experiment; several earlier-version claims corrected, with all protocol changes documented in Appendix H

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Leveraging Mental Models for Human-Centered Explanations: A Systematic Design Approach Illustrated by Explainable Fake Review Identification
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Explainable AI (XAI) often prioritizes model fidelity over user intelligibility, yielding explanations that satisfy technical transparency yet fail to support human sense-making. We propose a human-centered approach, MIND-X (Mental-model INtegrated Design for eXplainability), which aligns explanations with users' mental models, commonsense concepts, and judgment heuristics. Using fake review detection as a case study, we contribute: (1) a qualitative study (n=10) that elicits how people assess review credibility and produces an actionable, design-guiding taxonomy of perceptual cues; (2) a set of design principles that link those cues to explanation strategies and prompt LLMs to generate adaptive, language-based explanations; and (3) a quantitative evaluation (n=166) showing that these explanations offer distinct advantages over token-level transparency methods widely used in explainable text classification in terms of understandability, satisfaction, perceived trust, persuasiveness, and decision-making support. Rather than claiming general superiority, our evaluation illustrates how grounding explanations in users' everyday reasoning practices can produce more intelligible and context-sensitive accounts. Our findings advance human-centered explanation design beyond a mere "gloss of transparency," demonstrating that a mental-model-aligned design process can improve intelligibility and support accountability across user-centered explanation tasks.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 38 pages, 10 figures, 8 tables. Keywords: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI); Human-centered AI; Mental models; Fake review detection; User-centered explanation design; Natural language explanations; Cognitive heuristics

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Predicting Individual Differences in Lipreading From Eye-Tracking and Pupillometry During Silent Visual Speech
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Lipreading ability varies widely, including among people who are hard of hearing. Although mouth-directed attention is linked to speechreading outcomes, it remains unclear how much lipreading skill can be inferred from viewing behavior and which signals carry this information. We examine whether individual differences in lipreading ability are reflected in viewing behavior during silent speech and quantify the contributions of gaze dynamics, pupil-linked signals, and spatial viewing allocation. We introduce the Lipreading Perception Study (LiPS) dataset and a tracker-independent preprocessing pipeline that synchronizes SR Research EyeLink gaze and pupil recordings with the stimuli. Twenty-four adults (age 32 $\pm$ 10 years) completed a four-alternative forced-choice silent lipreading task. An extreme-groups protocol yielded 18 participants labeled as stronger or weaker lipreaders. Each participant-trial included four aligned views: lip-region images, frame-level gaze, pupil summaries, and spatial viewing proportions. A four-branch neural network with cross-modal attention predicted labels using participant-disjoint splits and systematic ablations. The full model reached accuracy 0.680 $\pm$ 0.040 across five folds, outperforming naive fusion baselines in accuracy. The pupil and viewing-summary branch was most informative: removing it caused the largest degradation (0.618 accuracy, 0.623 AUC), while it alone achieved 0.675 accuracy. The lip-image stream contributed little to participant-level discrimination. Individual differences in lipreading are reflected in pupil-linked and frame-level gaze signals rather than in how much time a viewer spends looking at the mouth. Synchronized gaze and pupillary measures may provide objective markers of visual speech perception, warranting investigation in larger, clinically diverse populations. LiPS provides a resource for extending this work.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Submitted to the Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research. 5 figures, 2 tables

Human-Computer Interaction.title: A Simple Solution to Improving Human Supervision of Algorithms: Evidence from Smart Vending
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Organizations increasingly deploy autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems for operational decisions, such as inventory replenishment. Yet granting full override discretion can degrade performance because of human bias and judgment errors, while prohibiting overrides may overlook valuable private information. This raises a key question: How should override discretion be structured to improve human supervision of autonomous AI? We propose a constrained override policy that limits the number of overrides within each decision episode. When the constraint binds, humans prioritize overrides they consider most valuable, a process we call selective filtering. We evaluate the policy in a smart-vending field experiment, randomly assigning 553 workers to no, free, or constrained downward override, with the constrained policy capped at two stock-keeping units (SKUs) per machine replenishment. Relative to the no-override policy, free override reduces inventory by 1.95 log points but also lowers sales by 1.19 log points, whereas constrained override reduces inventory by 1.28 log points without a statistically significant sales decline. Local average treatment effect estimates support this contrast. Constrained override also reduces inventory without statistically significant sales losses among experienced workers, for top-sales and growth-stage SKUs, and with greater machine--SKU familiarity. Simulations suggest calibrating the cap to the firm's relative margin, worker experience, and machine--SKU familiarity. Constrained override offers a simple and scalable way to use workers' private information in inventory replenishment. Firms can limit override discretion through the replenishment interface without redesigning the algorithm, identifying useful overrides in advance, providing individualized feedback, or retraining workers.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Is User Calibration Still Necessary for Continuous Myoelectric Control? A Closed-Loop Comparison of Calibration-Free Controllers
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: The need for user-specific calibration remains an often-cited barrier to widespread adoption of myoelectric control. Cross-user models trained on large multi-user datasets can now recognize gestures from unseen users without calibration, but they have been evaluated almost exclusively offline, leaving open whether calibration is still needed in closed-loop control. This study compared six calibration-free controllers, trained on 306 users of the EMG-EPN-612 dataset and used without any calibration data from the test participant, against three calibrated controllers in a closed-loop Fitts' law target-acquisition task with sixteen participants. The calibrated controllers achieved higher offline balanced accuracy (90.6% against 73.1% for the best controller of each paradigm), but completion rates did not differ significantly between paradigms, and the highest completion rate was achieved by a calibration-free controller. Calibrated controllers moved faster on successful acquisitions, partly because of their individually fitted speed mappings, though not significantly after correction for multiple comparisons. However, every calibration-free controller produced more direct and stable trajectories than every calibrated controller, even after adjusting for cursor speed. Offline accuracy did not predict completion rate across controllers or within participants, and across paradigms higher offline accuracy was associated with poorer trajectory quality in 15 of 16 participants. Without any calibration data from the end user, a model trained across a large population matched calibrated control in completion rate and exceeded it in trajectory quality. The offline accuracy gained through calibration should therefore not be taken as evidence of a closed-loop benefit.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Collaborative Hand Drawing to Conceptualize Usable Privacy and Security Research Problems: Students' Perspectives (Extended Version)
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: In this paper, we explore students' perspectives on incorporating hand drawing to conceptualize usable privacy and security research problems. We surveyed 64 female students who participated in an in-class collaborative hand drawing activity to conceptualize usable privacy and security research problems as part of a group-based student research project on usable privacy and security in an information and computer security course for undergraduate students. Our survey responses suggest that students perceived the drawing exercise positively. That is, they found it helpful in several aspects, enjoyable, and they recommend it to other students taking the course. The students also said that they would like to have such an exercise in other courses, such as Principles of Human-Computer Interaction and Fundamentals of Data Networks. Only three students mentioned downsides of the exercise, namely doubts about their drawing skills. Our results provide useful insights for educators seeking to enhance the student learning experience.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: This document is the authors' extended preprint for a short paper in the proceedings of Koli Calling'26, ACM (DOI: 10.1145/3856208.3856277)

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Say It or Grab It? Conversational Control of UI Adaptations in Mixed Reality
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Mixed reality interfaces must continuously adapt to a user's changing task and environment, yet adaptation policies are fixed in advance, either preset by the system or configured by the user. Natural language offers a way to state changing needs mid-task, but whether users can express interface behavior this way, and what it gains over direct manipulation, is unknown. We first elicited how users verbalize adaptation needs (N=19). We then built ConverseMR, which translates a spoken request into adaptation objectives and constraints and satisfies them continuously as the user's context changes. In a within-subjects study (N=24), conversational and direct control proved complementary: direct manipulation for precision, ConverseMR for reach and expressive breadth, with their combination rated highest. Spoken commands were rarely final and users frequently refined and replaced them upon experiencing the result, characteristic of, what we call, user-led adaptation, where users communicate adaption needs and the system identifies a solution.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Trust Hinders Bidirectional Human-AI Alignment
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Trust calibration remains the dominant framing of AI-assisted decision making: the goal is to close the gap between perceived and actual trustworthiness of AI systems so that users rely on them appropriately. We argue that this approach, while useful for decision problems that are well-defined and clearly scoped, overly restricts what it means to make a decision with AI support. To overcome this limitation, we develop three dimensions of AI-assisted decision making. First, trusting AI is only one of several possible strategies for managing uncertainty. Second, trust calibration is often misapplied when AI models large-world decision problems, i.e., ill-defined situations where goals and states are only partially known or unknowable. Third, in such settings human-AI alignment requires addressing higher-order decision processes. We conclude by reflecting on the implications of our observations on the design of process-oriented human-AI coupled systems that jointly identify and negotiate uncertainty throughout the decision-making task.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: Dynamic Alignment in Human-AI Coupled System (BiAlign Workshop)

Human-Computer Interaction.title: What Drives Students' Use of AI Chatbots? Technology Acceptance in Conversational AI
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Conversational AI tools have been rapidly adopted by students and are becoming part of their learning routines. This widespread use comes amid ongoing concerns about the reliability of AI-generated responses and the appropriate role of AI in education. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, we examine how students' perceptions of conversational AI, including its usefulness, ease of use, trustworthiness, enjoyment, and social influence, relate to their intentions to use these tools for learning. We investigate both the direct and indirect relationships among these perceptions to understand how they are associated with students' behavioral intentions. Using survey data from 229 students and partial least squares structural equation modeling, we found that perceived usefulness was the strongest direct predictor of intention, followed by perceived enjoyment. Perceived ease of use, trust, and subjective norms did not have significant direct associations with intention. However, trust and subjective norms had significant total indirect associations, while perceived enjoyment had both significant direct and indirect associations. The model explained 70.2% of the variance in behavioral intention. These findings suggest that students' intentions to use conversational AI are associated less directly with effort-related considerations and more with perceived usefulness and affective experience. They also highlight the importance of understanding what students perceive as valuable in conversational AI interactions, particularly when designing tools intended to encourage engagement while supporting learning.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: JumpStarter: Human-AI Planning with Task-Structured Context Curation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Human-AI collaboration on complex planning goals is bottlenecked by how LLM interfaces handle context: users must manually curate and re-surface relevant information across long and unstructured chat histories. Despite advances in long-context prompting and memory-augmented retrieval, this burden remains unresolved: users still have to identify and supply the right context at each decision point, regardless of how much the model can store or surface. We propose JumpStarter, a system that enables LLMs to collaborate with humans on complex goals by dynamically decomposing tasks to help users manage context. We specifically introduce task-structured context curation, a framework that breaks down a user's goal into a hierarchy of actionable subtasks and scopes context to localized decision points, enabling finer-grained personalization and reuse. The framework is realized through three core mechanisms: context elicitation, selection, and reuse. In a within-subjects user study, plans produced with JumpStarter were rated substantially higher in quality than those produced with ChatGPT. A complementary automatic simulation study shows that JumpStarter consistently outperforms ChatGPT baselines, planning and memory agents, and workflow ablations. These findings show that effective human-AI planning depends not on the volume of context provided, but on attaching the right context to the right subtask at the right time.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: AACL 2026 Main, 29 pages, 20 Figures, 9 tables

Human-Computer Interaction.title: From Neglect to Resignation: Understanding the Evolution of Mobile Privacy
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: This decade-long longitudinal qualitative study follows 31 smartphone users in China across four interview waves (2014-2023) to examine how mobile privacy understanding evolves alongside shifting computing infrastructures. Findings reveal three stages shaped by distinct interactional mechanisms: early functional acceptance of permission-based data access, growing vigilance triggered by behavioral tracking feedback loops, and eventual resignation as AI-driven inference made ecosystem-level profiling feel inescapable. Rather than a stable attitude, digital resignation emerges through cumulative infrastructure exposure, as each new system layer retroactively reinterpreted earlier permissions and exhausted users' capacity for self-management. The study challenges permission-centric design assumptions and proposes inference visibility, context isolation, and automated privacy agency as system-level responses.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted by IMWUT 2026

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Vibe Coding XR: Accelerating AI + XR Prototyping with XR Blocks and Gemini
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: While large language models (LLMs) have accelerated traditional software development through intent-driven "vibe coding", prototyping intelligent Extended Reality (XR) experiences remains a major challenge. The fundamental barrier is not just the steep learning curve for human creators, but that low-level sensor APIs and complex game engine hierarchies are ill-suited for LLM reasoning, routinely exceeding context windows and inducing syntax hallucinations. To bridge this gap, we contribute XR Blocks, an open-source, LLM-native WebXR framework. Unlike traditional engines, XR Blocks introduces a semantic "Reality Model" that aligns spatial computing primitives (users, physical environments, and agents) with natural language, providing a robust, concise vocabulary optimized for generative AI. Building upon this foundation, we present Vibe Coding XR, an end-to-end prototyping workflow that leverages LLMs to translate high-level prompts (e.g., "create a dandelion that reacts to my hand") directly into functional, physics-aware mixed-reality applications. To minimize the friction of on-device testing, the workflow introduces a seamless desktop "simulated reality" to headset deployment loop. Finally, we introduce VCXR60, a pilot dataset of 60 XR prompts paired with an automated evaluation pipeline. Our technical evaluation demonstrates high one-shot execution success, enabling practitioners to bypass low-level hurdles and rapidly move from "idea to reality". Code and demo are available at https://github.com/google/xrblocks and https://goo.gle/BuildXR.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: ACM VRST 2026

Human-Computer Interaction.title: GazeAgent: VLM-Guided Implicit Gaze Calibration from Egocentric Multimodal Behavior for AI Glasses
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: AI glasses typically require explicit, user-specific eye-tracker calibration, and accuracy can drift when the device shifts during use. We present GazeAgent, a VLM-guided framework that continuously and adaptively improves gaze-calibration accuracy from naturally occurring behavior without asking users to interrupt their activities. GazeAgent identifies precise visual attention (PVA) events from multimodal streams of inertial measurement unit (IMU), gaze, and wearer-hand signals, validates their task relevance, and localizes functional targets as pseudo-calibration targets. In a 10-participant scripted study, the system detected all 820 predefined PVA opportunities and, under device disturbance, reduced median gaze error by 44.1% compared with explicit calibration. In a five-participant case study, autonomous calibration produced the lowest workload and interruption ratings, and all participants preferred it for routine use. By deriving task-critical targets from natural multimodal behavior, GazeAgent demonstrates the potential for continuous, adaptive, and low-burden gaze interaction on egocentric AI glasses.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 27 pages, 14 figures, 3 tables

Information Theory.title: Query-Dependent Reading for Quantized Inner-Product Estimation: A Minimax Separation
Information Theory.summary:
We study quantization for inner-product estimation when storage and reading have separate budgets. In the static bit-probe model [Yao, 1981], an encoder stores $w$ bits about $x$ before seeing a query $y$, and a reader probes at most $r<w$ bits to estimate $x^\top y$. Both vectors lie in the $d$-dimensional Euclidean unit ball. Protocols may be randomized, and computation is unrestricted. Performance is measured by $d$ times the worst-case mean-squared error over $x,y$, averaged over protocol randomness.
  First, we show that query-independent reading cannot benefit from extra storage. Any such reader is equivalent to fully reading an $r$-bit message, even when later reads depend on previously returned bits. At fixed positive rates $W=w/d$ and $R=r/d$, the normalized minimax error converges to $1/(4^R-1)$, independent of $W$. The upper bound was already known [Ordentlich and Polyanskiy, 2025]. We prove the matching lower bound for arbitrary scalar decoders, extending the result for unbiased compressors [Safaryan et al., 2020].
  Then, we show that query-dependent reading makes extra storage useful. We construct a two-batch protocol using Gaussian projections and random thresholds, with asymptotic normalized error at most $(π+o(1))/[4R\log(W/R)]$ as $W/R\to\infty$. At fixed $R$, this error vanishes as storage grows, giving an unbounded advantage over query-independent reading. We also prove a finite-dimensional lower bound for arbitrary encoders, decoders, and fully branching readers. In the doubly sparse regime $W/R\to\infty$ and $R\log(W/R)\to0$, it gives normalized error at least $(1-o(1))/[2R\log(W/R)]$. Thus, our protocol is optimal within a factor of $π/2$ in the leading constant.

Information Theory.title: Undirected Network Coding and Faster External-Memory Integer Sorting
Information Theory.summary:
Network coding allows intermediate nodes to combine messages. Fractional routing instead splits each message among source-destination paths and forwards its parts without combining different messages. For undirected networks carrying independent messages between multiple source-destination pairs, the multiple-unicast conjecture asserts that the two methods achieve the same combinations of message rates. We give a finite counterexample and use its linear structure to accelerate external-memory integer sorting, addressing the question of whether integer operations can beat the comparison-sorting input/output (I/O) bound posed by Aggarwal and Vitter in 1988.
  We give a deterministic sorting algorithm: for $N$ integers of $Θ(\log N)$ bits, a memory holding $M$ integers, and block transfers of $B$ integers, where $2B\le M\le N$, the number of block transfers is $O\!\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+\frac{\log N}{(\log(M/B))^{1-\varepsilon}(\log M)^\varepsilon}\right]\right)$, where $\varepsilon=1.5\times10^{-5}$ is an absolute constant. In some parameter ranges, this bound is asymptotically smaller than the classical comparison-sorting bound. Under the external-memory model specified in this paper, we have formally verified the algorithm's correctness and I/O complexity bound in Lean.
Information Theory.comment: 34 pages, 5 figures. Revised construction and improved exponent

Information Theory.title: The Causal Description Gap: Information-Theoretic Separations Across Pearl's Hierarchy
Information Theory.summary: Pearl's causal hierarchy shows that observational, interventional, and counterfactual queries are qualitatively distinct. We ask a quantitative version of this question: how many additional bits are needed to specify higher-rung causal answers once lower-rung answers are known? We formalize this via query-class description length, the Kolmogorov complexity of the answers a structural causal model (SCM) gives to a class of queries, with system size given. Our main construction gives acyclic SCMs on $n$ binary variables whose common observational distribution has constant description length, while single-variable intervention answers can require $Θ(n^2)$ additional bits. For SCMs with independent noises, fixed finite gate-schema and noise libraries, and at most $d$ parents per variable, a degree-sensitive upper bound gives an observational-interventional gap of at most $O(nd\log(en/d)+n\log n)$. This makes the quadratic construction order-optimal in the dense regime and a rooted-tree construction order-optimal for bounded indegree. The quadratic separation persists under $\varepsilon$-accurate total-variation descriptions for every fixed $\varepsilon<1/4$. At the next rung, even knowing every hard-intervention distribution can leave a $Θ(n)$ counterfactual description gap; a masked-parity construction extends this to $Θ(n^2)$. These separation rates hold in the worst case and with high probability under uniform hidden parameters. A general ambiguity-to-bits theorem and Shannon analogue, together with explicit encodings, show that the gaps in our constructions equal the logarithm of residual higher-rung ambiguity up to lower-order terms.
Information Theory.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 26 pages (10 main text, appendices A to E)

Information Theory.title: Information Theory of Random Composition Trees
Information Theory.summary: Random composition trees model the hierarchical semantic structures of meaningful texts as a statistical ensemble generated by recursively splitting texts into coherent chunks. A recent study shows that different text types can be described by random composition trees with distinct branching factors, and that the entropy rates of these trees exhibit a similar dependence across text types as the entropy rates of the actual texts. Motivated by this correspondence, we analyze information-theoretic properties of this stochastic splitting model. First, we demonstrate that the entropy of random composition trees grows linearly with the root size, and we derive an analytical expression for the entropy rate as a function of the branching factor. Second, we prove that large trees exhibit typicality: with high probability, they belong to a typical set in which each tree is approximately equally likely. Our analysis reveals that the random composition tree model shares two key information-theoretic properties of language when modeled as a stationary and ergodic stochastic process: linear entropy growth and typicality.

Information Theory.title: Reduced APN permutations and a disproof of the Galois-ring lifting conjecture
Information Theory.summary: We construct infinite families of reduced almost perfect nonlinear (APN) permutations of $\mathbb{F}_{2^m}$ that admit coefficientwise permutation lifts to $\mathrm{GR}(2^k,m)$ for every $k>1$. These families disprove Conjecture~2 of Rønjom and Sandrib (Cryptogr. Commun., 2026), even for reduced polynomial representatives. For every odd $m\ge5$ with $3\nmid m$, we obtain explicit seven-term polynomials over $\mathbb{F}_2$ with formal derivative identically one. We derive them from a complete criterion for the reduced representative of $A(x)^{2^s+1}$ to have no critical point in $\mathbb{F}_{2^m}$, where $A$ is an invertible linearized polynomial and $\gcd(s,m)=1$. We then apply the cube case to construct a second family of degree $2^{m-1}+2$, whose nonconstant derivatives avoid zero by an explicit trace identity. A fixed parameter in $\mathbb{F}_{32}$ gives this family in every dimension $m=5r$ with $r$ odd, including a degree-$18$ example over $\mathbb{F}_{32}$. Both constructions remain in Gold linear equivalence classes, so liftability of reduced representatives is not invariant under invertible $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear input changes. We obtain the lifting conclusions from the standard Galois-ring permutation criterion. We also verify a degree-$24$ example supplied by Zhang and Haobo, prove a trace-adjoint criterion for reduced quadratic functions, and interpret the derivative condition through ramification at rational points.

Information Theory.title: Sample complexity of weak-signal latent-variable models
Information Theory.summary: We study parametric estimation in latent-variable models in the weak-signal regime, where a small signal-strength parameter $β$ controls the dependence of the observations on the unknown parameter. At $β=0$, this dependence disappears, so all parameter values induce the same observed distribution, which we call the null law. We develop a unified framework for analyzing sample complexity in the weak-signal regime by expanding the likelihood ratio around this shared null law in powers of $β$. We prove that if the unknown parameter is first globally identifiable at order $r$ in this expansion, then estimation to fixed accuracy requires at least on the order of $β^{-2r}$ samples. We further identify a likelihood-separation stability condition that is necessary for any estimator to attain this rate and, under mild regularity conditions, sufficient for both maximum likelihood and method-of-moments estimators to attain it. We also study the regime in which the target accuracy vanishes together with the signal strength, and show that global localization and local refinement may be governed by different likelihood orders, leading to distinct statistical scales. Finally, we apply our framework to broad classes of algebraically structured latent-variable models, including additive-noise channels and exponential-family models.

Information Theory.title: Optimal single-track Gray codes from Gray-ordered necklaces
Information Theory.summary: A single-track Gray code of length $n$ is a cyclic Gray code of $n$-bit words in which every column is a cyclic shift of the first. For prime $n$ the longest possible period is $2^n-2$. Whether it is attained for every prime has been open since Hiltgen, Paterson and Brandestini introduced these codes in 1996, and optimal codes were known for primes $n\le 19$. We show that a conjecture of Degni and Drisko (2007) on the reflected Gray code order of necklaces implies optimal single-track Gray codes for every prime. Their list of necklaces, conjecturally a Gray path for prime $n$, closes into a Hamilton cycle of the necklace graph after $(n-3)/2$ explicit Pósa rotations, and such a cycle lifts to an optimal code. This implication is formalized in Lean 4. Together with computation it gives optimal single-track Gray codes for every odd prime $n\le 47$: for $n\le 37$ explicit codes checked word by word by a program independent of the generator, and for $n=41$, $43$ and $47$ codes obtained from the implication after the Degni-Drisko property was verified at these lengths by two independently written programs.
Information Theory.comment: 7 pages, 1 table. Ancillary files: Lean 4 formalization, construction and verification programs, the codes for n <= 23, and verification logs. All codes (n <= 31): https://github.com/dzoba/single-track-gray-codes

Information Theory.title: Code Equivalence, Point Set Equivalence, and Polynomial Isomorphism
Information Theory.summary: The linear code equivalence (LCE) problem is known to be equivalent to the point set equivalence (PSE) problem, i.e., the problem to check whether two sets of points in a projective space over a finite field differ by a linear change of coordinates. For such a point set $\mathbb{X}$, let $R$ be its homogeneous coordinate ring and $\mathfrak{J}_{\mathbb{X}}$ its canonical ideal. Then the LCE problem is shown to be equivalent to an algebra isomorphism problem for the doubling $R/\mathfrak{J}_{\mathbb{X}}$. As this doubling is an Artinian Gorenstein algebra, we can use its Macaulay inverse system to reduce the LCE problem to a Polynomial Isomorphism (PI) problem for homogeneous polynomials. The last step is polynomial time under some mild assumptions about the codes. Moreover, for indecomposable iso-dual codes we can reduce the LCE search problem to the PI search problem of degree 3 by noting that the corresponding point sets are self-associated and arithmetically Gorenstein, so that we can use the isomorphism problem for the Artinian reductions of the coordinate rings and form their Macaulay inverse systems.
Information Theory.comment: minor corrections and clarifications; Lemma 2.10 added; to appear in Designs, Codes and Cryptography

Information Theory.title: Reed-Solomon Codes with Optimal Repair Bandwidth: A Basis-Transformation Approach
Information Theory.summary: Maximum distance separable (MDS) codes are widely used in distributed storage, but naively repairing a single failure in an $(n,k)$ MDS code requires downloading the full contents of $k$ surviving nodes. Minimum storage regenerating (MSR) codes, introduced by Dimakis et al., minimize repair bandwidth while preserving the MDS property by contacting $d>k$ helper nodes and downloading only a fraction of each helper. For scalar MDS codes, Guruswami and Wootters established a linear repair framework, and Tamo, Ye, and Barg subsequently gave the first explicit Reed-Solomon (RS) codes achieving the MSR point. Their construction yields RS-MSR codes with subpacketization $\ell=s\prod_{i=1}^n p_i$, where $s=d+1-k$ and the distinct primes $p_i$ satisfy $p_i\equiv 1\pmod{s}$. In this paper, we show that this congruence condition is not intrinsic to the RS repair problem. We develop a basis-transformation approach to the construction of repair-enabling subspaces. The approach consists of three deterministic operations -- Euclidean Square Partition, Transposition, and Column Aggregation -- which construct the required repair-enabling subspaces directly from the standard monomial basis of the repair field. Consequently, we obtain RS-MSR codes with subpacketization $\ell=s\prod_{i=1}^n p_i$ for arbitrary distinct primes $p_i>s$. For fixed $s$, this improves the subpacketization of the Tamo--Ye--Barg construction by a factor asymptotic to $\varphi(s)^{n+\mathrm{o}(n)}$, where $\varphi(\cdot)$ denotes Euler's totient function.

Information Theory.title: Spectra of Multivariate Vandermonde Matrices and Min-max Error Bounds for the High-dimensional Super-resolution Problem
Information Theory.summary:
We study multivariate rectangular Vandermonde matrices $U_N$ whose rows are indexed by the grid $G_N=\{-N,\ldots,N\}^d, $ and whose columns correspond to irregularly spaced points on the unit $d$-dimensional torus. Motivated by the problem of super-resolution (recovery of spike trains from low frequency noisy measurements), we consider configurations in which the points form several clusters, with points within each cluster separated by at most $h$ and distinct clusters are well-separated. We show that the column subspaces associated with different clusters are nearly orthogonal, i.e. for $N \rightarrow \infty, Nh \ll 1$, the minimal principal angle between any such pair is at least $
  {π\over 2} - \frac{C_1}{N} - C_2Nh - \frac{C_3}{\sqrt{N}}, $ for some constants $C_1,C_2,C_3$ independent of $N$ and $h$. This near-orthogonality enables the spectral analysis of such $U_N$ to be reduced to the analysis of each individual cluster.
  As a consequence, we derive sharp scaling for all singular values of $U_N$, revealing how the geometry of clustered points controls the conditioning of the high-dimensional super-resolution problems. Then we establish min-max error bounds for the recovery of clustered point sources, requiring only an upper bound on the largest cluster size and no knowledge of the geometry within the clusters. These bounds coincide with the optimal rates known in the one-dimensional setting. Furthermore, when the clustered points are in generic position (i.e. do not lie on a low-dimensional algebraic variety) our results indicate that super-resolution in high dimensions is more stable than in one dimension.

Information Theory.title: Discrete Phase-Shift Optimization of Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces using Uniform Reference Directions
Information Theory.summary: Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RISs) enable programmable control of the wireless propagation environment through adjustable reflecting elements. A fundamental challenge in RIS-assisted communications is the optimization of discrete phase shifts to maximize the received signal power. While recently developed algorithms can obtain optimal solutions with linear complexity, their computational cost may still be excessive in applications requiring large-scale simulations, real-time adaptation, or repeated optimization over numerous channel realizations. This paper proposes a low-complexity discrete phase-shift optimization algorithm based on multiple reference directions within the feasible optimality sector. By evaluating candidate phase configurations generated from uniformly distributed reference directions, the proposed method systematically improves upon existing approximation approaches that rely on a fixed set of reference directions. The number of reference directions serves as a design parameter that enables a controllable trade-off between computational complexity and optimality. Extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves substantial computational speedups while maintaining a small optimality gap relative to the optimal solution. The results further show that increasing the number of reference directions progressively reduces the optimality gap, providing flexible operating points that can be tailored to application-specific complexity and performance requirements.

Information Theory.title: Derivation Depth as an Information Metric: Axioms, Coding Theorems, and Storage--Computation Tradeoffs
Information Theory.summary: We introduce derivation depth-a computable metric of the reasoning effort needed to answer a query based on a given set of premises. We model information as a two-layered structure linking abstract knowledge with physical carriers, and separate essential core facts from operational shortcuts. For any finite premise base, we define and prove the computability of derivation depth. By encoding reasoning traces and applying information-theoretic incompressibility arguments, we establish fundamental bounds linking depth to the descriptive complexity of queries. For frequently asked, information-rich queries, the minimal description length grows proportionally to depth times the logarithm of the knowledge base size. This leads to a practical storage-computation tradeoff: queries accessed beyond a critical threshold become cheaper to cache than recompute. We formulate optimal cache allocation as a mathematical optimization problem solvable with approximation guarantees and extend the framework to handle noisy or incomplete knowledge bases.

Information Theory.title: Private Evaluation of High-Dimensional Functions
Information Theory.summary:
We study differentially private black-box evaluation of arbitrary high-dimensional functions. Given a dataset $S$ and query access to a function $f$---whose sensitivity may be unknown or unbounded---the goal is to privately output an approximation to $f(S)$. The black-box evaluator can only query the value of $f$ over a down neighborhood of $S$ (i.e., those subsets of $S$ that are obtained by removing a bounded number of elements from $S$). We design generic black-box evaluators for both pure and approximate differential privacy through a reduction to high-dimensional private quasi-concave optimization (QCO).
  Our black-box evaluator enjoys a geometric notion of utility. Consider the vectors obtained by applying $f$ on sets in a down neighborhood of $S$. With high probability, the evaluator's output is guaranteed to be in the convex hull of these vectors.
  Our work generalizes the result of Linder et al. [LRSS25] for real-valued function evaluation to high dimensions. It also recovers the private center-point guarantees of Beimel et al. [BMNS19], with an explicit additive approximation to maximum Tukey depth. We also apply our evaluators to user-level quasi-concave and convex optimization, showing how they can improve upon the sample-and-aggregate baseline of Nissim et al. [NRS07] by replacing the multiplicative data overhead with an additive overhead.
  Finally, we show that our formulation of high dimensional black-box evaluation and high dimensional private QCO are equivalent up to a factor of the dimension: the hardest private evaluation instances already arise from the cases that $f$ is a (non-private) quasi-concave optimizer.

Information Theory.title: Decentralized Decoding with Adaptive Local Combining for Cell-Free Massive MIMO
Information Theory.summary: In existing literature, a two-stage architecture comprising of large-scale fading decoding (LSFD) at the central processing unit (CPU) and local combining at the access points (APs) is commonly deployed for uplink processing in scalable cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-mMIMO) systems. However, centralized LSFD (c-LSFD) requires cross-AP channel statistics at the CPU and local combining uses schemes that either do not suppress interference optimally or result in analytically intractable solutions. We provide novel schemes to address both concerns. First, we propose the decentralized LSFD (d-LSFD) scheme that maximizes a surrogate signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio built only from local interference covariance statistics and identify covariance-action regime where it is equivalent to c-LSFD. Second, based on the fact that the antennas at each AP provide spatial degrees of freedom (DoFs) for both interference suppression and coherent array gain, we interpret every combining scheme as solving the optimal DoF allocation problem over available DoFs. Selective zero-forcing (ZF) schemes solve this problem over both the dimension and composition of the local ZF subspace. We then provide the DoF-adaptive ZF-subspace (DAZS) combining scheme, which lets each AP select the optimal directions in the ZF subspace by maximizing its local sum spectral efficiency. Our numerical results establish the efficacy and efficiency of the proposed schemes compared to the corresponding existing schemes.

Information Theory.title: A Linearly Convergent Algorithm for Petz-Augustin Means with Applications to Computing Petz-Augustin Capacity and Equilibrium Prices in Fisher Markets
Information Theory.summary:
We study the computation of the Petz-Augustin mean of order $α\in (0,1) \cup (1,\infty)$, defined as the minimizer of a weighted sum of $n$ Petz-Rényi divergences of order $α$ over the set of $d$-by-$d$ quantum states, where the Petz-Rényi divergence is a quantum generalization of the classical Rényi divergence. We propose the first algorithm with a non-asymptotic convergence guarantee for solving this optimization problem. The iterates are guaranteed to converge to the Petz-Augustin mean at a linear rate of $O\left( \lvert 1 - 1/α\rvert^T \right)$ with respect to the Thompson metric for $α\in(1/2,1)\cup(1,\infty)$, where $T$ denotes the number of iterations. The algorithm has an initialization time complexity of $O\left(nd^3\right)$ and a per-iteration time complexity of $O\left(nd^2 + d^3\right)$.
  Two applications follow. The first application concerns the Petz-Augustin capacity of order $α\in(1/2,1)$, which generalizes the quantum channel capacity and characterizes the optimal error exponent in classical-quantum channel coding. To compute this quantity, we propose the first iterative method with a non-asymptotic convergence guarantee, which uses our algorithm for computing the Petz-Augustin mean as a subroutine. The second application concerns the equilibrium prices in Fisher markets with constant elasticity of substitution (CES) utilities. We establish that when all buyers have CES utilities of common elasticity, the equilibrium prices are equivalent to the Petz-Augustin mean when all quantum states commute. In this case, our proposed algorithm is a tâtonnement process à la Walras. We further extend the algorithm to inhomogeneous Fisher markets, where buyers have CES utilities with different elasticities, and prove a faster convergence rate than existing tâtonnement-type algorithms.

Information Theory.title: Rate-Cost Tradeoffs in Nonlinear Control
Information Theory.summary: We study finite-horizon rate-cost tradeoffs for general stochastic control systems, including nonlinear systems. Under an average control cost constraint, we show that the minimum expected communication rate lies within an additive logarithmic gap above the normalized directed information minimized over causal control policies. This establishes directed information as the operationally relevant quantity governing rate-limited control, extending its previously established roles in causal source coding and linear quadratic Gaussian (LQG) control to general nonlinear control systems.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Cyclic Graphs and Memoization in Pure $λ$-Calculus
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
Purely functional programming makes immutability and non-strict evaluation its defaults; we push further, making interning and memoization the defaults of computation. In prior operational semantics for the pure $λ$-calculus, representing and transforming cyclic and infinite data requires an added recursion construct, a $\texttt{letrec}$, a $μ$-binder, or a built-in $Y$ for graph reduction, and sharing the repeated work of a memoized or dynamic-programming function requires an impure cache. We show that no extension is needed. We apply tabling, the standard method for solving a least-fixpoint equation, to weak-head reduction; this defines a new operational semantics for the pure $λ$-calculus that keeps each term's standard lazy meaning. A term that reaches finitely many distinct states, each solved in finitely many steps, comes out as a finite graph, possibly cyclic; the calculus stays pure, and the graph is faithful and independent of reduction order. We implemented this operational semantics as a $λ$-calculus interpreter. It does dynamic programming automatically, sharing repeated subproblems with no memoization table. It creates and transforms cyclic graphs with no added recursion construct. And it decides in finite time that some terms have no weak head normal form, returning $\bot$ for $Ω$.
  What the evaluator returns is a graph, so the $λ$-calculus becomes a DSL for graph computation: the memo table of dynamic programming, the transposition table of game search, and the derived-fact table of Datalog reachability and points-to analysis are all tabling on state identity, and none of them is written by hand. Compilation is one more such problem: we write a bootstrap compiler that compiles its own source, all as a pure $λ$-term.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Formalizing a Many-Sorted Hybrid Polyadic Modal Logic in Lean
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
We present a Lean formalization of a general hybrid modal logic with many-sorted signatures and polyadic modal operators. The system borrows ideas from both algebraic specification and dynamic logics, and is designed to serve as a uniform axiomatic foundation for specifying and verifying programming languages and security protocols. We expose a DSL for users to define languages and protocols as many-sorted signatures, specify the relevant domain-specific axioms, and reason about program executions or protocol runs. We provide a machine-checked proof of its soundness theorem and showcase the framework's versatility through several applications: an imperative programming language for code verification, a BAN logic and an epistemic logic used for security protocols, and the modal system S5. We have designed our formalization to be intrinsically sorted, that is, well-sorted formulas in the base language are well-typed terms in Lean. Thanks to intrinsic sorting, all domain specific applications can be easily embedded in our framework via the DSL, at no additional syntactic overhead required for the user to prove.
  All code presented in this paper is openly accessible in the following repository: https://github.com/alexoltean61/msphml-lean

Logic in Computer Science.title: A Dichotomy Theorem for Homomorphism Problems on Automatic Structures
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
The field of constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) studies homomorphism problems between relational structures where the target structure is fixed. Classifying the complexity of these problems has been a central quest of the field, notably when both sides are finite structures. In this paper, we study the generalization where the input is an automatic structure---potentially infinite, but describable by finite automata.
  We prove a striking dichotomy: homomorphism problems over automatic structures are either decidable in non-deterministic logarithmic space (NL), or undecidable. We show that structures for which the problem is decidable are exactly those with finite duality, which is a classical property of target structures asserting that the existence of a homomorphism into them can be characterized by the absence of a finite set of obstructions in the source structure. Notably, this property precisely characterizes target structures whose homomorphism problem is definable in first-order logic, which is well-known to be decidable over automatic structures.
  We also consider a natural variant of the problem. While automatic structures are finitely describable, homomorphisms from them into finite structures need not be. This leads to the notion of "regular homomorphism", where the homomorphism itself must be describable by finite automata. Remarkably, we prove that this variant exhibits the same dichotomy, with the same characterization for decidability.

Logic in Computer Science.title: The Myhill isomorphism theorem does not generalize much
Logic in Computer Science.summary: The Myhill isomorphism is a variant of the Cantor-Bernstein theorem. It states that, from two injections that reduce two subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ to one another, there exists a bijection $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ that preserves them. This theorem can be proven constructively. We investigate to which extent the theorem can be extended to infinite sets other than $\mathbb{N}$. We show that, assuming Markov's principle, the theorem can be extended to the conatural numbers $\mathbb{N}_{\infty}$ provided that we only require that bicomplemented sets are preserved by the bijection. This restriction is essential. Otherwise, the picture is overall negative: among other things, it is impossible to extend that result to either $2 \times \mathbb{N}_{\infty}$, $\mathbb{N} + \mathbb{N}_{\infty}$, $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}_{\infty}$, $\mathbb{N}_{\infty}^2$, $2^{\mathbb{N}}$ or $\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}$.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 26 pages, 6 figures, fixes followed a reviewer's comments

Logic in Computer Science.title: Verifying Human-Written Reasoning References
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Evaluating the reasoning of AI systems often relies on human-written reasoning chains as references, yet the logical support for their individual steps is rarely verified. Although prior neuro-symbolic approaches have formalized and checked reasoning, their reported evaluations do not systematically assess whether step conclusions in human-written reference derivations are entailed by their cited premise sets or investigate the sources of failures in those references. To address these limitations, we present a novel reference-centred assessment method for human-written derivations that combines entailment checking against cited premise sets, full-premise rechecking, and failure attribution to examine the reliability of these derivations and their formal representations. We evaluate it on P-FOLIO, using a large language model (LLM) to translate step conclusions into first-order logic (FOL) and the Z3 SMT solver to check entailment. Of 386 derivations examined, 202 (52.3%) meet all our checking criteria, meaning that every translated step is entailed by its stated support and the required target is established under the available FOL representations. Among 230 steps not entailed by their stated support, 191 become entailed when checked against the complete original premises, indicating that most initial failures reflect incomplete or mismatched support rather than unsupported claims. Manual analysis of the remaining 39 cases identifies 21 human reasoning errors, 11 FOL translation errors, and 7 dataset annotation errors. A separate manual audit of 50 randomly sampled steps that passed the entailment checks found 46 faithful FOL translations (92%). These findings suggest that disagreement with a human-written reasoning reference may originate in the reference or its formal representation rather than in the AI system being evaluated.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 24 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Preprint

Logic in Computer Science.title: Terminal Coalgebras in Countably Many Steps
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
We present a collection of results that imply that an endofunctor on a category has a terminal coalgebra obtainable as a countable limit of its terminal-coalgebra chain. This holds for finitary endofunctors on locally finitely presentable categories under conditions on both the functor and the category. We adapt finiteness arguments that were originally advanced by Worrell concerning terminal coalgebras for finitary set functors. Examples include the categories of sets, posets, vector spaces, graphs, nominal sets, and presheaves on finite sets. Worrell also described, without proof, the terminal-coalgebra chain of the finite power-set functor. We provide a detailed proof following his ideas.
  We then turn to polynomial endofunctors on the categories of Hausdorff topological spaces and metric spaces. The Vietoris space of compact subsets yields an endofunctor $\mathscr{V}$ on the category of Hausdorff spaces. Vietoris polynomial endofunctors are built from $ \mathscr{V}$, the identity and constant functors by forming products, coproducts and compositions. Their terminal coalgebras are obtained in $ω$ steps. We then turn to the class of Hausdorff polynomial functors on the category of metric spaces, which is analogous but uses in lieu of $\mathscr{V}$ the Hausdorff functor $\mathcal{H}$. We prove they have terminal coalgebras obtained in $ω+ ω$ steps. Finally, we show that every finitary endofunctor on the category of vector spaces over a fixed field again has a terminal coalgebra obtained in $ω+ω$ steps.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: Joint journal version of previous CALCO 2023 pearl paper (previous arXiv version) and CALCO 2025 paper

Logic in Computer Science.title: The Lattice of Coalition Logics between MCL and CL: Coatoms and Compact Meets
Logic in Computer Science.summary: For a fixed finite set $N$ of at least two agents, we investigate the lattice $L_N$ of coalition logics between minimal coalition logic (MCL) and classical coalition logic (CL), with extensions required to be structural. This lattice is order-dual to an interval in the subvariety lattice of Boolean coalition algebras. The eight basic extensions obtained by imposing seriality, independence of agents, and determinism form a Boolean cube under inclusion, but not a sublattice of $L_N$. Our main results concern coatoms and compact meets. First, finite critical coalition algebras, realized as complex algebras of finite general concurrent games, yield three infinite families of pairwise distinct coatoms containing seriality, distinguished by failures of independence, determinism, or both. An explicit splitting characterizes the unique coatom omitting seriality. Second, the meet of two basic extensions is compact if and only if the extensions are comparable. For incomparable pairs, no axiomatization of the meet can use formulas of uniformly bounded modal depth, even with infinitely many axioms. Consequently, $L_N$ and three natural principal intervals are non-coherent algebraic lattices. These results reveal lattice-theoretic phenomena beyond the inclusion order of the eight basic extensions.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 19 pages, one table; supplementary finite-checking Python program in ancillary files

Logic in Computer Science.title: Tactix: Towards a Programmable Strategy Interface for Flexible SAT Solving
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Modern SAT solvers combine a rich repertoire of proof rules with sophisticated strategies that determine when and how to apply them. Often, the internal implementations are tightly coupled to particular strategies, making it inconvenient to define new strategies without changing solver internals. We present Tactix, a proof-producing sequential CDCL solver that incorporates a wide range of techniques in state-of-the-art solvers with a clean separation of proof rules from solving strategies. This separation enables a public interface through which users can invoke particular techniques, observe their effects, and program a wide range of solving strategies. The default strategy of Tactix is programmable over this interface and outperforms state-of-the-art solvers on benchmarks from the 2024--2026 SAT Competitions. We also use the interface to develop novel strategies tailored to challenging benchmarks from two application domains, which led to performance gains over strong baselines. We intend Tactix to serve as an infrastructure for designing and evaluating novel solving strategies. Finally, we also present a self-study of the AI-assisted development process behind Tactix.
